surprises.description: Innventure reported only $1.0 million of Q2 revenue, far below the preview’s $3.42 million consensus and roughly $3 million implied Accelsius contribution. Accelsius generated just $0.9 million, and consolidated revenue fell from $1.4 million in Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 2026 revenue was $1 million,” with “Accelsius contributing 96% ($0.9 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 consensus” revenue was “$3.42M”; the preview said the implied path was “roughly Q2 ~$3M.”

surprises.description: Management went beyond the preview’s possible target reframe: it suspended all Accelsius revenue targets and pushed expected breakeven beyond 2026. The preview described a softer “entering 2027” target as a likely risk, but not the withdrawal of all targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management suspended all Accelsius revenue targets” and “no longer expects it to exit this year near cash flow breakeven at a ~$100 million annualized run rate, extending breakeven beyond 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether the December target was “reaffirmed, softened, or reframed,” and identified “run rate entering 2027” as a likely reframe.

surprises.description: Innventure abandoned its goal of consolidated positive cash flow by 2028, an additional setback beyond the delayed Accelsius target. The preview did not anticipate the company withdrawing this longer-term consolidated goal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Innventure abandoned its prior goal of consolidated positive cash flow by 2028 due to Accelsius's delayed path to profitability.”

surprises.description: The DarkNX purchase order was removed from the 2026 forecast after the customer lost its development site, with transfer to another location uncertain. The preview had flagged the DarkNX campus as something to monitor but did not anticipate the order dropping out of the forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The DarkNX purchase order was removed from the 2026 forecast after the customer lost its development site due to power envelope constraints,” and a transfer to an alternate location is on “an uncertain timeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “progress on the DarkNX 300MW Ontario campus” among the items to watch.

surprises.description: Management signaled that further dilutive capital raises may be needed in the second half, adding financing pressure. However, the roughly $13 million already raised at an average $6.21 was at a much higher price than the preview’s anticipated sub-$4 SEPA draws, making that completed issuance less dilutive than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Accelsius raised approximately $13 million through its standby equity purchase agreement at an average price of $6.21,” and Dave “signaled potential additional dilutive capital raises in the second half of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to expect “continued SEPA draws at sub-$4” in its base case and warned that raising capital at the current $3.69 price would be more dilutive.

surprises.description: A third-party benchmark showed materially better NeuCool cold-plate performance than the preview had any evidence to expect: cooler GPUs with substantially less coolant flow and a higher viable facility-water temperature. This is positive technical validation, though the preview had emphasized that Accelsius had not disclosed unit economics or demonstrated the ramp in revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: The benchmark showed GPUs running “9–14°C cooler” using “roughly one-third of the coolant flow,” extending viable facility water temperatures from “~45°C to 54°C and beyond.”

surprises.description: Accelsius is now focusing on large hyperscalers, whose two-to-three-year adoption cycles leave no visibility into 2027 revenue. That shifts the commercial focus toward slower-cycle customers and adds a longer-term visibility concern beyond the preview’s focus on near-term shipments and backlog conversion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Accelsius is now targeting large hyperscalers rather than small early adopters,” but “hyperscaler adoption cycles run two to three years, making 2027 revenue visibility unavailable.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on whether “any HyperStart-program hyperscaler has converted to a purchase order” and whether Q2 backlog was converting to shipments.

surprises.description: The two-phase market forecast was raised to $9 billion by 2030, a favorable market-size update that the preview had not anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The two-phase market forecast raised to $9 billion by 2030.”

in_line: Quarter-end cash of $46.5 million was within the preview’s estimated $40–47 million range, and the implied Q2 operating cash use was about $25.5 million ($59.5 million year-to-date less $34.0 million in Q1), within its anticipated $25–30 million burn range.

surprises.description: Revenue was $12.3 million, below the preview’s $13.29–$13.70 million consensus range and even below its $12.5 million bear-case threshold. The preview’s revenue expectation was therefore meaningfully missed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue declined about 14% to $12.3 million in Q2 2026 from $14.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $13.29M (MarketBeat) / $13.70M (Investing.com)” and the bear case was “Revenue | <$12.5M.”

surprises.description: Industrial Assets produced only about $600,000 of operating income, well below the preview’s $1.2 million Q1 run-rate reference despite the preview describing Q2 as seasonally the strongest quarter. Smaller deals and the absence of larger auctions weighed on results; consolidated adjusted EBITDA also fell to $1.2 million from $2.8 million a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Industrial Assets Division's operating income fell to roughly $600,000 in Q2 2026 from $1.3 million a year earlier, hurt by an absence of larger auctions and prevalence of smaller-scale deals”; “adjusted EBITDA fell to $1.2 million from $2.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 run-rate was Industrial $1.2M + Financial Assets $1.0M − DebtX $(0.6)M” and “Q2 is seasonally the strongest quarter.”

in_line: The $21.7 million non-cash HGC write-down was within the preview’s expected $18–24 million range and below its $23.7 million nonaccrual balance anchor.
The post-quarter Boston Note acquisition had already been flagged in the preview as closed Aug. 3 and not contributing to Q2.

surprises.description: Ending ARR was $11.6 million, far below the preview’s roughly $15.8 million estimate and below the $15.9 million year-ago level. The preview expected a modest sequential recovery; instead, a June contract reduction helped drive another substantial decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ending ARR fell to $11.6 million” from $15.9 million a year ago, including “a $2.6 million contract reduction in June 2026,” partially offset by $1.5 million of net ARR growth.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates (base): … ARR $15.8M”; the preview also identified “Ending ARR vs. $15.9M” as the key metric and described a base case of “$15.6–16.1M.”

surprises.description: Management withdrew its original goal of significant ARR growth by year-end 2026, rather than reaffirming it or providing the quantified ARR target the preview said investors were looking for. The preview expected the goal might be repeated without detail, not withdrawn.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management withdrew its original target for significant ARR growth by year-end 2026,” citing the contract reduction, no committed upsell, and limited time remaining.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had “repeatedly promised ‘significant ARR growth’ in 2026” and described the base case as “‘significant ARR growth’ repeated without quantification.”

surprises.description: Subscription revenue was $3.7 million, $0.6 million below the preview’s $4.3 million estimate. The reported decline was larger than expected and was attributed to the expired contract.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Subscription revenue dropping $900,000 to $3.7 million” due to the expired October 2025 contract.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates (base): Revenue $7.2M (subscription $4.3M, service $2.9M).”

surprises.description: Service revenue came in at $3.6 million, $0.7 million above the preview’s $2.9 million estimate, offsetting some of the subscription shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: Service revenue “increased $300,000 to $3.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates (base): Revenue $7.2M (subscription $4.3M, service $2.9M).”

surprises.description: Total revenue of $7.4 million modestly exceeded the preview’s $7.09–$7.32 million consensus range and $7.2 million base estimate, despite the subscription miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 revenue” was $7.4 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus was “$7.09M … / $7.32M”; the preview’s base estimate was “Revenue $7.2M.”

surprises.description: GAAP loss per share widened to $0.54, substantially worse than the preview’s roughly $0.33 loss estimate. The call attributed much of the loss to stock-based compensation and severance for the former CEO.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss per diluted share widened to $0.54” from $0.38, largely due to “$5.4 million of stock-based compensation and $700,000 of severance for the former CEO.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus EPS was “–$0.33”; the preview’s GAAP EPS estimate was “–$0.31.”

surprises.description: On the non-GAAP basis, loss per share was $0.08, better than the preview’s $0.10–$0.15 expected loss and its $0.12 base estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net loss per share improved to $0.08 from $0.11.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “non-GAAP EPS –$0.12” and said the comparable was closer to “–$0.10 to –$0.15.”

surprises.description: Secure gift card revenue is now not expected to add anything for the rest of 2026, including the holiday season, and meaningful ARR growth has shifted to late Q4 2026 or early Q1 2027. The preview already knew one large rollout had moved to January 2027, but was watching for retailer conversions before the holidays; the lack of any committed 2026 revenue is a further setback.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Meaningful gift card ARR growth has been deferred a few quarters to late Q4 2026/early Q1 2027”; there is “no incremental gift card revenue committed for the balance of 2026 including the holiday season.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether the pipeline would “convert to signed orders before holiday season” and called a “second slip” the highest-probability bear catalyst.

surprises.description: Secure gift card demand showed more concrete traction than the preview had established: the pipeline grew more than 30-fold, two more retailers committed to deployments, and the previously postponed retailer will run a smaller pilot in September. That adds near-term activity even though broad revenue contribution remains delayed.
surprises.fact_evidence: The pipeline grew “over 30x” to “more than 31 large and midsized retailers”; “two additional retailers have committed” to deploy, and the postponed retailer will start a smaller pilot in September.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a pipeline of “15 North American retailers / 8 of top 20 by sales” and asked whether it would convert to signed orders before the holiday season.

surprises.description: The company is planning a capital raise and expects to use over 90% of proceeds to build go-to-market teams and programs. The preview already noted the $17.5 million ATM, but did not anticipate this specific allocation of proceeds toward rebuilding commercial capacity.
surprises.fact_evidence: With “only $8.8 million in cash and short-term investments and no debt,” the company is “planning a capital raise with over 90% of proceeds earmarked for building out go-to-market teams and programs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that Digimarc had put “a $17.5M ATM in place” and expected approximately “$8.5M at 6/30 ex-ATM.”

surprises.description: The new CEO has moved quickly to add commercial leadership, hiring a VP of Retail Solutions in addition to the CRO already noted in the preview, with the full senior team expected by the end of Q3. This is more concrete organizational action than the preview’s expectation that the CEO might still be assessing the business.
surprises.fact_evidence: The CEO was “only 30 days into the role” and had “already hired a Chief Revenue Officer and a VP of Retail Solutions,” with the full senior leadership team expected by the end of Q3 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the realistic outcome was “‘I’m 5 weeks in, plan at a later date’” and asked whether rebuilding the sales organization would push costs back up; it noted the CRO had already been hired.

surprises.description: Digimarc is narrowing its direct commercial focus to retail and CPG and shifting several other verticals to a partner-led approach. The preview did not flag this change in go-to-market scope.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is “narrowing its commercial focus to retail and CPG” while shifting pharma, life sciences, media, technology, and government “to a partner-led approach.”

in_line: Ending cash of $8.8 million was close to the preview’s approximately $8.5 million estimate.
The previously postponed large retailer still aims for broader deployment in Q1 2027, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a January 2027 rollout.

surprises.description: The preview expected management to reaffirm FY2026 revenue guidance of at least $50 million; instead, management declined to reaffirm it, citing timing shifts in an international 5G deployment. It said no backlog orders had been canceled, but the guidance stance was materially weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management declined to reaffirm its prior full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $50 million, citing timing shifts in an international 5G deployment, while insisting no backlog orders have been canceled.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 revenue guidance of ‘at least $50 million’” and “Watch for the exact construction. ‘Reaffirm at least $50 million’ is one outcome.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin was 27.9%, well below the preview's 42% estimate and 40–44% base-case range. It also fell sharply from Q1's roughly 48% as product mix shifted, despite the large year-over-year improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 gross margin expanded to 27.9% from 7.8% in Q2 2025 … but sequentially margin fell from roughly 48% in Q1 to 28% due to product mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026E … Gross margin … 42%” and the base scenario expected “GM … 40–44%.”

surprises.description: The loss was much larger than the preview's operating model implied: it estimated about $4.4 million of quarterly opex and a $0.37 million net loss, while the company reported roughly $3.09 million of net loss. SG&A nearly doubled and R&D more than doubled, including substantial 5G development spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company posted a Q2 operating loss of approximately $3.2 million and a net loss of approximately $3.09 million, driven by deliberate investments ahead of revenue”; “SG&A expenses nearly doubled to about $4.08 million … while R&D more than doubled to $1.37 million (of which $1.08 million was 5G development).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Opex (implied) … ~$4.4M” and “Net income … –$0.37M.”

surprises.description: The preview's own Q2 revenue estimate was $9.0 million, with a base-case range of $8.5–10 million; actual revenue was $8.1 million, slightly below that build. It was nevertheless essentially in line with the $8.0 million consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was approximately $8.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026E (base) … Revenue … $9.0M” and the base scenario expected “Revenue … $8.5–10M”; consensus was “$8.00M.”

surprises.description: Orders from the customer associated with the original $40 million LOI have already exceeded that LOI's amount, a stronger cumulative conversion update than the preview's specific expectation of more than $6 million in July follow-on orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $6 million in follow-on purchase orders in July 2026 alone, and stated its original $40 million LOI has already been exceeded in orders from the same customer.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “July added >$6M in follow-on orders (~$4M under the North American MNO LOI, ~$2M other).”

surprises.description: The preview expected roughly $36–38 million of pro forma cash after the Series A proceeds; the reported June 30 cash and marketable securities plus the July net proceeds total about $33 million. The gross rights proceeds were close to the preview's expected subscription amount, but net proceeds and the resulting pro forma total were lower.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The July 2026 exercise of Series A rights generated approximately $21.92 million gross and $20.12 million net proceeds, adding to the roughly $13 million cash/marketable securities … at June 30.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Series A rights closed at ~$21.9M in subscriptions” and “Pro forma cash should be ~$36–38M.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was essentially in line with the $8.0 million consensus estimate, and the year-over-year revenue decline was anticipated because Q2 2025 included lower-margin acquired 5G Titan sales.
Revenue rose substantially from Q1, consistent with the preview's expectation that Q2 would be much higher than Q1.
The $6 million of July follow-on orders was broadly consistent with the preview's expectation of more than $6 million in July orders.
The Series A rights exercise raised about $21.9 million gross, in line with the preview's stated subscription amount.
The $76 million reseller LOI remained active but larger-order adoption was still delayed; the preview had flagged delayed deployment schedules and the lack of concrete LOI conversion as a key risk.

surprises.description: Q2 net sales were $2.4 million, below the preview’s roughly $3.0–$3.1 million expectation. The shortfall reflected a $0.7 million Simpliderm decline tied to a contract-manufacturer disruption, partly offset by a $0.4 million cardiovascular gain as Elutia returned to direct sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales of $2.4 million”; a “$0.7 million decline in Simpliderm (from a contract manufacturer production disruption)” was “partially offset” by a “$0.4 million cardiovascular gain from returning to direct sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (as-reported basis) ~ $3.0M”; the base-case model expected “Revenue $3.1M (SimpliDerm $2.1M + Cardio $1.0M).”

surprises.description: Elutia secured a new $15 million Avenue Capital credit facility, with $10 million already received, and said its current and projected cash sources total about $54 million, supporting a runway through at least 2028. That is materially stronger funding visibility than the preview’s tight-runway assessment and expectation of no new capital in the base case, although some proceeds depend on future milestones or transactions.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company secured “up to $26 million in new capital without an equity offering,” including a “$15 million Avenue Capital credit facility ($10 million already received).” It reported “about $54 million” in current and projected cash sources, providing “runway through at least 2028”; another “$5 million” from Avenue is available upon NXT 41X clearance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described total liquidity of “~$44.5M” as covering “roughly five to six quarters” and “tight, not comfortable,” and its base case assumed “no new capital raised.”

surprises.description: Despite the improved financing outlook, quarter-end cash was below the preview’s expected range: $19.9 million versus an estimated $22–24 million. This is a negative cash-balance variance even though the newly disclosed financing and sale proceeds improve the forward runway picture.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Elutia ended the quarter with $19.9 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “Cash 6/30 ~$22–24M”; its catalyst checklist used “~$23M” as the reference point.

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached 70.7%, up 8 percentage points year over year, a favorable result not anticipated in the preview’s margin estimate. GAAP gross margin of 59.6%, by contrast, was within the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded 8 percentage points to 70.7% from 62.7%, while GAAP gross margin rose to 59.6% from 52.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base-case model estimated “GAAP GM ~58–60%.”

surprises.description: Management reported unusually strong stated interest in NXT 41X from a blinded survey of 50 board-certified plastic surgeons, including willingness to champion it at hospitals and use it for high-risk patients. The preview did not flag this survey evidence, which adds favorable product-adoption commentary beyond the expected regulatory timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: In a survey of 50 surgeons, “96% expressed interest in adopting NXT 41X,” “92% said they would champion it at their hospital’s value analysis committee,” and “100% would use it for high-risk patients.”

surprises.description: Elutia said its in-house facility could support at least $300 million of revenue capacity when NXT 41X launches, with further expansion requiring only more personnel and shifts, and targeted gross margins above 80% at scale. The preview did not include these manufacturing-capacity or scaled-margin claims.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company expects “at least $300 million of revenue capacity at NXT 41X launch” from its Gaithersburg GMP facility, says further expansion requires “only added personnel and shifts,” and “targets gross margins above 80% at scale.”

in_line: The Q4 2026 NXT 41 clearance and H1 2027 NXT 41X clearance timelines, followed by a soft launch in H2 2027 and full launch in 2028, matched the preview’s expected timetable.
GAAP gross margin of 59.6% was within the preview’s estimated 58–60% range.
The $7.6 million net loss and $4.6 million adjusted EBITDA loss were broadly near the preview’s modeled $7.0–7.5 million net loss and approximately $4.5 million adjusted EBITDA loss.
The Simpliderm sale’s stated proceeds of up to $11 million, including $8 million cash at closing, were consistent with the preview’s disclosed transaction terms.

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 cash at $6–8 million and flagged a balance below $5 million as a major concern; CXAI reported $11.7 million at June 30. The reported cash balance was well above the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company held $11.7 million in cash as of June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Est. Q2 exit cash $6–8M — verify”; “Anything below ~$5M forces another raise.”

surprises.description: The preview emphasized that investors needed organic revenue disclosed separately, but the reported facts give only total Q2 revenue and no organic-versus-EngineRoom breakdown. That leaves the preview’s central question about the health of CXAI’s standalone business unanswered.
surprises.fact_evidence: The reported Q2 revenue is given as “about $1.7 million”; no organic revenue figure is provided in the reported facts.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic (ex-EngineRoom) revenue” was ranked the top metric to watch; “a company confident in its core will break it out.”

surprises.description: The preview said a reverse-split ratio and effective date were a critical near-term catalyst, with silence on the ratio described as bearish. No ratio or effective date is reported in the call facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: The reported call facts contain no reverse-split ratio or effective-date announcement.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Silence on the ratio today is a meaningfully bearish signal”; “the split must be effective on or about Aug 24, 2026.”

surprises.description: CXAI set breakeven for the second half of 2027. The preview called for a dated target and cited H1 2027 as the breakeven timing in its bull scenario, so the target is specific but later than that optimistic benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management targets breakeven in the second half of 2027 followed by profitable growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario called for a “credible EBITDA-breakeven date (H1'27)”; the preview also said the path-to-profitability discussion needed “a quarter, not a direction.”

surprises.description: CXAI reported ARR of $11.5 million, up from $3.6 million quarter over quarter and 156% year over year from $4.5 million. The preview focused on reported revenue and acquisition run-rate rather than this substantially higher recurring-revenue figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Annual recurring revenue jumped from $3.6 million to $11.5 million quarter-over-quarter, a 156% year-over-year increase from $4.5 million.”

surprises.description: A new three-year multimillion-dollar financial-services contract came through a competitive RFP, alongside renewals from two Fortune 500 customers; management said new enterprise wins are expected to add roughly one-third to revenue. The preview expected Q1 enterprise bookings to begin converting but did not anticipate these specific wins or the stated uplift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed a new 3-year multimillion-dollar financial services deal via competitive RFP and secured renewals from two Fortune 500 customers, with new enterprise wins expected to add roughly one-third revenue uplift.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1’s “$5M TCV across three 3-year enterprise deals should begin converting.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses rose only 5.6% while revenue grew 79% sequentially, a favorable divergence that the preview did not forecast. Cash EBITDA remained negative, but improved modestly from Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash EBITDA improved modestly to negative $2.68 million in Q2 from negative $3 million in Q1, while operating expenses rose only 5.6% against 79% revenue growth.”

surprises.description: CXAI reported NRR of 99.3%, up from the preview’s Q1 reference of 98%. The improvement is positive, though relatively small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net revenue retention improving to 99.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “NRR 98%” as the Q1 FY26 reference and called its trend a key quality signal.

surprises.description: The call reported Sky 2.0 entering production deployment, the Events module reaching general availability in September, and BEAT expected to launch in Q4. The preview did not flag these product milestones; their financial impact was not quantified in the reported facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sky 2.0 moved into production deployment, a new Events module reaches general availability in September, and the personal productivity product BEAT is expected to launch in Q4.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was about $1.7 million, broadly in line with the preview’s $1.50–1.68 million implied range and $1.50–1.70 million base scenario; the preview had already cautioned that a headline beat over $1.20 million consensus would be largely mechanical.

EngineRoom’s contribution and run-rate were broadly as anticipated: the preview cited roughly $8.1 million annualized revenue, $1.6 million adjusted EBITDA, 50-plus customers, and a greater-than-$12-million combined annualized run-rate. The reported facts give more than $8 million in EngineRoom revenue, approximately $1.6 million adjusted EBITDA, over 50 customers, and combined annualized revenue above $12 million.

Including only June’s EngineRoom revenue in Q2 and expecting the full three-month combined impact in Q3 was consistent with the preview’s estimate that only about one month of EngineRoom revenue would appear in Q2.

surprises.description: Caliber’s platform adjusted EBITDA reached about $0.3 million of profit, better than the preview’s expectation of breakeven or near breakeven and the base case of a small loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Platform adjusted EBITDA turned positive at approximately $0.3 million,” improving about $0.4 million from a $0.1 million loss a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side's real bar” was “breakeven or better”; the base scenario expected “-$0.1 to -$0.3M.”

surprises.description: Platform revenue fell to $3.7 million, missing the preview’s $4 million-or-more bar. The shortfall came as development and construction fees were pushed to later periods, rather than arriving in Q2 as the preview’s Steamboat financing thesis anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Platform revenue declined approximately 10% year-over-year to $3.7 million from $4.1 million,” driven by “the timing of project financings shifting to later periods.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the buy-side bar was “platform revenue ≥ $4M” and identified the Steamboat financing, which “closed in April 2026,” as the “single most likely source of an upside surprise.”

surprises.description: Caliber sold far more LINK during the quarter than the preview’s prior-quarter sale suggested, ending Q2 with fewer than half the Q1-end tokens. The sale generated $2.5 million for redeployment into real estate, but the scale of the reduction was not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company sold approximately 278,357 LINK tokens for $2.5 million in proceeds during the quarter” and held “229,204 LINK tokens valued at $1.7 million at quarter-end,” redeploying capital into its real estate platform.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported “507,560 LINK tokens” at Q1-end and noted that “~55,000 tokens were sold in Q1 for $0.5M”; it flagged the June 30 mark as a swing factor but did not anticipate a comparable Q2 sale.

surprises.description: Platform expenses rose despite lower platform revenue, with additional bad-debt reserves on uncollectible development and construction fees contributing to the increase. The preview did not flag this cost or collection pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Platform expenses rose approximately 11% to $5.9 million from $5.3 million,” primarily due to “increased bad debt charges from additional reserves on uncollectible development and construction fees.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a sizable near-term maturity burden among unsecured notes: $21 million of roughly $26 million principal comes due within 12 months. Refinancing and conversions provide some relief, but the preview had not identified this specific maturity schedule.
surprises.fact_evidence: Caliber had “148 unsecured notes totaling ~$26 million principal, of which $21 million matures within 12 months,” and had refinanced $6.4 million into a 36-month program and converted about $5.3 million into equity through August 13.

surprises.description: Caliber reported additional hotel-platform activity not anticipated in the preview: a pipeline of eight CHT acquisition assets, six hotels moved to an owner-centric model, and purchase of a Hyatt Studios site near the planned TSMC investment. The pipeline includes only one asset under an executed letter of intent, so much of the reported pipeline is not yet a completed acquisition.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “grew its CHT hotel acquisition pipeline to eight assets with one under executed letter of intent,” “transitioned six hotels to a new owner-centric management model,” and “purchased a 2.5-acre Hyatt Studios site near TSMC's $265 billion Phoenix semiconductor investment.”

in_line: Caliber reaffirmed full-year 2026 guidance of $18–22 million in revenue and positive adjusted EBITDA, as the preview expected; the stated 60%/40% sources of revenue growth also matched the preview’s back-half financing and capital-formation framework.

The first fund tokenization and planned expansion across an initial slate of roughly $100 million in managed assets were anticipated in the preview. The call did not provide a fundraising figure attributable to tokenization.

Managed capital was broadly stable, rising from about $489 million in the prior quarter to $495.6 million, while remaining 0.6% below the year-ago level; the preview’s base case expected AUM to be roughly flat.

surprises.description: HIT reaffirmed its $45–50 million FY2026 revenue guidance rather than trimming it, as the preview expected investors to fear. The company cited contracted and pipeline revenue metrics in support of the range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $45 million to $50 million, supported by contracted and pipeline revenue metrics.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side expects a cut”; the preview’s base case said “FY guide trimmed to ~$40–45M or steered ‘toward the low end,’” and its bear case expected a cut or withdrawal.

surprises.description: The amount of contracted revenue expected in the second half was only $14 million, well below the preview’s >$25 million benchmark for contracted revenue remaining in 2026. The reported pipeline was $66.3 million, but $64.4 million was not yet contracted and carried only a 15%–40% expected conversion rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Contracted revenue totaled $32.3 million for the first half of 2026, with $17.3 million already recognized, $14 million expected in the second half, and $1 million in 2027.” The pipeline was “$66.3 million as of July 31,” with “the remaining $64.4 million” carrying a “15%-40% expected conversion rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “> $25M” in contracted revenue remaining in 2026 and said this was “the single cleanest” measure of whether new business was landing.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $8.1 million, below the preview’s $9.3 million estimate and its $9.0–10.5 million base-case range; revenue also fell 13.5% year over year rather than being roughly flat. It did beat the preview’s low-confidence $7.55 million consensus, but the preview had already described a beat versus that figure as likely.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 GAAP revenue fell 13.5% year-over-year to $8.1 million from $9.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Q2 revenue estimate is $9.3M, roughly flat YoY”; the base scenario forecast “$9.0–10.5M” and said “a headline revenue beat versus $7.55M is the high-probability outcome.”

surprises.description: Cash was $6.5 million, well below the preview’s expectation of more than $9 million. The sharp rise in AR days to 55 from 20 also disclosed a collection-timing strain associated with the carrier transition that the preview had not quantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents declined to $6.5 million from $8.1 million a year ago, while AR days rose sharply to 55 days in the first half from 20 days in the prior-year period due to the carrier transition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s cash metric said “Loss narrowing; cash >$9M” and flagged $10.3 million of Q1 cash.

surprises.description: Management said the switch to an A-rated stop-loss carrier, expected within 30 days, could lift projections by 20%–30% by opening access to large brokerages that require A-rated carriers. The preview did not anticipate this potential source of a substantial increase in projections.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is switching to an A-rated stop-loss carrier, expected within 30 days,” which management believes “could lift projections by 20% to 30%” by unlocking business from large “alpha” brokerages.

surprises.description: The distribution network reached 933 partners, short of the preview’s >950 “good looks” threshold. The reported 19.9% year-over-year growth was also consistent with the preview’s concern that partner growth was decelerating.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The distribution partner network grew 19.9% year-over-year to 933 brokers, TPAs and agencies from 778.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “>950” partners would be good and noted growth was “Decelerating from +87% YoY (Q2'25) and +34% (Q4'25).”

surprises.description: HIT said its HitRix large-group stop-loss marketplace would launch within 2–3 weeks. The preview did not flag this near-term launch as a catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to launch its HitRix large-group stop-loss marketplace within 2-3 weeks.”

surprises.description: Management reported an anticipated pipeline of roughly 30 monthly submissions from municipalities and government agencies for the rate-stabilization program, a specific prospective source of activity not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “secured its first employer group under its 3-year rate stabilization program, with an anticipated pipeline of roughly 30 submissions per month from municipalities and government agencies.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was a $1.3 million Q2 loss, within the preview’s expected loss range of $1.0–$1.5 million.
Diluted EPS was a $0.04 loss, in line with the preview’s base-case range of a $0.03–$0.04 loss, though slightly worse than the cited $0.03 loss consensus.
The first employer group under the 3-year rate-stabilization program met the preview’s expectation of at least one signed contract in Q2.
Revenue exceeded the preview’s low-confidence $7.55 million consensus, as the preview said a beat of that figure was likely.

surprises.description: LIVE reported diluted EPS of -$0.34, well below the preview’s modeled -$0.03, and swung to a $1.1 million net loss. The loss was materially deeper than the near-breakeven result the model anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company swung to a net loss of approximately $1.1 million (loss per share of $0.34) versus net income of $5.4 million and diluted EPS of $1.24 in the prior year period.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Diluted EPS: Q3 FY2026 est. ~$(0.03).

surprises.description: Retail-Flooring revenue fell to $21.4 million, below the preview’s $23.4 million estimate, and its year-over-year decline was steeper than the model’s expected decline. The segment’s deterioration was worse than the already-weak trajectory the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: Retail-Flooring segment revenue fell 29.4% to $21.4 million due to continued weakness in new home construction and home refurbishment markets.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Retail-Flooring Q3 FY2026 estimated revenue: $23.4M; Q3 FY2025 revenue: $30.4M.

surprises.description: Operating income was $5.3 million, above the preview’s $3.8 million model estimate, despite declining 34% year over year. The reported result was substantially better than the forecasted year-over-year decline of 53%.
surprises.fact_evidence: Operating income decreased 34% to $5.3 million from $8 million, hurt by lower gross profit and higher operating expenses.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Operating income: Q3 FY2026 est. ~$3.8M, YoY –53%.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA came in at $9.3 million, above the preview’s $7.8 million estimate. Its 29.5% year-over-year decline was also less severe than the model’s expected 41% decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EBITDA dropped 29.5% (about $3.9 million) to $9.3 million, down from $13.2 million a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Adjusted EBITDA: Q3 FY2026 est. ~$7.8M, YoY –41%.

surprises.description: Steel Manufacturing revenue reached $36.3 million, above the preview’s $33.0 million estimate, while operating income surged 68.9% against a model that estimated $1.4 million of operating income. The segment performed considerably better than the preview’s expectation that Steel would stabilize around that level.
surprises.fact_evidence: Steel Manufacturing segment revenue rose 7.3% to $36.3 million, with operating income surging 68.9% and adjusted EBITDA up 16.3%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Steel Mfg Q3 FY2026 estimated revenue / operating income: $33.0M / $1.4M. The base case said, “Steel returns to ~$1.5M operating income.”

surprises.description: Gross margin improved to 34.1% rather than declining to the preview’s estimated 33.5%. Gross profit still fell, but the margin result was better than the expected 50-basis-point year-over-year contraction.
surprises.fact_evidence: Gross margin improved slightly by 10 basis points to 34.1%, while gross profit declined 3.1% to $37.1 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Gross margin: Q3 FY2026 est. ~33.5%, YoY –50 bps.

surprises.description: Retail-Entertainment revenue was modestly above the preview’s estimate, and operating income growth was much stronger than the model implied. The preview estimated operating income of $2.6 million, versus the prior-year $2.3 million, while the call reported 33.8% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Retail-Entertainment segment revenue grew 12.7% to $21.4 million with operating income up 33.8% and adjusted EBITDA up 28.9%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Retail-Entertainment Q3 FY2026 estimated revenue / operating income: $20.9M / $2.6M.

surprises.description: Consolidated revenue was $108.9 million, above the preview’s roughly $105 million estimate, making the year-over-year decline milder than the modeled 6.7% decline. The beat came despite the sharper-than-expected Retail-Flooring contraction.
surprises.fact_evidence: Total revenue declined 3.2% year-over-year to $108.9 million, down from $112.5 million, driven primarily by a $9 million drop in the Retail-Flooring segment.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Revenue: Q3 FY2026 est. ~$105M, YoY –6.7%.

in_line: The prior-year comparison included the $2.8 million of one-time gains ($1.5 million from employee retention credits and $1.3 million from a holdback settlement) that the preview had already identified as inflating Q3 FY2025 results.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $63 million, below the preview’s $70–75 million estimate. The call attributed about $5 million of the decline to insurance and legal reserve adjustments, which the preview had not flagged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA fell to $63 million from $82 million a year ago, with about $5 million of the decline driven by insurance and legal reserve adjustments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA *no published consensus; my est. $70–75M*.”

surprises.description: KinderCare cut its FY26 outlook: adjusted EBITDA is now $200–220 million versus prior guidance of $215–235 million, and revenue is $2.66–2.70 billion versus $2.70–2.75 billion. Q3 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $44–48 million also sits below Q2’s $63 million, offering little evidence of the material second-half progress the preview said management had guided toward.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was updated to revenue of $2.66–$2.7 billion, adjusted EBITDA of $200–$220 million, and adjusted EPS of $0.05–$0.15.” Q3 guidance is “revenue of $660–$680 million and adjusted EBITDA of $44–$48 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guide of $215–235M”; “FY26 revenue: $2.71B (FY guide $2.70–2.75B)”; management had guided “gradual improvement through the first half, material progress in the second half.”

surprises.description: The 68.6% occupancy headline was within the preview’s 68–69% range, but consolidations contributed a 70-basis-point benefit. Without that benefit, occupancy would be about 67.9%, implying a year-over-year decline of roughly 310 basis points rather than the expected narrowing to 200–250 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Same-center occupancy fell 240 basis points to 68.6%, though consolidations added a 70 basis point occupancy benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bar: a Y/Y gap that narrows to ~200–250bps (i.e., 68–69%).”

surprises.description: Enrollment fell 4% year over year, worse than the preview’s stated threshold of -2% or better and also weaker than Q1’s -3.0%. This indicates the enrollment trend did not improve as the preview hoped.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total enrollment declined 4% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Needs to be -2% or better to validate the trajectory”; Q1 enrollment was “-3.0% Y/Y.”

surprises.description: The closure program proved much larger than the preview’s 25–35-center base-case framing: KinderCare closed 49 centers in Q2 alone and expects 80–85 closures by year-end. The closures are expected to reduce annual revenue by about $57 million, though management estimates an $8 million adjusted EBITDA benefit and roughly 150 basis points of occupancy improvement once completed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “KinderCare closed 49 centers in Q2 … and expects total closures to reach 80 to 85 by year-end.” Once complete, optimization is estimated to be “a ~$57 million annual revenue headwind but a ~$8 million adjusted EBITDA benefit” and improve occupancy “by roughly 150 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “more than the usual 15–20” centers and its base scenario described “closures at ‘25–35 centers.’”

surprises.description: Full-year free cash flow is now expected to be less than $10 million, a steep shortfall against the preview’s $35–40 million guide. The call linked the shortfall to elevated optimization costs, including substantial lease-exit payments, with some exits potentially extending into 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow for the year is now expected to be less than $10 million due to elevated optimization costs, including ~$20–25 million of lease exit payments tied to about 36 identified lease exits, some potentially extending into 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY FCF guide $35–40M.”

surprises.description: Management lowered the expected tuition contribution to revenue growth to about 2.5% for the year, citing slower state subsidy reimbursement increases. That is below the preview’s bullish operating case, which depended on tuition holding above 3% on new enrollments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tuition contribution to revenue growth lowered to ~2.5% for the year due to slower state subsidy reimbursement increases.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Tuition holds >3% on new enrollments without volume attrition.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $698 million, essentially matching the preview’s $697.98 million consensus.
Q2 adjusted EPS was $0.08, matching the preview’s $0.08 consensus.
The reported occupancy headline of 68.6% was within the preview’s expected 68–69% range, though the consolidation benefit makes the underlying comparison weaker.
Champions grew revenue 13% year over year, remaining above the preview’s stated concern threshold of growth decelerating below about 12%.

surprises.description: Revenue was $46.1 million, well above the preview’s $37–39 million estimate, despite the expected production moderation. The preview’s working consensus was lower still, at roughly $33 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $46.1 million,” up approximately 15% sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Q2 est.” revenue was “$37–39M”; working consensus was “~$33M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA fell short of the preview’s $20–22 million estimate, coming in around $18.5–18.7 million. This was a miss even though revenue substantially exceeded the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $18.5-18.7 million in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Q2 est.” adjusted EBITDA was “$20–22M.”

surprises.description: Production averaged 6,800 BOE per day, below the preview’s 7,000–7,300 estimate and below its expectation that volumes would moderate from Q1. The result was within the company’s previously stated 6,500–7,000 guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Production averaged approximately 6,800 BOE per day,” a “16% sequential decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Q2 est.” production was “7,000–7,300 Boe/d”; the preview said volumes were expected to moderate through mid-year.

surprises.description: The reported average realized oil price of $94.07 per barrel was far above the preview’s estimate of roughly $73–75 per barrel. The preview had expected hedge structures and differentials to limit the company’s capture of the oil-price strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average realized oil price rose 53% year-over-year to $94.07 per barrel.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q2 realizations “should land near $73–75/Bbl” and flagged “hedge-capped upside.”

surprises.description: GAAP EPS was $1.31, materially below the preview’s forecast of $2.00–$2.80, despite a non-cash derivative gain. The reported gain was $13.1 million and was partly offset by $8.1 million in realized hedge settlement losses.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income was $17.5 million ($1.31 per share),” including “a $13.1 million non-cash unrealized derivative gain” that offset “$8.1 million in realized hedge settlement losses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “GAAP EPS: +$2.00 to +$2.80” and expected a “large non-cash derivative gain.”

surprises.description: Management reported plans to participate in over 20 gross wells and said BLM litigation resolution unlocked permitting for top-tier Powder River Basin wells, expanding the second-half development program beyond prior expectations. However, contributions are expected only in late 2026 and early 2027, and full program details are still forthcoming.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management plans to “drill and participate in over 20 gross wells”; BLM litigation resolution “unlocked permitting” and “expand[ed] the second-half development program beyond prior expectations,” with contributions expected “only in late 2026 and early 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview watched for a “D-J Basin DUC” completion targeted for mid-summer and whether the “Permian San Andres program gets sanctioned for the back half.”

surprises.description: The company repaid $13 million of debt, taking net funded debt to about $73 million from the preview’s roughly $87 million net-debt figure. Quarter-end undrawn credit availability was also reported at $40 million, above the preview’s roughly $27 million estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repaid $13 million of debt,” reducing the revolver balance to $85 million and net funded debt to “approximately $73 million”; it had “$40 million of undrawn credit facility availability at quarter end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed net debt of “~$87M” and “~$27M of revolver availability.”

in_line: Management reiterated full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $60–70 million, matching the preview’s base-case expectation that guidance would be reaffirmed.

surprises.description: The preview modeled a Q2 net loss of $4.5 million, but Stardust reported $3.9 million. Loss per share was also narrower than the preview's $0.44 estimate, at $0.35; the company attributed the EPS improvement primarily to a higher weighted-average share count, not better operating performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported a Q2 net loss of $3.9 million”; “Basic and diluted loss per share improved to $0.35”; the EPS change was “primarily due to a higher weighted average share count following capital raises.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's Q2 2026E base estimates were “Net loss $(4.5)M” and “Loss per share $(0.44).”

surprises.description: June 30 cash was about $0.5 million, below the preview's roughly $0.8 million base estimate. That is a modest shortfall against the estimate, although it remains within the preview's stated $0.3–$2.0 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents falling to approximately $0.5 million as of June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Cash & equivalents (EOP) ~$0.8M,” with a range of “$0.3M – $2.0M.”

surprises.description: After quarter end, the ATM raised about $2.9 million in net proceeds—an unexpectedly sizable near-term cash infusion, though it came through equity issuance and therefore adds dilution. The preview anticipated incremental ATM or equity-line dilution but did not specify a raise of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: The $5 million ATM “raised about $151,000 during the quarter and an additional approximately $2.9 million in net proceeds subsequent to quarter end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base case included “incremental ATM/equity-line dilution.”

surprises.description: Investing cash use fell to just $0.2 million for the first half, versus $2.2 million a year earlier, as the company shifted to a more phased capital deployment. The preview emphasized project scale and funding needs but did not anticipate this sharply reduced investment outflow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash used in investing activities dropped sharply to $0.2 million from $2.2 million” and reflected “a more phased deployment of capital.”

in_line: The company remained pre-revenue, as the preview said it would have no revenue for years.
First-half operating cash use was $4.0 million, roughly consistent with the preview's estimate of about $2.0 million of Q2 operating cash burn following Q1 burn of $2.07 million.

Management said meeting working-capital and capital-expenditure needs over the next 12 months depends on raising additional capital, consistent with the preview's emphasis on limited runway and ongoing financing needs.

There was no material progress in feedstock, offtake, or strategic financing discussions. The preview described the relevant arrangements as non-binding LOIs and flagged silence on project financing as informative.

Management is evaluating alternatives to address Nasdaq continued-listing requirements, including the minimum market-value threshold, but the facts report no concrete cure. The preview had already highlighted the October 21 deadline and delisting risk.

surprises.description: The preview’s independent build expected a Q2 net loss of about $55–60 million, EPS of roughly –$1.65 to –$1.80, and R&D expense of $48–55 million. Nektar reported a $40.6 million loss, or –$1.23 per share, with $39.1 million of R&D; it also narrowed FY26 R&D guidance to $210–230 million from the previously cited $200–250 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss was $40.6 million ($1.23 per share), with R&D expense of $39.1 million and full-year R&D guidance of $210-230 million reflecting Phase III ramp-up.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net loss ~$55–60M, EPS ~–$1.65 to –$1.80”; “R&D ~$48–55M.” The preview also cites management’s FY26 R&D guide of “$200–250M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected a single AA registrational study of about 600 patients. Nektar finalized a single study, as expected, but it is planned to enroll 850 patients, a substantially larger trial; the early-2027 start remains aligned with the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Finalized its single registrational Phase III ZENITH-AA study in alopecia areata (850 patients, primary endpoint SALT ≤20 at week 52), planned to start early 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side has already underwritten one ~600-patient study starting early 2027.”

surprises.description: Nektar raised its year-end cash outlook above the preview’s $800–825 million expectation, to approximately $815–840 million. The company also said its $1.02 billion cash balance and no-debt position fund operations into Q3 2028, past the initial AD readouts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its year-end 2026 cash guidance to approximately $815 million to $840 million”; it ended Q2 with “$1.02 billion in cash and investments and no debt,” with runway “extending into Q3 2028 past the initial AD data readouts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Year-end guide is $800–825M with runway ‘into 2028.’”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue came in below the preview’s estimate of roughly $10.7–10.9 million. Full-year revenue guidance remained $40–45 million, consistent with the preview’s expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 noncash royalty revenue was $10.1 million, with full-year 2026 revenue still expected at $40-45 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ~$10.7–10.9M”; FY26 revenue consensus was “$40.6M” and company guidance was “$40–45M.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed favorable prescriber research that the preview had not discussed: nearly all surveyed high-volume physicians said injection-site reactions would not deter prescribing, and physicians favored REZPEG’s T-reg mechanism in light of the reported infection-risk and conjunctivitis profile.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Market research with 151 high-volume prescribers found 150 of 151 physicians said injection site reactions were not a barrier to prescribing, and physicians favored REZPEG's novel T-reg mechanism given no increased infection risk and no conjunctivitis observed.”

surprises.description: Although the preview noted pending securities class actions and the possibility of legal costs, it did not flag a scheduled jury trial. Management disclosed a federal-court jury trial date of September 8, 2026, and declined to comment further because litigation is ongoing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A jury trial in federal court in San Francisco is scheduled for September 8, 2026, on which management declined to comment further citing ongoing litigation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described securities class actions and said to “watch whether” legal costs reverse their Q1 decline.

in_line: The two initial ZENITH-AD studies started in July with 510 patients each, and the third treatment-experienced study was set to start by the end of September, consistent with the preview’s expected AD-3 September start and the stated trial plans.
The single-study AA path and planned early-2027 start matched the preview; the unexpected difference was the 850-patient size rather than the expected roughly 600 patients.
Q4 2026 REZOLVE-AA 24-week off-treatment data remained a planned catalyst, as the preview expected.
Full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $40–45 million was maintained, matching the preview’s cited company guidance.

surprises.description: TSSI reported Q2 revenue of $35.1M, about 25% below the $47.1M consensus and the preview’s roughly $47.7M segment build. The revenue decline was substantially worse than expected, despite the preview anticipating a pullback in low-margin Procurement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue declined 20% year-over-year to $35.1 million”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Q2 FY26 Consensus | $47.1M”; the preview’s segment build estimated “Total … ~$47.7M.”

surprises.description: Procurement revenue fell to $18.2M, far below the preview’s $30M estimate. The preview expected a pullback from the prior-year $33M, but not one this deep.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Procurement revenue from $33 million to $18.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Procurement … Q2 FY26E | $30M”; the preview also described it as “Low-margin, lumpy, zero visibility.”

surprises.description: Systems Integration revenue was $13.9M, below the preview’s $15–16M expectation and just under its roughly $14M threshold for sustaining the growth narrative. It still grew 46% year over year and reached 39% of revenue, but the reported dollar amount missed the expected level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Systems Integration revenue grew 46% year-over-year to $13.9 million and now represents 39% of total revenue versus 22% a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Systems Integration … $16.0M” and said “SI below ~$14M breaks that narrative”; it also cited “~$15.5M implied consensus.”

surprises.description: Blended gross margin rose to 22.8%, materially above the preview’s roughly 17.5% estimate. Gross profit also increased despite the revenue decline, reflecting a much stronger margin outcome than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Blended gross margin improved 640 basis points to 22.8% from 16.4%, and consolidated gross profit rose 11% to $8 million despite the overall revenue decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s segment build estimated “Gross margin … ~17.5%.”

surprises.description: Q2 Adjusted EBITDA was $4.5M, below the preview’s approximately $5.0M estimate. However, management kept full-year guidance toward the upper end of the $20–22M range, as the preview expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased 12% year-over-year to $4.5 million in Q2 and 5% to $9.8 million year-to-date, with management reaffirming full-year guidance toward the upper end of the $20-22 million range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 Adjusted EBITDA at “~$5.0M” and said the buy-side wanted “‘high end’ reaffirmed or a raise above $22M.”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $0.05, below both the $0.06 consensus and the preview’s roughly $0.07 estimate. Net income was essentially flat to slightly lower, with higher tax expense cited as a pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income was essentially flat to slightly down at $1.4 million ($0.05 per diluted share) versus $1.5 million ($0.06) a year ago, pressured by higher income tax expense ($413,000 vs. $69,000).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS | Q2 FY26 Consensus | $0.06”; the preview’s segment build estimated “Diluted EPS … ~$0.07.”

surprises.description: The cash balance was $67.7M, above the preview’s concern that cash might exit Q2 in the low $50Ms after the prior-quarter draw and planned investment. Debt was also slightly below the preview’s roughly $17M estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company maintains a strong balance sheet with $67.7 million in cash and only $16.1 million in total debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “If cash exits Q2 in the low $50Ms with working capital still absorbing, expect financing questions,” and cited debt of “~$17M.”

surprises.description: Facilities Management revenue reached $2.7M, well above the preview’s $1.7M estimate. Maintenance revenue declined as customers did not renew agreements on older MDCs, but discrete project work lifted the segment above expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Facilities Management revenue grew 84% year-over-year to $2.7 million, though maintenance revenue declined to $746,000 from $1 million … offset by discrete project work rising to nearly $2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Facilities Mgmt … Q2 FY26E | $1.7M”; the preview characterized the segment as “Noise.”

surprises.description: Management identified supply-chain constraints, rather than demand or the validation-test bottleneck emphasized in the preview, as the main limit on Systems Integration growth. Georgetown has 2–3 times the capacity required by its contractual minimum, so capacity exists but is not yet fully usable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Georgetown facility has 2x to 3x capacity above the contractual minimum, with supply chain constraints (rather than demand) cited as the primary gating factor limiting Systems Integration growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted a “validation-test bottleneck” and said scaling depended on Georgetown “throughput scaling faster than the validation-test bottleneck”; it also described the potential to halve validation-test time to deliver “2x the volume with current load.”

surprises.description: The Vera Rubin investment is expected to generate incremental recurring revenue mainly in Q4, a revenue contribution the preview did not specify when discussing the roughly $17M capex program. This adds a more concrete near-term payoff to the planned capacity investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is “investing approximately $17 million” in power and cooling capacity for NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform, with completion expected by mid-September and “incremental recurring revenue mainly in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the “$17M next-gen (Vera Rubin-class power/cooling) capex program completes ‘at some point in the third quarter,’” but did not state that it would drive incremental recurring revenue mainly in Q4.

in_line: Management reaffirmed FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $20–22M toward the upper end, matching the preview’s expectation that the “high end” language would be maintained.
The Vera Rubin capacity project remained on a Q3 completion timeline, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it would complete “at some point in the third quarter.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $15.1 million versus the preview’s $10.8 million model, but about $4.4 million came from newly presenting pass-through electricity costs gross. Excluding that presentation change, revenue was about $10.7 million—essentially in line with the model rather than a comparable $4.3 million beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $15.1 million”; reported growth was 145%, “but only 73% excluding a new gross presentation of pass-through electricity costs that added ~$4.4 million to both revenue and cost of revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base revenue: $10.8M.”

surprises.description: The net loss was substantially larger than the preview’s estimate implied: the preview translated its $(0.11) EPS estimate into an expected loss of roughly $14–15 million, while the reported loss was $22.6 million. The call attributed major items to stock compensation, interest expense, and a debt-extinguishment loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $22.6 million from $7.8 million a year earlier,” driven by “$9.4 million of noncash stock compensation, $3.2 million interest expense, and a $4.2 million loss on debt extinguishment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A $(0.11) EPS on ~130M shares implies a ~$14–15M net loss.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA remained a loss and was worse than the preview’s $(1.0) million base model, at $(1.6) million. The sequential improvement was real, but the result did not reach the modeled level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $1.6 million,” a 25% sequential improvement.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base Adj. EBITDA: $(1.0)M.”

surprises.description: Gross profit fell to $766,000, with new-site ramp costs and Briscoe repairs weighing on the quarter; Briscoe itself posted a gross loss. That was weaker than the preview’s expectation that hosting segment margin would hold around 35–40%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit compressed 35% year-over-year to $766,000,” hurt by “new-site ramp costs at Kati 1” and “roughly $1.5 million of front-loaded turbine repairs” at Briscoe, which “posted a $787,000 gross loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Hosting >$8M with segment margin holding ~35–40% validates the pivot.”

surprises.description: The company had a much larger cash position than the preview’s downside scenario contemplated, ending Q2 with $113 million of cash and a 2.1x current ratio. That liquidity was built alongside substantial ATM issuance, so the stronger funding position came with meaningful shareholder dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised $159.4 million in Q2 (primarily $113.5 million via ATM) plus an additional $23.6 million through the ATM since quarter-end by issuing about 18.8 million shares”; it ended Q2 with “$113 million cash” and a “current ratio of 2.1x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “$68.6M unrestricted at 3/31 against a heavy capex program” and identified “cash <$50M with continued ATM issuance” as a bear-case condition.

surprises.description: Proprietary mining revenue fell more sharply than the preview’s base case, which modeled mining revenue around $2.2 million. The preview did flag weak hashprice, but the reported 40% revenue decline shows a larger realized drag than that base estimate assumed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Proprietary Bitcoin mining revenue fell $1.1 million (40%) as hash price dropped from ~$51 to ~$34.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case assumed “mining ~$2.2M”; the preview also said hashprice was “volatile and weak in Q2.”

surprises.description: The renewable-power and AI development footprint was ahead of the preview’s operating-scale reference: 192 MW was operating, with a 206 MW target by the end of summer, and the pipeline exceeded 6.3 GW. The preview’s operational scenario described MW under management moving from 147 toward roughly 170.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The renewable power pipeline grew 47% this year to over 6.3 gigawatts,” with “192 MW currently operating,” “14 MW under construction (targeting 206 MW by end of summer),” and “over 1.6 GW of AI capacity in development.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base operational case anticipated “MW under management stepping from 147 toward ~170.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a specific proposed financing structure for AI builds: 70–80% project-level debt, arranged after a lease is signed, with an illustrative stabilized NOI figure. The preview was waiting for financing specifics, but this is a proposed playbook rather than a disclosed committed financing facility.
surprises.fact_evidence: For each 100 MW AI build-out, management plans to fund “70–80% with project-level debt raised within 8–12 weeks of a signed lease,” with “an illustrative ~$180 million of stabilized annual net operating income under a 15-year triple-net contract.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a bank was engaged but “no structure disclosed,” and asked whether financing would be “project-level debt/JV equity (good — non-dilutive at HoldCo) vs. more ATM equity.”

surprises.description: The call supplied a concrete timeline for Kati 2, saying initial ready-for-service would take roughly 15 months after contract signing. The preview explicitly noted that numeric guidance would be new, so this adds clarity but also makes the build-out timeline explicit.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management guided to “roughly 15 months from contract signing to initial ready-for-service.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any guidance at all” was a key watch item; the preview said even “a MW-energized or run-rate revenue target would be new information.”

surprises.description: Soluna completed the Briscoe acquisition and bought out partners in Dorothy 1A and 1B, achieving full vertical integration across Project Dorothy 1. The preview discussed Briscoe as a potential REC-sales contributor but did not anticipate this completed set of transactions or the Dorothy integration update.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “closed the $53 million Briscoe Wind Farm acquisition on April 1 and bought out partners at Dorothy 1A and 1B, achieving full vertical integration of power generation and compute across Project Dorothy 1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview mentioned “Briscoe REC sales” as a possible bull-case driver but did not describe the acquisition close or the Dorothy partner buyouts.

surprises.description: The Series B preferred shares were fully retired through conversion into common stock, and accumulated dividends were paid. The preview flagged a possible preferred-share resolution as a dilution event, but the specific conversion and cash payment were not yet known.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “fully retired all 62,500 Series B preferred shares (converting into ~6.5 million common shares at $0.96) and paid $2.1 million in accumulated dividends.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “$1.8M Series B preferred dividends in arrears” and said “any resolution, exchange, or conversion is a dilution event worth pricing.”

in_line: Kati 2 had not yet converted to an executed lease: the call reported a signed tenant LOI with lease negotiations underway, consistent with the preview’s base case of negotiations continuing rather than a completed lease.
Adjusted EBITDA improved sequentially but remained negative; the preview expected movement toward breakeven and described a first positive quarter as a genuine surprise.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $24.3 million, below the preview’s $28.3–28.9 million consensus range and even below management’s earlier $25–30 million-plus framing. Management attributed the shortfall to delayed DoD public-sector spending diverted to the Iran conflict.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $24.3 million” and was “slightly short of expectations due to delayed DoD public sector spending diverted to the Iran conflict.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue **~$28.3–28.9M**”; management’s preliminary Q2 framing was “**$25–30M+**.”

surprises.description: The company lowered FY2026 revenue guidance to $100–150 million from its prior $130–145 million range. The new midpoint is lower, with the reduction driven primarily by federal delays and reduced VDR contribution expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Veritone lowered full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $100 million-$150 million,” with the reduction driven primarily by “Department of War/Federal delays and reduced VDR contribution expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 revenue: $135.0M (Street) vs. **$130–145M co. guide**”; the preview said a cut to “**$105–120M**” was the honest outcome in its base scenario.

surprises.description: VDR conversion looked less immediate than the preview’s Q2 opportunity suggested: the call described $15 million of active pipeline as potentially closing in Q3/Q4, with only 2–3 months of delivery visibility, rather than establishing that the preview’s Q2 revenue bogey had been achieved. Management also lowered expected VDR contribution to the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: VDR had “an additional $15 million active pipeline potentially closing in Q3/Q4 2026,” but timing was outside the company’s control with “only 2-3 months of delivery visibility”; reduced VDR contribution expectations also contributed to the guidance reduction.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview set a bogey of “**$8M+ of recognized VDR revenue**” and said “~$20M of active pipeline” could close in Q2.

surprises.description: Cost reductions were progressing much more slowly than the preview’s end-of-Q2 target: the company had implemented about 11% of its cost structure in annualized savings, while the preview expected a 30% consolidated opex cut by the end of Q2. Management now targets 30% total savings by early 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company had implemented “approximately $11.3 million in annualized cost savings (about 11% of its cost structure),” targeting $15–20 million by fiscal year-end and “up to 30% total savings by early 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “~30% consolidated opex cut targeted for end of Q2” and cited Q2 opex below $34 million as the bogey.

surprises.description: The profitability timeline moved later: management now targets non-GAAP breakeven as early as the first half of 2027, rather than the preview’s expectation of operating profitability as early as Q4 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management targets “breakeven non-GAAP profitability as early as the first half of 2027,” shifting the profitability timeline from earlier expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the cost-cut plan “underpins the ‘operating profitability as early as Q4 2026’ claim.”

surprises.description: The restructuring carried a specific one-time severance and transition charge that the preview did not anticipate: 62 employees, about 14% of the workforce, were eliminated and the charge was $4.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 restructuring eliminated 62 full-time employees, roughly 14% of the workforce,” contributing to “a $4.5 million one-time severance and transition charge.”

surprises.description: Debt reduction and lower carry costs were a positive development not reflected in the preview’s focus on the roughly $45.6 million of near-term converts: total debt was down about $85 million from a year earlier, reducing annualized carry costs by more than $13 million. The call facts do not, however, describe a separate solution to the November maturity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total debt was reduced to approximately $45 million” from “about $130 million a year earlier,” an “$85 million improvement” and “over $13 million in reduced annualized carry costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “$45.6M of 1.75% converts maturing **November 15, 2026**” and asked for a refinancing or exchange plan.

in_line: Cash and restricted cash was $12.7 million, within the preview’s base-case cash range of $8–14 million, though below its stated greater-than-$20-million relief threshold.

surprises.description: Q2 sales of $41.3 million exceeded the preview’s $34–37 million estimate and its $38 million bull-case threshold. The preview cautioned that published consensus was stale, but the result also came in well above its own bottom-up forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales surged 244% year-over-year to $41.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate: $34–37M”; the bull scenario projected “$38M+.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $3.0 million, above the preview’s $0.5–1.5 million base estimate and above its bull-case threshold of $2.5 million. It reached the low end of the quarterly pace the preview said was needed to support the full-year guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA jumped to $3.0 million in Q2 2026 from just $0.1 million a year earlier,” reflecting acquired-business contributions and early synergy realization.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “$0.5–1.5M” in its base case and said “EBITDA ≥$2.5M” in the bull case; it also said the full-year guide required “~$3.0–4.4M per quarter” across Q2–Q4.

surprises.description: Management reaffirmed the entire $138–148 million sales and $8–12 million adjusted EBITDA ranges rather than narrowing EBITDA toward the low end. The CFO also said she would be personally disappointed if revenue finished below the guidance midpoint, a more confident stance than the preview’s expectation of a low-end outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reaffirmed full-year 2026 guidance of $138 million to $148 million in net sales and $8 million to $12 million in adjusted EBITDA”; the CFO said she “would be personally disappointed if full-year revenue lands below the midpoint of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected revenue guidance to be “Reaffirm at low end” and projected to “Narrow toward $8M” for adjusted EBITDA.

surprises.description: The preview expected low-to-mid-30s gross margins in the second half, with commodity relief and tariff refunds as potential support. Management instead described low-30s as the appropriate go-forward range, indicating that a meaningful margin recovery should not be assumed even though Q2’s 30.3% was within the preview’s estimated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management flagged low-30s% as the appropriate go-forward gross margin range,” reflecting the confirmed lower profitability of Terrasoul.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had guided to “low-to-mid 30s in H2 on commodity relief and tariff refunds,” and estimated Q2 gross margin at “30–33%.”

surprises.description: GAAP net loss was substantially worse than the preview’s EPS range, despite the strong adjusted EBITDA result. The reported loss included sizeable business-combination and integration costs and intangible amortization.
