surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net loss widened to $1.8 million (-$0.25 per share) from $0.4 million (-$0.03) a year ago,” driven by “$3.5 million of business combination/integration costs and $1.1 million of intangible amortization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave a GAAP EPS estimate of “-$0.05 to +$0.02” and cited consensus of “-$0.033.”

surprises.description: The Walmart launch was in more than 1,000 stores, but essentially all of its revenue contribution is expected in Q3 and Q4. That pushes the sales impact later than the preview’s expectation that the new distribution would start showing up in the current results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company launched 5 coffee and creamer SKUs into more than 1,000 Walmart stores nationwide, with essentially all revenue impact expected in Q3 and Q4 rather than Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Walmart distribution “should start showing up” and included the new Walmart/Target distribution in its discussion of the expected second-half step-up.

surprises.description: Management reported early synergy realization from the acquisitions, a positive development against the preview’s expectation that operational integration and production shifts would occur later.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EBITDA growth reflected “early synergy realization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said production shifting to Terrasoul’s facility was expected “later in 2026 or beyond,” and that “any pull-forward is a genuine positive.”

in_line: Q2 gross margin of 30.3% was within the preview’s 30–33% estimate, though near its lower end.
The CFO’s departure at the end of August was already disclosed in the preview; the call facts do not indicate a new change to that transition.

surprises.description: Revenue was $191.3 million, about 3.2% below the $197.7 million consensus and down 14% year over year, a steeper decline than the preview’s expected 11.1% decline. The result also missed the preview’s expected slight sequential increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue was $191.3 million, down 14% year-over-year on a pro forma basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 FY2026 consensus $197.70M … Implied Δ −11.1% YoY, +0.3% QoQ.”

surprises.description: Normalized EBITDA reached $21.9 million, well above the preview’s $17–19 million base case and the $15.6 million level it said the quarter needed to exceed. It also rose 8.4% year over year, rather than merely improving sequentially as management had committed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 normalized EBITDA reached $21.9 million, up 8.4% year-over-year and 40.6% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Normalized EBITDA (must be > $15.6M)” and the base case was “$17–19M”; management had committed to EBITDA “increasing in Q2.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached a record 24.9%, above the preview’s 23.3–24.0% base-case range and its 24.5% bull-case threshold. The fourth consecutive quarterly expansion itself was expected, but the margin level exceeded those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded for the fourth consecutive quarter to a record 24.9%, up 290 basis points year-over-year and 140 basis points sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “23.3–24.0%” and its bull case was “24.5%+”; it also asked whether gross margin would achieve a “4th straight expansion.”

surprises.description: New ACV bookings rose to $36 million, beating the preview’s $32 million bull-case marker and reversing the prior quarter’s 3.7% year-over-year decline. Total contract value also increased to $121.3 million from Q1’s $108.1 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New ACV bookings reached $36 million, up 57% year-over-year and 32.1% sequentially, while total contract value closed at $121.3 million, up 51.6% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch new ACV “vs. the ~$27–30M trailing average,” noted Q1 new ACV was “$27.3M (−3.7%),” and set “new ACV >$32M” as a bull-case marker.

surprises.description: Technology revenue grew 9.8% year over year and its adjusted gross margin expanded to 64.2%, sharply better than the preview’s concern that the segment’s 26.4% Q1 revenue decline might continue. This also materially strengthens the segment’s performance relative to the preview’s discussion of it as a possible divestiture candidate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The technology segment grew revenue 9.8% year-over-year to $24.5 million with adjusted gross margin expanding 690 basis points to 64.2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Technology had “Q1: $18.7M, −26.4%, 52.4% GM” and warned that “a −26% decline there undercuts” the separate-asset thesis.

surprises.description: Applied Workflow Automation revenue fell 16.7%, a steeper decline than its 12.6% Q1 decline and beyond the preview’s 14% decline marker for its bear case. That indicates greater weakness in the segment the preview identified as the main source of revenue declines.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The applied workflow automation segment revenue fell 16.7% to $166.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited AWA’s “Q1: $178.4M, −12.6%” and defined the bear case as an “AWA decline steepens past −14%.”

surprises.description: Management raised its annualized operational-efficiency target to $65–75 million from $55–60 million and projected about $35 million of benefit during 2026. The higher target was an improvement beyond the cost-savings program the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its targeted annualized operational efficiency range to $65-75 million (up from $55-60 million), with an expected in-year 2026 benefit of approximately $35 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a “$55–60M annualized target” and said roughly half was implemented but “not yet visible in the P&L.”

surprises.description: The strategic-alternatives process advanced to hiring a financial advisor. The preview wanted evidence that the process was active, including bankers being named, but reported no news since the May announcement.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “has engaged a financial advisor for its previously announced strategic alternatives process.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the market wanted “evidence of a live process — bankers named, a signed LOI, or a disposal of the Technology segment,” and noted “No timeline given, no news since.”

surprises.description: The reported sales pipeline was $2.5 billion, up 17.2% year over year. The preview focused on bookings but did not discuss or set an expectation for pipeline size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The total sales pipeline stood at $2.5 billion as of June 30th, a 17.2% increase year-over-year.”

surprises.description: Management highlighted revenue per employee rising to about $89,000 from $82,000 last quarter, with a projection near $100,000 by year-end. The preview anticipated cost savings beginning to show in the P&L but did not forecast this productivity measure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue per employee grew to approximately $89,000 from $82,000 last quarter and is projected to approach $100,000 by year-end.”

in_line: Management’s expectation of a second-half 2026 revenue inflection was consistent with the preview’s expectation that growth would resume in H2 2026.

The projected approximate 20% workforce reduction by year-end 2026 was consistent with the preview’s discussion of a 20% headcount reduction and its concern about whether that target would slip into 2027.

surprises.description: AirJoule raised full-year 2026 cash-spend guidance to $27–28 million from $25 million, above the preview’s expectation that spending would track the roughly $25 million guide. Management said the added spending is for accelerated JV commercialization and deployments, tempering the negative cash-spend surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 cash spend guidance was raised slightly to $27-28 million (from $25 million), with the incremental spend directed toward accelerated JV commercialization and deployments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “burn in line with $25M FY guide”

surprises.description: AirJoule disclosed a Core DH dehumidifier product aimed at an estimated 1.2 million installed conventional desiccant-wheel systems, with a targeted 2027 product timeline. The preview focused on the Core AWG launch and did not anticipate this additional product opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Core DH dehumidifier product targets an estimated 1.2 million installed base of conventional desiccant wheel systems, focusing on facilities operating at 30%-50% relative humidity, with a targeted 2027 product timeline.”

surprises.description: The first full-scale Prime system is already commissioned and running 24/7, and is tracking toward its target of up to 2,000 liters per day. The preview looked for confirmation of the European deployment timing but did not anticipate this operating-performance update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The first full-scale Prime system, commissioned in Newark in May and running 24/7, is tracking toward its target of up to 2,000 liters per day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AirJoule Prime European deployment ... — timing confirmation.”

surprises.description: AirJoule said it is preparing for contract manufacturing targeted for 2027 and exploring partners to reduce its internal CapEx needs. The preview highlighted cash and commercialization milestones but did not anticipate this manufacturing approach.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is advancing contract manufacturing preparations targeting 2027 ... and is exploring partners to reduce internal CapEx needs.”

in_line: Combined cash was $43 million with no debt, within the preview’s estimate of roughly $40–43 million and above its $40 million watch threshold; management also said liquidity supports operations, the JV, and planned deployments into 2028.
Quarterly net operating expenses of $4.1 million were within the preview’s $4.0–4.5 million estimate for parent net opex.

The company expected only modest paid deployment revenue in 2026, with more meaningful revenue beginning in 2027, consistent with the preview’s expectation of little Q2 revenue and its pre-commercial outlook.
The two Kubota Core systems are to be deployed starting later this quarter, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Kubota units would deploy in Q3.
The Prime system is scheduled to ship to Europe this quarter, providing the deployment-timing confirmation the preview was watching for.

surprises.description: The preview estimated about $9.5 million of cash at June 30 and treated less than 12 months of runway as the base case. Acurx reported $10.7 million and said it funds the PATHFINDER trial and operations for at least one year.
surprises.fact_evidence: Acurx ended Q2 2026 with $10.7 million in cash, up from $7.6 million at year-end 2025, which management says funds the Pathfinder trial and operations for at least one year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate: ... cash at 6/30 **≈ $9.5M**”; the preview also said Q1 had stated cash “would **not** fund 12 months.”

surprises.description: The preview expected PATHFINDER’s first enrollment by August 2026, but management now anticipates enrollment in Q4. The study is fully funded, which is reassuring, but it does not offset the delay against the stated timing expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The 20-patient open-label PATHFINDER trial is fully funded, with enrollment anticipated to begin in Q4 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had guided to “first enrollment **by August 2026**” and listed “rCDI pilot first-patient-in” as a key metric to confirm.

surprises.description: The preview noted the FDA’s general single-Phase-III pathway guidance, but the call added that the FDA is open to reviewing the totality of evidence at a pre-NDA meeting after ASPIRE and PATHFINDER, particularly if efficacy is robust. That is a more specific and encouraging indication of regulatory receptiveness than the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: The FDA indicated it is open to reviewing the totality of evidence at a pre-NDA meeting after completion of a single Phase III trial (Ibez ASPIRE) plus the PATHFINDER study, particularly if efficacy results are robust.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited the Aug. 3 FDA guidance PR on a “single-Phase-3 pathway” and flagged “pre-NDA meeting timing” as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: The preview modeled a net loss of $1.9–2.1 million. The reported $2.3 million loss was higher than that estimate, although the $0.53 per-share loss was better than the preview’s cited consensus of $0.57 per share.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 net loss widened to $2.3 million ($0.53 per diluted share) from a $0.2 million net loss in Q2 2025, reflecting higher R&D spending.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate: net loss **$1.9–2.1M**, EPS **≈ −$0.50**”; consensus Q2 FY26 EPS was **−$0.57**.

in_line: The pivotal ASPIRE trial still needs additional funding, and management has not secured a funding source. The preview described the trial as subject to funding and expected no named funding path in its base case.

surprises.description: FFAI reported Q2 revenue of $836,000, far below the preview’s roughly $1.7–2.2 million estimate and $1.79 million consensus. The result was less than half the preview’s bottom-up range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue reached $836,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 revenue ~ $1.79M”; the preview’s bottom-up estimate was “Total revenue ~ $1.7–2.2M.”

surprises.description: The reported cumulative shipments imply about 220 units shipped in Q2, using 242 units at quarter-end less 22 at the end of Q1. That is slightly above the preview’s estimate of roughly 195–210 Q2 units, even as revenue fell well short of its estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cumulative robot sales and shipments grew from 22 units in Q1 to 242 by end of Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EAI robot units shipped ~195–210.”

surprises.description: Q2 liabilities were about $278 million, above the preview’s expected roughly $200–215 million and also above its cited Q1 figure of $230 million. The stated goal of reducing liabilities below $100 million within three to four quarters was retained, but the Q2 level was less favorable than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total liabilities declined about $61 million to roughly $278 million,” with management targeting “under $100 million within the next three to four quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “liabilities ~$200–215M”; the preview cited “$230M at Q1’26” and the “<$100M four-quarter goal.”

surprises.description: The call facts report $70 million in institutional commitments, including $25 million in convertible notes, while the preview’s cash estimate already counted $45 million in institutional financing. The additional financing is helpful, but $42.5 million was classified as restricted cash, and the provided facts do not give a June 30 cash balance or runway.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured $70 million in cumulative new institutional commitments during Q2, including $45 million in secured notes and $25 million in convertible notes, though $42.5 million was classified as restricted cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Cash (30 Jun) ~$10–25M” based partly on “$45M institutional,” and said “If cash is under ~$15M with no committed facility, nothing else on the page matters.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted positive gross margin on robotics as an important test. The call facts instead report a $10.7 million consolidated gross loss; they do not provide a robotics-only gross margin or ecosystem revenue share, so the specific expected segment performance cannot be confirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross loss narrowed to $10.7 million from $26.9 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 delivered positive gross margin on robotics with ecosystem at 26% of revenue. Sustaining both is the entire ‘this is a real business, not a story’ argument.”

surprises.description: FFAI reported canceling about 5.36 million Class A warrants in July, bringing cumulative permanent cancellations to about 49.9 million units. The preview flagged dilution and share count as key concerns but did not anticipate these specific cancellations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Canceled approximately 5.36 million Class A warrants in July, bringing cumulative permanent warrant cancellations to about 49.9 million units since December 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called share count “the dilution meter” and highlighted the “$300M shelf and $90M ATM on file.”

surprises.description: Management described a production ramp for the EAI Data Factory and a top-customer order that could be worth over $400,000, developments not covered in the preview. The figures are targets and potential order value, rather than reported realized revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The EAI Data Factory targets monthly production of 2,100 qualified real-world data collection hours by end of August, scaling to 20,000 hours by December and 50,000 hours for the full year, with a top customer order potentially worth over $400,000.”

surprises.description: Management cited the FCC’s addition of foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots to its covered list as a structural tailwind for FFAI’s U.S.-based manufacturing strategy. This policy development was not anticipated in the preview, and the facts describe a potential strategic benefit rather than a quantified result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On July 28, 2026, the FCC added foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots to its covered list, which management frames as a structural tailwind for its U.S.-based ‘built-in USA’ three-phase manufacturing strategy.”

in_line: The company reaffirmed its 2,000-unit full-year target, as the preview’s base case expected that target to be reiterated.
The reported 394 cumulative units by the end of July matched the preview’s stated figure.
The $5-per-share convertible-note floor was retained, consistent with the preview’s focus on whether the announced floor would be honored.
The target of reducing liabilities below $100 million within three to four quarters was reiterated, as the preview expected.
The 1-for-150 reverse split and regained Nasdaq minimum-bid compliance were already reflected in the preview.

surprises.description: Revenue was about $3.6 million, above the preview's $3.38 million consensus estimate, a modest beat. The reported 12.8% year-over-year growth also exceeded the preview's implied 9% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 12.8% year-over-year to approximately $3.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $3.38M” and “Implied Y/Y | +9%.”

surprises.description: The company reported positive gross profit of roughly $0.6 million, whereas the preview's base case expected gross margin to remain negative. This was a clear reversal from the negative gross-profit quarters the preview highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit stayed essentially flat at roughly $0.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base case expected “gross margin still negative,” and noted that “two consecutive quarters” had negative gross margin.

surprises.description: Net loss was about $3.3 million, better than the preview's roughly $4.0 million consensus translation and below its base-case range of $4.0–$5.5 million. SG&A fell about $0.9 million, or 21.5%, which accompanied the lower loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss improved to approximately $3.3 million from about $4 million”; “SG&A expenses declined approximately $0.9 million or 21.5% to $3.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied net loss | ~$4.0M”; the base scenario projected a net loss of “$(4.0)–(5.5)M.”

surprises.description: The company secured $13.5 million of new financing for the Prairie Hills facility, taking total debt to about $14.2 million. The financing addresses the preview's question about how the facility would be funded, but the resulting debt is a substantial increase from the debt level it cited.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total debt rose to approximately $14.2 million from $1.9 million at year-end, reflecting $13.5 million of new financing for the Prairie Hills facility in Iowa.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 gross debt of “$2.699M” and asked “how a 400,000 sq ft Prairie Hills ... facility gets funded off a ~$2M cash balance.”

surprises.description: Despite reporting $10.7 million in cash and restricted cash, about $10 million was restricted for the Iowa facility, leaving only about $0.7 million available for operations. That is less usable cash than the preview's roughly $2 million baseline suggested and leaves operating liquidity very limited.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Of approximately $10.7 million in cash and restricted cash, about $10 million is restricted for the Iowa facility, leaving only about $0.7 million available for operations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 cash of “$1.952M” and described the Prairie Hills facility as needing funding “off a ~$2M cash balance.”

surprises.description: Management now expects co-manufacturer production to begin at the end of Q4 2026, later than the preview's anticipated September 2026 start. The delay pushes back the planned early production used to capture demand ahead of the Prairie Hills facility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management plans to begin production through a co-manufacturer at the end of Q4 2026 to capture demand early.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “confirmation that co-manufacturer production starts September 2026” as a milestone to watch.

surprises.description: Management said all capacity at the planned Prairie Hills RTD facility—over 100 million beverage units annually—is already presold across owned brands and private label. The preview discussed the facility's funding and timing but did not anticipate that its full capacity was already committed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Prairie Hills RTD facility is being built for over 100 million beverage units annually ... and 100% of capacity already presold across owned brands and private label.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow was positive for the first six months, at about $0.9 million, compared with $6.8 million used in the prior-year period. This extends the positive cash-flow result noted for Q1, although the preview had emphasized that Q1's positive cash flow was working-capital driven.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow was positive for a second consecutive quarter at approximately $0.9 million for the first six months, versus $6.8 million cash used in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q1 operating cash flow of “+$251K (first positive in 5 quarters, working-capital driven).”

in_line: Fresh-cut sales rose more than 42% year over year, consistent with the preview's warning that growth could remain cut-herb-led; the preview noted Q1 Cut Herbs growth of 45.9% and flagged the sales mix as a key debate.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $9 million, below the preview’s $12–14 million estimate and the $13.10 million consensus. That is a substantial miss against the expected quarter, despite first-half revenue growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $9 million, essentially flat versus $9.1 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates: revenue $12–14M”; consensus revenue was “$13.10M.”

surprises.description: Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash reached $48.9 million, far above the preview’s $22–26 million estimate. The increase was primarily funded by common stock issuance, so the stronger liquidity came with an equity-issuance tradeoff.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash rose to $48.9 million at June 30, 2026 from $17.1 million at year-end 2025, primarily due to proceeds from common stock issuance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates: ... quarter-end cash $22–26M”; the preview also said a print above “~$25M” would support the liquidity narrative.

surprises.description: The Shougang-LanzaTech stake was valued at roughly $110 million, versus the preview’s estimate of about $63 million based on the IPO valuation. The reported JV market capitalization was also higher than the preview’s roughly $750 million estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LanzaTech's 8.3% retained stake in the Shougang-LanzaTech JV ... was valued at roughly $110 million as of August 12, with the JV's market cap at approximately $1.32 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “roughly $63M of marketable securities” and cited an “~$750M implied market cap.”

surprises.description: LanzaTech reported that its China facility is undergoing ISCC-EU certification for recycled carbon fuels, with certified ethanol sales expected to begin supporting demand and pricing from Q4; it is also negotiating its first sale. The preview did not flag this certification-linked sales opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LanzaTech is undergoing the world's first ISCC-EU certification for recycled carbon fuels at its China facility,” which “could unlock certified ethanol sales expected to begin driving demand and pricing improvement starting in Q4”; the company is “in active negotiations for its first sale of ISCC-EU certified ethanol.”

surprises.description: The company reinstated full-year 2026 guidance after the preview said it had not issued explicit guidance. The $50–55 million revenue target implies a substantial second-half step-up from first-half revenue of $21 million, though there was no prior full-year target to compare against.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reinstated full-year 2026 guidance of $50-$55 million in revenue, an adjusted EBITDA loss of $22-$26 million, and operating expenses of $51-$55 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The company has not issued explicit FY2026 financial guidance, so there is no guidance line to beat or miss.”

surprises.description: Q2 R&D expense fell to $2 million, below the preview’s Q1 run-rate reference of $4 million. That indicates deeper R&D cost cutting rather than a Q2 re-acceleration, while the preview had also raised the possibility that such a low level could represent under-investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D expense was cut dramatically to $2 million in Q2 2026 from $14.9 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether “R&D at $4.0M ... is a sustainable run rate ... or an under-investment that shows up as a re-acceleration in Q2.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA loss was $7.6 million in Q2, within the preview’s expected range of $7–9 million.
Operating expenses of $11.7 million were consistent with the preview’s base-case expectation that the cost base would hold below $13 million.
LanzaJet’s approximate $650 million valuation was consistent with the preview’s cited $650 million pre-money valuation and its estimate of LanzaTech’s roughly 46% stake.

surprises.description: Gross margin was 67.2%, well below the preview’s roughly 72% expectation and even below its bear-case threshold of about 68%. Management attributed the decline to product and customer mix and higher costs, including tariffs on imported components.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined to 67.2% from 69.6% year-over-year, pressured by product/customer mix and increased costs including tariffs on imported components.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~72%”; the bear case cited “GM compresses below ~68%.”

surprises.description: Management forecast Q3 revenue of $2.3–$2.5 million, a sequential decline from Q2, citing non-recurring international orders and summer seasonality. The preview had not laid out a Q3 decline, although it noted that the full-year target required $4.8–$5.2 million in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q3 2026 revenue down sequentially to a range of $2.3 million to $2.5 million due to non-recurring international orders and seasonal summer slowness”; Q2 included “approximately $500,000 in international upside,” including a large dental order not expected to recur in Q3.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $9.8–10.2M guide requires $4.8–5.2M in 2H — roughly flat half-over-half.”

surprises.description: The company reaffirmed its $9.8–$10.2 million full-year revenue range rather than raising it after Q2 revenue had been pre-announced above the prior consensus. The preview treated a raise as plausible and said a bare reaffirmation after the revenue beat would read as soft.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $9.8 million to $10.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A guidance raise is plausible given the Q2 upside; a mere reaffirm after a 12% revenue beat would read as soft.”

surprises.description: Medical segment growth was 231% year over year, below the preview’s roughly 300% expectation. Management also cautioned that CompuFlo is still scaling from a small base.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Medical segment (CompuFlo) grew 231% versus Q2 2025, though management stressed it is still scaling from a small base.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Medical segment | ~$0.4M implied (+300% YoY).”

surprises.description: Management reported $325 Medicare reimbursement payments under Novitas and First Coast fee schedules across three regions and 13 states. This provided a specific reimbursement amount and coverage footprint, though the call facts do not give paid-claim counts or average dollars per claim, which the preview identified as the useful proof point.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CompuFlo has secured $325 Medicare reimbursement payments under Novitas and First Coast fee schedules covering 3 regions and 13 states, representing roughly 30% to 35% of the population.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “paid-claim count (not submitted), average paid amount per claim” and said “Paid claims with disclosed dollar amounts is the metric that converts this from story to model.”

surprises.description: Despite the preview’s concern about near-term financing risk, management said it was not currently planning to raise additional capital. The reported $2.1 million cash balance was within the preview’s estimated $2.0–$2.5 million range, so the positive difference is the stated lack of a current fundraising plan, not a cash-balance beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company holds $2.1 million in cash, $3.7 million in working capital, and $466,000 in convertible debt, and stated it is not currently planning to raise additional capital following its $2.51 million April private placement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a repeat going-concern flag with “sub-$2M cash makes another dilutive raise near-certain” and described the balance-sheet risk as skewing negative.

in_line: Q2 revenue was $2.8 million and first-half revenue was $5.0 million, both already disclosed before the release; the preview explicitly said the Q2 print was “not a revenue event.”
Cash was $2.1 million, within the preview’s estimated $2.0–$2.5 million range. The provided facts do not report whether the going-concern language changed.
The Red One Medical agreement and Q4 2026 target for first orders were already flagged in the preview; the reported access to federal healthcare markets is consistent with that discussion.
Six-month operating expenses were down 20% (about $1.4 million) year over year, consistent with the preview’s focus on continued cost discipline rather than the feared expense re-acceleration.

surprises.description: The preview described Project Permian as an 80 MW gas-turbine project paired with post-combustion capture, with capture above 90%. Management instead said near-term capital will go to unabated gas generation and that capture is only a possible later-phase add-on; the initial Permian phase will have no post-combustion capture.
surprises.fact_evidence: NET Power announced a major strategic pivot, redirecting near-term capital toward unabated natural gas power generation while retaining carbon capture as an optional later-phase add-on. Project Permian's initial phase will not deploy post-combustion carbon capture.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Project Permian Phase 1 was described as conventional Siemens A35 gas turbines paired with Entropy's amine-based post-combustion capture; the preview cited a capture rate of >90%.

surprises.description: The preview treated a signed offtake agreement or binding term sheet as the key expected proof point, and said anything short of one would disappoint. Management confirmed there is no signed offtake yet and only expects to share more within the next couple of months.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management emphasized it has no signed offtake agreement yet but expects to share more within the next couple of months.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything short of an executed or term-sheeted agreement is a disappointment at this point in the calendar”; the preview also noted an unpublished whisper of “signed or term-sheeted by the Q2 call.”

surprises.description: Project Permian was expected to start at 80 MW and scale to 800 MW on the site. Management now describes a data-center-oriented, behind-the-meter redesign with capacity of about 1 to 1.5 GW across phases, a substantially larger potential deployment.
surprises.fact_evidence: Project Permian is being redesigned for colocated data center demand with capacity for approximately 1 to 1.5 gigawatts across multiple phases.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Project Permian Phase 1 rescoped to 80 MW”; “scalable to 800 MW (10 units) on the same site.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 cash and investments at $250–275 million and cited about $3.6 million of debt at quarter-end Q1. NET Power reported approximately $310 million and no debt, better than those balance-sheet estimates, although the cash total was below Q1's $319 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended Q2 2026 with approximately $310 million in cash, cash equivalents and investments and no debt.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash & investments (est.): ~$250–275M”; “Balance sheet: $319M cash & investments at 3/31/26, ~$3.6M total debt.”

surprises.description: The preview laid out a $125–175 million NET Power equity check for the expected 80 MW project, alongside project debt and Entropy equity. Management now says completing Permian will require additional project-level financing, partner capital, or new equity, leaving a funding need beyond the reported cash balance without a stated funding plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management acknowledged that completing Project Permian will require additional project-level financing, partner capital, or new equity.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “NET Power equity check” of $125M–$175M, with the balance funded by project debt and Entropy equity, and highlighted a catalyst of explaining how the check gets funded “without an equity raise.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the Entropy joint development agreement to be finalized in Q2, with exclusive U.S. rights and possible project equity participation. Instead, the relationship is being restructured and capture is reserved for possible later phases, with no near-term CCS capital commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Entropy carbon capture relationship is being restructured into a revised framework for potential deployment only in later phases, with no near-term capital commitment for CCS.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the Entropy JDA was “Guided to finalize in Q2” and would grant NET Power exclusive U.S. power-generation rights through 2032, with Entropy able to take up to 49% project equity.

surprises.description: The preview described Siemens/RPS turbine packages as contracted for the 80 MW phase. Management now says it is working with a potential customer to secure another 120 MW of gas-power equipment, which could bring first-phase secured capacity to nearly 200 MW—though the additional equipment is not yet secured.
surprises.fact_evidence: NET Power is working with a potential customer to secure an additional 120 megawatts of gas power equipment; combined with already-secured turbines, this would bring total secured capacity to nearly 200 megawatts for the first phase.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Equipment contracted | $77M Siemens/RPS turbine packages” for the 80 MW Phase 1.

surprises.description: The preview's project description centered on turbine generation with capture and an early-2029 commercial operation date; it did not flag a 99.9% reliability design constraint. Management says a single large turbine cannot meet the target because of maintenance downtime, so the plan relies on a mix of batteries, reciprocating engines, and gas turbines on a 2028 timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is targeting three 9s (99.9%) reliability using a mix of battery storage, reciprocating engines, and gas turbines, on a 2028 timeline. A single large turbine unit cannot meet the target due to maintenance downtime.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described contracted Siemens A35 turbine packages for Phase 1 and cited a target COD of “Early 2029.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on a clean-power product and a target power price of at least $100/MWh, but did not anticipate that customers would not be asked to pay upfront for clean or carbon-capture power. Management says dropping capture from the initial phase frees capital to roughly double installed megawatts for behind-the-meter deployment, easing the customer's upfront burden while shifting the initial product away from the expected captured-power offering.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management confirmed it does not expect to require customers to pay for clean/carbon-capture power upfront, and said dropping post-combustion capture frees capital to roughly double installed megawatts for behind-the-meter deployment.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “Target power price: ≥$100/MWh” and described Phase 1 as a gas-turbine project paired with post-combustion capture.

surprises.description: The preview discussed data-center demand and grid constraints as part of the market backdrop, but did not project how long shortages could last. Management now says the constrained-power environment may persist well into 2040 or beyond, with ERCOT queues backed up into the 2030s, supporting a longer-lived demand opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management estimates the power shortage/grid-constraint environment could persist from the early 2030s at the earliest to 2040 and beyond, with ERCOT queues now backed up into the 2030s.

surprises.description: Management projected that LightNava could exceed $500 million in peak U.S. annual sales by 2030, with another roughly $300 million of upside if the compounded/repackaged bevacizumab market is disrupted. The preview discussed the U.S. market opportunity but did not give a company sales forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LightNava could generate more than $500 million in peak U.S. annual sales by 2030,” assuming repackaged bevacizumab remains available; management estimated “roughly $300 million of additional upside” if that market is disrupted.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described an “$8.5B US retina TAM” but gave no LightNava peak-sales estimate.

surprises.description: The company supplied a first-year post-U.S.-launch revenue forecast of $50–75 million, including a 10–15% contribution from Europe, and described a sharply back-loaded launch ramp. The preview focused on quarterly revenue and launch details but did not provide a first-year sales or ramp forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management guided first 12-month post-U.S.-launch total net revenue of “$50–75 million,” with Europe contributing “about 10–15%”; about 10% of first-year revenue was expected in the first three months, rising to about 50% in the fourth quarter following launch.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the company had committed to availability “before year-end 2026” and asked for launch specifics; it gave no first-year revenue forecast.

surprises.description: LightNava’s NORS 2 result showed a substantially higher share of patients gaining at least 15 letters than ranibizumab. The preview did not discuss an efficacy comparison, so this was new positive clinical information.
surprises.fact_evidence: In NORS 2, “41.7% of LightNava-treated patients gained at least 15 letters at month 11 versus 23.1% for ranibizumab.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a WAC price below $500 per vial and said it was targeting competitiveness with biosimilars and other anti-VEGF therapies. The preview said pricing was undisclosed and highlighted the risk that the product would struggle against lower-cost alternatives, so the price target answers a key open question but does not establish competitiveness with compounded Avastin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The WAC price for LightNava is expected to fall below $500 per vial,” targeting competitiveness with biosimilars and other anti-VEGF therapies.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Not yet disclosed. This single variable determines whether the $8.5B US retina TAM … is addressable or theoretical”; the preview also said LightNava competes against “compounded Avastin at roughly $50–100 per dose.”

surprises.description: Management projected a substantial increase in quarterly SG&A as the launch approaches: roughly double current levels by the end of calendar 2026, with another approximately 10% increase in 2027. The preview anticipated launch hiring but did not forecast this scale of expense growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects quarterly SG&A to “roughly double from current levels by end of calendar 2026,” with a further “~10% increase in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked about “the size of the retina sales force being hired” and noted the company’s financing and cash-burn concerns, but gave no SG&A forecast.

surprises.description: LightNava was described as the only FDA-approved ophthalmic formulation of bevacizumab in the U.S. The preview already knew of the FDA approval, but did not state this distinctive market position.
surprises.fact_evidence: The FDA approved LightNava, “making it the only FDA-approved ophthalmic formulation of bevacizumab in the U.S.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview stated that the FDA “approved LYTENAVA … for wet AMD on July 24, 2026,” but did not mention that it was the only FDA-approved ophthalmic bevacizumab formulation.

surprises.description: The adjusted quarterly loss was narrower than the preview’s base-case range: $0.09 per share versus an expected adjusted loss of $0.14–$0.18 per share. This was a better result than the preview’s central expectation, though it was close to the preview’s bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q3 fiscal 2026 adjusted net loss was “$10.9 million ($0.09/share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “−$0.14 to −$0.18” adjusted EPS; its bull case was “−$0.10 or better.”

in_line: FDA approval for wet AMD was already known before the call: the preview said LightNava had been approved on July 24, 2026.
The June 30 cash figure and $55 million offering were broadly as previewed: it cited preliminary cash of $11.2 million and a $55 million offering expected to close on August 14.
The permanent J-code timing was consistent with the preview’s expectation that a permanent code would require a multi-quarter process; management anticipated one in April 2027.

surprises.description: The preview put Q2 gross revenue consensus at about $3.43 million, implying 14% year-over-year growth. Super League reported about $3 million and flat year over year; although the call characterized that as in line with analyst expectations, it was below the preview’s stated consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 gross revenue was approximately $3 million, essentially flat both year-over-year and sequentially, and in line with analyst expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross revenue | ~$3.43M (+14% YoY)”

surprises.description: The preview estimated quarter-end cash and securities of $7.3–$7.9 million. The reported $6.7 million was below that range, though above the preview’s $6.5 million level associated with especially concerning burn.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with approximately $6.7 million in cash and investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Estimated 6/30/26 cash + securities | ~$7.3M – $7.9M”; the preview also said “Anything below ~$6.5M” would imply re-accelerated burn.

surprises.description: The preview emphasized the possibility that the effective shelf and Aegis arrangements signaled an upcoming financing. Management instead said it did not anticipate needing to raise additional capital, a reassuring statement against that concern, though the facts do not say management directly reconciled the shelf or Aegis arrangements.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “stated it does not anticipate needing to raise additional capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the shelf and Aegis waiver “the strongest signal yet that a raise is being prepared” and said financing was the dominant risk.

surprises.description: The preview modeled gross margin at roughly 36–38% and warned that Misfits’ programmatic mix could pull it toward 32%. Instead, gross margin rose to 41%, above the preview’s modeled range and Q1’s 36%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to 41% from 36% in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | No published consensus (model ~36–38%)”; the preview also warned that margin could “fall back toward 32%.”

surprises.description: The preview said reaching Q4 adjusted EBITDA profitability would require a roughly $1.5 million-per-quarter swing and noted Q1’s 11% year-over-year cash-EBITDA improvement. The reported adjusted EBITDA loss improved about 20% year over year, a stronger improvement rate than that recent comparison suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss improved approximately 20% year-over-year to roughly $1.7 million, versus a loss of approximately $2.1 million in the prior year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 delivered an 11% YoY cash-EBITDA improvement”; reaching breakeven “requires roughly a $1.5M+/quarter swing.”

surprises.description: The preview cited pipeline per salesperson of $1.78 million as the Q1 starting point and highlighted pipeline conversion as important to the second-half revenue build. Pipeline per seller rose about 57% to $2.8 million by Q2 end, a substantial increase in this leading indicator.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Weighted pipeline per seller rose about 57% to approximately $2.8 million at the end of Q2, up from roughly $1.78 million at Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “pipeline per salesperson $1.78M” and said to watch “Operating KPIs and the 2H revenue build.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated Misfits’ partial-quarter contribution but warned that its lower-margin programmatic mix could create a margin problem. The call said the acquisition added no cost base and that headcount was below pre-acquisition levels, indicating cost absorption or savings not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Super League completed the May 2026 acquisition of Misfits Ads assets without increasing its cost base, with total headcount now below pre-acquisition levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Misfits was “programmatic” and “structurally lower gross margin,” and expected a partial-quarter contribution; it did not forecast that the acquisition would add no cost base or leave headcount below pre-acquisition levels.

surprises.description: The preview stressed the need for visible cost discipline and a path to breakeven, but did not anticipate the reported improvement in billable use of delivery capacity or management’s indication that roughly $5 million of GAAP OpEx was near the go-forward baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Billable client utilization of cost-of-goods team capacity increased approximately 30% relative to Q1,” and management said “GAAP OpEx of roughly $5 million is near its go-forward baseline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said breakeven required “either opex comes down hard or 2H revenue steps up materially” and called for visible opex control.

surprises.description: The preview did not flag the removal of preferred stock as a Q2 development. The company said it eliminated all preferred stock outstanding, further simplifying its capital structure after eliminating debt last year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company eliminated all preferred stock outstanding for the first time in several years, building on last year's debt elimination to simplify its capital structure.”

surprises.description: The preview discussed prior client wins and new commercial initiatives but did not anticipate the specific Q2 and Q3-to-date first-time client activity. The company reported six first-time clients, including Dodge for a Fortnite program, while retaining several named renewal clients.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company closed 6 first-time clients during Q2 and Q3-to-date, including Dodge as its inaugural partner for a Fortnite program, while retaining renewal clients such as USGA, Logitech, GoGo squeeZ, and Regal Cinemas.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed its target of achieving adjusted EBITDA profitability in Q4 2026, as the preview specifically highlighted reaffirmation of that target as a key expectation.

surprises.description: The preview expected roughly a $5.8 million non-cash loss on the Lucid stake and a GAAP net loss of $11–14 million. Instead, the stake was valued at $33 million using a $1.07 share price, and PAVmed reported a $6.6 million GAAP net loss before NCI and preferred dividends; the reported loss was substantially narrower than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PAVmed’s equity method investment” was valued at “$33 million based on Lucid’s $1.07 June 30 closing price, down from $1.15 at March 31.” GAAP net loss was “$6.6 million (before NCI and preferred dividends),” and non-cash fair value charges were “$3.1 million versus $10.8 million prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “31.3M × ($1.15 − $0.965) ≈ $5.8M non-cash equity-method loss in Q2” and “That alone should push GAAP net loss wider than Q1’s $7.0M, plausibly to $11–14M.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP loss per share was better than the preview’s estimated range, at $0.27 versus an expected loss of $0.35–$0.45 per share. The preview warned that a larger share count could mechanically reduce the per-share loss, so this does not by itself establish better operating performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net loss was $1.7 million, or $0.27 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP adj. EPS” estimate: “-$0.35 to -$0.45.” The preview also said a smaller per-share loss could result from “denominator arithmetic.”

surprises.description: Veris’s 510(k) submission target moved later than expected: the preview anticipated a late-2026 submission, while the call put the target in early 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Veris’ implantable physiologic monitor is targeting an early 2027 FDA 510(k) submission.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Veris was “targeting late-2026 510(k)” and the preview asked whether “late 2026” would survive the quarter.

surprises.description: Veris’s battery milestone was better than expected: battery life now exceeds the two-year target, and design freeze is expected this month, whereas the preview described battery optimization to the two-year target as a gating engineering item.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Battery life [is] now exceeding the two-year target and design freeze [is] expected this month.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Battery optimization (two-year life) is the gating engineering item.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a potentially less burdensome regulatory route for Port IO than the de novo pathway previously expected: it may qualify for 510(k), with early human results also reported as favorable. This was not a development identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Port IO may qualify for a faster, less capital-intensive 510(k) pathway rather than the previously expected de novo pathway,” following results showing “100% device patency and 90% completion across 10 patients.”

surprises.description: PAVmed disclosed an Octaris esophageal imaging program licensed from Duke, with USC clinical validation planned, a pipeline development the preview did not identify. Its potential is distant because commercialization remains several years away.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Octaris esophageal imaging platform, licensed with worldwide rights from Duke, expects IRB approval in October for USC clinical validation but remains several years from commercialization.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating expenses rose above the prior-quarter level and the four-quarter average, with the increase attributed to Veris implantable-device R&D. The preview highlighted the prior quarter’s elevated costs and specifically flagged the possibility of further opex creep.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP quarterly operating expenses rose to $6.1 million, about $200,000 above the prior quarter and $400,000 above the four-quarter average, reflecting increased Veris implantable device R&D.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged whether the widened loss was “the LUCD fair-value mark, not opex creep” and noted, “Q1 already ran $1.1M hot.”

in_line: Cash at June 30 was $3.8 million, within the preview’s estimated $3.5–5.5 million range, though near its low end.
The Ohio State registry retained the previewed target of enrolling 1,000 patients within one year; the call also said enrollment was accelerating.

surprises.description: The preview described more than a dozen licensing discussions but said there had been zero signed agreements; management now reports four signed agreements with Werfen, Sysmex, Revvity, and Hologic. That is a substantial step beyond discussion-stage pipeline activity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Volition now has four signed agreements with multibillion-dollar companies (Werfen, Sysmex, Revvity, Hologic)” and is “in discussions with over a dozen additional diagnostic/liquid biopsy firms and governments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Twelve months of ‘discussions’ with zero signed agreements is the pattern to test. One signed term sheet with a disclosed upfront would materially change the funding math.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses were $4.6 million, well below the preview's $5.5–6.0 million estimate. The reported 32% year-over-year reduction and 27% headcount cut indicate a larger expense reduction than the preview's base estimate anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses fell 32% year-over-year to $4.6 million,” including “a 27% headcount reduction versus 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26E (mine)” operating expenses: “$5.5–6.0M.”

surprises.description: The sepsis finger-prick prototype showed approximately 90% correlation with the automated assay, above the preview's reported correlation of approximately 0.85. Management also described potential use in point-of-care settings and low-income countries.
surprises.fact_evidence: The lateral flow prototype “demonstrated approximately 90% correlation with its CE-marked automated Nu.Q NETs assay,” potentially expanding the market into “point-of-care and low-income countries.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the Aug. 12 sepsis data as “r ≈ 0.85 vs automated Nu.Q NETs.”

surprises.description: Management gave no 2026 revenue guidance, citing lumpiness and difficulty predicting revenue; Discover Services generated no revenue in Q2 because of project timing. The preview modeled FY2026 revenue but did not anticipate this explicit lack of company outlook or a zero-revenue quarter for Discover Services.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “declined to provide 2026 revenue guidance, citing that revenue remains lumpy and difficult to predict, with Discover Services revenue at $0 in Q2 due to project timing.”

surprises.description: Management said a Mayo Clinic i10 analyzer placement is expected this quarter, adding a specific near-term placement opportunity that the preview did not identify.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company reported “a Mayo Clinic i10 analyzer placement expected this quarter.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was approximately $0.4 million, within the preview's $0.30–0.45 million estimate.
Quarter-end cash of approximately $2.8 million was within the preview's $2.3–3.2 million estimate.
The $7.3 million net loss was within the preview's $5.5–7.5 million expected range; the preview also identified derivative or warrant remeasurement as a potential swing factor.
The feline lymphoma publication was still pending and taking longer than hoped, consistent with the preview's warning that the milestone could remain under review or be delayed.
The French lung cancer reimbursement process remained on the preview's expected timeline: a formal submission is anticipated by Q3 2026, with potential clinical use in 2027.
The Capture-Seq market opportunity cited on the call was consistent with the preview's discussion of the approximately $23 billion MCED and $13 billion-plus MRD markets.

surprises.description: Gross margin was 33.9%, far below the preview’s 43.5% estimate. The company attributed the decline to lower manufacturing output, about $150,000 of scrap, and the Re-Tain cost shift; monthly production also fell from more than 450,000 units in Q1 to about 350,000 in Q2, rather than maintaining the output level the preview viewed as a margin tailwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin fell to 33.9% in Q2 2026 from 43.7% a year earlier, and declined 11.1 points sequentially, driven by 7.5 points from lower manufacturing output, 2.1 points from ~$150,000 of scrap, and 1.9 points from the Re-Tain cost shift.” Monthly production fell “from a record 450,000+ units in Q1 to about 350,000 units in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Estimate” for Q2 gross margin was 43.5%; the preview said “Below 42% is a problem” and described yield gains above 450K units/month as a tailwind.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.7 million, well above the preview’s $1.05–1.15 million estimate. The reported figure included the $2 million legal settlement, so it was not solely a reflection of underlying operating performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.7 million in Q2 2026 (up from $1.4 million) … including the $2 million settlement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adj. EBITDA” of “$1.05–1.15M.”

surprises.description: Reported EPS was $0.20, below the preview’s $0.26 conditional estimate if the settlement was booked, although above its $0.04 estimate excluding the settlement. Net income and first-half results were boosted by the $2 million settlement, which the preview had identified as an unresolved accounting question.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income was $1.8 million ($0.20 per share) … though both quarter and six-month results were boosted by a $2 million legal settlement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “EPS (GAAP, if settlement booked)” at “$0.26” and “EPS (ex-settlement)” at “$0.04”; it said the settlement’s accounting treatment was undetermined.

surprises.description: Commercial indicators showed stronger traction than the preview quantified: distributor out-the-door volume grew 28% year over year in Q2, and First Defense increased its share of animals treated from about 15% to 19%, with its share of producer spending rising from about 29% to 38%. The preview discussed product sales and Canadian demand but did not set expectations for these sell-through or market-share measures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Distributor out-the-door volume growth was 21% in Q1 and 28% in Q2 2026 year-over-year, averaging 24% for the first half.” First Defense’s treated-animal share rose “from ~15% in December 2025 to ~19% by June 2026,” and spending share rose “from ~29% to ~38%.”

surprises.description: The company described an approximately $8 million capacity investment, financed mostly with cash on hand, that is intended to more than triple capacity and shorten processing time. The preview discussed a $3.5 million first phase, a broader multi-year program, and possible equity dilution, but did not anticipate this total investment amount or specify cash as the primary funding source.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is investing “approximately $8 million” in freeze-drying and liquids processing “to more than triple current capacity,” with processing time reduced “from 2-3 months to under one month,” “financed mostly with cash on hand.” It ended Q2 with $8.9 million in cash and working capital of $16.6 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “$3.5M phase one plus phase two” as a multi-year capital program and called an equity raise a “live dilution risk.”

in_line: Q2 product sales were $7.2 million, up 11.5%, matching the July pre-announcement; first-half sales of $17.5 million, up 20.9%, were also already disclosed.

Domestic sales of $6.2 million, up 27.7%, and international sales of about $1 million, down 38.9%, matched the preview’s pre-announced figures. The explanation that the international decline mainly reflected Canada’s 2025 backorder-clearing orders was consistent with the preview’s expectation that the comparison was a restocking artifact.
The $2 million settlement was expected to land in Q2; the surprise was its effect on reported earnings relative to the preview’s conditional EPS estimate, not its timing.

surprises.description: The remaining unguaranteed SBA book was more heavily reserved and smaller than the preview’s roughly $159 million balance and its 18–20% coverage threshold for a clearing event. BayFirst reported 33% reserves on BOLT, 25% on FlashCap, and unguaranteed SBA 7(a) balances down to $142 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $60 million BOLT portfolio at a 33% reserve and the $29 million FlashCap portfolio at 25%, while total unguaranteed SBA 7(a) balances declined to $142 million from $159.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~$159M of unguaranteed SBA 7(a) remains”; the higher-risk Bolt and FlashCap paper was “reserved at ~13%,” and “If the $37.0M resolution pushes coverage to 18–20%, that reads as a genuine clearing event.”

surprises.description: Normalized NIM was 4.07%, well above the preview’s 3.25–3.45% estimate. Even reported NIM of 3.48% was slightly above that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Normalized net interest margin excluding one-time impacts was 4.07% versus the reported 3.48%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net interest margin” estimated at “3.25–3.45%.”

surprises.description: Core operating performance was much closer to break-even than the preview’s estimated $4–6 million pre-provision core loss. Excluding one-time items, the reported quarterly core operating loss was only about $200,000.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Core operating loss for the quarter was only about $200,000, roughly breakeven excluding all one-time items.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pre-provision core loss” estimated at “−$4 to −$6M.”

surprises.description: Tangible book value per share was $4.82, above the preview’s $3.50–$4.05 pro forma estimate, despite the quarter’s large charges and dilution from preferred-share conversion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tangible book value per share collapsed to $4.82 from a restated $14.22 at the end of Q1 2026, reflecting the asset resolution charges and dilution from converting preferred shares.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s tangible common equity walk estimated “Pro forma TBV/share” of “~$3.50–$4.05.”

surprises.description: The one-time charges exceeded the previously announced $40.1 million by $3.7 million. The net loss was nevertheless slightly less severe than the preview’s estimated range, at $32.7 million versus a forecast range starting at $33 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$43.8 million in one-time asset resolution and nonrecurring charges out of the $44 million pretax loss”; “net loss of $32.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pre-announced charges” of “−$40.1M”; estimated net loss of “−$33M to −$45M.”

surprises.description: BayFirst plans to open a South Tampa branch in September and return to 12 retail locations, an expansion detail not anticipated in the preview, which focused on branch closure and expense reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Plans to open a new South Tampa branch in September to return to 12 retail locations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked about the “go-forward expense base after the Sarasota branch closure and SBA wind-down.”

in_line: The $32.7 million net loss was within the preview’s estimated $33–$45 million loss range, and the preview had already warned that the headline loss would be dominated by the announced charges.
The reported total capital ratio of 12.77% was within the preview’s estimated 11–13% range for post-charge total risk-based capital, and restored the ratio above the 10% well-capitalized threshold.

Deposits fell $97 million in the quarter, close to the preview’s expectation of another decline similar to Q1’s $98 million. The preview also anticipated intentional runoff of high-rate promotional and brokered deposits.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case put June 30 unrestricted cash at about $1.0–1.8 million, with below $1.0 million flagged as a near-term financing concern. Xcel reported only about $400,000, well below that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended the quarter with only about $400,000 in unrestricted cash, roughly $12 million in debt, and about $12 million in stockholders' equity.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case anticipated “cash ~$1.0–1.8M”; the preview also said “Anything under ~$1.0M unrestricted” with burn still running would force near-term financing.

surprises.description: The preview’s own model expected $1.30 million of revenue, while Q2 revenue was $1.1 million. The result also fell well short of the $1.80 million consensus figure, which the preview cautioned was unreliable and likely too high.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 revenue declined to $1.1 million from $1.3 million a year earlier, primarily due to the divestiture of the Judith Ripka brand.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Xcel model was “Revenue $1.30M”; its consensus table showed “Revenue $1.80M,” while warning that the consensus was “low-quality” and appeared aggressive.

surprises.description: The preview said the Judith Ripka sale gain could leave GAAP results near breakeven or positive. Instead, Xcel reported a $2.5 million quarterly net loss, although that was narrower than the prior-year loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net loss for Q2 2026 was approximately $2.5 million (-$0.40 per share), compared with a $4 million loss in the prior-year quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “GAAP net income could print near breakeven or positive on the Ripka gain alone,” while cautioning that GAAP would be noisy.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a long-term target not included in the preview: each of Xcel’s eight existing brands is to average $7 million a year in royalty income by the end of 2030. This adds a specific portfolio-wide growth ambition, but the preview provided no comparable expectation to assess it against.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management targets each of its 8 existing brands generating an average of $7 million per year in royalty income by the end of 2030.

surprises.description: The preview focused on low cash and possible dilution but did not mention that most current interest is being paid in kind, with no cash payment due until 2027. That provides a near-term cash-flow cushion relative to the liquidity concern it emphasized.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cited a majority of current interest being paid in kind, with no cash payment until 2027.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called June 30 cash the “single most important line” and said cash below about $1.0 million could force near-term financing.

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA loss of about $480,000 was within the preview’s expected range of a $400,000–$700,000 loss and close to its $550,000 loss model.
The Judith Ripka sale closed at approximately 6x gross royalty income, matching the preview’s stated expectation of a sale at about 6x.
The fall launches and one launch deferred to 2027 broadly matched the preview’s expectations for fall 2026 launches and a 2027 launch.
The influencer-led portfolio’s following exceeding 46 million was consistent with the preview’s reference to 46 million followers and its 100 million target.

surprises.description: About 300,000 of the newly issued warrants had already been exercised within days of the financing. That was earlier than the preview expected, which said the warrants were unlikely to be exercised near-term while the stock was below the $4.06 strike.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly 300,000 of the newly issued 1.2 million warrants … have already been exercised in the days following the raise.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “With the stock at $3.05 those warrants are underwater, so they won't be exercised near-term.”

surprises.description: Management said the Central Bank of Jordan initiative could scale over the next two to three quarters to annual recurring revenue comparable to a South African bank customer generating over $1 million. The preview flagged the Jordan win but had no such potential scale or timing estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Central Bank of Jordan initiative was won sole-source in a competitive bid and could scale over the next two to three quarters toward ARR comparable to a South African bank customer generating over $1 million in ARR.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dollar values, timing, and whether any of these are in 2H guidance are the single most useful thing they can give.”

surprises.description: Service revenue was about $231,000, below the preview’s implied estimate of roughly $260,000, and fell 28% rather than the approximately 20% decline implied there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue dropped 28% to $231,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Services/maint. (implied) ~$0.26M” and “~−20%.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed that roughly half of new U.S. business and virtually all international business comes through channel partners, which receive 20–30% software discounts. The preview did not discuss this channel mix or discount structure, which adds a potential constraint on realized software economics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly half of new U.S. business and virtually all international business flows through channel partners (who receive 20-30% software discounts).”

surprises.description: Management flagged growing EMEA pipeline deals across government, defense, financial services, and education, a commercial pipeline update not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management flagged growing EMEA pipeline deals across government, defense, financial services, and education.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $1.92 million, about 31% below the roughly $2.8 million May guidance, with a large hardware order slipping into the second half; the preview had already identified the miss and hardware deferral.
The Q2 net loss and first-half loss were inconsistent with the preview’s cited profitability guidance; the preview had already flagged that shortfall.

License revenue growth, hardware revenue decline, and the 87% gross margin were already reported in the preview, including its warning that the margin was driven by favorable mix and could compress as hardware returns.
The warrant inducement, roughly $2.3–$2.4 million of net proceeds, and cash above $4.5 million were already described in the preview.
The reverse split, return to Nasdaq trading, and June 30 stockholders’ equity of $4.3 million were already noted in the preview.

surprises.description: Lantern reported a $7.1 million net loss, or $0.57 per share, far worse than the preview’s $3.2–$3.6 million estimated loss and $0.27 estimated loss per share. A $3.6 million warrant-related expense from the May offering drove the gap; the preview warned that warrant accounting could distort GAAP results, but not that the reported loss would be this large.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A $3.6 million warrant-related expense” drove net loss to “$7.1 million ($0.57/share)” versus $4.3 million ($0.40/share) a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Net loss $3.2M – $3.6M” and “EPS ... -$0.27”; it also cautioned that warrant-related movement could distort GAAP net loss “in either direction.”

surprises.description: Although cash of approximately $7.4 million landed within the preview’s range, management flagged additional funding as a top priority. That is less reassuring than the preview’s base-case expectation of reaffirming runway into mid-Q1 2027, though the call facts do not state a revised runway date.
surprises.fact_evidence: Cash and marketable securities were approximately “$7.4 million” at June 30, and management flagged “additional funding as a top priority.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected runway to be reaffirmed “into mid-Q1 2027”; it identified runway language as the dominant issue.

surprises.description: Lantern disclosed that Open Medicine AI is a 100%-owned separate entity that intends to raise its own capital and could eventually list separately, with Lantern potentially distributing shares to its holders. The preview had highlighted ownership and funding as unresolved, so this adds a clearer path to separate value, but no outside capital raise or cash proceeds for Lantern were reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: OMAI was established as a “separate, 100%-owned entity” that “intends to raise its own capital” and “eventually become a separately listed company”; Lantern may distribute shares to its holders.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Lantern’s “retained ownership percentage” and “whether OMAI has raised outside capital” had not been disclosed and were important.

surprises.description: Management introduced a sizeable new estimate for the AI opportunity: a $9–10+ billion market by 2030–2031 and potential standalone growth of Open Medicine’s AI tools to several hundred million dollars. The preview discussed AI commercialization but did not flag these quantified estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management estimated the AI-enabled drug discovery market could reach “$9–10+ billion by 2030–2031,” with Open Medicine’s tools potentially growing to “several hundred million dollars standalone.”

surprises.description: Lantern reported new regulatory progress for LP-184: clearance for a 39-patient bladder cancer trial in Denmark and an approximately 40-patient triple-negative breast cancer trial, plus a patient-selection patent notice of allowance. The preview anticipated LP-184 trial activity generally, but did not identify these specific clearances or the patent milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: LP-184 received “EMA clearance for a 39-patient” bladder cancer trial, “FDA clearance for a ~40-patient” triple-negative breast cancer trial, and “a notice of allowance” on a patient-selection patent.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that R&D spending might rise as “the pediatric CNS and LP-184 trials initiate.”

surprises.description: Lantern highlighted four potential priority review vouchers from its Starlight pediatric brain cancer program and cited recent voucher transfers of $150–200 million or more each. The preview did not identify this potential source of substantial non-dilutive value; the vouchers and their possible value remain conditional.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company said it holds “four potential priority review vouchers” via STAR-001 and noted recent transfers “for $150–200 million or more each.”

surprises.description: Management added claims about the clinical pipeline’s potential scale and development efficiency: over $15 billion in combined annual market potential, first-in-human trials in under three years, and roughly $2–3 million per program versus industry norms of five to ten years and $25–100 million. These quantified claims were not part of the preview’s expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management estimated “over $15 billion” in combined annual market potential and said the pipeline reached first-in-human trials “in under 3 years at roughly $2–3 million per program” versus “5–10 years and $25–100 million.”

in_line: June 30 cash and marketable securities of approximately $7.4 million were within the preview’s $6.5–$7.5 million estimate and close to its approximately $7.2 million central expectation.
R&D expense of $1.8 million was within the preview’s $1.6–$2.0 million estimate; the reported 25% year-over-year operating-expense reduction also matched its expectation of continued cost discipline.

The LP-300 update’s 8.9-month median PFS and 77% clinical benefit rate for L858R patients, along with the L858R-enriched, eight-cycle single-arm trial design, were consistent with the preview’s reported data and description of the amended protocol.

surprises.description: DTST reported a $1.2 million net loss attributable to common shareholders, much worse than the preview’s base-case EPS range of $(0.13)–$(0.18), which implies a substantially smaller loss. SG&A rose 33.2% to $1.5 million, above the preview’s $1.0–$1.2 million base case; the increase included a 99.1% jump in non-cash stock compensation and higher professional fees.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss attributable to common shareholders widened to $1.2 million from $732,000”; “SG&A expenses increased 33.2% to $1.5 million,” primarily due to a “99.1% ($328,000) jump in non-cash stock-based compensation” and a 26.2% rise in professional fees.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case forecast EPS of “$(0.13)–(0.18)” and SG&A of “$1.0–1.2M”; it said SG&A “stays ≥$1.4M on cash professional fees + SaiS spend” in the bear case.

surprises.description: Gross margin was 47%, below the preview’s expected 52–56% range, despite gross profit increasing. Management attributed the margin expansion versus the prior year to favorable mix and operating leverage, but the reported margin still fell short of the preview’s Q2 expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit rose 21.9% to $168,000, with gross margin expanding to 47% from 42.1%,” attributed to “favorable sales mix and operating leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin” base case: “52–56%.”
