surprises.description: Management described a more concrete and near-term acquisition process than the preview’s general discussion of acquisition risk: it had evaluated roughly 124 companies, screened over 15 reverse-merger proposals, aims to sign a non-binding LOI within 45–60 days, and targets closing an acquisition by the end of Q4 2026 or Q1 2027. The plan is tempered by stated capital constraints, unrealistic target valuations, and proposed cash-plus-earn-out structures.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management had “evaluated roughly 124 companies and screened over 15 reverse-merger proposals”; the CEO set an objective to “sign a non-binding LOI within 45–60 days” and “close an acquisition by the end of Q4 2026 or in Q1 2027.” Acquisitions would use “upfront cash plus earn-outs,” with the CEO citing “capital constraints” and many targets’ “valuations as unrealistic.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview characterized acquisition as one alternative to funding SaiS and referred to a possible “transformative-acquisition tease that would consume the cash pile,” but did not flag a specific screening scale or LOI/closing timetable.

in_line: Continuing-operations revenue was $359,000, within the preview’s $355–375K base case; its 9.3% year-over-year growth was also within the preview’s expected 5–10% range.
Cash and marketable securities ended at approximately $9.3 million, within the preview’s $9.2–9.5M estimate.
The company had no long-term debt, consistent with the preview’s description of DTST as debt-free.

surprises.description: Star Equity announced an unanticipated agreement to acquire Hart-Hanks for about $30 million, funded half in cash and half in preferred stock, with no common shares issued or external capital required. Management expects $10 million of cost synergies and a combined business with about $400 million in revenue and $30 million in adjusted EBITDA once those synergies are realized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Star Equity announced a merger agreement to acquire Hart-Hanks for $5 per share (~$30 million on a fully diluted basis), funded half in cash and half in Star preferred stock, with no common shares issued and no external capital needed.” Management targets “$10 million in cost synergies” and expects “combined pro forma revenue of ~$400 million and adjusted EBITDA of ~$30 million once synergies are realized.”

surprises.description: Building Solutions earnings came in well below the preview’s estimate: adjusted EBITDA was $0.5 million versus $1.2 million expected. A large project that the preview expected to land in Q2 instead shifts into Q3, alongside market softness.
surprises.fact_evidence: Building Solutions reported “revenue of $14.6 million,” “gross profit of $3.2 million,” and “adjusted EBITDA of $0.5 million,” hurt by “market softness and a large project whose revenue shifts to Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Building Solutions Q2 revenue / adjusted EBITDA at “15.0 / 1.2” and said management had indicated “delayed projects would close in Q2.”

surprises.description: Building Solutions backlog improved from the preview’s $8.0 million entry point, but remained below the level the preview said was needed to signal a strong rebuild; Q2 orders also fell short of the cited normal run rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Building solutions backlog rose to $10.6 million with Q2 orders of $17.3 million, still below the $20 million normal run rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “>$12M backlog and book-to-bill ≥1.0” and described backlog rebuilding as central to the 2H outlook.

surprises.description: Business Services’ gross profit did not show the conversion the preview was looking for: it declined even though revenue grew. However, adjusted EBITDA of $1.6 million exceeded the preview’s $1.0 million estimate, making the segment result mixed rather than a clean earnings miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: Business Services revenue “grew 2% to $36.4 million,” while “gross profit declined 4% to $17.8 million” and adjusted EBITDA was “$1.6 million,” with $1.5 million of growth investments versus $0.8 million a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Business Services revenue / adjusted EBITDA at “37.5 / 1.0” and said Q2 was when signed business “should convert to gross profit.”

surprises.description: Business Services new-logo wins were much weaker than the preview’s setup suggested: the preview highlighted unusually strong Q1 wins and expected signed business to begin converting, while reported year-to-date new-logo annual contract value was only $2.1 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New logo wins in business services were weak at just $2.1 million year-to-date annual contract value versus a much higher expectation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 new-business wins “significantly exceeded any 2025 quarterly level” and flagged Q2 as when “signed business should convert to gross profit.”

surprises.description: Cash fell below the preview’s $9 million downside marker, leaving less liquidity than the preview’s Q1 cash figure. The facts do not say whether the preferred-stock ATM was used.
surprises.fact_evidence: Star ended Q2 with “$8.9 million in cash (including $2.1 million restricted)” and working capital excluding cash of $21.5 million, down from $22.4 million at year-end.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 cash of “$10.3M (incl. $2.2M restricted)” and included “cash <$9M” in its bear-case conditions.

surprises.description: Hudson merger synergies reached about $3 million, above the original $2 million target and ahead of the preview’s $2.6 million annualized realized figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Hudson merger cost synergies reached approximately $3 million, exceeding the originally projected $2 million,” while corporate costs fell to $3.6 million for the first half from $5.1 million pro forma a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$2.6M annualized realized vs. $2.0M original target” and said a raise to “$3M+” would be a positive.

in_line: Energy Services was broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of a clean grower: revenue was $3.9 million versus the $3.9 million estimate, and adjusted EBITDA was $1.2 million versus about $1.1 million expected.
Star repurchased about $0.2 million of shares in Q2 and said it plans to continue buybacks, broadly matching the preview’s expectation that repurchases would continue with authorization remaining.

surprises.description: The preview pointed to an EPS loss of $0.11 per share, while TOMI reported a loss of $0.05 per share, a smaller loss and a beat of about $0.06 per share.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 net loss was approximately $382,000, or $0.05 per share.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS | $(0.11) — H.C. Wainwright … | $(0.05) | Beat by ~$0.06”

surprises.description: The preview’s July 9 framing implied a 70% gross margin, but TOMI reported 61.7%, an 8.3-point shortfall. The preview also noted the margin was down year over year, but the gap versus 70% was materially worse than that framing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to 61.7% from 50.3% in Q1 2026, though it remained below the 65.7% recorded in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | 70% implied by July 9 pre-announcement | 61.7% | Miss vs. pre-announced framing.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on the $6.2 million of booked or expected orders and the $8.6 million advanced-stage bucket, but did not cite a broader $35 million commercial pipeline. Management reported a pipeline of approximately $35 million alongside the booked-order support for the revenue guide; the pipeline is not the same as committed revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance of at least $12 million, supported by booked orders and expected completions exceeding $6.2 million and a broader commercial pipeline of approximately $35 million.”

surprises.description: The preview did not identify the merger-related costs in Q2. TOMI reported roughly $300,000 of elevated advisory, legal, and diligence expense tied to the pending Carbonium Core merger, which management expects to decline after closing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 operating expenses included roughly $300,000 in elevated advisory, legal, and diligence costs tied to the pending Carbonium Core merger, which management expects to decline once the deal closes.”

surprises.description: The preview did not state a baseline timeline for breakeven; it described positive operating income in the second half as a bull-case signal. Management now expects to reach breakeven comfortably by Q4 2026, providing a specific timing expectation for that improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating loss narrowed 78% year-over-year to approximately $244,000, and management stated it expects to reach breakeven comfortably by Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull-case signal was “explicit path to positive operating income in 2H”; it did not give a baseline breakeven forecast.

in_line: Q2 revenue was approximately $2.25 million, in line with the preview’s approximately $2.3 million expectation; the strong year-over-year growth itself was not a surprise.
TOMI reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of at least $12 million, as the preview expected.
The $2.6 million current sales backlog matched the preview’s cited post-quarter backlog figure.
Applicator sales of $355,000 versus $13,000 a year earlier matched the preview’s cited figures.
Cash of about $322,000 and working capital of $1.82 million were in line with the preview’s liquidity figures; continued ELOC reliance was also anticipated.

The $10 million minimum concurrent financing condition for the Carbonium Core merger remained under negotiation, consistent with the preview’s base case of financing in process without committed terms.

surprises.description: Barfresh reported a Q2 Adjusted EBITDA loss of about $1.2 million, far worse than the preview's estimate of a $0.2–0.3 million loss; net loss also widened to $1.9 million versus the preview's EPS estimate of -$0.05 to -$0.06. The annual outlook was more severe still: instead of the preview's estimated positive $1–2 million of FY26 Adjusted EBITDA, management guided to a $1–2 million loss, with the second half expected to range from a $500,000 loss to breakeven.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss doubled to approximately $1.2 million from $600,000” and “Net loss widened to $1.9 million from $880,000.” Management “cut full-year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance to negative $1 million to $2 million” and “now expects back-half Adjusted EBITDA of negative $500,000 to breakeven.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 Adjusted EBITDA of “-$0.25M” and GAAP EPS of “-$0.05 to -$0.06”; its FY26 estimate was “$1.0–2.0M” of Adjusted EBITDA.

surprises.description: Gross margin fell far below the preview's 22–24% estimate: Barfresh reported a gross loss and a -3.2% margin, rather than merely missing the preview's 20% pass/fail threshold. The loss was attributed to Arps startup costs and low productivity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross loss of $150,000 (negative 3.2% of revenue) versus a gross profit of $506,000 (31.1% margin) a year earlier,” driven by “startup costs and low productivity at the Arps facility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Gross margin” of “22–24%” and said “Anything below ~20% means no sequential progress.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue missed the operative company guide, not just the stale published consensus: revenue was $4.7 million, below the guide's $5.2–5.6 million range and the preview's $5.5 million estimate. The reported 190% year-over-year growth was therefore not enough to meet the expected quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 190% year-over-year to $4.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified the operative Q2 company guide as “$5.2–5.6M” and estimated “$5.5M”; it cautioned that the published $6.4–6.6M consensus was stale.

surprises.description: Management set FY26 revenue guidance at $23–26 million, below even the preview's expected trimmed range of $26–29 million. The preview had already expected a trim from the prior $28–32 million guide, but the reported range went further down.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was set at $23 million to $26 million,” lowered partly because of “removal of ice cream mix production and slower recovery from prior school-year supply issues.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's own estimate was “$26–29M”; its base case was a trim to “low end of $28-32M” or “$26-29M.”

surprises.description: Barfresh removed its higher-margin ice cream mix business from the Arps facility because the aging plant could not reliably run both product lines at once. The preview did not anticipate the company exiting this production while waiting for operations to stabilize.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Barfresh removed its higher-margin ice cream mix business from the Arps facility because aging infrastructure could not reliably run both product lines simultaneously,” with plans to resume it only “after production stabilizes.”

surprises.description: The legacy Barfresh segment grew 9% year over year, better than the preview's Q1-based implication that the business was flat to down. However, the call also said supply-constraint damage was still lingering and customer recovery had shifted into the 2026–2027 school year, limiting the near-term improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The legacy Barfresh frozen beverage and food segment grew only 9% year-over-year,” with lingering damage from supply constraints pushing customer recovery into the “2026-2027 school year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said implied Q1 core revenue was “~$2.6-2.7M vs. $2.9M in Q1'25 — i.e., the legacy business was flat-to-down,” while noting that Q2 “captures almost none” of the 2026–27 school-year rollout.

surprises.description: Liquidity appeared thinner than the preview's March snapshot suggested: cash and accounts receivable together were about $1.4 million at June 30, compared with $4.1 million of cash plus receivables cited at March 31. The preview had flagged liquidity as a key issue, but the reported balance was materially lower.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly $1.4 million of cash and accounts receivable and $2.2 million of inventory as of June 30, 2026,” following a “$7.5 million convertible note that paid off the Defiance property mortgage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview stated “Cash + AR was $4.1M at 3/31/26” and flagged liquidity and progress on refinancing as items to watch.

surprises.description: Construction costs for the Defiance facility had risen more than anticipated, a cost overrun the preview did not flag. Management said it would use a new mortgage and equipment financing rather than an equity raise; the preview had expected a facility remortgage, so the mortgage itself was not new, but the cost increase and equipment-financing need were.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Construction costs have risen more than anticipated, requiring a new mortgage and equipment financing rather than an equity raise.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified a “promised facility remortgage” and said to watch for “the promised facility remortgage”; it did not mention construction costs rising more than anticipated or equipment financing.

in_line: Defiance commissioning remained targeted for before the end of 2026, consistent with the preview's expectation that the facility would still be a Q4 project.
Arps contributed $3.2 million of Q2 revenue, broadly near the preview's cited roughly $2.9 million per-quarter Arps contribution.

surprises.description: The preview modeled Q2 revenue of $3.8 million, implying 47% year-over-year growth. Using reported first-half revenue of $7.6 million less Q1 revenue of $4.03 million, Q2 revenue was approximately $3.57 million—about 6% below the model and roughly 38% above the prior year.
surprises.fact_evidence: First half 2026 revenue reached $7.6 million; Q1 2026 revenue was $4.03 million (from the preview). These figures imply Q2 revenue of approximately $3.57 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue … MSGME Q2'26 … $3.8M (+47% YoY, −6% QoQ)”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $0.8 million, below the preview’s roughly $1.0 million estimate, even though first-half adjusted EBITDA more than doubled year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA for H1 2026 was $2.2 million, more than double the $1 million in the prior year period, though Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA fell to $0.8 million from $1.4 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA … MSGME Q2'26 … ~$1.0M”

surprises.description: RaceControl’s Q2 contribution appears short of the preview’s targets: subtracting the preview’s Q1 subscription revenue from the reported H1 total implies about $0.6 million in Q2, or roughly 17% of estimated Q2 revenue, below the preview’s 22% share target. Its $2.9 million ARR also equates to about $242,000 of monthly recurring revenue, just below the preview’s $250,000-plus target for June.
surprises.fact_evidence: “RaceControl subscription revenue grew ~349% year-over-year to approximately $1.4 million in H1 2026, now representing 18% of total revenue”; “RaceControl is running at approximately $2.9 million in annual recurring revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Look for: MRR >$250K exiting June, subscription share ≥22% of revenue.” The preview also reports Q1 RaceControl revenue of $0.8 million.

surprises.description: The preview expected Le Mans Ultimate engagement to be flat to slightly soft based on Steam concurrent-user trends, but management reported that April set a record for average daily active users. This points to stronger peak user activity than the preview’s engagement read suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “April marking the highest-ever month for average daily active users.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Steam concurrents corroborate a flat-to-slightly-soft quarter”; Q2 average concurrent users were estimated at about 3,243 versus 3,355 in Q1.

surprises.description: The company retired all Class B super-voting shares, giving every outstanding share equal voting rights. The preview discussed the Driven Lifestyle buyback and governance signals but did not anticipate this change in voting structure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased $3.7 million of Class A shares from Driven Lifestyle Group and retired all Class B super voting shares, giving all outstanding shares equal voting rights.”

in_line: Management said detailed roadmap plans for the new game title and long-term project would be disclosed on the Q3 call, consistent with the preview’s expectation that roadmap detail would be deferred until then.
Cash was $3.9 million at quarter-end, close to the preview’s $3.8 million post-buyback estimate; the preview also already noted the $1.2 million revolver draw and February 2028 maturity extension.

surprises.description: The preview modeled $0.45 million of net income and $0.04 diluted EPS, but CSPI reported an $846,000 net loss, or $0.09 per share. That was a substantial reversal from the expected return to profitability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company posted a Q3 net loss of $846,000 ($0.09 per share), widening from a net loss of $264,000 ($0.03 per share) in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net income … $0.45M”; “EPS (diluted) … $0.04.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $14.4 million, well below the preview’s $15.5 million estimate and down from $15.4 million a year earlier. The preview had identified $15.4 million as the key year-over-year threshold for keeping the full-year growth math on track.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 FY2026 revenue declined to $14.4 million from $15.4 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue … Q3 FY26 — my base est. $15.5M”; “Revenue ≥ $15.4M (the YoY comp) — the single cleanest pass/fail.”

surprises.description: Service revenue fell to $4.5 million versus the preview’s $5.3 million estimate, a much sharper shortfall than the preview’s roughly flat-services base case. The reported reason was vendor delivery delays.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue falling to $4.5 million from $5.3 million due to vendor delivery delays.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Service revenue … Q3 FY26 — my base est. $5.3M”; “<$5.0M = the recurring-revenue narrative is in trouble.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 30.1%, below the preview’s 32.0% estimate and its watchpoint for a recovery to 32% or better. Product gross margin improved sharply, but service gross margin fell year over year, so the overall recovery was weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Overall gross margin expanded more than 100 basis points to 30.1% of sales, driven by product gross margin rising to 20.7% from 15.7%, even as service gross margin dipped to 51.2% from 53.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin … Q3 FY26 — my base est. 32.0%”; “Gross margin ≥ 32% alongside revenue growth.”

surprises.description: A 65% year-over-year increase in Technology Solutions backlog indicates strong demand, but the accompanying delivery delays are a new obstacle to the preview’s expected second-half growth: vendor lead times have stretched beyond 200 days and management expects the constraint to persist for at least a year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Technology Solutions backlog is now 65% higher than a year ago because hardware vendor delivery times have stretched from a historical 30-60 days to over 200 days, a supply constraint management expects to persist for at least a year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said in May it is ‘on track to generate growth during the second half’”; matching FY25 requires “$30.7M” in H2 and growth requires “$31.5M+.”

surprises.description: CSPI reported two sizeable new managed-service wins—a six-year, seven-figure agreement with a professional sports team and a three-year food-distributor deal expected to generate mid-six-figure annual recurring revenue. The preview had described AZT Protect’s existing contract dollars as small and hoped for commercial proof, but did not anticipate these specific wins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed a 6-year, 7-figure managed service agreement with a nationally recognized professional sports team and a 3-year deal with a food distributor expected to generate mid-6-figure annual recurring revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The dollars are still small … this is a narrative/multiple driver, not a Q3 numbers driver.”

surprises.description: AZT Protect reported 100% renewals among customer sites reaching their one-year mark and no customer breaches to date, adding concrete retention and security-performance evidence beyond the preview’s focus on early commercial traction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AZT Protect achieved a 100% renewal rate on all customer sites reaching their one-year mark, and no AZT Protect customer has experienced a breach to date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AZT PROTECT commercial proof, not slideware”; the preview asked for land-and-expand orders, customer-base information, and an ARR-like disclosure.

surprises.description: AZT Protect’s enterprise opportunities may take 18–24 months to close, longer than the preview’s emphasis on near-term commercial proof suggests. One major opportunity has advanced to the final two vendors, while smaller wastewater deals can close in six weeks, making the sales outlook mixed rather than uniformly slow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Large enterprise AZT Protect deals carry 18-to-24-month sales cycles, with one major opportunity having narrowed from 15 competing products down to a final two, while smaller wastewater deals have closed in as little as 6 weeks.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AZT PROTECT commercial proof, not slideware”; the preview framed it as a narrative driver and asked for evidence of land-and-expand activity.

surprises.description: Cash ended at $24.7 million, up from the $23.1 million reported at March 31, rather than showing the further drawdown the preview warned could pressure the company’s cash position. However, about $8.3 million of financed receivables is longer-term, so part of the balance remains tied up beyond a year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $24.7 million in cash and cash equivalents, and financed receivables total about $8.3 million longer-term (over one year).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash fell from $26.3M (6/30/25) to $23.1M (3/31/26)”; “a further meaningful draw would tighten the valuation floor.”

surprises.description: The company incurred a couple hundred thousand dollars in costs from the U.K. pension buyout/sale, an expense not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Incurring a couple hundred thousand dollars in costs from the U.K. pension buyout/sale.”

in_line: CSPI declared a $0.03 per-share dividend, matching the preview’s expectation of a $0.03 declaration.

surprises.description: The preview expected total Q2 revenue of $2.7–3.0 million, including $0.2–0.5 million of advisory, platform, or other revenue. Revenue was $2.5 million and came entirely from staking, so the anticipated non-staking revenue did not appear in the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $2.5 million, entirely from staking.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue: $2.7–3.0M”; “Advisory / platform / other: $0.2–0.5M.”

surprises.description: Reported G&A was far above the preview’s $4.2–4.8 million estimate, reaching $11.1 million. The gap was largely a one-time $6.8 million severance charge related to the PoNS divestiture; management said G&A should normalize toward Q1 levels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 G&A expenses jumped to $11.1 million from $3.3 million a year earlier, including $6.8 million of nonrecurring severance from the PoNS divestiture, with management guiding G&A to normalize back toward Q1 levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “G&A: $4.2–4.8M”; the preview expected “PoNS exit + cost actions.”

surprises.description: The net loss was larger than the preview’s modeled range: $30.3 million versus an expected $20–22 million. The preview expected the smaller SOL decline to sharply reduce the loss; the reported result was still driven largely by non-cash digital-asset fair-value losses, alongside the unexpected severance expense.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss of $30.3 million ($0.38 per share) … driven largely by non-cash digital asset fair value losses.”

surprises.description: Average net staking yield fell to 6.14%, below the preview’s expectation that yield would hold around 6.9%. It still beat the network average, but by 46 basis points rather than the preview’s cited 90-basis-point Q1 advantage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average net staking yield was 6.14% APY in Q2 2026, outperforming the Solana network average of 5.68% by 46 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base … staking yield holds ~6.9%”; the preview described Q1’s “6.9% net vs a 6.0% system average — a genuine 90bp edge.”

surprises.description: The quarter-end SOL holding count was about 2.3 million, above the preview’s 2.071 million recent-10-Q base case. That resolves the preview’s flagged discrepancy toward the higher tracker and Q1-call figures, rather than the lower filing figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company held approximately 2.3 million SOL across all categories at quarter-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview used “2,071,127” SOL from the most recent 10-Q as its base case and flagged a discrepancy with “2.30–2.33M” tracker figures and the Q1-call remark of “2.37M.”

surprises.description: The company secured its first institutional third-party stake commitment of roughly 0.5 million SOL, with validator revenue expected to begin in Q3. The preview discussed potential advisory and platform contracts, but did not anticipate this specific institutional staking commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured its first institutional third-party stake commitment of roughly 0.5 million SOL, with initial validator revenue expected to be recognized in Q3 2026.”

surprises.description: The company completed a new $8 million strategic institutional raise led by Mirae Asset with Hashkey Capital. The preview described the prior $8 million Q1 raise as the last capital raise and focused on the risk of a below-NAV ATM, so this additional financing was not anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed an $8 million strategic institutional raise led by Mirae Asset with Hashkey Capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Last capital raise: $8M @ $2.60 (Q1 2026).”

surprises.description: The PoNS divestiture produced a $3.1 million gain, an additional favorable one-off beyond the preview’s expectation that the divestiture would be completed and bring cost savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “divested the cash-consuming PoNS medical device business for a $3.1 million gain.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the company “completed the divestiture of the PoNS neurostimulation device business during Q2 FY2026” and flagged the need to quantify its terms and cost savings.

surprises.description: The company acquired a Hong Kong regulated trust company for $2 million, a transaction not anticipated in the preview. It adds a new regulated business asset but also uses capital; the provided facts do not state its expected contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “acquired a Hong Kong regulated trust company for $2 million.”

surprises.description: SOL fell approximately 12% in Q2, somewhat more than the preview’s modeled 10.4% decline. This modestly worsened the treasury’s fair-value backdrop versus the preview’s assumed price move.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SOL's price declined approximately 12% during Q2, following a 33% drop in Q1, weighing on reported fair value but not cash or token holdings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled SOL moving from “$83.11 (3/31) → $74.45 (6/30),” describing Q2’s drawdown as “‑10.4%.”

in_line: Staking revenue was $2.5 million, within the preview’s $2.4–2.6 million estimate for staking rewards.
The PoNS business divestiture was completed in Q2, as the preview expected.
Year-to-date buybacks were approximately $5.9 million, broadly near the preview’s stated $5.0 million already disclosed; Q2 buybacks were $2.3 million.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case put Q2 gross margin at 20–28%, but Nuvve reported just 2.6%. Margins excluding grants were also negative at -14.5%, with the company citing a $1.2 million Troy project write-down, a higher mix of low-margin hardware, and elevated DC charger warranty costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margins collapsed to 2.6% in Q2 2026 from 26.1% a year ago,” hurt by “a $1.2 million write-down on the Troy project,” low-margin hardware sales, and warranty costs; excluding grants, product and service margins were “-14.5% versus +11.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin” estimates: Bear “<15%”; Base “20–28%”; Bull “>30%.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case expected $0.8–1.5 million of ending cash and $2.0–3.0 million of operating cash burn. Nuvve ended with only $0.5 million of cash (plus restricted cash) after using $3.6 million in operating activities, landing near the preview’s bear-case cash level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash fell to just $0.5 million as of June 30, 2026 (plus $0.3 million restricted), a $1.4 million sequential decline, with $3.6 million used in operating activities during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Ending cash estimates: Bear “<$0.5M”; Base “$0.8–1.5M.” Operating cash burn estimates: Base “$(2.0)–(3.0)M.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $1.23 million came in just below the preview’s $1.3–1.8 million base range. The reported growth came mainly from charging-station shipments and grants, rather than a clearly identified step-up from the Mino project discussed as a possible revenue swing factor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue rose 268% year-over-year to $1.23 million,” driven mainly by “higher product shipments of charging stations and increased grant revenues.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Revenue estimates: Bear “<$1.0M”; Base “$1.3–1.8M”; Bull “$2.5M+.” The preview also said whether the April Mino milestone would be recognized over time could make Q2 revenue “step up materially.”

surprises.description: Nuvve reported $5.3 million of backlog, up $0.9 million sequentially, despite the preview highlighting the earlier Fresno-related backlog decline and saying a quantified backlog would be a genuine positive. The increase is a modest positive indication of new business converting toward 2026 sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog grew to $5.3 million at June 30, 2026, up $0.9 million from $4.4 million at March 31, 2026, tied to new contracts expected to convert to sales in 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted the “$15.7M backlog decline (Fresno termination)” and said “A quantified backlog figure would be a genuine positive.”

surprises.description: Although the preview described a strategic pivot toward stationary BESS, nearly all reported megawatts under management were still EV chargers: only 0.2 MW came from stationary batteries versus 29.7 MW from chargers. That makes the reported capacity mix a mismatch with the pivot narrative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Megawatts under management rose 3.1% sequentially and 16.8% year-over-year to 29.9 MW,” but stationary batteries contributed “only 0.2 MW versus 29.7 MW from EV chargers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “the pivot from V2G hardware to stationary BESS aggregation in Europe and Japan” and said management had guided to “growth in megawatts under management.”

surprises.description: Nuvve was already delisted in the preview, which listed it on OTC Pink, but it now trades on OTCQB and management is targeting a return to a senior exchange within months. This is better-than-described progress on the listing-tier issue, though the senior-exchange return remains a target rather than a completed step.
surprises.fact_evidence: Nuvve “now trades on the OTCQB under symbol NVVE, with management targeting a return to a senior exchange within months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed the company as “OTC Markets — Pink Limited Information Tier” and said an upgrade to Pink Current or OTCQB “would modestly improve liquidity.”

surprises.description: The company raised $1.2 million through stock and warrant issuance during the quarter, whereas the preview said there had been no publicly announced financing since the June loan and treated a financing with the print as a possible bull-case development. The raise provided some funding but also involved equity issuance, and it did not prevent ending cash from falling to $0.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised $1.2 million through issuance of common and preferred stock and warrant exercises,” and took on $1.4 million in debt during the quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Nothing has been publicly announced since the June 12 term loan” and described “a new financing announced with the print” as the most likely bull catalyst.

surprises.description: Accrued expenses increased sharply during the quarter, an additional sign of balance-sheet pressure beyond the low cash balance emphasized in the preview. The preview identified negative working capital, but did not flag this specific sequential build in accrued expenses.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Accrued expenses jumped $2.8 million sequentially to $5.0 million, while accounts payable stood at $4.4 million.”

in_line: Megawatts under management increased, consistent with the preview’s note that management had guided to growth in this metric.

surprises.description: Sidus disclosed that it joined the Russell 3000, Russell 2000, and Russell Microcap Indexes in the June reconstitution. The preview did not anticipate this development; the company said it expands institutional investor eligibility and is expected to improve trading liquidity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sidus joined the Russell 3000, Russell 2000, and Russell Microcap Indexes in the June 2026 reconstitution,” expanding institutional investor eligibility and expected trading liquidity.

surprises.description: Sidus said full commercial availability of Fortis VPX is anticipated in early 2027, subject to integration and customer qualifications. The preview highlighted potential first commercial orders but did not provide this availability timeline, so the disclosure adds a later-dated commercialization milestone rather than evidence of an immediate launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full commercial availability of the Fortis VPX platform is anticipated in early 2027, subject to final integration and customer qualifications currently underway.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “first commercial orders for FeatherEdge / Orlaith / Fortis VPX” as a key issue, but gave no full-availability date.

surprises.description: First-half SG&A implies Q2 expense of about $5.1 million—$9.5 million for the first half less the preview's $4.42 million Q1 figure—slightly above the preview's $4.4–5.0 million Q2 estimate. Sidus attributed some of the increase to professional fees related to the CFO transition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A rose 9% to $9.5 million partly on higher professional fees tied to the CFO transition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's Q2 estimate was “SG&A $4.4–5.0M”; it listed Q1 2026 actual SG&A as “$4.42M.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of approximately $583,000 and its 54% year-over-year decline were within the preview's $0.45–0.60 million estimate and anticipated decline of 55%–65%.
The $4.8 million Q2 net loss was within the preview's $4.8–5.5 million estimate.
June 30 cash of $166.5 million was within the preview's estimated $165–175 million range; the preview also expected no term debt.
The 101.1 million period-end Class A shares were essentially in line with the preview's 101.2 million estimate.
Progress toward the next LizzieSat flight and the Fortis Maxima TRL-9 path was broadly in line with the preview's focus on the planned testing and qualification milestones.

surprises.description: The original CGuard delivery-system FDA approval slipped from the expected Q3 timing to Q4 2026. The preview identified a Q3 approval and U.S. restart as the key near-term milestone, so the delay pushes the restart later than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FDA approval timing for the original CGuard delivery system slipped from Q3 to Q4 as management adopted more conservative regulatory timeline assumptions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided to Q3 2026 approval and a Q3 U.S. re-entry using the original CGuard delivery system.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was far worse than the preview’s expectation of roughly breakeven to about 5%: InspireMD reported a negative 43.7% margin. The preview anticipated the recall credit and inventory impairment, but not a gross loss of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit was a loss of $0.8 million (negative 43.7% margin) … hurt by the credit and a $612,000 inventory impairment charge.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates: … GAAP gross margin ~5%”; the base case also expected “GAAP GM near zero.”

surprises.description: International revenue was $2.1 million, below the preview’s $2.3–2.6 million expectation and below its $2.2 million warning threshold, despite growing 21% year over year. The preview identified a result below $2.2 million as evidence of softer ex-U.S. demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International revenue grew approximately 21% year-over-year to $2.1 million, driven entirely by demand with immaterial FX impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Look for $2.3–2.6M”; “Anything below $2.2M means the recall headline is bleeding into ex-U.S. ordering behavior.”

surprises.description: Total revenue was $1.8 million, below the preview’s $2.54 million consensus and its $2.0 million estimate. However, the preview noted a lower $1.8–2.1 million whisper range and anticipated that the recall returns provision could suppress reported revenue, so the result was less surprising against that lower baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue was $1.8 million, essentially flat versus Q2 2025, as international growth offset the U.S. revenue impact of the voluntary recall.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026E Revenue $2.54M”; “My estimates: Revenue $2.0M”; the “buy-side whisper is materially lower than $2.54M — closer to $1.8–2.1M.”

surprises.description: Management announced a nearly 20% workforce reduction with about $9 million in annual savings, rather than merely the hiring pause the preview said to watch for. The savings come with a $900,000–$1.2 million Q3 charge, with the full run-rate benefit not expected until Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A workforce reduction of nearly 20% initiated in Q3 is expected to save approximately $9 million annually, with a $900,000-$1.2 million restructuring charge in Q3 and the full run-rate benefit visible in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said it would ‘pause’ headcount adds pending FDA clarity”; the preview said to watch for “OpEx below Q1’s $14.7M” as evidence of that pause.

surprises.description: Net loss was $14.3 million, worse than the preview’s $13.4 million estimate, and the $0.17 per-share loss was worse than its $0.155 estimate. But the per-share loss was better than the preview’s cited $0.183 consensus, making the earnings result mixed rather than a clear miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $14.3 million ($0.17 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates: … net loss $13.4M, LPS $(0.155)”; consensus EPS was “$(0.183).”

in_line: The $734,000 customer credit was close to the preview’s estimate of approximately $700,000 for customer returns.
The $612,000 inventory impairment was close to the preview’s approximately $650,000 estimate.
Quarter-end cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of $30.4 million were broadly in line with the preview’s ~$29–30 million expectation.
Prime 80 / TCAR approval was expected in H2 2026; management’s Q4 2026 target falls within that window.
The redesigned Prime 135 delivery system’s first-half 2027 U.S. reentry target is consistent with the preview’s H1 2027 framing.

surprises.description: DocGo widened its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA loss guidance to $17–$22 million, versus the prior $5–$10 million loss estimate the preview expected to hold. The company attributed the change to slower-than-expected cost cuts and lower first-half gross margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year adjusted EBITDA loss guidance to $17-$22 million, substantially wider than the prior $5-$10 million loss estimate, citing slower-than-expected cost cuts and lower gross margins in the first half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If Q2 adj. EBITDA is better than –$6M and the FY guide holds, the bridge is credible.” The base case also expected the “FY EBITDA guide [to be] maintained.”

surprises.description: The preview looked for positive EPS by Q3 and a credible H2 profitability bridge; management instead described reaching a positive adjusted EBITDA run rate only as DocGo exits the year, excluding Hicuity. That is a later and narrower profitability milestone than the preview highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expects to reach a positive adjusted EBITDA run rate as it exits the year, excluding any Hicuity contribution.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “reaffirmation (or not) of ‘positive EPS by Q3 2026’ and H2 adjusted EBITDA profitability.”

surprises.description: DocGo agreed to buy Hicuity Health, its largest acquisition to date, a deal not anticipated in the preview. Hicuity brings meaningful revenue and growth, but DocGo will assume debt and issue equity, making the announcement a mixed development for shareholders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Signed a definitive agreement to acquire St. Louis-based virtual care provider Hicuity Health, its largest acquisition to date,” with “approximately $65 million in trailing 12-month revenue and $4.5 million in adjusted EBITDA” and 10%–12% growth. DocGo will assume “~$52 million of existing” debt and issue equity equal to 2% of fully diluted shares, with a further 3.5% earnout possible.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Most likely outcome on this call remains ‘no update’” on strategic alternatives; the preview did not anticipate an acquisition.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was below the preview’s roughly $75–$77 million expectation, coming in at $73.4 million. The preview expected the migrant-program wind-down to be essentially lapped, while the reported total still fell year over year because of that wind-down.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue fell to $73.4 million from $80.4 million a year earlier due to migrant project wind-down.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case is an in-line-to-slightly-light revenue print (~$76M),” with consensus of $75.35 million and $75.57 million; the preview said “the migrant-program wind-down is essentially lapped.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA loss was slightly worse than the preview’s expected range: $6.3 million versus a buy-side range centered on $4–$6 million and a base case of $5–$6 million. The sequential improvement and cost reductions were in line with the expected cost-cutting story, but the result landed just below its anticipated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA loss improved nearly 40% sequentially to negative $6.3 million from negative $10.3 million,” alongside a corporate reduction in force that cut annual SG&A by approximately $4.5 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buy-side centers –$4M to –$6M”; the base case expected adjusted EBITDA “around –$5M” and a “sequential EBITDA improvement of ~$4–5M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin fell to 30.5%, rather than recovering above the 32% level the preview identified as the test of whether temporary labor and fuel pressures were easing. Management cited higher field labor wages, sharply higher fuel costs, and temporarily lower SteadyMD margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated adjusted gross margin declined to 30.5% from 31.6% year-over-year,” pressured by higher field labor wages, fuel at $4.27 per gallon versus $3.16, and temporarily lower SteadyMD margins from aggressive hiring.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A move back above 32% validates the ‘temporary’ characterization; a flat or down print undermines it.”

surprises.description: Reported organic revenue growth was about 5% after excluding migrant and SteadyMD contributions, well below the preview’s description of the core business compounding at roughly 20%–25%. The measures may not cover identical business components, but the reported growth figure was materially slower than that expectation suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding migrant and SteadyMD contributions, organic revenue grew about 5% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the core business as “compounding ~20–25%.”

surprises.description: Available cash was $25.2 million and total cash including restricted cash was $48.1 million, below the preview’s expected $50–$56 million ending liquidity range. The preview had highlighted cash erosion as a key risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total cash and equivalents including restricted cash fell to $48.1 million from $59.9 million quarter-over-quarter, with available cash dropping to $25.2 million from $35.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s “Base case ending liquidity” was “$50–56M.”

surprises.description: Perceptive Advisors committed up to $50 million of additional financing, including an initial $12.5 million tranche, and the term loan will replace DocGo’s existing asset-backed credit line. This was not anticipated in the preview and offers financing support while also adding debt financing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Perceptive Advisors committed up to $50 million of additional financing to DocGo in multiple tranches, with the first $12.5 million funded upon execution of a pre-closing management services agreement,” and “the term loan will replace DocGo’s existing asset-backed credit line.”

surprises.description: Management discussed a proposed CMS rule that could remove Medicare RPM reimbursement in 2027, but said only about 2,000 of its 55,000 monitored patients could be affected and that most are cardiac implantable-device patients not subject to the change. The regulatory issue was not flagged in the preview, and management described limited exposure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A proposed CMS rule could eliminate Medicare RPM reimbursement in 2027,” but “only about 2,000 patients face potential risk” while “the vast majority of its 55,000 monitored patients are cardiac implantable-device patients that are unaffected.”

in_line: FY2026 revenue guidance was narrowed to $305–$310 million, broadly in line with the preview’s $305.1 million consensus estimate.

Q2 adjusted EBITDA improved substantially sequentially, consistent with the preview’s expectation that cost reductions would begin to show up in Q2, even though the loss was slightly worse than its expected range.

surprises.description: The preview expected Phase 1 construction to have broken ground by the end of Q2 2026. Instead, the company said it had obtained the county permits and expects site grading to begin in the coming weeks, indicating the anticipated start had not yet occurred.
surprises.fact_evidence: “obtained its construction permits … and expects to begin site grading in the coming weeks”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guided to break ground by end of Q2 2026 — i.e., this quarter. Did it happen?”

surprises.description: The preview described the Macquarie facility’s $270 million as available, but the call said $240 million of it depends on securing a final lease. That makes most of the undrawn capacity conditional on a milestone that remains outstanding.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$270 million undrawn … though $240 million … is contingent on securing a final lease.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$20M of $290M funded, $270M available.”

surprises.description: Rather than only remaining in advanced lease negotiations, New Era gained the opportunity to negotiate the Phase 1 power purchase agreement in its own name, and management said it is substantially in final form. It is still pending approvals, so this is progress toward—but not confirmation of—a completed agreement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In early July, New Era gained the opportunity to negotiate the Phase 1 power purchase agreement in its own name” and “the contract is substantially in final form pending approvals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Lease still ‘advanced negotiations, no signature’”

surprises.description: The project’s contemplated combined gross capacity rose from about 650 MW to roughly 757 MW, principally because Phase 2 increased from about 450 MW to 550 MW. The preview had described the 450 MW Phase 2 and roughly 650 MW combined project.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Phase 2 capacity was increased from approximately 450 MW to 550 MW” and combined Phase 1 and Phase 2 capacity is “roughly 757 MW versus the ~650 MW previously contemplated.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Phase 1 = 200 MW; Phase 2 = +450 MW behind-the-meter.”

surprises.description: The preview expected cash above $60 million and noted more than $80 million as of April, but did not anticipate the quarter’s cash increase being driven largely by cash-paid warrant exercises. The $84.8 million ending balance is supportive of liquidity, while the warrant exercises are a financing source not flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ended Q2 2026 with $84.8 million in cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash, an increase from the prior period despite CAPEX and burn, driven largely by the exercise of $2-struck cash-paid warrants.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash >$60M” and “Cash >$80M as of April 30, 2026.”

surprises.description: Management said it had significantly expanded the leadership team and was positioning the company to pursue growth beyond TCDC. The preview discussed the new CEO, CFO and COO and identified some executive backgrounds, but did not flag this broader team expansion or beyond-TCDC growth push.
surprises.fact_evidence: “significantly expanded its leadership team with hires from Microsoft, AWS, TikTok, CoreWeave, Switch, and EdgeConneX, positioning the company to pursue growth beyond TCDC.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “new CEO Charlie Nelson … Ted Warner as President & CFO, Jose Rodriguez (ex-Microsoft/AWS/TikTok) as COO.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated a policy tailwind from the governor’s directive and the company’s behind-the-meter positioning. Management went further, claiming TCDC already meets the standards and has attracted interest from essentially every major potential tenant—stronger tenant-interest commentary than the preview identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “management claims TCDC already meets the standards and has attracted interest from essentially every major potential tenant.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Policy tailwind: company publicly backed Governor Abbott’s Aug 2026 directive tightening oversight … consistent with its behind-the-meter, non-grid-queue positioning.”

in_line: The company reported $84.8 million of cash, above the preview’s >$60 million threshold; the preview also noted cash above $80 million as of April.
The company reported $270 million undrawn on the Macquarie facility, matching the preview’s stated $270 million available, although the call clarified that most of it is conditional on a final lease.
The 54-acre corridor acquisition brought owned land to 492 acres, consistent with the preview’s stated expansion from 438 to 492 acres.
The Q4 2027 targeted initial power timeline falls within the preview’s broader 2H 2027 first-power target.

surprises.description: The preview expected a first-quarter revolver draw and a newly levered balance sheet, but Flexsteel ended fiscal 2026 debt-free while generating more than $47 million of free cash flow. It also had $16.7 million in cash after the share repurchase and dividend payments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “generated over $47 million in free cash flow”; “maintained a debt-free balance sheet with $16.7 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the April buyback was “funded with cash plus a first-ever revolver draw” and estimated “a ~$25–35M draw.”

surprises.description: Flexsteel is exiting Home Styles, a ready-to-assemble category that generated about $12 million of fiscal 2026 sales but had below-average gross margins. The preview did not anticipate the exit; excluding the category, the company says sales growth would have been stronger than reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: “exiting its Home Styles ready-to-assemble product category,” which “contributed roughly $12 million in fiscal 2026 sales at below-average gross profit margins”; excluding it, fiscal-year growth would have been “closer to 6.5%-7%” and Q4 growth “about 2.3%.”

surprises.description: Q4 GAAP operating margin was 14.2%, but that figure included a large, unanticipated benefit from tariff refunds; adjusted margin was 7.1%. The refund benefit therefore made the headline GAAP margin much stronger than the underlying result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 GAAP operating margin of 14.2% was inflated by a 780 basis point benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds,” while adjusted operating margin was 7.1%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q4 margin anchor was “op margin ‘similar to Q3’ (≈7.1%)” and it did not mention IEEPA tariff refunds.

surprises.description: For Q1 FY2027, Flexsteel guided to 1%-4% sales growth, whereas the preview identified a guide below flat as a key downside risk. That is a better sales outlook than the preview’s downside scenario, although the range still implies modest growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 guidance calls for net sales of $111 million to $115 million (1%-4% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “any revenue guide below flat” was a major risk and described a guide below flat as a potential source of a sharp drawdown.

surprises.description: Q4 sales slightly exceeded the company’s flat-sales guidance and the preview’s key $114.6 million comparison, rather than merely landing within the preview’s lower-consensus beat scenario. The beat was modest, and growth remained weak at 0.7%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 net sales were $115.4 million, up just 0.7% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited company guidance of “flat to prior year (≈$114.6M)” and called revenue of “≥ ~$113M” confirmation of guidance.

surprises.description: Despite average pricing rising about 10%-11% in Q4, unit volumes declined; growth was concentrated in health and wellness and strategic accounts. The preview discussed pricing as a possible way to offset inflation but did not flag this price-versus-volume pattern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average pricing rose approximately 10%-11% in Q4, with unit volume declines that did not fully offset the pricing gains, while health and wellness and strategic accounts posted volume growth.”

surprises.description: Fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS came in a little above the preview’s implied estimate, though the gap was small and the preview warned that headline EPS beats were a recurring pattern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “record adjusted EPS of $4.94.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base-case bridge implied “FY26: ~$458M revenue (+3.9%) and ~$4.82 diluted EPS.”

in_line: Fiscal 2026 sales of approximately $459 million, up 4%, were close to the preview’s implied estimate of approximately $458 million and 3.9% growth.
Q4 adjusted operating margin of 7.1% matched the preview’s expected margin of approximately 7.1%; the preview also anticipated pressure from rising freight and other costs.
The 25% dividend increase was in line with the preview, which noted that the dividend had already been raised 25% to about $0.20 per quarter.

surprises.description: StreamX reported its first revenue—$146,000 of gold lease income, including about $134,000 earned in the quarter—above the preview’s estimate of roughly $0–0.1 million. It was still well below the $0.4 million consensus figure, so the result is a modest positive against the preview’s operating estimate but a miss against consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “StreamX recognized its first-ever revenue of $146,000 in gold lease income in Q2 2026 (approximately $134,000 earned in the quarter).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “my estimate) ~$0.0–0.1M in Q2”; consensus revenue was “$0.4M.”

surprises.description: Operating costs and cash burn were much lower than the preview’s roughly $15 million per-quarter burn estimate: operating expenses fell 57.1% from Q1, Q2 burn was about $1.6 million per month, and management expects about $1.1 million per month in Q3. The resulting estimate of roughly 18 months of runway on immediately available funds is substantially longer than the preview’s roughly two-quarter runway.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses fell 57.1% ($20.4 million) versus Q1”; “Cash burn was ~$1.6 million per month in Q2, expected to drop to ~$1.1 million per month in Q3,” giving “roughly 18 months of runway on immediately available funds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$45.85M (3/31) → ~$30.6M currently ⇒ ~$15M/qtr burn, ~2 quarters left.”

surprises.description: The $41.8 million total-liquidity figure includes assets that are not immediately accessible: only about $19.5 million is available, with $5 million loaned to Wintermute, a locked-up MetaLayer investment, and $15.5 million in physical gold inventory. That makes the headline liquidity less usable than the preview’s focus on current cash suggested, even though the lower burn extends runway.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$41.8 million in total liquidity with no debt, but only ~$19.5 million is immediately available,” with $5 million loaned to Wintermute, a locked-up MetaLayer investment, and $15.5 million of physical gold inventory.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash & runway” was expected at “$28–32M”; the preview estimated “~$30.6M currently.”

surprises.description: The preview expected stock-based compensation below $10 million, but Q2 included $32.5 million. The reported loss also included about $12 million of non-cash interest and a $3.1 million debt-extinguishment loss, adding costs not anticipated in that estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed 69% to $14.6 million in Q2 from $46.7 million in Q1, though it included $32.5 million of non-cash stock-based compensation, ~$12 million of non-cash interest, and a $3.1 million loss on debt extinguishment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s SBC bar was “<$10M.”

surprises.description: Management pushed the silver product launch from Q3 2026 to 2027, rather than providing a near-term launch that could support the FY26 revenue ramp the preview highlighted. This removes the anticipated Q3 timing and delays the second-commodity opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “delayed the silver product launch from Q3 2026 to 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged the “2nd commodity launch date (silver)” as a key watch item and described the second product as a potential path to the FY26 revenue ramp.

surprises.description: Management repeatedly pointed to a first significant institutional GLDY allocation arriving in Q3 2026 as the key inflection point. The preview’s base case anticipated flat ounces and no hard guidance, so this gives a specific near-term catalyst, though the allocation had not yet arrived.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “repeatedly guided to the first significant institutional GLDY allocation arriving in Q3 2026 as the key inflection point.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “Ounces flat” and “no hard guidance”; its bull case required evidence that channels “convert to actual inflows.”

surprises.description: The company introduced GLDC, a permissionless, fee-free gold token backed one-to-one by yield-bearing GLDY, creating an additional potential revenue line that the preview did not identify. Management’s example of about $3.5 million annually per $100 million of GLDC is illustrative, not guidance, so the opportunity is not yet realized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is introducing GLDC, a permissionless, fee-free gold token backed one-to-one by yield-bearing GLDY,” and said a 3.5% reserve rate “could generate ~$3.5 million annually per $100 million of GLDC (illustrative, not guidance).”

surprises.description: Although the preview already expected little or no net AUM growth, the call disclosed that StreamX and exchangeable shares hold about 91% of GLDY, leaving only about 9%—roughly 280 ounces—in external ownership. That makes the existing AUM base much more dependent on company-funded seeding than the preview’s flat-ounce estimate alone conveyed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “StreamX (including exchangeable shares) holds about 91% of GLDY, meaning external ownership is only ~9% (about 280 ounces), as the company seeded the reserve with its own capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described GLDY at about 3,118 ounces and concluded “GLDY net inflows were approximately zero in Q2”; it did not estimate the external ownership share.

surprises.description: The call disclosed that material weaknesses in internal controls remained unremediated and that disclosure controls were not effective. The preview mentioned the auditor change to EisnerAmper as already announced, but did not flag these control deficiencies.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Material weaknesses in internal controls remained unremediated as of June 30 and disclosure controls were concluded not effective,” and the company switched auditors from CBiz to EisnerAmper.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview mentioned “EisnerAmper” among qualitative news already released, but did not state an expectation of unresolved material weaknesses or ineffective disclosure controls.

surprises.description: The board authorized a buyback of up to 10 million shares at no more than $2 per share, a new capital-allocation measure that could counter dilution concerns. No shares had yet been repurchased, so it was only an authorization rather than an executed reduction in share count.
surprises.fact_evidence: There was “a board-authorized buyback of up to 10 million shares (max $2/share) with no shares yet repurchased.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on dilution, warning that “Another raise near $1.00 is deeply dilutive,” and said “Silence = relief” on a new ATM or shelf takedown.

in_line: GLDY AUM in ounces was essentially flat: 3,111 ounces at quarter-end versus the preview’s calculated estimate of about 3,118 ounces and its expectation of approximately zero net inflows.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was expected to be about $4.71, but Home Depot reported $4.92, a $0.21 (about 4.5%) beat and 5.1% year-over-year growth versus the preview’s expected 0.6% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS was $4.92, up 5.1% from $4.68 a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS: $4.71 (range $4.71–4.73)” and the preview says the consensus implied “+0.6%” year-over-year growth.

surprises.description: The preview expected gross margin to fall about 60 basis points, but the quarter included a $685 million tariff refund that lifted gross margin by roughly 145 basis points. Underlying pressure excluding the refund was about 120 basis points, and management said the refund benefit would be fully offset by unplanned costs over the year, shifting pressure from Q2 into Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $730 million in IEEPA tariff refunds late in June, of which $685 million reduced Q2 cost of goods sold and boosted gross margin by roughly 145 basis points”; “Excluding the tariff refund, gross margin faced about 120 basis points of pressure”; management expects refunds “to be fully offset by unplanned cost pressures over the year, creating a Q2-to-Q3 timing shift.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “Gross margin ~32.8% (–60bp)” and said Q2 pressure was expected to continue, “but not quite to the degree” of Q1’s –75bp.

surprises.description: Sales came in at $47.9 billion versus the preview’s $47.5 billion consensus, a modest beat; year-over-year growth was 5.7% rather than the expected 4.9%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 sales rose 5.7% year-over-year to $47.9 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $47.5B (range $47.0–47.5B)” and “+4.9%” year-over-year.

surprises.description: Total comps were 1.7%, above the preview’s derived range of roughly 1.0%–1.5%, and management said both total and U.S. comps exceeded company expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total comp sales up 1.7% and U.S. comps up 1.3%, both exceeding company expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview derived comparable sales of “~+1.0% to +1.5%” and described the base case as “+1.0–1.5%.”

surprises.description: Comp transactions fell 1%, less than the preview’s expected 1.5% decline, improving on the weak transaction trend that the preview identified as a key risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comp average ticket rose 2.8% while comp transactions fell 1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s consensus table expected retail transactions down “–1.5%,” and it flagged a transaction result worse than Q1’s –1.3% as a concern.

surprises.description: Big-ticket transactions over $1,000 rose 2.4%, a notable improvement from the +0.8% reported in Q1 despite the preview’s concern about continued weakness in large discretionary projects.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Big-ticket transactions over $1,000 up 2.4% amid continued weakness in large discretionary projects.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified big-ticket transactions as “the cleanest read on discretionary project demand” and gave Q1’s result as “+0.8% in Q1.”

surprises.description: Comps strengthened month by month, and management said Q3 had started in line with Q2 demand trends, providing a firmer near-term demand signal than the preview’s base case of demand remaining relatively similar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comps accelerated through the quarter (total: May +1.2%, June +1.5%, July +2.3%), and management said Q3 has started consistent with Q2 demand trends.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “underlying demand relatively similar” and described ticket-led comps with transactions down 1% to 1.5%.

surprises.description: SRS had positive comps above Home Depot’s company average, with positive comps across all its verticals, reversing the slightly negative SRS comps noted in Q1 and addressing a key watch item in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SRS comped above the company average with positive comps across all verticals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q1 SRS comps as “slightly negative (roofing weak)” and flagged the “SRS/GMS organic trend” as a key metric to watch.

in_line: Home Depot reaffirmed its fiscal 2026 guidance, as the preview expected: flat-to-2% comp growth, 2.5%–4.5% total sales growth, about 33.1% gross margin, 12.4%–12.6% operating margin, and flat-to-4% EPS growth.
Comp average ticket rose 2.8%, essentially matching the preview’s 2.7% estimate.

surprises.description: Keysight reported Q3 revenue of $1.846 billion, above the preview’s $1.78–$1.82 billion whisper range and well above the $1.75 billion consensus. The result exceeded even the preview’s bull-case revenue range of $1.80–$1.84 billion at its midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue of $1.846 billion grew 36% reported (31% core), exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Applying even a normalized beat to $2.47 puts the buy-side bar at ~$2.60–$2.70 on EPS and $1.78–$1.82B on revenue”; the bull scenario forecast revenue of “$1.80–1.84B.”

surprises.description: Q3 EPS of $3.07 substantially topped the preview’s $2.60–$2.70 inferred buy-side bar, not just the $2.46–$2.48 consensus. It also exceeded the preview’s bull-case range of $2.70–$2.85.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Applying even a normalized beat to $2.47 puts the buy-side bar at ~$2.60–$2.70 on EPS”; the bull scenario forecast “$2.70–2.85.”

surprises.description: Orders reached $2.91 billion, far above the preview’s $1.9–$2.1 billion base range and even its bull case of more than $2.1 billion. Book-to-bill stayed above 1.1 for a second straight quarter, alongside an all-time-high sales pipeline and record monthly funnel intake.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 orders reached $2.91 billion, up 56% reported (52% core)”; “Book-to-bill has exceeded 1.1 for two straight quarters, with the sales pipeline at an all-time high and highest-ever monthly funnel intake reported last month.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said orders “Below ~$1.9B (book-to-bill <1.1x) breaks the acceleration story,” gave a base range of “$1.9–2.1B / ~1.1x,” and a bull case of “>$2.1B / >1.15x.”

surprises.description: Q4 guidance came in materially above the preview’s expected range: revenue of $1.930–$1.950 billion versus roughly $1.80–$1.86 billion, and EPS of $3.34–$3.40 versus roughly $2.70–$2.95. The EPS guide also cleared the preview’s bull-case threshold of $3.00.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 guidance calls for revenue of $1.930-1.950 billion … and EPS of $3.34-3.40.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected Q4 revenue of “~$1.78–1.86B and EPS of roughly $2.60–$2.95”; its base case was “Rev $1.80–1.86B, EPS $2.70–2.90,” and bull case EPS was “≥$3.00.”

surprises.description: Operating margin reached 33.2%, far above the preview’s roughly 28% implied blended margin and its concern that the manufacturing-test ramp might dilute incrementals. It also surpassed Keysight’s stated long-term target range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin expanded 820 basis points year-over-year to 33.2%, surpassing the long-term target range of 31%-32%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said segment consensus implied “~28%” blended operating margin and flagged whether the ramp would “start diluting incrementals”; it also noted the key risk of incrementals “below ~40%.”

surprises.description: Commercial Communications revenue was $1.06 billion, well above the preview’s $910 million estimate, with 56% growth versus an expected 41%. The business also crossed $1 billion for the first time, and wireline revenue surpassed wireless for the first time.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The commercial communications business posted its first-ever $1 billion quarter at $1.06 billion revenue (up 56%), with wireline revenue exceeding wireless for the first time.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Commercial Communications revenue of “$910M, +41%” and described the Q2 growth rate of “+40%” as the comp to beat.

surprises.description: Management raised the implied FY2026 revenue growth outlook to 32%, above the preview’s expectation of “high-20s%” growth. This is a stronger full-year outlook in addition to the unusually high Q4 guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 guidance was said to imply “full-year FY2026 revenue growth of 32%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had raised FY26 revenue growth to “high-20s%” and described the expected framework as “high-20s%.”

surprises.description: The acquisition integration was completed a quarter ahead of schedule, and management now expects 80%–90% of the $100 million in cost synergies to be realized on a run-rate basis exiting the fiscal year. The preview expected the synergy target and 80% realization by year-end, but did not anticipate the early completion or an additional roughly $50 million synergy contribution in FY2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Acquisition integration completed a quarter ahead of schedule, with 80%-90% of $100 million in cost synergies expected to be realized on a run-rate basis exiting the fiscal year, and ~$50 million incremental synergy contribution expected in FY2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected confirmation of “the $375M revenue and >$100M synergy targets” and noted “80% realized by year-end.”

surprises.description: Despite the record order book and strong pipeline, management said constrained component supply—not demand—will limit near-term revenue over the next two quarters. The preview emphasized the manufacturing ramp and strong demand but did not flag component availability as a near-term revenue constraint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects supply chain, not demand, to be the governor of near-term revenue over the next two quarters, particularly due to constrained incoming component parts.”

surprises.description: IRIDEX reported Q2 revenue of $12.6 million, below the preview’s $13.0–$13.4 million base case and both cited consensus estimates of $12.98 million and $13.59 million. The shortfall was material against the preview’s expected range, though it fell within the preview’s bear-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $12.6 million, down 7% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $13.59M”; “Revenue (alt.) $12.98M”; base case: “Revenue | $13.0–13.4M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 34.2%, essentially unchanged from 34.5% a year earlier, rather than recovering toward the preview’s 39–41% estimate or its stated threshold of at least 40%. That is a gap of roughly five to seven percentage points from the preview’s expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin was essentially flat at 34.2% versus 34.5% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin ~39–41% (my est.)”; “Gross margin ≥40%”; the base case expected “margin recovery vs. the 34.5% comp.”

surprises.description: The GAAP loss was worse than expected: IRIDEX lost $0.07 per share, versus consensus estimates of a $0.01–$0.02 loss and the preview’s base case of a $0.01 loss to breakeven. The net loss also widened year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $1.3 million ($0.07 per share) from $1.0 million ($0.06 per share).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA turned into a loss instead of the preview’s expected profit. The reported $0.4 million loss was about $0.9–$1.2 million below the preview’s $0.5–$0.8 million base-case estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA turned to a $0.4 million loss versus $21,000 income a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$0.5–0.8M (my est.)”; base case: “$0.5–0.8M.”

surprises.description: Retina revenue was $6.5 million, below the preview’s $7.2–$7.5 million base-case build. The preview expected retina to remain soft but improve sequentially; the reported year-over-year decline deepened to about 19%, although revenue did rise from Q1’s $5.8 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retina [revenue declined] from $8.0 million to $6.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base-case build: “retina $7.2–7.5M”; the base case also described “Retina still soft but improving sequentially.”

surprises.description: Glaucoma probe demand was stronger than the preview’s roughly 10% growth expectation: probe volume rose about 35%, and G6 family revenue grew 19% to $3.9 million. Management said underlying probe growth still exceeded 15% even after removing relocation-related pre-orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cyclo-G6 probe volume rose approximately 35% year-over-year to 17,700 units, and G6 product family revenue grew 19% to $3.9 million”; excluding pre-orders, “underlying glaucoma probe growth was still over 15%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “glaucoma +10%”; it said two consecutive quarters of double-digit probe growth would be “the strongest fundamental datapoint of the year.”

surprises.description: Cyclo-G6 system placements fell to 18, versus 35 in the year-ago quarter. The preview described placements as lumpy, but did not anticipate the reported order-timing issues in EMEA or competitive pressure on console placements in the GmbH business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cyclo-G6 system placements fell to 18 units versus 35 in the prior year, driven by order timing in EMEA and competitive pressure on console placements in the GmbH business.”

surprises.description: Management said relocation-related safety-stock buildup is expected to pressure cash through 2026, with the cash benefit reversing in 2027. That added a near-term cash-use headwind not identified in the preview’s discussion of cash-flow breakeven and liquidity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Headquarters relocation-related safety stock buildup is expected to pressure cash through 2026 before reversing as a tailwind in 2027.”
