surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had promised “positive operating cash flow for FY2026” and described Q2 cash that was “flat-to-up” as supporting the story.

in_line: FY2026 revenue guidance was reaffirmed at $51–$53 million, as the preview’s base case expected; the preview also noted that the guide excludes the Middle East.
Q2 cash was flat-to-up versus the preview’s expectation: cash ended at $4.7 million, up $0.1 million sequentially, and the company reported positive cash flow.
The annual adjusted operating-expense guide of $19–$19.5 million was consistent with the preview’s stated full-year guide.

The second-half outlook remained broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of soft-but-improving retina and continued double-digit glaucoma growth: management expected low-single-digit retina growth and low-double-digit glaucoma growth.

surprises.description: The preview put adjusted EPS consensus at $2.25–$2.35 and the buy-side bar above $2.40. Reported EPS was $4.11, including a $1.65 tariff-refund benefit; even excluding that benefit, EPS was about $2.46, above the buy-side bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 GAAP and adjusted EPS reached $4.11” including “a $1.65 benefit” from the tariff refund; “excluding refunds, EPS rose approximately 20%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (adj.)” consensus “$2.25–2.35”; the buy-side bar was “EPS above $2.40.”

surprises.description: The preview expected full-year operating margin to improve by 20 basis points or more. Management guided to an improvement of about 50 basis points excluding tariff refunds, a stronger stated increase than the preview’s 20-basis-point reference.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year operating margin rate, “excluding tariff refunds,” was guided to “about 0.5 percentage points above last year's adjusted rate of 4.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Standing guidance was “operating margin +20bps or more vs. 2025's 4.6% adjusted.”

surprises.description: The preview cited full-year net sales growth guidance of about 4%. Target raised that outlook to around 5%, a one-percentage-point increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year net sales growth guidance was raised to around 5%, one percentage point higher than the prior outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Standing FY2026 guidance” was “net sales growth ~4%.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a return to share repurchases. Target said it plans to resume buybacks in the second half after pausing them, alongside its dividend payments and move toward a 40% payout ratio.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to resume share repurchases in the back half of the year, having paused them,” and paid “$518 million in Q2 dividends” while “moving toward a 40% payout ratio.”

in_line: Underlying full-year EPS guidance was broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of a raise toward about $9 ex-tariffs: the headline range rose to $9.90–$10.90, but excluding the $1.65 tariff-refund benefit the midpoint increased by only $0.75.
SG&A remained a pressure point, as the preview anticipated: the rate was 21.6%, about 30 basis points above last year, despite being below the 21.9% rate cited for Q1.
Weakness in Apparel and Home was consistent with the preview’s warning about softness in those categories; management said their growth was only flattish and that it was not satisfied.

surprises.description: Mercury's Q4 bookings were far above the preview's already-raised bar for a strong quarter: bookings reached $660 million, rather than merely exceeding the prior $348 million record.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY26 bookings hit a record $660 million, up 93.1% year-over-year and nearly double the previous record, yielding a 2.28 book-to-bill ratio.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “management said Q4 bookings ‘have the potential to be the strongest of the year.’ That sets a bar of >$348M and a record.”

surprises.description: The FY27 revenue outlook was higher than the preview's $1.05 billion Street expectation: management said revenue would approach $1.1 billion, or nearly double-digit growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For FY27, management guided revenue approaching $1.1 billion (approaching double-digit growth).”

surprises.description: FY26 free cash flow was only $68 million, well below the preview's expectation that Q4 cash generation could bring the year roughly flat to up versus FY25's $119 million. Given $39.8 million of free cash flow for the first nine months, the full-year figure also implies a positive but much lighter Q4 contribution than the preview's $60–80 million scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$68 million of full-year free cash flow (down from $119 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 FCF ~$60–80M gets FY26 roughly flat-to-up.”

surprises.description: Management expects FY27 free cash flow conversion of only about 35%, materially below the 50% conversion target highlighted in the preview. It also anticipates an unusually large Q1 cash outflow because of early material receipts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 free cash flow conversion is expected to approach only 35%, below the 50% target, with Q1 anticipated to be a larger-than-normal cash outflow due to early material receipts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management's medium-term target is above-market growth, low-to-mid 20% adj. EBITDA margin, ~50% FCF conversion.”

surprises.description: Backlog was substantially stronger than the preview's latest cited levels: total backlog exceeded $1.9 billion and the next-12-month portion reached $1 billion, providing a record level of near-term conversion visibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record total backlog reached over $1.9 billion (up 38.4% year-over-year), with next 12-month backlog hitting a record $1 billion (up 23.3%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted the “12-month convertible slice (was $807M at Q2)” as more important than the total backlog, while citing Q3 total backlog of “~$1.6B.”

surprises.description: Sales diverged sharply by geography: domestic revenue, which accounts for most sales, grew organically, while international revenue fell because of a delivery slowdown at a contract manufacturer. Management expects that international issue to unwind over the next couple of quarters; the preview did not flag this regional split or delivery issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Domestic revenue, representing 85.8% of FY26 sales, grew 13% organically, while international sales declined roughly 15% due to a temporary contract-manufacturer delivery slowdown expected to unwind over the next couple of quarters.”

surprises.description: Mercury reported a new Palantir AI partnership as a potential source of upside, which was not mentioned in the preview. Management said the FY27 and FY28 outlook does not include any benefit from it, and no financial contribution was quantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 and FY28 outlooks exclude ... any benefit from the new Palantir AI partnership, framing these as upside opportunities.”

surprises.description: Net debt fell to $227 million after a $150 million payment against the revolving credit facility. The preview discussed possible appetite for tuck-in M&A but did not anticipate this specific debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt was reduced to $227 million (down 19.5% year-over-year), aided by a $150 million payment against the revolving credit facility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said SolderMask “suggests appetite for tuck-in M&A over buyback.”

in_line: Q4 adjusted EPS was $0.37 versus the preview's approximately $0.38 consensus estimate.
Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin was 16.7%, within the preview's estimated 16.5–17.5% range; the preview had already identified margin pressure as the quarter's soft spot.
Management's long-term low-double-digit organic growth target is broadly consistent with the preview's expectation that investors wanted a credible path to low-double-digit growth.

Management continued to exclude potential munitions, space, and missile-defense framework benefits from its outlook; the preview had already noted that these opportunities were excluded and that quantification was uncertain.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $6.7 million, well below even the lower $15.5 million consensus estimate and below the preview’s $8–20 million base case. The preview’s functional test was whether the back-half ramp was visibly starting; this small print does not show that.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue of only $6.7 million”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $15.5M” (alternative: “$45.0M”); base case: “$8–20M.”

surprises.description: Management kept the $200 million FY26 target, as expected, but said Q3 would bring only a modest bump and a “very significant” Q4 jump depends on launching the exchanges in mid-September after Fiserv integration. That makes the already steep second-half ramp especially dependent on a specific launch and leaves little evidence of an early ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “reiterated full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $200 million”; it expects “a modest revenue bump in Q3 and a ‘very significant’ jump in Q4,” contingent on mid-September exchange launches after Fiserv integration.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The guide was “≥$200M” and “explicitly back-half weighted”; the preview asked whether the “back-half ramp [was] visibly starting.”

surprises.description: The signed tokenization pipeline was reported at $2.5 billion of intended issuance and $213 million of fees, versus the preview’s roughly $800 million of contracts carrying about $90 million in fees. The larger pipeline is a positive change in stated potential, though none of those fees had appeared in reported revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Signed tokenization contracts total $2.5 billion in intended token issuance, representing $213 million in fees”; “none has yet appeared in reported revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “~$800M of signed tokenization contracts carrying ~$90M of fees.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a roughly $200 million expected liquidity stack, including BTC sales, Vivisol/Silex receivables and a $120 million non-dilutive Silex revenue-share deal. The preview highlighted that funding sources were unclear; however, these are expected sources to fund the Available Network rollout, not confirmation that the cash has already been collected or that CyberCatch is funded.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cited “roughly $200 million in expected 2026 liquidity” from BTC sales, Vivisol/Silex receivables, “a $120 million non-dilutive Silex rev-share deal,” and the morning’s financing, to fund the Available network rollout.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the “funding source is undisclosed” for CyberCatch and noted management’s claim of “>$250M of available funding,” while questioning how that reconciled with the reported cash balance.

surprises.description: The company said it had raised $60 million in Q2, primarily for its initial payment into the Available Networks/Quest structure. The preview focused on the cash shortfall and funding of the all-cash CyberCatch deal, so this financing is new, but its stated use does not resolve that specific question.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Datavault raised $60 million in Q2, primarily to fund its initial payment into the Available Networks/Quest token structure.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the funding of the “$94.5M all-cash acquisition” its “single most important disclosure” and said the funding source was undisclosed.

surprises.description: Management expected approximately 1 billion shares outstanding by quarter-end, up from the preview’s 855.6 million, with another 45–50 million shares to be issued for BankWise and the morning’s financing. That is more dilution than the preview’s starting share count implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects to end the quarter with approximately 1 billion shares outstanding”; “an additional 45-50 million shares” are to be issued for BankWise and the morning’s financing.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported “Shares out: 855.6M” and flagged that every financing headline is “read as dilution first.”

surprises.description: Management said the company can remain listed through February under an equity exemption without a reverse split, and that it is refusing to execute one. This is a clearer and more favorable near-term path than the preview’s expectation that an extension required a formal reverse-split commitment or that a split might be needed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An equity exemption [allows it] to remain listed through February without a reverse split, which it is refusing to execute.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a second extension “requires … a formal commitment to a reverse split,” and identified the Aug. 24 deadline as a key unresolved issue.

surprises.description: CyberCatch had been listed among the Q3 objectives to close, but management now described the $94 million all-cash deal as closing in Q4. That pushes the expected close later than the preview’s milestone checklist implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: CyberCatch is “a $94 million all-cash deal closing in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q3 objectives list included “closing CyberCatch and NYIAX.”

surprises.description: Management claimed Project Questrel could generate more than $10 billion in revenue at completion under a 50-50 split, and said $1 billion in coins had already been minted with some sold to a Fortune 500 company. The preview anticipated a $1 billion phase-one deployment and initial offering, but did not flag this larger revenue claim or reported sale.
surprises.fact_evidence: Project Questrel “could generate over $10 billion in revenue at completion, with a 50-50 revenue split”; management said it had “already minted $1 billion in coins and sold some to a Fortune 500 company.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed a “$1B Project Qestrel phase-one deployment and initial token offering this quarter.”

surprises.description: The company described a share-swap chain in which 50 million Datavault shares for Vivisol shares became $150 million of Phoenix Asia Holdings stock, intended to enhance the balance sheet and support Genius Act compliance. This specific asset transaction and compliance rationale were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A share-swap chain converted 50 million Datavault shares for Vivisol shares into $150 million of Phoenix Asia Holdings stock,” intended as a balance-sheet enhancement for Genius Act compliance.

in_line: Management reiterated the FY26 revenue target of $200 million, consistent with the preview’s stated ≥$200 million guidance, although the timing and dependence of the ramp were more specific.
The BankWise acquisition broadly matched the preview’s expectation that the company would acquire a U.S. bank with a digital-asset charter.

surprises.description: Q4 EPS was $0.39 versus the preview’s $0.31–$0.32 consensus, and full-year diluted EPS was $2.51 versus the $2.43 FY26 consensus. The reported figures were above expectations, though the preview’s consensus was labeled adjusted EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 EPS jumping to $0.39 from $0.09 a year earlier”; “Diluted EPS grew 66% for the full year to $2.51.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS: $0.31–$0.32” for Q4; “Adjusted EPS: $2.43” for FY26 consensus.

surprises.description: Q4 organic sales growth reached 5%, above the preview’s expected 2–3% and making Q4 the strongest quarter of the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The fourth quarter delivering the strongest performance at 5% organic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic net sales growth: ~+2–3%” for Q4.

surprises.description: FY26 operating margin was 11.2%, above the preview’s 10.7–11.0% company-guidance range. The call also reported gross margin up 150 basis points, a margin improvement the preview did not specifically forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin expanded 320 basis points to 11.2%, while gross margin rose 150 basis points to 75.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted op. margin: 10.7%–11.0%” for FY26 company guidance.

surprises.description: The FY27 operating-margin outlook was raised above the preview’s preliminary 12.5–13.0% framework, to 12.7–13.5%. The EPS range of $3.10–$3.35 straddles the $3.18 consensus, with a midpoint only slightly above it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its operating margin outlook to 12.7%–13.5%, with diluted EPS of $3.10 to $3.35.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Prelim: +3–5% organic, 12.5–13.0% adj OM”; “FY27 Adjusted EPS consensus: $3.18.”

surprises.description: PRGP savings are expected to take longer to reach their full annualized level than the preview anticipated: the preview said the “vast majority” would arrive in FY27, while the call said full annualized savings benefits would flow through in FY28.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full annualized savings benefits are expected to flow through in fiscal ’28.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “May commentary said ‘vast majority’” of PRGP benefits would land in FY27.

surprises.description: Mainland China grew 9%, ahead of the preview’s mid-single-digit expectation for improvement in the China ecosystem, and the company marked a sixth consecutive quarter of prestige beauty share gains.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Mainland China led regional performance with 9% organic sales growth, marking a sixth consecutive quarter of prestige beauty share gains.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The FY27 guide assumes China ecosystem retail improves to mid-single digits.”

surprises.description: Travel Retail returned to positive global territory in June and July, with double-digit growth in Hainan. The preview expected recovery to be a key test against a very weak comparison, but this reported return to growth—especially in Hainan—was a favorable signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Travel Retail, about 15% of reported sales, returned to positive territory globally in June and July for the first time in three years, led by double-digit growth in Hainan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Asia/Pacific and travel retail — the easiest comp in the model”; “Anything short of a large positive APAC number here is a genuine disappointment.”

surprises.description: North America returned to organic growth in Q4, with retail sales up mid-single digits, after the preview highlighted flat Americas growth in Q2 and Q3 and a negative Q4 comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North America returned to organic sales growth in Q4 with retail sales up mid-single digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Americas: flat” in Q2 and Q3, with “Q4 FY25 (comp): –4%.”

surprises.description: Makeup’s organic sales trend improved by 500 basis points, better than the preview’s expectation of flat-to-slightly-negative performance. The call did not say that makeup had turned positive, only that its trend improved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Makeup improved its organic sales trend by 500 basis points led by M.A.C and TOM FORD.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case anticipated “makeup flat-to-slightly-negative”; the preview also said makeup had been “flat for two quarters.”

surprises.description: Online sales reached a record 34% of reported sales, up 3 percentage points from FY25. The preview did not identify this channel milestone as an expectation or key debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Online sales grew double digits and reached a record 34% of reported sales, up 3 percentage points from fiscal ’25.”

surprises.description: Jo Malone London and TOM FORD each crossed $1 billion in sales, while The Ordinary posted double-digit growth—brand-level milestones and growth the preview did not specifically anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Jo Malone London and TOM FORD each surpassed $1 billion in sales”; “The Ordinary posted double-digit growth.”

in_line: FY26 organic sales grew 3%, in line with the preview’s approximately 3% organic-growth expectation for the year.
FY27 organic sales guidance of 3%–5% matched the preliminary framework in the preview.
FY27 diluted EPS guidance of $3.10–$3.35 spans the preview’s $3.18 consensus; its midpoint is close to consensus.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.43, below the preview’s $0.49 consensus estimate (and $0.50 alternative), a shortfall of about 12–14%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “adjusted EPS of $0.43”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS $0.49” and “Adj. EPS (alt.) $0.50”

surprises.description: Consolidated adjusted operating margin was 3.9%, below the preview’s roughly 4.8–5.0% expectation and just under the company’s 4.0% guidance floor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated adjusted operating margin declined to 3.9% from 4.8% a year ago”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating margin ~4.8–5.0%” and company guidance of “4.0–5.5%”

surprises.description: The Q2 adjusted operating margin guide of 4.0–5.5% fell well short of the preview’s 7%-or-better bogey, despite the preview expecting Q2 pricing increases to begin showing up. Management also noted that the prior-year quarter had a nonrecurring 110-basis-point warranty benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q2 … adjusted operating margin of 4%-5.5%, versus a prior-year quarter that included a nonrecurring 110 basis point warranty benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side wants a Q2 adjusted operating margin guide with a 7%-handle or better” and “tariff-driven price increases management said they took ‘for Q2 onward’ show up.”

surprises.description: Retail written same-store sales turned positive at 3%, beating the preview’s base-case expectation of flat to down 2% and improving from the cited Q4 decline of 2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retail segment written sales grew 16% with same-store written sales up 3%, a significant sequential improvement from Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “SSS ~flat to –2%”; the preview also identified a positive written same-store sales print as the key upside catalyst.

surprises.description: Management said La-Z-Boy’s EIPA tariff refunds are significantly smaller than peers’, limiting its ability to fund promotions while competitors reinvest their refunds. That qualifies the preview’s expectation that domestic manufacturing would provide a competitive advantage amid tariffs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EIPA tariff refunds are significantly smaller than industry peers, limiting its ability to fund promotions as competitors reinvest refunds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the “~90% domestic upholstery manufacturing mix” as a “genuine relative advantage” and said it could convert into “visible share gain against import-exposed competitors.”

in_line: Fiscal 2027 capital expenditures of $90–$110 million matched the preview’s stated capex guidance of $90–$110 million.

The ongoing Joybird manufacturing consolidation and its continuing drag until the consolidation completes by fiscal year-end were consistent with the preview’s expectation that manufacturing would be folded into La-Z-Boy plants during FY2027.
The company’s domestic upholstery production share of over 90% was broadly in line with the preview’s estimate of approximately 90%.

surprises.description: Toll Brothers reported EPS of $2.97, above the preview’s $2.89–$2.93 consensus range, though the beat was only 4 cents above its upper end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EPS of $2.97, beating guidance on units, dollars, and earnings.”

surprises.description: Q4 gross-margin guidance came in at 26.0%, below the 26.3% level the preview identified as the load-bearing expectation. The shortfall is 30 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 guidance projects … 26.0% gross margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 to ~26.3%”; the preview called Q4’s 26.3% margin reaffirmation “the load-bearing assumption for the entire FY26 guide.”

surprises.description: Net signed contracts rose 5% year over year, reaching the preview’s bull-case threshold and exceeding its base-case expectation of flat to down 5%. Management attributed the increase to community-count expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net signed contracts rose 5% year-over-year to 2,508 units ($2.5 billion), driven by community count expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … Orders (YoY) 0% to −5%”; the preview described “flat-to-positive units” as a strong signal and set “+5% or better” in its bull case.

surprises.description: Pricing was firmer than the preview’s expected stable incentive rate: incentives declined to about 7.5% from roughly 8%, and about 30% of communities raised prices.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Incentives declined to approximately 7.5% of gross sales price from about 8% over the past year, and roughly 30% of communities saw price increases during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Incentives have been flat at 8.0% of gross sales price for four consecutive quarters”; the base case also expected “incentives 8%.”

surprises.description: Management raised the full-year average delivered-price outlook to $995,000–$1 million, adding about $53 million in revenue, rather than merely maintaining the existing outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year average delivered price to $995,000-$1 million (adding ~$53 million in revenue).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said that, after raising FY guidance at Q2, “FY26 maintained” was the base case and warned that “a trim would be read harshly.”

surprises.description: Toll raised its full-year stock-repurchase projection to $700 million from $650 million, exceeding the preview’s stated target rather than merely delivering the expected pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its full-year 2026 stock repurchase projection to $700 million from $650 million and returned approximately $231 million to shareholders in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$226M repurchased through H1 against a $650M FY target.”

surprises.description: Despite the 5% year-over-year increase in contracts, management said the sales environment was still subdued in the first 2.5 weeks of Q4, adding a near-term demand caution not reflected in the preview’s expected clean Q4 margin reaffirmation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management noted the sales environment remained subdued into the first 2.5 weeks of Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected Q4’s 26.3% margin to be “reaffirmed with conviction” in its bull case and described TOL as having “a demand story … that is actually holding.”

in_line: Deliveries were 2,662, essentially matching the preview’s estimate of about 2,669 and within company guidance of 2,600–2,700; home-sales revenue of $2.6 billion was also within the $2.60–$2.62 billion consensus range.
Adjusted gross margin of 25.6% was within the preview’s 25.4%–25.6% base-case range and in line with its expectation that consensus required a modest beat over the 25.25% guide.
Q4 delivery guidance of 3,450–3,550 was within the preview’s expected range of roughly 3,400–3,600.
Finished spec inventory fell to 1.9 homes per community, in line with the preview’s expectation of “near 2.0/community.”
Community growth remained on track for 480–490 at year-end, with similar 8%–10% growth reaffirmed for FY2027, as the preview anticipated.
The 69% loan-to-value ratio for financed buyers matched the preview’s stated 69% expectation; the 25% all-cash share was close to its 23% reference.

surprises.description: JKHY’s Q4 non-GAAP revenue was $633 million, above the preview’s implied range of about $616–628 million and its roughly $616 million non-GAAP consensus estimate. The beat was modest relative to the quarter’s size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 non-GAAP revenue was $633 million, up 7% year-over-year and above implied guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP revenue” was implied at “~$616–628M”; the preview also cited “Revenue (non-GAAP basis) ~$616.3M.”

surprises.description: The initial FY2027 non-GAAP margin expansion guide of 20–40 basis points is below the preview’s stated 50-basis-point threshold for defending the margin outlook. Management also flagged near-term cost pressures, though it said margin upside could come later in the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027” guidance includes “non-GAAP margin expansion of 20-40 basis points”; management flagged pressure from “normalizing self-insured medical costs, cyber/frontier model investments, and the EC 2030 data center consolidation project,” with “margin upside possible later in the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 needs ≥50bp to defend the multiple”; the preview also said the bear case would involve “FY27 margin expansion” that is “flat-to-down.”

surprises.description: JKHY guided FY2027 GAAP EPS to $7.33–$7.38, modestly above the preview’s approximately $7.20 statutory consensus. The preview cautioned that EPS estimates differed by basis, but identified $7.20 as the statutory figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP EPS of $7.33-$7.38 (5%-6% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 consensus EPS | ~$7.20 statutory (Zacks carries $6.54 — different basis).”

surprises.description: The 58 fiscal 2026 core wins exceeded the preview’s target of more than 55 and its base-case estimate of about 56. The preview already anticipated strong trifecta selling, and the full-year 59% attach rate was close to its 58% year-to-date figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A record 58 competitive core wins in fiscal 2026, up from 51 the prior year”; trifecta deals were “59% of the 58 core wins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Core wins for the full year (target: >55, vs. 51 in FY25)” and the base-case scenario anticipated “wins ~56”; trifecta wins were “58% of wins YTD.”

surprises.description: Management said Q1 FY2027 non-GAAP revenue growth would be modestly below the low end of the full-year range, citing a 1% impact from moving the Connect conference into Q2 and timing of one-time items. The preview did not flag this specific Q1 softness or conference timing shift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q1 fiscal 2027 non-GAAP revenue growth to come in modestly below the low end of the full-year range,” driven by “a 1% impact from shifting the Connect conference into Q2” and “timing of onetime items.”

surprises.description: The company returned 122% of free cash flow to shareholders, a substantial buyback and dividend payout not anticipated in the preview. It ended with only $40 million of debt, so it came close to—but did not fully meet—the preview’s debt-free-by-year-end expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2026 free cash flow rose 31% to $539 million,” and JKHY “returned 122% of free cash flow to shareholders” through “$448 million in buybacks” and “$170 million in dividends,” ending with “just $40 million in debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said debt was “$90M at Q3 with management targeting debt-free by fiscal year-end” and that the Street wanted confirmation FCF conversion settled into the “95–105% normalized range.”

in_line: FY2027 non-GAAP revenue growth guidance of 6.3%–7.3% was broadly in line with the preview’s approximately 6.5% Street estimate and its 6.5%–7.5% base-case range.
FY2026 non-GAAP operating margin expanded 92 basis points, within the preview’s stated 75–95 basis-point FY2026 margin-expansion outlook.
Full-year non-GAAP revenue growth of 7% was within the preview’s implied FY2026 range of approximately 6.6%–7.1%.
Faster-payment transaction volume growth of 45% was close to the preview’s cited 47% year-over-year growth expectation.
The 59% full-year trifecta share was broadly consistent with the preview’s 58% year-to-date figure and its expectation of strong cross-selling.

surprises.description: The preview expected Q4 revenue of roughly $4.0–4.1 billion, with $4.15 billion or more as the bull trigger. ADI guided to $4.3 billion, well above both the expected range and that trigger.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 guidance calls for revenue of $4.3 billion (+/- $100 million)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus FY2026 revenue of ~$14.8B implies an October-quarter bar of roughly $4.0–4.1B”; “$4.15B+ is the bull trigger.”

surprises.description: The preview put Q4 EPS at roughly $3.60–3.80. ADI guided to $3.86, above that range and just above the preview’s $3.85 bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 guidance calls for … EPS of $3.86 (+/- $0.15)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The EPS bar derives to roughly $3.60–3.80”; bull case: “≥$3.85.”

surprises.description: The preview expected automotive growth of about 8–11% year over year, while ADI reported 16% growth. The auto business therefore accelerated more than the preview’s model allowed for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Automotive (25%) grew 16% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview segment estimate: automotive “+8–11%” year over year; it also noted FQ2 auto “grew just 2% Y/Y.”

surprises.description: The preview expected industrial growth of 45–50% year over year. ADI reported 53%, modestly exceeding that already-strong expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Industrial (49% of revenue) grew 53% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview segment estimate for industrial: “+45–50%” year over year.

surprises.description: The preview modeled consumer growth of 10–15% year over year, but ADI reported 6%. Consumer performance was weaker than expected despite growth overall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consumer (10%) grew 6% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview segment estimate for consumer: “+10–15%” year over year.

surprises.description: The preview described a roughly 50-basis-point gross-margin decline in Q3 and little utilization upside. ADI instead expects Q4 gross margin to rise about 150 basis points to roughly 74%, near its 2022 peak levels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Q4 gross margin to rise ~150 bps to about 74%, back near 2022 peak levels, driven by favorable mix, higher fixed cost absorption, and price adjustments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management explicitly flagged ~50 bps of decline in FQ3”; “utilization offers minimal further upside.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted inventory as a risk, citing 168 days on hand and watching for a further increase. Instead, days inventory fell to 156, and distributor inventory moved below the 6–7 week target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Distributor channel inventory fell below the 6-7 week target and days inventory declined to 156.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “days of inventory (168 in FQ2, elevated), channel weeks (6–7, lean)” and warned about “days-of-inventory … with softening bookings.”

surprises.description: The preview expected ADI’s data-center share to be above 75% of communications revenue. Management reported 80%, with both optical and power growing more than 100% year over year, indicating stronger scale and growth in those businesses than the preview had specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Data center now represents 80% of communications revenue, with both optical and power businesses each growing more than 100% year-over-year in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said data center “is now >75% of Communications” and identified it as “the swing factor.”

surprises.description: The preview said a bull case would require a quantified data-center trajectory and a raise to the 2030 opportunity framework. Management said its 2030 data-center and energy opportunity had more than doubled versus its assessment a year earlier, and gave growth targets for OCS revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management's 2030 data center and energy revenue opportunity has more than doubled versus its assessment just one year ago, with OCS revenue set to roughly double in 2026 and targeting similar growth in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case required management to “volunteer a quantified data center trajectory” and flagged “any raise to the $20B-by-2030 framework.”

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate management signaling that the analog industry could grow at double-digit rates for years, a marked step up from ADI’s former 5–7% long-term model. Management also characterized FY2027 as a “brisk growth year.”
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management signaled potential for double-digit annual analog industry growth for years, raising expectations above the prior 5%-7% long-term model set in 2021, and expects a ‘brisk growth year’ in fiscal 2027.”

in_line: Communications grew 84% year over year, within the preview’s estimated 75–85% range. Its approximate 16% share of Q3 revenue also implies sequential growth around the preview’s low-to-mid-teens expectation.

surprises.description: Lowe’s moved its full-year outlook to the bottom of the prior range—about $92 billion of sales, flat comps, 11.6% adjusted operating margin and $12.25 adjusted EPS—rather than affirming the guidance, which the preview called the base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cut full-year 2026 guidance to the bottom of its prior range, now expecting ~$92 billion in sales, roughly flat comps, ~11.6% adjusted operating margin, and ~$12.25 adjusted EPS.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (~50%): … FY guide affirmed, not raised”; prior FY guidance was sales of $92–94B, comps flat to +2%, adjusted operating margin of 11.6–11.8%, and adjusted EPS of $12.25–12.75.

surprises.description: Comparable sales were only 0.2%, below the preview’s inferred buy-side expectation of roughly 0.5–1.0%, despite remaining positive for a fifth consecutive quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable sales rising just 0.2%, marking the fifth consecutive quarter of positive comps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comparable sales: ~+0.5–1.0% (buy-side)” and “near bottom of guide range.”

surprises.description: Sales of $26 billion fell short of the $26.14–26.18 billion consensus range, even though sales grew 8.3% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 sales reached $26 billion, up 8.3% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $4.40, above the preview’s $4.22–$4.26 consensus range; the $0.11 tariff-refund benefit did not account for the whole beat, as EPS exceeded expectations even excluding it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS was $4.40 (GAAP $4.27), which included an $0.11 benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds, and exceeded expectations even excluding that benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | $4.22 (some feeds $4.26).”

surprises.description: The quarter weakened sharply by July: after June comps rose 1.7%, July comps fell 1.2%, with competitors using tariff refunds to cut prices in seasonal categories. The preview anticipated outdoor-category weather risk, but not this tariff-refund-driven competitive pricing pressure or the late-quarter reversal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Monthly comps were uneven at May down 0.4%, June up 1.7%, and July down 1.2%, with July hurt by competitors using tariff refunds to aggressively cut prices in seasonal categories like grills, patio and live goods.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Drought and unfavorable weather were cited as a specific Q2 risk to outdoor/seasonal categories.”

surprises.description: Comparable transactions fell 2.1%, a steeper decline than the preview’s HD read-through of transactions down 1.0%; ticket growth of 2.3% did not prevent traffic from contracting.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable average ticket rose 2.3% while comparable transactions fell 2.1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Transactions vs. ticket” and noted HD’s “transactions down 1.0%”; it said to watch whether Lowe’s showed the same shape.

surprises.description: The near-term outlook indicated a weak second half: Q3 adjusted EPS is expected to be about 7% below the prior year, and Q4 comps are implied to be negative, partly because of the winter-storm comparison. That contrasts with the preview’s focus on transactions improving later in FY26 to support the back-half earnings requirement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for comps in line with the flat full-year outlook and adjusted EPS approximately 7% below prior year, with Q4 implied to be negative partly due to a ~50 basis point drag from cycling last year's winter storm.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the H2 outlook required “transactions to inflect” and noted Lowe’s had said it expected transactions “to improve later in FY26.”

surprises.description: Management said any second-half tariff refunds are excluded from guidance and would be reinvested in customer-facing pricing actions, rather than being treated as an earnings benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The guidance excludes any second-half tariff refunds, which management said would be reinvested in customer-facing pricing actions.”

surprises.description: Customers using Lowe’s Mylow AI agent converted at triple the rate of non-users, a new and potentially favorable operating detail not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Customers using the Mylow AI agent converting at triple the rate of non-users.”

in_line: Gross margin fell 80 basis points and adjusted operating margin fell 62 basis points, broadly within the preview’s expected range of roughly 60–80 basis points of operating-margin compression amid fuel, transportation and acquisition-mix pressure.
Online sales grew 15.7%, close to the 15.5% growth cited in the preview as the Q1 benchmark.

surprises.description: Marmaxx comped only 1%, well below the preview’s 2.7% estimate and the 4%+ performance described as necessary for the bull case. Management attributed the weakness entirely to correctable merchandise-mix execution issues, making the shortfall a company-specific execution problem rather than a broad customer-demand issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marmaxx, TJX's largest division, comped only 1% versus 6-7% at the other three divisions, with management attributing the shortfall entirely to self-inflicted, correctable merchandise-mix execution issues.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Marmaxx” comp estimate: “+2.7%”; the preview also said “a 4%+ Marmaxx comp is what a bull case is built on.”

surprises.description: Adjusted pretax margin was 11.9%, above the preview’s expected 11.7–11.8% base-case range and the company’s 11.4–11.5% plan. The 70-basis-point gross-margin increase was largely attributed to tariff-related merchandise-margin favorability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted Q2 pretax profit margin was 11.9%, up 50 basis points year-over-year, with adjusted gross margin of 31.4% (up 70 bps) largely driven by tariff-related merchandise margin favorability.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “margin ~11.7–11.8%”; its consensus table listed pretax margin of “~11.5–11.6% (implied)” and company guidance of “11.4%–11.5%.”

surprises.description: Q3 guidance points to a margin decline and only 2–3% EPS growth, a pullback from the strong Q2 profitability and the raised full-year outlook. The preview discussed fuel-price sensitivity but did not anticipate this specific near-term guidance profile.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance implies a margin pullback, with adjusted pretax margin of 12.3-12.4% (down 30-40 bps) and EPS of $1.30-$1.32 (up just 2-3%), pressured by higher fuel and freight costs.”

surprises.description: TJX Canada and International comps appear to have substantially exceeded their preview estimates: the call said the three divisions other than Marmaxx each comped 6–7%, versus estimates of 2.8% for Canada and 3.0% for International. This indicates considerably stronger performance in those divisions than the preview assumed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marmaxx…comped only 1% versus 6-7% at the other three divisions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Segment consensus estimated comps of “+2.8%” for TJX Canada and “+3.0%” for TJX International.

surprises.description: HomeGoods comped 7%, one point above the preview’s 6% estimate. Its 12.4% segment profit margin was also up 240 basis points year over year, although the preview gave no specific Q2 margin estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HomeGoods delivered a standout 7% comp with adjusted segment profit margin of 12.4%, up 240 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: HomeGoods comp estimate: “+6.0%”; the preview also flagged “HomeGoods margin durability” after a Q1 margin of 12.9%.

surprises.description: The full-year adjusted pretax margin range was raised to 12.0–12.1%, modestly above the preview’s stated existing range of 11.9–12.0%.
surprises.fact_evidence: TJX “lifted full-year adjusted pretax margin guidance to 12.0-12.1%, up 30-40 bps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed the current FY27 pretax margin guide as “11.9–12.0%.”

surprises.description: TJX raised its long-term store target by 500 to 7,500 and plans to increase annual store growth from 3% to 4% next year. The preview discussed store count but did not flag a higher long-term target or faster growth plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “TJX raised its long-term store target by 500 units to 7,500 stores and plans to accelerate annual store growth to 4% starting next year (from 3%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview included a store-count estimate of “5,292” and described growth versus the prior year, but did not anticipate a revised long-term target or accelerated annual growth.

surprises.description: Inventory was up 7% overall but only 2% per store, a moderation from the Q1 per-store increase noted in the preview. Management also characterized inventory as well-positioned amid abundant buying opportunities, rather than as a markdown concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Balance sheet inventory rose 7% (up 2% per store), which management views as well-positioned amid abundant buying opportunities across a network of ~21,000 vendors and 1,400+ buyers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted inventory per store was “+7% reported / +6% cc at Q1 end” and flagged whether elevated inventory would be a “forward margin asset” or “a markdown liability.”

in_line: Consolidated comps were 4%: above the 3.2% consensus and company’s 2–3% plan, but in line with the preview’s working whisper of about +4%.
Adjusted EPS of $1.22 exceeded the $1.18–$1.19 consensus and company plan, but was within the preview’s $1.21–$1.23 working whisper and $1.21–$1.24 base-case range.
Full-year adjusted EPS guidance of $5.15–$5.20 was raised from $5.08–$5.15, matching the preview’s base case of $5.15–$5.25 and reaching the stated $5.20 buy-side threshold at the top of the range.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case put June backlog around $6–8 million, with at least $9 million needed to show that orders were replacing shipments. Backlog was $5.4 million after substantial shipments, closer to the preview’s catch-up-risk case and suggesting weaker replenishment than the base case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog ended June at $5.4 million after the company converted a substantial portion into shipments during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (~50%): … backlog ~$6–8M”; “If June-30 backlog holds ≥$9M, orders replaced shipments”; “If it drops to $5–6M, Q2 was a one-time catch-up.”

surprises.description: The preview expected a GAAP loss of about $4.4 million, or $0.20 per share; BEEM reported a $3.1 million loss, or $0.14 per share. The loss was meaningfully narrower than the consensus bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $3.1 million ($0.14 per share) from $4.3 million ($0.28 per share) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 EPS: –$0.20”; “Implies net loss ≈ –$4.4M.”

surprises.description: The preview said opex of about $5 million or less would indicate the cost program was taking hold. Opex came in at $4.5 million, below that threshold, with management also citing roughly $0.5 million of first-half cost reductions; the prior-year comparison is partly affected by a $1.4 million stock grant.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses fell to $4.5 million from $5.9 million a year ago (which included a $1.4 million stock grant), reflecting roughly $0.5 million in first-half cost reductions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A GAAP opex print at or below ~$5.0M would signal the cost program is real.”

surprises.description: The preview raised concern about possible going-concern language or a dilutive financing need, given the low starting cash balance. The call facts instead report that BEEM remained debt-free, had a fully unused $100 million credit line, and had no going-concern qualification; the facts do not provide the quarter-end cash balance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company remains debt-free with a fully unused $100 million line of credit and no going concern qualification.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for: going-concern language in the 10-Q”; the preview also said the quarter was a “liquidity binary” and raised the possibility of ATM reliance or a dilutive raise.

surprises.description: The preview anticipated $2.7 million of lease savings over five years and described labor savings as unquantified. Management gave a $2.7–3 million lease-savings estimate and specified that Yuma labor costs are about 75% of San Diego rates, adding detail and a slightly higher upper-end lease estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The relocation of manufacturing from San Diego to Yuma, Arizona is expected to save approximately $2.7-3 million in rent over the 5-year lease, plus labor costs at about 75% of San Diego rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company cites $2.7M of lease savings over five years from the Yuma relocation plus unquantified labor savings.”

surprises.description: The preview did not identify a customer-specific credit-loss provision. BEEM reported a $1 million noncash provision tied to one customer balance that it is still trying to collect, an unanticipated loss item and collection risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half results absorbed a $1 million noncash provision for credit losses tied to a single customer balance, which the company is still working to collect.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted international growth and U.S. market headwinds, but did not anticipate Europe generating roughly as much revenue as the U.S. or the cited 35% year-over-year growth in European EV sales. This adds evidence of regional demand outside the U.S.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Europe now generates roughly the same amount of revenue as the United States, and management cited European EV sales up 35% year-over-year despite US market weakness.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “international 51% of revenue” in Q1 and said “Federal EV spending remains a stated headwind,” but gave no Europe-specific revenue or EV-sales expectation.

in_line: Revenue was $8.6 million, consistent with the already disclosed preliminary result of more than $8.5 million and the preview’s company-set bar of at least $8.5 million.

GAAP gross margin of 17.8% was within the preview’s expected 15–18% range. Adjusted non-GAAP gross margin of 26.2% was near the top of the preview’s estimated 23–26% range, while still below the prior-year margin as anticipated.
The preview had already flagged more than $0.5 million of drone and robotics battery orders in one week; the call’s report of over $0.5 million in such orders is consistent with that expectation.

surprises.description: Accuray reported Q4 revenue of $100.9 million, below the preview’s roughly $108 million base case, although it was above the preview’s most recently refreshed estimate of about $95.8 million. Full-year revenue of $402 million was also below the preview’s roughly $409 million base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 net revenue fell 21% year-over-year to $100.9 million,” and “full-year revenue declined 12% to $402 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base case: ~$108M”; “Investing.com (post-Q3) ~$95.8M”; and “Base case implies FY26 revenue of ~$409M.”

surprises.description: Product sales fell far more sharply than the preview’s base case assumption of a normal Q4 seasonal product uplift. Q4 product revenue declined 42%, and the company attributed roughly $58 million of its full-year product-revenue decline to China.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 product revenue dropped 42% to $40.8 million and full-year product revenue fell 27% to $173 million,” with “roughly $58 million of the annual decline attributable to reduced sales in China amid geopolitical tension and tariff uncertainty.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case assumed “Normal Q4 seasonal product uplift, MENA still blocked”; the preview also said “Two consecutive quarters of order collapse would mean the FY27 revenue base is impaired.”

surprises.description: Service revenue proved more resilient than the recent trend suggested: it grew in Q4 and for the full year, despite Q3 service revenue having declined year over year. Pricing actions and the larger installed base supported the growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue grew 6% in Q4 to $60.1 million and 4% for the full year to $229 million, supported by pricing actions and a larger installed base, with contract capture rate near 90%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q3 service revenue of “$55.1M” and “-1%” year over year.

surprises.description: Accuray again withheld formal FY2027 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance instead of providing the Q4 update the preview was watching for. The company cited tariffs, geopolitical conditions, and macroeconomic uncertainty affecting product demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company will not provide formal FY2027 revenue or adjusted EBITDA guidance, citing tariff impacts, China and Middle East conditions, and macroeconomic uncertainty affecting product demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said they'd update at Q4. Reinstating guidance signals confidence; a second withdrawal is damaging.”

surprises.description: The company’s FY2026 transformation savings substantially exceeded the preview’s expectation that roughly $10 million of a $12 million target had been achieved through Q3. Accuray said it delivered over $20 million in bottom-line improvements for the full year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Transformation initiatives delivered over $20 million in bottom-line improvements in FY2026, well above the $12 million target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “confirmation of the $25M annualized cost benefit by FY27 (vs. ~$10M of a $12M FY26 target achieved through Q3).”

surprises.description: The expected gross-margin recovery was weaker beneath the reported product-margin figure: Q4 product gross margin of 31.7% included $5.8 million of EPA tariff favorability, and adjusted product gross margin was only 17.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 product gross margin of 31.7% was inflated by $5.8 million of EPA tariff favorability; excluding this, adjusted product gross margin was only 17.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “GM ~28%” and warned that “anything under 27% says the cost program isn't reaching the P&L.”

surprises.description: Demand indicators remained weak in Q4: book-to-bill was 0.9 and backlog was about $313 million, below the preview’s stated stabilization marker of book-to-bill above 1.0 and down from the Q3 backlog of $356.2 million. The full-year ratio was 1.1, but still below the company’s targeted healthy level of 1.2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year book-to-bill ratio was 1.1, below the company's targeted healthy level of 1.2, with Q4 book-to-bill at 0.9 and backlog of approximately $313 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s catalyst checklist asked whether “Gross orders and book-to-bill” would be “>1.0x” to stabilize the FY27 revenue narrative; Q3 backlog was reported at “$356.2M.”

surprises.description: Year-end cash was above the preview’s stated level of concern: Accuray reported $48.8 million, rather than a balance below roughly $30 million that would make the TCW investment look like a lifeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and equivalents at $48.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “Anything under ~$30M reframes the $15M TCW infusion as a lifeline rather than a bridge,” and cited Q3 cash of $38.1 million.

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA was stronger than the preview’s base case implied: the preview expected Q4 adjusted EBITDA of $5–8 million after nine-month adjusted EBITDA of negative $2.3 million, while the reported full-year figure was $10.6 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EBITDA fell to $10.6 million from $28.3 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case: … Adj. EBITDA ~$5–8M”; the preview also reported nine-month FY26 adjusted EBITDA of “$(2.3)M.”

in_line: The TCW recapitalization’s core terms were already described in the preview: $55 million in total, including a $15 million cash investment, preferred equity with an 8% dividend and conversion around $0.50, and covenant relief through December 2027. The reported transaction terms and the fact that shareholder approval is still needed did not materially depart from that preview.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case anticipated a discrete reporting issue without a restatement, but Solésence said it filed an NT 10-Q and is restating historical financials because indirect manufacturing costs were improperly allocated in its inventory costing methodology. Management said the error does not affect cash flows or operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company filed a Form NT 10-Q and is restating historical financials due to an inventory costing methodology error involving improper allocation of indirect manufacturing costs,” while management said it “does not affect cash flows or operations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “a discrete, non-restatement item”; it also said that a clean filing without an ICFR change would be a relief outcome.

surprises.description: Solésence guided to a much stronger second half than the preview’s base case of roughly $13–15 million per quarter implied: management expects about $35 million in second-half revenue and full-year 2026 revenue above 2025. The preview had framed a rationalized revenue level and softened targets as the base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management now expects full-year 2026 revenue “to exceed 2025,” with the second half “approximately $35 million,” described as the strongest second half in company history.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case described revenue normalizing at “the ~$13–15M quarterly level” and said targets might be softened.

surprises.description: Gross margin came in at 31%, above the preview’s roughly 28% estimate and management’s 30% floor, rather than remaining below that floor. The company said it held margin around that level despite much lower revenue, reflecting improved labor efficiency.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin held roughly steady at 31% versus a restated 32% a year earlier,” despite 25% lower revenue, “signaling improved labor efficiency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated gross margin at “~28%” and highlighted the “30% gross profit margin floor”; its base case anticipated “GM 27–29%, below the 30% floor.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was weaker than the preview’s modeled 5–7% margin: $523,000 on $15.3 million of revenue is about 3.4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA fell to $523,000 from $3.7 million in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated an “Adj. EBITDA margin” of “~5–7%.”

surprises.description: The quarter’s net loss was smaller than the preview’s modeled loss, even with the Refy charge and without the prior-year ERC payment. Solésence reported a $158,000 loss versus the preview’s $400,000 loss estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 “swung to a net loss of $158,000” from $3.2 million of net income, partly due to a “one-time $938,000 charge related to Refy” and the absence of a “$1.4 million ERC payment received in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Net income” of “-$0.4M.”

surprises.description: The reported shipped and on-hand order total was higher than the year-earlier figure, providing a positive demand and order-visibility datapoint that the preview did not quantify.
surprises.fact_evidence: “As of August 17, shipped and on-hand orders for 2026 totaled $64.9 million, up from $60 million in the same period of 2025.”

surprises.description: Revenue was slightly above the preview’s model, though it still fell sharply year over year as expected given the tough comparison. The $15.3 million result was $0.3 million above the $15.0 million estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 revenue was “$15.3 million,” down 25% year over year from $20.4 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 FY2026 base estimate was “$15.0M (-26% YoY).”

in_line: Revenue recovered sequentially from Q1 and exceeded the preview’s $15 million threshold for a recovery quarter.
The approximately $938,000 Refy-related charge was anticipated in the preview.
The July hair-and-scalp SPF extension was flagged in the preview as a development to watch.

surprises.description: Coty framed FY27 as a transition year, targeting EBITDA and free cash flow close to FY26 levels rather than growth. The preview anticipated a conservative year with first-half contraction offset by second-half expansion, but did not state an expectation for flat full-year results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guiding fiscal 2027 as a transition year, targeting full-year EBITDA and free cash flow close to fiscal 2026 levels rather than growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “RBC expects conservative FY27 with 1H contraction offset by 2H expansion.”

surprises.description: Management said Q1 FY27 sellout should remain similar to the prior two soft quarters before improving sequentially. That points to continued near-term weakness rather than the improvement the preview highlighted as an operational tell.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 [is expected] to show a sellout trend similar to the prior two soft quarters before sequential improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “‘Sequential improvement’ without a quantified FY27 EBITDA range = base case”; the preview also said to watch for “Prestige sell-out growth.”

surprises.description: Coty disclosed that sellout has trailed category growth for several quarters, contributing to lower sell-in and inventory swings. The preview emphasized sellout as a focus and a potential growth tell, but did not anticipate this sustained company-wide shortfall or its inventory consequences.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Coty's sellout has been trailing category growth for several quarters, driving lower sell-in and inventory swings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “‘Coty.Curated’ (fewer launches, sell-out focus, AI-driven cost takeout) needs to show up in the GM line”; “Operational tells by scenario: Bull needs Prestige sell-out (not sell-in) growth.”

surprises.description: The company is changing its bonus system to make market share and sellout key measures alongside sales and EBITDA, explicitly shifting away from its historically sell-in-focused culture. The preview discussed a sellout focus but did not anticipate this compensation change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Restructured its fiscal 2027 bonus system to make market share and sellout a key KPI, alongside sales and a strong EBITDA component, marking a shift from its historically sell-in-focused culture.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “‘Coty.Curated’ (fewer launches, sell-out focus, AI-driven cost takeout)…”

surprises.description: Management quantified an oil-price headwind of roughly $20–30 million. The preview noted prior tariff-related gross-margin pressure but did not identify this additional current cost.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Elevated oil prices between $90 and $100 are costing Coty roughly $20-30 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Down 250 bps adj. in Q3 on tariffs, E&O, and low asset utilization.”

surprises.description: Coty said a potential tariff refund of about $30 million could provide upside, though it remains unconfirmed. The preview mentioned tariffs as a cost pressure but did not flag a possible refund.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A potential ~$30 million tariff refund remains a possible but unconfirmed upside.”

surprises.description: CoverGirl and Sally Hansen have substantially narrowed their U.S. market gap, and Sally Hansen is now growing ahead of its category through equity-building advertising rather than promotions. The preview did not anticipate this brand-level improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CoverGirl and Sally Hansen have substantially narrowed the gap to market, with Sally Hansen now growing ahead of the category, driven by equity-building advertising rather than promotions.”

surprises.description: Coty plans to remove 20% of on-shelf SKUs and expects no material sales impact, while reducing returns and obsolescence costs that have weighed on Consumer Beauty EBITDA. The preview did not identify this specific action or expected cost benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Plans a 20% SKU reduction on shelf, which management expects to occur without material sales impact while reducing returns and obsolescence costs that have weighed on Consumer Beauty EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Coty set an aspiration to return the underlying portfolio, excluding Gucci, to growth in FY28 through incremental innovation with halo effects on core brands. The preview highlighted the FY28 Gucci revenue cliff but did not describe this specific underlying-growth target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Targets returning its underlying portfolio (excluding Gucci) to growth in fiscal 2028, relying on incremental innovation with halo effects on core global brands like Burberry and Hugo Boss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 revenue still largely carries Gucci, meaning the revenue cliff is FY28, not FY27.”

surprises.description: Management said the cost-savings and restructuring program alone is intended to offset the financial impact of Gucci’s departure, despite Gucci representing a low-double-digit percentage of sales with healthy profit. The preview highlighted the FY28 revenue cliff but did not anticipate a commitment to fully offset its financial impact through savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cost-savings and restructuring program alone [to] offset the financial impact of the Gucci license departure (a low-double-digit percentage of sales with healthy profit), targeting savings in allocated overhead, manufacturing, distribution, and central functions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 revenue still largely carries Gucci, meaning the revenue cliff is FY28, not FY27.”

surprises.description: ClearSign booked six M-Series burner orders, including five large M1 units for two top-tier Permian Basin customers. The preview discussed M-Series revenue as a possible base-case source, but did not anticipate this order count or customer detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Since the prior call, the company booked orders for 6 M-Series burners”—about 10–12% of its roughly 50-proposal pipeline—with “5 large M1 units going to two top-tier Permian Basin customers.”

surprises.description: The 36-burner Texas process-burner project is now on hold because the customer has not resolved its financing. The preview noted the project was not yet a firm equipment order, but did not flag financing as a hurdle.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 36-burner Texas process burner project is on hold due to unresolved customer financing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the Texas project as “not yet booked as firm equipment orders” and flagged “timing of the Texas 36-burner equipment phase.”

surprises.description: The California 32-burner project has advanced to the test-furnace stage, a constructive development even though the preview highlighted conversion to the equipment order as a key question and no firm equipment order was reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 32-burner California flat-flame project is progressing to test-furnace stage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “conversion of the California 32-burner engineering phase (~$0.5M) into the ~$3.2M equipment order” as a key item, while its base case anticipated “no backlog number given.”

surprises.description: One three-burner order uses a licensing arrangement: the customer builds from ClearSign’s drawings, lowering reported revenue per unit while keeping profit-margin dollars unchanged. The preview did not anticipate this revenue-recognition nuance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “One of the 3-burner orders was structured as a licensing/royalty deal” that reduces revenue per unit “but preserv[es] the same profit-margin dollars.”

surprises.description: Management described a path to a $6–7 million run rate from midstream and flare products alone, and said double-digit-million annual revenue is feasible as process-burner installations activate. The preview focused on lumpy 2H revenue and the October startup, but did not set out this scale of revenue potential.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management sees “a path to a $6-7 million run rate from midstream and flare product lines alone” and views “double-digit-million annual revenue as feasible as process burner installations activate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the key question was “whether 2H26 is being framed as another Q4-weighted year” and described the base case as “spare parts + M-series + flare revenue only.”

surprises.description: Operating cash use rose to about $1.2 million from roughly $511,000 a year earlier, with management attributing the increase to customer cash-collection timing. The preview emphasized burn and runway but did not anticipate this year-over-year increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash used in operations jumped to about $1.2 million in Q2 2026 from roughly $511,000 a year ago,” driven by “customer cash collection timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Cash and burn” and said “Runway matters more than EPS here,” but gave no expectation for Q2 operating cash use.

surprises.description: The year-over-year loss improvement came almost entirely from lower G&A legal fees associated with a dissolved Board special committee, rather than clearly indicating recurring operating-cost discipline. That makes the improvement less indicative of ongoing savings than the preview’s cost-control framing suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net loss narrowed by $373,000, “primarily due to a $368,000 drop in G&A expenses tied to reduced legal fees from a dissolved Board special committee.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a lower operating loss would “mark real cost control” and highlighted “Opex discipline.”

in_line: Revenue was approximately $560,000, matching the preview’s already-reported apparent figure, although it was well below the $1.34 million consensus estimate the preview cited.
EPS was $(0.22), matching the preview’s apparent result and its statement that this would beat the $(0.28) consensus estimate.
Gross margin was approximately 41%, in line with the preview’s apparent result and its expectation of a 35–45% recovery.
The Gulf Coast 26-burner startup remained on track for October, as the preview expected.
No hard backlog total was disclosed; the preview described silence on a quantified backlog as the base case.
The July private placement and resulting cash position were broadly in line with the preview, which already cited the 500,000-share offering and estimated cash of about $9.8 million.

surprises.description: The preview's Q1 whisper was roughly $150–165 million of total revenue, but management guided to $140–160 million of device revenue alone. Q4 device revenue was $106 million, so the device outlook signals a strong sequential increase, although the call facts do not give total Q1 revenue for a direct comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 guidance calls for device revenue of $140 million to $160 million.” Q4 device revenue was “~$106 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Whisper sits around $150–165M”; the key question was whether the company guides to “the first sequential growth quarter in over two years.”

surprises.description: The preview wanted an EBITDA or cash-flow breakeven date or at least a FY2027 framework, but management provided no timeline. Instead, it said gross-margin breakeven requires roughly an $800 million annual revenue run rate, with the exact level depending on mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management estimates a roughly $800 million annual revenue run rate is needed to reach breakeven gross margin,” while the “exact point depends on product mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side expects a date or at least an FY2027 framework”; “Silence here is a bear signal.”

surprises.description: The Q1 operating-expense outlook of $62–66 million is above the preview's roughly $61 million flat-cost expectation. That leaves less room for operating-cost reductions than the preview's base case assumed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q1 FY2027 guidance newly disclosed “operating expenses of $62 million to $66 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave operating expenses of “~$61M” and said the base case assumed “Cost discipline holds.”

surprises.description: Management highlighted a refinancing opportunity in roughly $630 million of first-lien debt carrying about 16% interest, a specific high-cost debt burden and potential cash-burn lever not featured in the preview's account of manageable debt service. Any benefit is prospective, not a completed refinancing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First lien debt of roughly $630 million carries ~16% interest,” representing “a major refinancing opportunity that could meaningfully reduce the company's $54 million quarterly operating cash burn.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described debt service as “fixed and manageable” and cited cash interest of “~$145M/yr” after emergence.

surprises.description: Gross capital expenditures fell to $5 million from $38 million in the prior quarter, a sharp reduction the preview had not forecast for Q4. The preview did flag FY2027 capex plans, but gave no Q4 gross-capex expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross capital expenditures fell sharply to $5 million in Q4 from $38 million in the prior quarter.”

surprises.description: A $41 million inventory reduction boosted operating cash flow, providing a substantial working-capital benefit that the preview did not anticipate. The call facts do not state the resulting total operating cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory reduction contributed a $41 million benefit to operating cash flow.”

surprises.description: Holders converted $46 million of convertible notes to equity during the quarter, reducing debt and annual interest expense but also bringing forward some equity dilution that the preview had identified as a risk to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Holders of $46 million of convertible notes voluntarily converted debt to equity during Q4, saving approximately $1 million in annual interest expense.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “any signal on ~44M shares of potential convert dilution.”

in_line: Q4 revenue was $150 million, matching the preview's $150 million consensus and the midpoint of company guidance.
Q4 adjusted non-GAAP gross margin was negative 19.9%, within the preview's implied range of roughly negative 18% to negative 21%; the preview also expected gross margin to remain negative.
Adjusted EBITDA of negative $62 million was at the low end of the preview's estimated negative $55 million to negative $62 million range.
Q4 operating expenses were $62 million versus the preview's roughly $61 million estimate, broadly consistent with its expectation of flat costs.
AI data-center revenue remained unquantified in dollars, as the preview's base case anticipated; the reported sequential growth and more-than-doubling year over year reaffirmed strong expansion.

surprises.description: The preview looked for FY27 core revenue growth of about 13–14%, with 13%+ described as preserving the durable-growth narrative. BILL guided to 11–14%, a midpoint of 12.5%, and cited a three-point growth headwind from spend-and-expense dynamics and bank channels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 core revenue guidance of $1.669B-$1.719B implies 11%-14% growth,” including “3 points of year-over-year growth headwind (2 points from spend & expense dynamics and 1 point from bank channels).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A first FY27 guide of 13%+ preserves the durable-growth narrative”; the modeled buy-side bar was “~13–14% core.”

surprises.description: The preview expected roughly 3,800 or more Q4 net adds and flagged fewer than 3,500 as a sign of post-restructuring disruption. BILL added only about 1,800; management attributed the shortfall to restructuring and deliberate focus on its ideal customer profile.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added only ~1,800 net new customers in Q4,” below recent trends due to “organizational restructuring and deliberate ideal-customer-profile focus.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Net adds ≥~3,800” and said net adds “<3,500” would signal RIF disruption.

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP operating margin reached 23%, well above the roughly 19.5% implied by the preview’s expected operating income and revenue. The margin also expanded substantially year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin reached 23%, expanding 860 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q4 non-GAAP operating income at “~$84M” on consensus revenue of “$430.5M,” implying a margin of about 19.5%.

surprises.description: The preview put Q4 core revenue consensus at about $397 million. BILL reported $400.5 million, a modest beat and slightly above the preview’s expected 15% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 core revenue grew 16% year-over-year to $400.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Core subscription and transaction revenue consensus was “~$397M (implied),” with “+15%” implied year-over-year growth.

surprises.description: The preview anticipated a Rule-of-40 framework and a GAAP margin roadmap, but BILL provided a specific FY27 profitability outlook: it expects to exceed the Rule of 40 exiting the year and generate well over $125 million of GAAP profits for the full year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects to exceed the Rule of 40 (net revenue growth plus operating margin) exiting FY27 and to generate well over $125 million of GAAP profits for the full year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Rule of 40 and GAAP margin expansion were deferred to this call, and flagged a “no-show” on the framework or GAAP roadmap as a risk.
