surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided fiscal 2028 revenue growth of approximately 70%, describing it as supply-constrained since unconstrained demand points to roughly 100% (doubling) growth.”

surprises.description: The call quantified a major AWS deployment commitment that the preview had not specified: AWS is to deploy an additional 2 million GPUs over several quarters, providing concrete multi-quarter demand visibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AWS is deploying an additional 2 million GPUs from this quarter through Q2 fiscal 2029.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “inference mix and backlog/supply commentary” and said “any quantified visibility (multi-quarter booked demand) supports the durability case,” but gave no deployment figure.

surprises.description: Management disclosed a substantial AI-lab financing and investment effort not anticipated in the preview: nearly $50B invested in Frontier AI labs and partnerships to raise over $500B in third-party financing. This adds a new, large funding channel to the demand outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “NVIDIA's revenue opportunity per gigawatt has expanded from ~$18 billion with Hopper to $25 billion with Blackwell to $40 billion with Vera Rubin, and is expected to rise further.”

surprises.description: The call newly indicated that AI labs using NVIDIA’s balance sheet are expected to account for roughly one-quarter of next year’s business. That is a substantial, previously unquantified source of demand, though it also ties some of the outlook to NVIDIA-backed financing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects demand from AI labs that leverage NVIDIA's balance sheet to contribute roughly one-quarter of next year's business.”

in_line: China data center compute remained excluded from the forward outlook, as the preview expected in its base case. The call said Q2 China H200 shipments were less than 1% of Data Center revenue and dilutive to gross margins.
Vera CPU shipments to AWS begin this quarter, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Vera shipments would start in Q3.

surprises.description: Ooma raised FY2027 revenue guidance to $332–333.5 million, above the preview’s cited prior range of $326–328.5 million and beyond its base-case expectation of a nudge to roughly $328–330 million. The new adjusted EBITDA and EPS ranges also exceed the prior ranges, with EPS reaching $1.35–$1.38.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year fiscal 2027 guidance projects revenue of $332-333.5 million”; “Full-year fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA is guided to $47.5-48.3 million with non-GAAP EPS of $1.35-$1.38.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year FY2027 guidance (raised at Q1): revenue $326.0M–$328.5M; non-GAAP EPS $1.29–$1.34; adj. EBITDA $45.0M–$46.5M.” The preview’s base case expected guidance “nudged to high end (~$328–330M / $1.32–1.35).”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $83.2 million exceeded the preview’s $82.3 million high end of company guidance. The beat was also well above the roughly $80.2 million consensus figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue reached $83.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Q2 FY27 Company Guidance … $81.6M – $82.3M | Street Consensus … ~$80.2M.” The preview called the “real bar” the “high end of guidance (~$82.3M).”

surprises.description: Q2 profitability came in above the preview’s already-strong expectations: non-GAAP EPS was $0.35 versus a $0.34 guidance high end, while adjusted EBITDA was $12.4 million versus an implied range topping out around $12.0 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA hit a record $12.4 million (15% of revenue), up 74% year-over-year, while non-GAAP net income grew 58% to $10.2 million ($0.35 diluted EPS).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP diluted EPS | $0.33 – $0.34”; “Adj. EBITDA (implied) | ~$11.5M – $12.0M.”

surprises.description: Ooma raised its residential outlook from an expected decline to expected growth, improving the segment outlook beyond the preview’s flat-to-1% decline plan. The preview had identified a second consecutive quarter of residential user growth as a possible narrative upgrade, but did not anticipate this stronger revenue outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Residential revenue outlook was raised from a 1-2% decline to flat-to-1% growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 plan assumes residential subscription flat to -1%.”

surprises.description: Ooma reported a record $30.2 million of trailing-12-month free cash flow and $17.6 million of buybacks over four quarters, neither of which the preview anticipated; the preview focused instead on debt reduction and capacity for possible acquisitions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated record trailing-12-month free cash flow of $30.2 million, spent $17.6 million on buybacks over four quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “continued quarterly paydowns to rebuild capacity for further tuck-in North American UCaaS deals” and said another acquisition was “a live possibility.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed 8% blended ARPU growth and a core-user count of 1.427 million, with business users now 49% of the total. The preview specifically said it did not expect ARPU or core-user metrics to be disclosed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Blended ARPU rose 8% year-over-year to $16.95, and business users now represent 49% of the 1,427,000 total core users.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Ooma does not disclose net dollar subscription retention or ARPU in its releases, and stopped emphasizing a ‘core users’ count — do not expect those metrics.”

surprises.description: Business-user additions were held down by IWG churn and a one-time count correction: reported growth was 4,000 users, versus 11,000 without those factors. The preview focused on organic business subscription growth but did not flag these specific headwinds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Business user growth was dampened by 4,000 users of IWG churn and a one-time count correction, without which business users would have grown 11,000 instead of the reported 4,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “organic business subscription growth (ex-FluentStream/Phone.com)” and cited a 9% Q1 organic rate, without mentioning IWG churn or a count correction.

surprises.description: MyPhone was already expected to be available through Walmart.com, with in-store shelf placement expected in the fall, but the call reported sales through Costco, Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Target. The wider set of named retail channels was not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Residential additions were “driven largely by the newly launched MyPhone product now sold at Costco, Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said MyPhone was “on walmart.com with in-store shelf placement expected this fall.”

in_line: Ooma added more than 3,000 residential users, consistent with the preview’s expectation that a second consecutive quarter of residential user growth was possible.
AirDial remained a strong growth driver: the preview expected continued momentum, and the call reported 75% year-over-year services-revenue growth and installations up 50% from the prior quarter.
The preview expected continued debt paydowns; the call reported a further $6.5 million Q2 repayment and debt of $47 million, down from $53.5 million.

The preview warned that acquisitions flattered reported growth and highlighted organic growth as a key debate. The call said revenue grew 8% excluding acquisitions, so acquisition dependence remained an issue; however, this is not directly comparable to the preview’s 9% organic business-subscription-growth figure.

surprises.description: Q3 non-GAAP EPS was $3.91, well above the $3.67 consensus and the $3.69 top of guidance. The preview’s own base case was $3.78, so the earnings beat was larger than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS was $3.91” and exceeded guidance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus $3.67”; guidance “$3.63–$3.69”; the preview’s base-case model was “non-GAAP EPS $3.78.”

surprises.description: Management raised full-year non-GAAP EPS guidance to $15.04–$15.10, a larger uplift than the preview’s expected modest increase to $14.80–$14.90. The new range is also well above the prior $14.72–$14.80 guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year non-GAAP EPS guidance by $0.31 at the midpoint to $15.04-$15.10.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected FY26 EPS to be “nudged to $14.80–14.90”; existing guidance was “$14.72–14.80.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow guidance rose by $600 million to about $2.6 billion, substantially above the preview’s $2.0 billion figure. Cash-from-operations guidance also increased and planned CapEx fell, contributing to the larger FCF outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow guidance was raised $600 million to approximately $2.6 billion,” cash from operations guidance was raised $500 million to about $2.8 billion, and CapEx was reduced to approximately $225 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY2026 guidance was “OCF ~$2,300M, FCF ~$2,000M, capex ~$300M.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue exceeded both the $2.44 billion consensus and the top of guidance, rather than landing merely within the range. The beat was modest in percentage terms.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 revenue reached $2.477 billion,” beating the high end of guidance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus was “$2.44B”; guidance was “$2,410–2,460M.”

surprises.description: Design IP revenue was $474 million, below the $487.4 million consensus, and growth of about 11% was below the preview’s expected 14%. The segment did return to growth, but its revenue recovery was weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Design IP segment returned to growth with revenue of $474 million, up approximately 11% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Design IP consensus was “$487.4M” and “+14%”; the preview said the Street needed “a second clean sequential quarter.”

surprises.description: Backlog edged down to $10.9 billion from the $11 billion reported at Q2, rather than rising. The decline was attributed to the processor IP solutions divestiture, which makes the signal less concerning than an unexplained decline but still falls short of the preview’s desired backlog progress.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog remained strong at $10.9 billion but declined modestly quarter-over-quarter due to the divestiture of the processor IP solutions business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$11B at Q2” and said “flat-to-down Synopsys backlog” would be a concern.

surprises.description: The reported non-GAAP operating margin of 41.6% exceeded the roughly 40% margin implied by the preview’s Q3 guidance discussion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin of 41.6%,” exceeding guidance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Guidance implies ~40% non-GAAP operating margin this quarter.”

surprises.description: Management now expects EDA to accelerate to double-digit organic growth in Q4 and for full-year 2026. The preview did not identify that acceleration outlook, making it a constructive growth-durability signal beyond the reported 8.5% Q3 growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EDA revenue grew 8.5% year-over-year” and management expects it “to accelerate to double-digit organic growth in Q4 and for full-year 2026.”

surprises.description: Synopsys reported record hardware-assisted verification revenue, with 12 new and 66 repeat customer wins. That was stronger evidence of hardware demand than the preview’s description of hardware/emulation timing as normalizing between Q3 and Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record hardware-assisted verification revenue,” with “12 new and 66 repeat HAV customer wins in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “hardware/emulation timing was framed as normalizing between Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: The preview cited a PCIe 7.0 win rate above 90%; management reported wins in over 95% of opportunities, alongside 25 LPDDR6 design wins year-to-date and a die-to-die business on pace to double. These were stronger and broader IP traction signals than the preview had specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Over 95% of PCIe 7 opportunities won, 25 LPDDR6 design wins year-to-date, and a die-to-die business on pace to double year-over-year with over 100 cumulative design wins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “PCIe 7.0 (>90% win rate), UCIe, HBM4 and custom AI silicon.”

surprises.description: The first joint Synopsys-ANSYS multiphysics Fusion solution launched with customer-validated design-closure improvements of up to 10x, an unanticipated product milestone. However, management said it will not contribute revenue until 2027, so monetization is not near term.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The first joint Synopsys-ANSYS multiphysics Fusion solution launched in Q3” with results of “up to 10x faster design closure,” but “revenue contribution is not expected to begin until 2027.”

surprises.description: GAAP EPS included a gain from the processor IP divestiture, an additional positive one-off item not quantified in the preview. The preview anticipated the sale’s closure but discussed it as a revenue headwind, not as a gain affecting reported GAAP EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP EPS was $2.84 including a gain from the processor IP divestiture.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “close of the Processor IP Solutions sale” and an “~$40M FY26 revenue headwind,” but did not mention a gain.

in_line: Full-year revenue guidance rose to $9.69–$9.74 billion, close to the preview’s base-case expectation of $9.68–$9.73 billion and consistent with its expected modest raise.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $928 million, above the preview’s $904–905 million consensus and $902–905 million company guide. The roughly 2.5% beat was stronger than the preview’s stated base-case range of $915–922 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 total revenue reached $928 million,” exceeding the company’s guidance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $904.1M (Zacks) / $905.3M (street composite) | $902–905M”; the base case was “$915–922M.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating income reached $416 million, well above the preview’s roughly $393 million consensus and $392–395 million guide. That also implies an operating margin around 44.8%, versus the preview’s expected roughly 43.6% and year-over-year compression.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income of $416 million,” exceeding the company’s guidance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income | ~$393M | $392–395M”; “Non-GAAP op margin | ~43.6%”; the preview described Q2 margin as down about 110 bps year over year.

surprises.description: Commercial subscription growth was about 13%, above the preview’s 11.3% estimate and contrary to its concern that this was the weaker side of the business. Growth was also double-digit excluding Crossix, with strength across CRM, content, data, and Crossix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The commercial subscription segment grew approximately 13% year-over-year, with double-digit growth even excluding Crossix,” driven by broad-based strength.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Commercial Solutions subscription growth (est. +11.3%). The weak side of the house”; the preview said a sub-11% print would undercut the CRM-win narrative.

surprises.description: CRM momentum appears ahead of the preview’s expectation that Veeva would win a majority of four remaining top-20 migration decisions: management reported 12 of the top 20 committed, with only two more expected to be decided by year-end. The call also identified Regeneron as a Vault CRM selection; Biogen’s selection had already been announced before the release.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Best CRM quarter ever,” including “Biogen and Regeneron selecting Vault CRM”; “12 of the top 20 biopharma companies committed to Vault CRM, with only 2 remaining that are expected to be decided by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had expected “to win the majority of the four remaining top-20 CRM migration decisions by fiscal year-end”; the preview also noted Biogen was already announced.

surprises.description: More than 180 CRM customers are now live, substantially above the preview’s cited installed-base reference of more than 125 exiting FY26. The preview flagged the live-customer count as a metric to watch but did not anticipate a figure this high.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Veeva has over 180 CRM customers live.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total live customers (was >125 exiting FY26).”

surprises.description: AI use has moved beyond general monetization discussion to a large-scale customer deployment: one top-20 customer activated AI across its entire sales force, while management said Salesforce had no customers live. The preview focused on Falcon economics and monetization rather than this adoption proof point.
surprises.fact_evidence: “One top 20 customer activated AI across its entire sales force this quarter, contrasting with Salesforce having no customers live.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “Veeva AI monetization detail” and described quantified Falcon bookings or revenue framing as the potential upside surprise.

surprises.description: Falcon has five early adopters and first go-lives are expected this year, but management said product readiness—not customer interest—is the constraint. That tempers the opportunity: the preview highlighted monetization proof and an upcoming early-adopter release, but did not flag Veeva’s own product readiness as the bottleneck.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Veeva Falcon … has 5 early adopters including one top 20 pharma, with first go-lives expected this year,” and management identified “being the rate-limiter on product readiness as the key constraint despite very high customer interest.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Falcon early adopters were expected ahead of a November release and described bookings, pipeline, or FY28 revenue framing as the key potential upside.

surprises.description: Management expects Falcon gross margins to be roughly similar to software margins, a more favorable cost outlook than the preview’s concern that AI investment was weighing on margins without yet producing AI revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Falcon gross margins to be roughly similar to software margins,” because much of the work is pushed into deterministic software and AI model prices are expected to decline.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said AI investment was “showing up in the P&L” and framed the bear case as “AI capex without AI revenue.”

surprises.description: Management described a longer-dated route to recapturing CRM customers that chose Salesforce: it expects some wins primarily in 2027–2028, before the backstop expires at the end of 2029. That provides a competitive opportunity but places the expected recovery mainly beyond the near term.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is targeting “maintained CRM market leadership of over 70% share” and expects to win back some customers who selected Salesforce, “primarily in 2027-2028 before the Veeva CRM backstop expires end of 2029.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted the Vault CRM scoreboard and asked when revenue from new wins would turn on, noting that near-term contribution was likely immaterial; it did not provide a win-back timeline.

surprises.description: Management disclosed a horizontal CRM startup, Aspen, with a simplified $50-per-user monthly price plus usage overages. The planned financial exposure is minimal and no revenue is included in plans, while management is confident the market exists but uncertain about execution—an unanticipated new initiative with both limited near-term downside and execution risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Aspen horizontal CRM startup carries minimal financial investment with no revenue factored into plans,” uses “$50 per user per month plus usage overages,” and management expressed “100% confidence the market exists but uncertainty on execution.”

surprises.description: HP reported Q3 non-GAAP EPS of $0.83, well above the $0.66 consensus bar and even the preview’s roughly $0.70 whisper. The $0.11 tariff-refund benefit helped, but EPS was still above the high end of company guidance without it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS was $0.83, up 11%, and included $0.11 from tariff refunds, though EPS still exceeded the top of guidance even excluding that benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Zacks consensus (as of the Aug 2026 preview) is $0.66”; “Treat $0.66 as the published bar and ~$0.70 as the whisper.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue of $15.7 billion substantially exceeded the preview’s $14.60 billion consensus estimate and was also above the preview’s bull-case range of $14.9–$15.2 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HP delivered record Q3 revenue of $15.7 billion, up 13% year-over-year (11% in constant currency).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $14.60B (Zacks)”; bull scenario: “Revenue $14.9–15.2B (+7–9%).”

surprises.description: HP raised FY26 EPS guidance to $3.19–$3.29 from $2.90–$3.10, a much stronger upward revision than the preview’s base case of no raise or a narrow-up. The new range includes an estimated $0.19 tariff-refund benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HP raised full-year EPS guidance to $3.19–$3.29 (from $2.90–$3.10) … including $0.19 of estimated tariff refund benefit for the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 EPS guide vs. $2.90–$3.10”; base case: “FY26 guide narrowed to ~$2.95–$3.10 (no cut, no raise)”; a floor increase was described as “a genuine surprise.”

surprises.description: The Q4 EPS outlook of $0.69–$0.79 was higher than the preview’s base-case expectation of about $0.65 and the roughly $0.67 implied by the prior full-year guide. The range includes $0.08 of tariff-refund benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 EPS guidance is $0.69–$0.79, including $0.08 of tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 EPS framed at ~$0.65”; the preview also said the old full-year guide implied Q4 EPS of “~$0.67.”

surprises.description: Personal Systems units fell about 16%, a sharper decline than the 7% drop cited for Q2, even as price and premium mix lifted segment revenue. That is a concerning indication of the unit elasticity the preview flagged as a key debate around PC price increases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Personal Systems revenue hit a record $11.8 billion, up 18%, with commercial up 22% and consumer up 10%, despite units declining ~16%, driven by pricing, premium mix, and services.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Units fell 7% in Q2 … even as revenue rose 13% — all growth was price/mix”; “the question is whether 15–20% price increases start destroying demand.”

surprises.description: Tariff refunds provided an unanticipated one-off boost to reported results: they contributed $0.11 to Q3 EPS and were the main reason Print operating margin rose year over year. The preview discussed trade-related costs but did not flag refunds as a benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS was $0.83 … and included $0.11 from tariff refunds”; Print margin was “~1 point higher year-over-year mainly due to tariff refunds.”

surprises.description: HP also raised FY26 free-cash-flow guidance to $3.0–$3.2 billion from $2.8–$3.0 billion, above the preview’s expected reaffirmation and back-half weighting.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HP raised … free cash flow guidance to $3.0–$3.2 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 FCF guide $2.8–$3.0B”; base case: “FCF reaffirmed but back-half weighted.”

surprises.description: Print revenue declined 2% (4% in constant currency), rather than holding around the flat level cited for Q2. The preview highlighted positive Q2 Supplies growth, so the reported contraction points to weaker segment momentum than that recent indicator suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Print revenue declined 2% (down 4% in constant currency).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Print is the profit engine: $4.2B revenue (flat)”; “Supplies +1% in Q2.”

surprises.description: HP reported that key growth areas grew 46% year over year, a strong growth disclosure not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Key growth areas grew 46% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: Tank printers delivered 42% unit growth and gained 4 points of share, an unexpectedly strong Print product result that the preview did not discuss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tank printers achieved 42% unit growth with 4 points of share gain.”

surprises.description: HP disclosed a new three-year, $100 million agreement with print services provider RRD, a commercial win not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HP signed a 3-year, $100 million agreement with print services provider RRD.”

in_line: Personal Systems operating margin was 4.6%, close to the preview’s roughly 4.5% base case and consistent with expectations that it would remain below the long-term range; the Q4 low point and improvement in FY27 were also anticipated.

Print operating margin was 18.1%; excluding tariff refunds it was at the low end of the long-term range, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of a margin near the lower end and its concern about a result below 18%.

AI PCs were 46% of Personal Systems shipment mix and are expected to reach 60–70% in 2027 and more than 70% in 2028, broadly consistent with the preview’s 60–70% next-fiscal-year and greater-than-70% FY28 targets.

Personal Systems revenue is expected to grow year over year but decline sequentially in Q4, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a Q4 trough. The call also said margins should improve in FY27, matching the preview’s focus on reaffirmation of sequential recovery.

surprises.description: Q2 comparable sales grew 4.1%, far above the roughly 1% company guide and above the preview’s 2%–3.5% whisper range. The result also exceeded the preview’s 3%–4% bull-case range at its upper end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 comparable sales grew 4.1%, significantly beating guidance of approximately 1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the whisper “+2% to +3.5%” and listed the company guide as “~+1.0%.”

surprises.description: Best Buy raised full-year guidance more than the preview’s expected modest increase: comps are now expected to grow 1.9%–3%, and adjusted EPS is $6.70–$6.90. Both ranges are above the preview’s base case of roughly +1% to +2% comps and $6.45–$6.70 EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Best Buy raised full-year fiscal 2027 guidance to comparable sales growth of 1.9%-3%, adjusted EPS of $6.70-$6.90, and revenue of $42.3-$42.8 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “comps +1% to +2% and adj. EPS $6.45–6.70”; it said the FY27 EPS guide might be raised to “$6.60–6.85” in the bull case.

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was $1.47, above the preview’s $1.34–$1.38 consensus range and the $1.40–$1.45 base-case range. It was just below the preview’s bull-case low of $1.48.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS rose 15% year-over-year to $1.47.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Adjusted diluted EPS” consensus of “$1.34–$1.38” and a base case of “$1.40–1.45.”

surprises.description: The adjusted operating income rate reached 4.3%, versus the preview’s expectation of about 3.9% and its assumption of a flat year-over-year rate. That is a notably stronger margin result than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income rate of 4.3%, up roughly 40 basis points versus last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed adjusted operating income rate consensus at “~3.9%” and described the guide as “~3.9% adjusted OI rate (flat y/y).”

surprises.description: Revenue of $9.8 billion exceeded the preview’s $9.58–$9.59 billion consensus estimate. The size of the beat was meaningful, though the result fell within the preview’s bull-case revenue range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue of $9.8 billion (up 3.6% year-over-year).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 revenue consensus was “$9.58–9.59B.”

surprises.description: Marketplace GMV was about $300 million in Q2 and the full-year target rose to $1.3 billion, above the preview’s stated $1.2 billion-or-more target. The preview had identified a run-rate above $1.2 billion as an important test.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The domestic marketplace generated ~$300 million GMV in Q2, with full-year GMV now expected to reach $1.3 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Marketplace did “~$250M GMV in Q1 against a ≥$1.2B FY27 target” and flagged a “run-rating above $1.2B.”

surprises.description: The margin outlook included a previously unanticipated $34 million tariff-refund benefit, with similar IEEPA refunds assumed in Q3. The preview emphasized Marketplace and Ads as the expected sources of gross-profit-rate improvement, so the reported refund contribution makes the margin support less purely structural than that framing suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit rate expansion included a $34 million tariff refund benefit, with similar IEEPA refunds assumed in Q3; full-year gross margin expected to improve 30-40 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for gross-profit-rate expansion “≥ +20bps” with Marketplace GMV and Ads, saying it would “prove the margin story is structural, not cost-cutting.”

surprises.description: The full-year domestic marketplace GMV plan also now includes adding international sellers later this quarter, a development the preview did not anticipate. This expands the marketplace plan beyond the domestic GMV target discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International sellers [are] being added later this quarter.”

surprises.description: Emerging categories such as AI glasses, trading cards and health rings more than doubled year over year and now contribute about one percentage point of comps. The preview did not flag this source of sales growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Emerging categories including AI glasses, trading cards and health rings more than doubled year-over-year and now contribute about 1 point of comp.”

surprises.description: Computing extended its positive-comp streak to a tenth consecutive quarter, versus the preview’s stated nine-quarter streak. That is a further quarter of durability than the preview had identified, although management expects growth to slow in the back half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Computing delivered its tenth consecutive quarter of positive comps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described computing as being on a “9-quarter positive comp streak.”

surprises.description: Memory-cost inflation is producing mid-teens growth in computing average selling prices while unit sales fall by high single digits, and management expects that pattern to persist through the year. The preview discussed whether the computing cycle was peaking but did not anticipate this specific price-and-volume split.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Memory cost increases drove computing ASPs up mid-teens while units declined high single digits, a dynamic expected to persist through the rest of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview framed the computing debate as whether the “AI PC + Windows refresh” cycle was peaking.

surprises.description: Domestic TV sales grew more than 10% year over year, a strong result for a home-theater area the preview had highlighted as slightly negative in Q1 and still awaiting the RGB television launch as a swing factor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Domestic TV sales grew more than 10% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “home theater … was slightly negative in Q1” and described the RGB television launch as “the swing factor for home theater.”

surprises.description: August quarter-to-date comps were tracking at the high end of the 1%–3% guidance range, providing a stronger early read on the next quarter than the preview’s cautious second-half framing suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3-to-date comps in August are tracking at the high end of the 1%-3% guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “cautious H2 language” and identified holiday promotional uncertainty as a concern.

surprises.description: Higher incentive compensation is adding about $130 million to full-year SG&A year over year, a specific cost pressure the preview did not mention. Management expects roughly a $100 million reduction in incentive compensation next year, so the pressure is expected to ease later.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Incentive compensation is pressuring SG&A, increasing approximately $130 million year-over-year for full year, and is expected to reset lower (~$100 million reduction) next year.”

in_line: Management expects computing growth to slow in the back half as it laps the Windows 10 end-of-support tailwind, consistent with the preview’s concern that the computing cycle could be peaking.

surprises.description: The preview expected storage deliveries of 2.8–3.2 GWh. e-STORAGE shipped 3.7 GWh and recognized revenue on 3.3 GWh, exceeding that range, although recognized revenue was only slightly above its top end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “e-STORAGE shipped 3.7 GWh and recognized revenue on 3.3 GWh, exceeding guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company guide — storage | 2.8–3.2 GWh (incl. ~0.4 GWh internal)”

surprises.description: The preview identified Jeffersonville’s first commercial module delivery in Q3 as the HJT milestone to watch. Canadian Solar reported that its first commercially operational US HJT cell facility had opened and was ramping Phase 1, with full production planned for October 1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company opened the first commercially operational HJT solar cell facility in the US (Jeffersonville), ramping Phase 1 to 2.1 GW-peak with full production October 1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Jeffersonville Phase I (2.1 GW) first commercial module delivery targeted Q3'26 — confirmation or slip.”

surprises.description: The preview discussed the HJT price premium but did not anticipate a large contracted backlog for domestically made HJT and TOPCon modules. Canadian Solar reported more than 13 GW-peak of contracted backlog worth over $4.5 billion, with deliveries extending through 2029.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CSI Solar has secured over 13 GW-peak of contracted backlog for domestically manufactured HJT and TOPCon modules valued at more than $4.5 billion, with deliveries through 2029.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “HJT is carrying a stated 10–15% price premium over TOPCon.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on FEOC/PFE and 45X clarity, but the call instead offered a favorable, unanticipated outlook on Section 232: management expects exemptions tied to US investment and expects policy-driven US pricing to benefit CSI Solar. It also said the existing module backlog excludes Section 232 pricing adjustments that could raise contract values as agreements are renegotiated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 13 GW backlog does not yet include any Section 232 polysilicon pricing adjustments, which management expects will push contract values upward as agreements are renegotiated”; management “expects to qualify for Section 232 tariff/MIP exemptions” and views the policy as “net positive and accretive to CSI Solar even without full rebates due to higher US module pricing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FEOC / Prohibited Foreign Entity status and 45X eligibility. Mizuho's upgrade rests entirely on CSIQ qualifying as non-PFE. Definitive commentary either way is a step-change.”

surprises.description: The preview modeled total segment operating income of about a $42 million loss, while the reported manufacturing and Recurrent losses together were about $68 million. The manufacturing loss was driven in part by Jeffersonville ramp-up expenses, making segment performance weaker than that estimate despite the in-line gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The manufacturing segment posted a $49 million operating loss”; Recurrent Energy posted “a $19 million operating loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Segment op income … Q2'26E (base) … ~−$42M.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged Recurrent project-sale timing as a risk and assumed no large sale would close in-quarter, but it did not anticipate an impairment charge on an upcoming sale. Recurrent recorded a $24 million impairment on a Latin America project sale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurrent Energy generated only $117 million of revenue and a $19 million operating loss, dragged by deferred project sales and a $24 million impairment on an upcoming Latin America project sale.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No large Recurrent project sale closing in-quarter”; the preview also identified “deferral of Recurrent project sales to 2027” as a bear-case signal.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue reached the high end of the company’s range and was slightly above the preview’s $1.17 billion consensus figure. The gap was small, and gross margin was within the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue reached $1.2 billion at the high end of guidance, with gross margin of 13.9% in line with expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $1.17B”; company guide was “$1.0–1.2B.”

in_line: Q2 gross margin was 13.9%, within the preview’s expected 13–15% range.

The $1.40 Q2 loss per share was within the preview’s modeled range of approximately −$1.20 to −$1.60; the preview specifically warned that vendor EPS estimates varied widely and that there was no reliable consensus beat/miss line.
Q3 revenue guidance of $1.3–1.5 billion was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of roughly $1.3 billion or more.
The storage contracted backlog of $3.5 billion covering 34 GWh was consistent with the preview’s cited $3.5 billion and 34 GWh.
The preview anticipated about $1.3 billion in FY26 CapEx and warned that debt was rising; the call projected around $1.3 billion of CapEx and reported higher debt.

surprises.description: Dollar Tree raised FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $7.70–$8.05, well above the preview’s expected new floor of about $6.90–$7.00 and top end of $7.15+. The updated range includes an approximately $0.60 net tariff-refund benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was updated to… adjusted EPS of $7.70-$8.05, including an approximately $0.60 net tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bar is a new floor of ~$6.90–7.00 and a top end of $7.15+.”

surprises.description: Underlying Q2 EPS was $1.39, above both the $1.00–$1.15 company outlook and the preview’s $1.11–$1.12 consensus. This was a genuine earnings beat even excluding the unusual tariff-related benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS was $2.70, of which $1.31 came from the net impact of tariff refunds, reinvestments, and certain duties, implying underlying EPS of $1.39 versus the $1.00-$1.15 outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS… Consensus: $1.11–1.12”; “Company Guide… $1.00–1.15.”

surprises.description: The company received $383 million in tariff refunds despite the preview’s assumption that refunds would be excluded from guidance and reinvested rather than flow through to EPS. The related tariff items contributed $1.31 to Q2 diluted EPS and 680 basis points to gross margin, creating a much larger reported benefit than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $383 million in tariff refunds (benefiting gross profit by $369 million)”; “Gross margin expanded 850 basis points to 42.9%, including a 680 basis point benefit from tariff-related items”; diluted EPS included “$1.31… from the net impact of tariff refunds, reinvestments, and certain duties.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management… explicitly assumes no tariff refunds in the outlook (any refunds would be reinvested, not dropped to EPS)”; “Refunds are excluded from guidance and management said they would be reinvested.”

surprises.description: Q2 sales and comps came in above published consensus: sales were $4.9 billion versus $4.85–$4.86 billion expected, and comps were 3.7% versus 3.1%. The comp was also above the preview’s 3.4%–3.8% functional-whisper range only at its lower-to-middle portion, so the upside was more noticeable against published consensus than against the buy-side bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales grew 7% to $4.9 billion with comparable store sales up 3.7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Consensus | $4.85–4.86B”; “Comparable store sales | +3.1%”; “functional whisper is therefore comp ~3.4–3.8%.”

surprises.description: Traffic was positive, as the preview’s central thesis hoped, but at +0.4% it was below the preview’s cited +1.4% Q2 foot-traffic data and far below July’s +4.5% reading. Ticket growth of 3.3% supplied most of the comp, rather than a stronger traffic contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable store sales up 3.7% (traffic +0.4%, ticket +3.3%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Placer.ai data… shows Q2 foot traffic +1.4%… and July at +4.5%”; “reported traffic turning positive.”

surprises.description: A helium supply shortage unexpectedly reduced sales by about $15 million, or roughly 30 basis points of comp. The preview did not flag this supply constraint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A helium supply shortage [was] estimated to have cut total sales by about $15 million or roughly 30 basis points of comp.”

surprises.description: Dollar Tree reported that stores in its “opportunity for improvement” category fell from about half the fleet at last October’s Investor Day to about one-third. The preview discussed execution and multi-price opportunities but did not anticipate this specific scale of store-level improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Stores in the ‘opportunity for improvement’ category declined from about half of the fleet at last October's Investor Day to about one-third today.”

in_line: The company repurchased $605 million of shares in Q2, consistent with the preview’s bull-case marker of at least $500 million; the approximately 8% trailing-12-month share-count reduction was also already cited in the preview.
Management’s warnings that gross margin would face fuel-driven freight and tariff-related pressure in the second half were consistent with the preview’s flagged 2H tariff, fuel, and freight risks.

surprises.description: Service revenue reached $124.4 million, above the preview’s $119–121 million estimate, and gross margin expanded to 74% despite the preview’s warning that temporarily low medical claims costs would reverse. Management attributed the margin improvement to AI-enabled service cost reductions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue up 6% to a record $124.4 million”; “Gross profit was a record $258 million (~74% of revenue), up from 71% a year earlier, driven by AI-enabled service cost reductions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Service revenue ~$119–121M (est.)”; management said “~$2M of the service-cost beat came from temporarily depressed employee medical claims” and was “pushed back into the forecast as non-sustainable.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $167 million, above the preview’s estimated $158–163 million range. The result also came with a record 48% adjusted EBITDA margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached a record $167 million, up 11% year-over-year, with a record adjusted EBITDA margin of 48%, up from 46% a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$158–163M (est.)” and “+5–8%” implied year-over-year.

surprises.description: New HSAs from sales grew 24%, accelerating from the preview’s cited Q1 pace of 172,000 accounts and 15% growth. That is a stronger sales result than the preview’s durability test implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New HSAs from sales up 24% year-over-year, setting a Q2 record and the strongest quarter outside open enrollment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 added 172K new HSAs, +15%” and the preview flagged “New HSAs from sales vs. 172K/+15%” as a key test.

surprises.description: Fiscal 2027 guidance increased only slightly on revenue and adjusted EBITDA, while the non-GAAP EPS range was unchanged. That fell short of the preview’s base-case expectation for an upward revenue narrowing and an EPS nudge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised fiscal 2027 guidance to revenue of $1.411–$1.421 billion, non-GAAP EPS of $4.66–$4.73, GAAP EPS of $2.88–$2.96, and adjusted EBITDA of $628–$636 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “FY27 revenue guide narrowed upward, EPS nudged to ~$4.72–4.80”; the prior guide was revenue “$1.410–1.420B” and non-GAAP EPS “$4.66–4.73/sh.”

surprises.description: GAAP EPS was $0.78, below the preview’s $0.85–0.94 estimate range, even though reported GAAP net income was a record. The company cited a $3.3 million one-time software disposal expense.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income was a record $65.6 million ($0.78 per diluted share), the latter including $3.3 million of one-time software disposal expense.”

surprises.description: Repurchases were about $108 million, below the preview’s expectation that a pace above roughly $125 million per quarter would support the share-count guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased approximately $108 million of shares at an average price below $90.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$123M repurchased in Q1” and said “Pace above ~$125M/quarter supports the ~84M share guide.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was $1.24, above the preview’s approximately $1.19 consensus estimate, though it remained within the preview’s base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net income was $103.8 million ($1.24 per diluted share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS ~ $1.19.”

surprises.description: Revenue came in modestly above the preview’s approximately $349 million consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue grew 8% year-over-year to approximately $351 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue ~ $349M.”

surprises.description: The company reported that investing HSA members grew more than 20%, above the preview’s cited 18% growth, and launched a no-fee SimplyInvest lineup—an additional product development not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Investing members grew over 20% (about 9% of total members) with a new SimplyInvest no-fee lineup launched.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “909K HSAs with investments (+18%)” and “invested balances +38%”; it did not mention a SimplyInvest launch.

surprises.description: Management reported that monthly active app users rose 62% year-over-year and that Health Savings Days drew 500,000 unique visitors, operating-engagement details not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marketplace ended the quarter with over 14,000 active members and drove 500,000 unique visitors during Health Savings Days”; “monthly active app users hit 1.4 million, up 62% year-over-year.”

in_line: Custodial revenue was $175.9 million, within the preview’s estimated $172–176 million range.
Interchange revenue was $50.4 million and grew 5%, matching the preview’s estimate of approximately $50–51 million and 5% growth.

surprises.description: Burlington’s Q2 adjusted EPS was $2.37 even excluding the $0.64 tariff-refund benefit, above the preview’s $2.19 consensus and the $2.20 top of guidance. That is a clear underlying earnings beat despite comps coming in below the preview’s expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EPS was $2.37, up 38% year-over-year (excluding a $0.64 tariff refund benefit) and above the guidance range of $2.05-$2.20.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS … Consensus $2.19”; the preview also says consensus was at the “high end of guide.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBIT margin expanded 100 basis points, well above the previewed consensus of about 50 basis points and the company’s 30–60-basis-point guidance. The 70-basis-point merchandise-margin gain was especially strong relative to the preview’s focus on whether the prior quarter’s merchandise-margin improvement could hold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBIT margin expanded 100 basis points to 7%, well above guidance of 30-60 basis points, driven by a 70bp merchandise margin gain, 20bp of supply chain leverage, and 50bp of SG&A leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Op. margin … Guidance +30 to +60 bps; Consensus ~+50 bps”; the preview also says, “Q1’s +20 bps needs to hold against +11% comp inventory.”

surprises.description: Comps rose only 2%, below the preview’s roughly 3–4% expectation and at the midpoint of company guidance. The preview’s share-gain debate therefore did not resolve with an above-consensus comp; transactions were flat and the increase came entirely from larger baskets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comp store sales rose only 2% (midpoint of the 1%-3% guidance), pressured by an elevated 1.5 percentage point cannibalization headwind from new store openings”; “Q2 comp was driven entirely by higher basket size with flat transactions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comp store sales … Consensus ~+3–4% (buy-side higher)”; the preview says a “4-handle or better” would validate the share-gain narrative.

surprises.description: Total sales grew 11%, slightly below the preview’s 11.8% consensus growth expectation, though still within company guidance. The sales growth result was therefore less strong than the headline consensus bar even as EPS and margins beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total sales grew 11%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales … Consensus $3.02B (+11.8%)”; the preview described consensus as at the “high end” of the +10% to +12% guidance.

surprises.description: The tariff refund was about $55 million, below the preview’s rough $100–130 million pre-tax estimate, and Burlington plans to reinvest all of it in sharper pricing rather than retain it as an earnings benefit. The preview flagged possible additive earnings treatment; instead, management said the full-year earnings impact would be neutral, with reinvestment weighing on Q3 and Q4 margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received approximately $55 million in tariff refunds in Q2 but plans to fully reinvest them into sharper pricing across Q3 (40%) and Q4 (60%), making the full-year earnings impact neutral.” Q3 and Q4 operating margins are expected to be down due to the reinvestment.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “a rough $100–130M pre-tax” refund and said to watch “whether it lands in GAAP EPS, whether adj. EPS excludes it, and whether any of it is reinvested in price.”

surprises.description: Management sounded more cautious about the consumer, citing persistently high gas prices and weak sector-wide Q2 comps. The preview discussed competitive and category risks, but did not flag gas prices as a concern Burlington management might emphasize.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management turned more cautious on the consumer, citing persistently elevated gas prices and weak sector-wide Q2 comps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a possible “off-price category” split and asked whether “Burlington’s value positioning should be fine,” but did not mention elevated gas prices or an explicitly more cautious consumer tone.

surprises.description: Burlington reported a record pace of store openings and strong new-store economics: 149 net openings over the trailing 12 months, with annual sales above $7 million and payback under two years. The preview cited a plan for 115 net and 135 gross openings for FY2026 but did not anticipate these reported trailing-12-month scale and productivity figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company opened 178 gross (149 net) new stores over the trailing 12 months—a company record—averaging ~27,000 sq ft, over $7 million in annual sales, and payback under 2 years, targeting 1,500+ stores by end of 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year FY2026 guide … 115 net new stores (135 gross).”

in_line: Full-year comp guidance of +3% to +4% and total-sales growth guidance of +10% to +11% remained within the preview’s expected ranges of +2% to +4% comps and +9% to +11% sales.
Full-year adjusted EPS guidance of $11.77–$11.97 was broadly in the preview’s base-case range of about $11.75–$12.00 and near the $11.84 Street estimate, rather than clearly exceeding the Street.

Comp-store inventories remained up 11%, close to the elevated inventory level highlighted in the preview, while reserve inventory was lower at 43% of total versus 50% a year ago—consistent with the preview’s focus on lower reserve inventory as a favorable composition signal.

surprises.description: Dollar General raised FY2026 EPS guidance to $7.80–$8.00, well above the preview’s expected raise to roughly $7.35–$7.55 and the prior $7.20–$7.45 range. The sales and comp guidance increases were also stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year fiscal 2026 guidance to net sales growth of 4%-4.3%, same-store sales growth of 2.5%-2.9%, and EPS of $7.80-$8.00.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 EPS guide: raise to ~$7.35–$7.55 vs. maintain $7.20–$7.45”; the bull scenario expected “Raised to $7.35–$7.55.”

surprises.description: Gross margin expanded 127 basis points, far above the preview’s roughly 35–40 basis-point bridge and even the 50–65 basis-point bull case. Tariff refunds contributed 81 basis points, but the reported expansion also included lower LIFO and improvements in shrink and damages.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 127 basis points to 32.6%, including an 81 basis point benefit from tariff refunds net of reinvestment, aided by lower LIFO, shrink and damage improvements, despite higher transportation costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s EPS bridge required “gross margin +35–40bps”; its bull scenario assumed “GM +50–65bps.”

surprises.description: The quarter’s headline EPS substantially exceeded the $2.00 consensus, reaching $2.48. The roughly $0.25 tariff-refund benefit was within the preview’s estimated refund range, but EPS excluding that benefit was still about $2.23, above consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EPS increased 33% to $2.48, including approximately $0.25 benefit from tariff refunds after related reinvestments, with operating profit up 29.2% to $769 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS: $2.00” consensus; the preview estimated a possible tariff-refund benefit of “$0.20–$0.80/share.”

surprises.description: Sales and same-store sales outpaced the preview’s expectations: net sales were $11.3 billion versus $11.17 billion consensus, while comps were 3.5% versus the derived 2.2–2.5% estimate. Traffic growth of 2% was a particularly strong component of the comp result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales rose 5.2% to $11.3 billion, with same-store sales up 3.5% driven by 2% traffic growth and 1.5% basket growth, marking the fifth consecutive quarter of traffic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $11.17B”; same-store sales were estimated at “~2.2–2.5% (derived).”

surprises.description: Dollar General will resume share repurchases in the second half of 2026, earlier than the preview’s expectation of no buybacks planned for 2026 and the long-term framework’s initial 2027 timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Dollar General will resume share repurchases in Q3, buying up to $700 million of stock in the second half funded with cash on hand, ahead of the initial 2027 timeline in its long-term framework.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “no share repurchases planned” for FY2026 and noted that any reopening of repurchases would be a “meaningful narrative shift.”

surprises.description: The expected contribution from shrink and damage improvements now looks stronger and more durable than the preview’s cautious margin assumptions: management expects about 50 basis points of additional gross-margin expansion on the 2025 base, beyond the 80-plus basis points already achieved in 2025, and said this exceeds original targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Shrink and damages are now expected to add about 50 basis points of gross margin expansion on the 2025 base, on top of 80-plus basis points achieved in 2025, exceeding original targets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the prior-year shrink tailwind was “largely lapped” and anticipated shrink contributing “~0–25bps”; it flagged damages as a possible offset but did not expect this stronger outlook.

in_line: Tariff refunds were recognized in Q2: the preview flagged a possible Q2 refund benefit of roughly $0.20–$0.80 per share, and the reported benefit was approximately $0.25 per share.

Delivery contributed less to comps than in the prior quarter as its contribution scaled down while lapping prior growth; the preview had flagged delivery’s prior-quarter contribution and expected it to be watched.

Management’s commentary on affluent-customer trade-down and continued pressure on lower-income core customers was broadly consistent with the preview’s discussion of accelerating higher-income trade-in and constrained core customers amid fuel costs.

surprises.description: Q4 net sales were $295.5 million, about 12% above the $263.9 million consensus and well above the company-guidance range of $261–267 million. The sales beat was substantially larger than the preview’s expected result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 fiscal 2026 net sales rose 42.7% to $295.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Q4 FY26 Consensus | $263.9M”; “Guidance-Implied | $261–267M.”

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EBITDA was $33.9 million, above the preview’s expected $29.5–31.5 million range and roughly $30 million consensus. The dollar result beat expectations even though the reported margin was close to the preview’s roughly 11.4% expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 fiscal 2026 net sales rose 42.7% to $295.5 million, with adjusted EBITDA up 72.7% to $33.9 million and margins expanding 200 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$30M”; “Guidance-Implied | $29.5–31.5M”; “Adj. EBITDA margin | ~11.4%.”

surprises.description: Full-year FY2026 sales reached $914.6 million, about $29 million above the raised guidance ceiling and well above the preview’s $883.2 million consensus. This exceeded the full-year revenue expectation by a meaningful amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year fiscal 2026 net sales reached $914.6 million (up 13.3%), about $29 million above the raised guidance top end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year FY2026: Guidance $880–886M net sales”; “Consensus $883.2M.”

surprises.description: Legacy Q4 sales were $234.3 million, well above the preview’s implied roughly $202–210 million and contrary to its expectation of roughly flat legacy revenue. Cobalt and saltwater fishing were strong, while Malibu itself grew only 3.2% on lower unit volumes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 legacy net sales grew 13.2% to $234.3 million, driven by Cobalt (+31% to $70.5 million) and saltwater fishing (+11.1% to $80.9 million) volume gains, while Malibu grew only 3.2% to $82.9 million on lower unit volumes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied Legacy Q4 FY26 | Net sales | ~$202–210M”; “Δ | ~flat.”

surprises.description: SACSTOR’s Q4 sales of $61.2 million exceeded the preview’s expected $57–59 million. That contributed to the stronger-than-expected quarter, though its margin disappointed separately.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The March 2 SACSTOR acquisition contributed $61.2 million in Q4 revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided Saxdor separately: $57–59M revenue.”

surprises.description: Despite SACSTOR revenue exceeding expectations, its Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin was below the guided 10–11% range: the roughly $4 million contribution on $61.2 million of sales implies a margin of about 6.5%. Ramp investment at Fort Pierce and higher input costs were cited as the reasons.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin (~$4 million contribution) came in below the guided 10-11% range due to Fort Pierce ramp investments and higher input costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Saxdor separately: $57–59M revenue at 10–11% adj. EBITDA margin.”

surprises.description: FY2027 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $101–109 million came in below the preview’s implied sell-side range of roughly $105–115 million at the low end and has a midpoint below that range’s midpoint. Revenue guidance, by contrast, starts at the preview’s $1.08 billion consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 guidance projects net sales of $1.080-$1.120 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $101-$109 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2027 consensus (the real bar): ~$1.08B revenue (+22%) and ~ $2.53 EPS”; “FY2027 revenue + adj. EBITDA guidance… Consensus ~$1.08B / implied EBITDA roughly $105–115M.”

surprises.description: Q1 FY2027 guidance calls for only $14–16 million of adjusted EBITDA, with first-half margins weighed down by SACSTOR ramp investment. The preview gave no Q1 estimate, so this is a newly disclosed near-term earnings constraint rather than a miss against a stated Q1 forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 guidance calls for net sales of $255-$265 million and adjusted EBITDA of only $14-$16 million, with first-half margins weighed down by SACSTOR ramp investment.”

surprises.description: Full-year GAAP net income fell to $1.7 million, or $0.09 per share, down 88.8%, primarily because of SACSTOR acquisition and integration expenses. The preview focused on adjusted EPS and did not set an expectation for this GAAP result or these costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year GAAP net income dropped 88.8% to $1.7 million ($0.09/share), primarily due to SACSTOR acquisition and integration expenses.”

in_line: Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin was about 11.5% ($33.9 million on $295.5 million of sales), close to the preview’s roughly 11.4% expectation; the reported 200-basis-point year-over-year expansion also broadly matched its implied margin improvement.
FY2026 adjusted EBITDA of $73.9 million was within the preview’s cited $72–74 million guidance range, despite the substantial revenue overage.

FY2027 revenue guidance began at $1.080 billion, matching the preview’s roughly $1.08 billion consensus, and its low-to-mid single-digit legacy growth assumption was broadly consistent with the preview’s flat-to-modestly-up legacy outlook.

The modest improvement in retail registrations was consistent with the preview’s base-case expectation of stabilization: registrations were down roughly 3%, compared with mid-single-digit declines in the March quarter.
The company continued share repurchases and announced a new $70 million authorization, consistent with the preview’s emphasis on buybacks and the existing authorization’s remaining capacity.

surprises.description: TITN’s consolidated equipment margin reached 8.5%, well above the preview’s 6.5–7.0% expected band for the rest of FY27 and even the preview’s 7.5% bull-case threshold. Management attributed the gain to inventory-health initiatives, not a recovery in underlying industry demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated equipment margin improved 190 basis points year-over-year to 8.5%, driven by inventory health initiatives rather than any improvement in underlying industry demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guided 6.5–7.0% for the rest of FY27”; the bull case expected “Equipment margin ≥7.5%.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 18.6%, above the preview’s estimated 17.0–17.5% range. That expansion helped keep gross profit essentially flat despite lower revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit held essentially flat at $92.4 million as gross margin expanded 150 basis points to 18.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin ~17.0–17.5%.”

surprises.description: Domestic Ag same-store sales fell 8.4%, a substantially milder decline than the preview’s expected 12–18% decline. The preview had cautioned that a result better than -10% could reflect pull-forward timing rather than underlying upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Domestic Ag segment sales fell 8.4% same-store to $310.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A Q2 Ag SSS print in the −12% to −18% band is consistent with plan; better than −10% likely means more pull-forward risk deferred to Q4, not upside.”

surprises.description: Europe’s full-year revenue outlook was cut to a 30–40% decline, far worse than the preview’s modeled 20–25% decline. Management said about $44 million of the decline would come from the German wind-down.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year outlook was cut to a decline of 30-40%, with ~$44 million of the drop from the German wind-down.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company modeling assumptions of “Europe −20/−25%” and said to watch for any change to “the −20/−25% range.”

surprises.description: Construction’s full-year growth outlook rose to 5–10%, above the preview’s modeled 0–5% range, alongside positive same-store growth and a swing to pretax income.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Construction was a bright spot, growing 9.2% same-store to $78.6 million with pretax income of $0.4 million versus a $1.2 million loss last year, prompting an upgraded full-year growth outlook to 5-10%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company modeling assumptions of “Construction 0/+5%.”

surprises.description: Australia’s full-year growth outlook was raised to about 15–20%, above the preview’s 10–15% assumption, although management said 8 percentage points of the growth came from FX.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year growth guidance was raised to about 15-20% though 8 points come purely from FX.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company modeling assumptions of “Australia +10/+15%.”

surprises.description: Floorplan and interest expense fell 30%, a somewhat larger reduction than the preview’s approximately 25% full-year decline assumption. The preview had already identified lower floorplan interest as a reliable source of earnings improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Floorplan and interest expense fell 30% to $8.1 million on lower interest-bearing inventory.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Floorplan interest | ~−25% Y/Y”; the preview also said Q1 was “−26%” and guided “~−25% for the year.”

in_line: Revenue was $496.4 million, above the $486.5 million consensus and within the preview’s $495–510 million base-case range; the preview expected another revenue beat.
Adjusted EBITDA of $4.6 million was within the preview’s estimated $4–6 million range.
Management reaffirmed the full-year adjusted EBITDA range of $17–29 million and adjusted diluted loss-per-share range of $1.25–$1.75, as the preview expected.

The forecast for weaker Domestic Ag equipment sales in the back half due to delivery pull-forward was consistent with the preview’s expectation that timing reversals would weigh more heavily in Q3 and Q4.
Australia’s large year-over-year sales increase was broadly anticipated: the preview highlighted the 50.1% comparison decline, acquisition additions and FX tailwinds as drivers of a large gain.

surprises.description: BBW reported Q2 revenue of $115.3 million, about 4.6% below the preview’s $120.8 million consensus and below the cited consensus range. The decline was also steeper than the preview’s expected 2.8% year-over-year decrease.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 fiscal 2026 total revenue fell 7.2% year-over-year to $115.3 million” and results “fell short of company projections.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Consensus | $120.8M (range $116.2M–$121.3M)” and implied Y/Y “–2.8%.”

surprises.description: The company cut full-year revenue guidance to $500–$525 million from $530–$550 million, and pre-tax income guidance to $60–$68 million from $72–$78 million. This was a deeper reset than the preview’s base case of narrowing the range to its low end, and the revenue range is below the prior guidance floor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered full-year revenue guidance to $500-$525 million (from $530-$550 million) and cut pre-tax income guidance to $60-$68 million (from $72-$78 million), citing weak traffic and the loss of the Walmart program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance: held, narrowed, or cut?” The base case anticipated “FY revenue narrowed to low end ($530–540M), adj. pre-tax held”; the bear case anticipated a cut “below $530M and/or adj. pre-tax below $65M.”

surprises.description: BBW reduced its full-year commercial growth outlook from at least 20% to essentially flat, reversing the preview’s expectation that commercial would remain a growth engine. The preview had highlighted Walmart as a swing factor, but the guidance cut also reflects slower-than-expected wholesale opportunities.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial segment growth guidance was slashed from at least +20% to essentially flat,” driven by the inability to repeat last year’s Walmart order and slower-than-expected wholesale opportunities.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called commercial “the bright spot: +34.1% in Q1, guided to +20%+ FY” and said it “needs >$11.5M and reaffirmed +20% FY to keep the asset-light growth story alive.”

surprises.description: Q2 pre-tax income of $11.6 million was slightly above the preview’s implied $10.5–$11.5 million range, despite being down sharply year over year and below company projections. This was a small positive versus the preview’s estimate, not an overall indication that results met management’s plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pre-tax income declining 24.1% to $11.6 million from $15.3 million a year earlier,” with results falling short of company projections.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pre-tax income | ~$10.5–11.5M (implied).”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 54.2%, down 340 basis points, as occupancy costs deleveraged and the company promoted underperforming summer products. That contrasted with the preview’s recent evidence of improved gross margin and promo discipline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin contracted 340 basis points to 54.2%, driven by occupancy cost deleverage and increased promotional activity to clear underperforming summer trend products.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Q1 GM ex-refund was +140bps on higher AUR and promo discipline — genuinely good” and flagged “Gross margin ex-tariff and SG&A” as an issue to watch.

surprises.description: The Halloween launch produced exceptionally strong sales, including a company-record non-Q4 week, but management said it was still slightly below prior expectations. The strong signal for Q3 trends was encouraging against the preview’s concern about traffic, while the shortfall from expectations tempered the positive read.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Halloween launch delivered the highest non-Q4 sales week in company history and the third-highest US e-commerce sales week ever,” signaling improving trends “despite still being slightly below prior expectations.”

surprises.description: Management attributed weak traffic partly to a less-customizable summer collection, while highly customizable products such as Chummy Shark sold out. The preview focused on traffic and e-commerce declines but did not anticipate this product-level explanation or the contrast between the collections.
surprises.fact_evidence: The “underperforming summer trend collection (slushy plushies, berry goods) was less customizable and drove weaker traffic,” while “highly customizable products like the Chummy Shark sold out.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed about $3 million of long-term investments within its guidance assumptions, an additional cost not identified in the preview. The stated tariff-cost amount was broadly near the preview’s estimate, although the assumed tariff rate was higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guidance reflects $10-$11 million of tariff-related costs at a 12.5% rate plus ~$3 million of long-term investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Net tariff ~$10M FY at a 10% rate” and did not identify the additional long-term investments.

in_line: E-commerce demand declined 15.6% year over year, within the preview’s base-case expectation of a 15%–25% decline; the sequential improvement from Q1 was also consistent with the preview’s focus on whether the decline would moderate.
The company remained on track for at least 50 net new locations this year, matching the preview’s stated full-year location guidance.

surprises.description: Hormel lowered its FY2026 organic net sales growth outlook to 1%-2% from 1%-4%, citing weaker market and consumer conditions. The preview presented the 1%-4% range as the reaffirmed outlook, so the cut to the top end is a negative change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered its full-year organic net sales growth expectation to 1%-2% from a prior range of 1%-4%, citing weaker market and consumer conditions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance (reaffirmed at Q2, May 28): Net sales $12.2–$12.5B, organic +1–4%”

surprises.description: Q3 organic net sales declined 2%, whereas the preview’s headline net sales consensus implied 0.5% growth. The measures are not identical, but the reported organic decline indicates weaker underlying sales than the preview’s topline expectation suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 organic net sales declined 2% year-over-year, driven by portfolio shaping actions, softer commodity markets, and a pressured consumer.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales … +0.5%”

surprises.description: Q4 EPS is now expected to be about $0.37 at the midpoint, below the prior expectation of about $0.40. This indicates a weaker finish to the year than previously anticipated, despite the higher FY2026 guidance floor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 EPS is now expected at ~$0.37 at the midpoint versus a prior ~$0.40 expectation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus $0.36 in Q3 implies $0.33–$0.41 in Q4.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating margin expanded to 9% rather than declining year over year as the preview’s base case anticipated. The preview specifically called holding around 9% a positive surprise given fuel, logistics, and utilization pressures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating margin expanded 60 basis points year-over-year to 9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … margin down Y/Y on fuel”; “holding ~9% here would be a genuine positive surprise.”

surprises.description: Hormel raised the lower end of its FY2026 adjusted EPS range to $1.45 from $1.43, while keeping the upper end at $1.51. That is better than the preview’s base case of reaffirming the range, though short of its bull-case expectation of narrowing to $1.47–$1.51.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hormel raised and narrowed its fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $1.45-$1.51 from the prior $1.43-$1.51.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “a straight reaffirm is neutral”; “Narrowing to $1.47–$1.51 is the bull outcome.”

surprises.description: Q3 adjusted EPS was $0.37, one cent above the $0.36 consensus estimate. The preview viewed $0.36 as the key benchmark for the noisy quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 adjusted EPS was $0.37, up 6% versus last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS $0.36”; “Adjusted EPS $0.36 vs. the whisper.”

surprises.description: A one-time legal-entity transition depressed SPAM export sales, a temporary sales disruption not identified in the preview’s discussion of portfolio changes or key risks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A one-time legal entity transition depressed SPAM export sales.”

surprises.description: Hormel recorded an impairment on its Indonesia minority investment, an unanticipated charge not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company … recorded an Indonesia minority investment impairment.”

in_line: Foodservice continued to show the growth and resilience the preview identified as important: it delivered its 12th consecutive quarter of organic net sales growth, with profit growth outpacing sales. The call facts do not provide growth rates to determine whether it exceeded the preview’s consensus estimates.

The preview anticipated portfolio-related noise in Retail, including the whole-bird turkey divestiture and private-label reductions. The reported high-single-digit volume decline was partly attributed to those actions, with about half tied to portfolio changes.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $4.7 million, well above the preview’s derived $1.5–$2.0 million range. The preview had no published quarterly consensus, but this was about 2.4–3.1 times its estimated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $4.7 million,” including “$3.1 million of TRISO product revenue and $1.6 million of government service revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “I am using ~ $1.75M as the Q2 base case”; the preview’s derived range was “Q2 $1.5–2.0M.”

surprises.description: The Q2 net loss was far smaller than the preview’s scenario expectation: $3.4 million versus a base-case loss of $9–$11 million. The loss also narrowed from Q1, despite the ramp in operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed sequentially from $7.7 million in Q1 to $3.4 million ($0.12 per share), driven by first commercial product revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “Net Loss −$9M to −$11M”; it also said management had signaled “losses widen as production scales ahead of revenue.”

surprises.description: The August agreements lifted total backlog to $576.9 million and funded backlog to $119.3 million—far above the preview’s cited backlog levels, with funded backlog nearly doubling after June. The preview had identified a funded-backlog step-up and possible Radiant contribution as important, but did not anticipate this scale of increase or the Entegris/Antares agreement.
surprises.fact_evidence: Total backlog “reached $576.9 million after the August Entegris/Antares agreement”; funded backlog “approximately doubled to $119.3 million after the August fuel supply agreement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$245M” total backlog and “$65M funded,” and said to watch “whether funded backlog steps up.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 67% in a quarter when the preview characterized the company’s margin as deeply negative and said margin percentages carried little signal. The reported result indicates positive gross margin on the quarter’s product and service revenue, despite process yield of 63.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company achieved 67% gross margin in the quarter at a 63.3% process yield,” with the coating step at “95%-97% yield.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported “Gross margin” of “−244%” for Q1 and said “margin percentages carry little signal this quarter.”
