surprises.description: Management reported stronger evidence of prolonged tanker-market disruption than the preview’s central framing of Hormuz as a binary reopening risk: oil majors were seeking two-to-three-year VLCC charters, and 2028 U.S. Gulf-to-Asia FFA paper was near $100,000/day. Those signals point to expectations of elevated rates persisting well beyond the immediate quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Long-term charter demand has deepened with oil majors seeking 2-3 year VLCC deals, and 2028 FFA paper (TD22, U.S. Gulf to Asia) is trading near $100,000/day, signaling expectations that disruptions persist.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Hormuz reopening as “the only true binary” and treated management signaling “structurally longer disruption” as a bull-scenario condition.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a sizeable VLCC orderbook relative to the commercially active fleet: about 33.5% of the total fleet and nearly 40% after excluding largely sanctioned, non-trading vessels. The preview did not flag this future supply overhang, and management said the active-fleet comparison approaches 2008–2009 levels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The VLCC order book stands at ~33.5% of the total fleet but nears 40% of the commercially active fleet once ~166-167 non-trading (largely sanctioned, 20-plus-year-old) vessels are excluded, approaching 2008-2009 levels.”

in_line: The Q3 VLCC booked rate of $156,900/day was within the preview’s $150,000–$175,000 base-case range, even though the 86% booking coverage was much higher than assumed.
Selling older vessels into strong secondhand values was anticipated as a capital-allocation possibility in the preview; it specifically flagged further asset sales as something to watch.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $1.9 billion, well above the $1.76 billion consensus and the preview’s $1.78–$1.80 billion whisper range. Organic growth was approximately 5%, though about 1 percentage point came from unplanned material purchases that management does not expect to recur.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue was $1.9 billion with organic growth of approximately 5%, though roughly 1 point came from unplanned material purchases that management does not expect to repeat.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 Consensus” revenue: “$1.76B”; “Whisper is likely $1.78–1.80B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS of $3.01 substantially exceeded the preview’s $2.31 consensus estimate. The year-over-year decline was attributed mainly to the prior-year legal settlement, an effect the preview had already cautioned was not a clean measure of deterioration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS was $3.01, down year-over-year primarily due to a prior-period favorable legal settlement, partially offset by a lower share count.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY27 Consensus” adjusted diluted EPS: “$2.31”; the preview also said the prior-year settlement made the “optical Y/Y decline” an “unclean read on deterioration.”

surprises.description: Quarterly book-to-bill was only 0.6x and trailing-twelve-month book-to-bill was 0.8x, below the preview’s expectation of at least 1.0x and management’s stated full-year goal. Management said the quarter’s figure would have been near 1.0x if a large recompete had been booked two days later, but that timing caveat does not change the reported result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Book-to-bill was a weak 0.6x for the quarter (0.8x trailing twelve months), with management noting it would have been near 1.0x had a large recompete not been booked two days after quarter close.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management guided for full-year book-to-bill “comfortably over 1.0” and described the base scenario as “B2B ~1.0–1.1x.”

surprises.description: SAIC raised FY27 revenue guidance to a $7.25 billion midpoint and adjusted EBITDA guidance by 4% at the midpoint, taking the margin range to 10.3%–10.5%. This was stronger than the preview’s existing revenue guidance ceiling of $7.2 billion and its scenario for a modest guide increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised FY27 guidance, lifting revenue 2% to a $7.25 billion midpoint, adjusted EBITDA 4% at midpoint (margins of 10.3%-10.5%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY27 revenue guidance of “$7.0–$7.2B” and adjusted EBITDA margin guidance of “10.1%–10.3%”; its base scenario anticipated FY EPS “nudged to ~$10.10–10.25.”

surprises.description: The RITS roll-off was described as creating an approximately 350-basis-point revenue headwind, somewhat greater than the preview’s estimate of about a 3% organic headwind in each of Q3 and Q4. The expected second-half margin step-down to the high-9% range, however, is broadly consistent with the preview’s full-year margin math.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Second-half margins are expected to step down to the high-9% range due to targeted investments, with the RITS contract roll-off creating an approximately 350 basis point revenue headwind.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview sized RITS at “~$200M of 2H revenue, ~3% organic headwind in each of Q3 and Q4” and said full-year guidance implied “~9.7–10.0% average across Q2–Q4.”

surprises.description: Project ORBIT was quantified at approximately $150 million in annual run-rate savings by the end of three years, a concrete figure the preview did not have. About two-thirds is earmarked for reinvestment, with the remainder supporting margin expansion, so the savings are not all expected to flow through to margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Project ORBIT targets approximately $150 million in annual run-rate savings by the end of a 3-year period, with about two-thirds ($100 million) reinvested and the rest supporting margin expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Quantification — dollars, timing, reinvestment vs. flow-through — is the main narrative swing factor,” without giving an expected savings amount.

surprises.description: Management set a path to mid-10% margins next year and approximately 11% by FY30, adding specific out-year margin targets that the preview had not provided.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management set margin targets of mid-10s% for next year and a path to approximately 11% by FY30.”

surprises.description: SAIC won a border security recompete after quarter-end, an additional win not identified in the preview’s list of expected awards or bookings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[The company] won a border security recompete after quarter-end.”

surprises.description: Net leverage declined to 3.0x from the 3.1x figure cited in the preview, a modestly better capital-structure outcome than the stated baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage declined to 3.0x this quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “net leverage 3.1x.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA margin was 10.3%, at the top of the preview’s estimated 10.0%–10.3% range; the preview also cautioned that comparisons with the prior year were affected by a favorable legal settlement.

Recompete win rate exceeded 90%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the rate would return near 90%; new-business win rates were also reported at or above 30% and back within target ranges.
Free cash flow guidance remained at least $600 million, or $14 per share, as the preview listed that level as the company’s existing guidance.

The first-half intel-space awards exceeded $1.6 billion, in line with the preview’s note that more than $1.6 billion of awards had been won in 1H and that the previously announced intel-agency recompete was likely to affect Q3 bookings.
The year-over-year EPS decline was primarily tied to the prior-period favorable legal settlement, as the preview had already flagged that settlement as distorting the comparison.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $56 million, above the preview’s $53.0 million consensus and $53.5 million base estimate, even though it fell year over year. The reported decline was 7.3%, milder than the preview’s implied 12.3% decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fourth quarter revenue declined 7.3% to $56 million”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $53.0M” and “Our estimates (base case): Revenue $53.5M”; the table showed implied Y/Y of “−12.3%.”

surprises.description: Consolidated same-store sales were substantially weaker than the preview’s Q4 expectation: growth was just 0.1% versus an estimated 2.0–2.5%. Supercuts also grew only 2.6% in Q4, below the preview’s 4.5% estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated same-store sales rose only 0.1% in Q4” and “Supercuts Q4 growth of 2.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consolidated SSS … Q4 +2.2%E” and “Supercuts SSS … Q4 +4.5%E”; the base case expected consolidated SSS of “+2.0–2.5%.”

surprises.description: Management expects salon closures to remain at roughly fiscal 2026 levels in fiscal 2027, suggesting the closure cycle will persist. The preview’s framing that closures might be winding down made that outlook worse than expected, although the reported fiscal 2026 net decline was close to the preview’s Q4 expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects fiscal 2027 closures to be similar to fiscal 2026 levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had previously called FY25 “the last year of closures in this order of magnitude” and framed “Under ~50 net” Q4 closures as evidence “the closure cycle is genuinely over.”

surprises.description: The company expects a $7–8 million excess-cash-flow sweep payment in September, reducing cash as well as debt. The preview highlighted cash generation and the debt balance but did not flag this near-term cash outflow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An excess cash flow sweep payment of $7-8 million [is] expected in September to reduce cash and debt.”

surprises.description: Company-owned segment adjusted EBITDA reached $2.8 million, above the preview’s stated $2.2 million threshold for its bull-case operating scenario. The facts also describe a $0.8 million improvement, but the preview did not set a base-case company-owned EBITDA estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Company-owned salons … improved segment adjusted EBITDA by $800,000 to $2.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case required “company-owned EBITDA ≥$2.2M.”

in_line: Fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $32.8 million, close to the preview’s $32.6 million estimate and approximately in line with its roughly $32.5–32.6 million framing.
The franchise portfolio’s 199-salon net decline was close to the preview’s expectation of about 50 net closures in Q4, based on a 150-salon decline through the first nine months.

The preview expected cash generated from core operations to increase meaningfully. Fiscal 2026 unrestricted cash from operations rose to $13.5 million from $5.4 million, consistent with that expectation.
Refinancing remained active but no completed transaction or timeline was reported, matching the preview’s base case of refinancing “in progress, no timeline.”
Supercuts traffic was still down about one point, consistent with the preview’s base-case expectation of traffic remaining flat or negative rather than the positive-traffic bull case.

surprises.description: Revenue of $50.8 million was well below the preview’s $65–75 million base case, although it landed at the bottom of the preview’s $50–60 million bear range. Bitcoin mining revenue was $47.4 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue was approximately $50.8 million, with about $47.4 million from Bitcoin mining, representing a roughly 50% sequential decline from Q1.”

surprises.description: Combined hashrate finished at 27.58 EH/s, below the preview’s 30–33 EH/s base range and just under its 28 EH/s bear-case threshold. Rightsizing may have been underway, but the exit rate was weaker than the base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company deliberately rightsized mining operations, ending Q2 with self-mining hashrate of 19.84 EH/s and lease hashrate of 7.74 EH/s for a combined 27.58 EH/s.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … Exit hashrate 30–33 EH/s”; “Bear: … <28 EH/s.”

surprises.description: The company recorded about $51 million of impairment and disposal losses on mining machines, primarily noncash, contributing to an $81.6 million continuing-operations net loss. The preview gave no quarterly loss estimate and did not flag these charges in its ex-ante scenario framework.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss from continuing operations was approximately $81.6 million, driven primarily by about $51 million in noncash impairment ($42.9 million) and disposal losses ($8.5 million) on mining machines.”

surprises.description: Cash mining cost was close to the preview’s expected range, but the reported all-in cost was $98,405 per Bitcoin—well above recent Bitcoin price levels. That indicates materially weaker economics after costs beyond the cash mining measure emphasized in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average cash mining cost fell about 5% sequentially to $73,313 per Bitcoin, while all-in cost was $98,405 per Bitcoin, exceeding recent Bitcoin price levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … Cash cost/BTC ~$72–75K.”

surprises.description: Cango introduced a Bitcoin hedging program using short-term BTC-denominated loans, an approach not anticipated in the preview’s ex-ante framework. The program coincided with a sharp narrowing in crypto fair-value losses, though it also adds short-term debt and limits some Bitcoin-price exposure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Loss from fair value changes in crypto assets narrowed sharply to $4.1 million from $151.8 million in Q1, aided by a newly implemented Bitcoin hedging program.” The program uses loans “sized to roughly one to two months of production,” with “around $8 million in short-term debt at quarter end.”

surprises.description: The company signed its first AI infrastructure customer contract after quarter-end, a concrete commercial step not specified in the preview’s ex-ante expectations. The positive development is tempered by management’s expectation that initial revenue will be modest and immaterial.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed its first AI infrastructure customer contract after June 30, with revenue recognition expected to begin in Q3 but described as modest and immaterial initially.”

in_line: Average cash mining cost was $73,313 per Bitcoin, within the preview’s base-case expectation of approximately $72,000–$75,000.
AI revenue recognition is expected to begin in Q3, consistent with the preview’s stated expectation of revenue in the second half of 2026.

surprises.description: MMED's U.S. revenue growth accelerated to 13.1% from 1.5% in Q4, well above the preview's ≥5% threshold for an inflection. U.S. new pump sales grew over 20%, and competitive conversions doubled year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. growing 13.1% (up from 1.5% in Q4)”; “U.S. new pumps sold grew over 20%”; “competitive conversions in the U.S. have doubled versus a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “U.S. revenue growth … What good looks like ≥+5%”; the base case expected “U.S. +3–5%.”

surprises.description: Even after excluding the extra week, organic growth was low double digits, ahead of the preview's ≥8% bar and its expectation that ex-week growth would approximate Q4's 8.7%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An extra week … contributed roughly 4-6 points to Q1 growth; excluding it, organic growth was low double digits versus 8.7% in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic growth ex-extra-week … What good looks like ≥8%”; management's phasing steer was that “ex-extra-week Q1 organic should approximate Q4 levels.”

surprises.description: Q1 adjusted EBITDA margin was 9.9%, far below the preview's ≥16.5% benchmark for the 14-week quarter. The disclosed investment pull-forward and FX charge explain part of the shortfall, but margin would still have been only 12.2% excluding them.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 adjusted EBITDA was $83 million (9.9% margin), reduced ~230 bps by an $8 million pull-forward of investment and a $12 million nonoperational FX remeasurement charge; excluding these, margin would have been 12.2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin … What good looks like ≥16.5% on 14 wks.”

surprises.description: Total Q1 new pump sales were 34,000, below the preview's 45–50k good-outcome threshold and also below its cited Q4 level of about 42k, despite the strong U.S. new-pump growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q1 new pumps sold of 34,000 (up 7.7%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “New pump sales (NPS) … ~42k Q4 … What good looks like ≥45–50k.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $843 million beat the published $828.4 million consensus but came in just below the preview's $845–855 million effective whisper and below its $850–860 million base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue was $843 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $828.4M”; “$845–855M as the effective whisper”; base case “$850–860M.”

surprises.description: MMED raised its FY27 organic revenue growth outlook from about 10% to about 10.5%. The preview said a raise—not merely reaffirming the outlook—was the bar, so this is positive but a smaller move than its bull-case 10–11% outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year fiscal 2027 organic revenue growth outlook to approximately 10.5% from prior guidance of approximately 10%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bar is now a raise, not just a reaffirm”; the bull case anticipated organic guidance of “10–11% or above high end.”

surprises.description: The MiniMed Fit patch pump's FDA filing was completed ahead of schedule, earlier than the preview's expectation of a submission in the fall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The MiniMed Fit patch pump 510(k) was filed with FDA ahead of schedule.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the “Fit patch pump FDA submission this fall.”

surprises.description: MiniMed Flex received its CE Mark ahead of target, and the company gave a November 2025 European commercial-launch expectation; the preview had not flagged this European milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “MiniMed Flex received CE Mark ahead of target, with European commercial launch expected in November 2025.”

surprises.description: Vivera completed U.S. pivotal-trial enrollment ahead of schedule, an earlier pipeline milestone than the preview's general discussion of a CY2027 algorithm launch had anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Vivera fully closed-loop algorithm completed U.S. pivotal trial enrollment ahead of schedule.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview mentioned the “CY2027 pipeline (Vivera algorithm)” but did not anticipate early completion of enrollment.

in_line: The extra fiscal week contributed roughly 4–6 points to Q1 growth, consistent with the preview's estimate of about 4.3–6.5 points.
CGM attachment reached 69%, matching the preview's ≥69–70% good-outcome range.
FY27 adjusted EBITDA margin guidance was reaffirmed at approximately 16%, consistent with the preview's base-case expectation of a reaffirmation.

surprises.description: The preview flagged weak professional-services economics and asked whether the drag was transitory, but did not anticipate Rory Read taking interim leadership of the services organization to accelerate improvements. That is an unanticipated management intervention in an area already identified as a concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: Rory Read said he would lead the services organization on an interim basis to accelerate improvements in the services area.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management attributed compression to “negative-margin professional services” and the preview asked whether management would frame the professional-services drag as “transitory.”

surprises.description: The call announced Jordi Ribas as a new board member, an appointment the preview did not mention. The provided information does not establish whether this is favorable or unfavorable for shareholders.
surprises.fact_evidence: Rory Read announced “Jordi Ribas as a member of Sprinklr's Board of Directors.”

in_line: The preview identified Tom Addis as the new Chief Revenue Officer; the call announced his addition as CRO.

surprises.description: Medtronic reported $9.8 billion of Q1 revenue, above the preview’s more realistic $9.55–$9.65 billion bar. That is a clear beat even after setting aside the stale $9.47 billion consensus figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 revenue reached $9.8 billion” and beat expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The real bar is ~$9.55–9.65B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $1.45 was above both the preview’s $1.39 consensus and the company-guide range of $1.38–$1.40. The reported EPS was also $0.06 above the guidance midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS of $1.45,” with EPS “$0.06 above the guidance midpoint and Street estimates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS $1.39”; company guide “$1.38–$1.40.”

surprises.description: Cardiac Ablation Solutions grew 88% worldwide and 139% in the U.S., far exceeding the preview’s roughly 50% base case and clearing even its >55% bull-case marker. It also reached $2 billion in trailing 12-month revenue ahead of schedule and gained 9 points of U.S. share.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cardiac Ablation Solutions delivered 88% worldwide growth (139% in the U.S.), surpassed $2 billion in trailing 12-month revenue ahead of schedule, and gained 9 points of U.S. share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case anticipated “CAS ~50%”; the bull case required “CAS holds >55% growth.”

surprises.description: Medtronic raised FY27 organic revenue guidance by 50 basis points, taking the range to 7.25%–7.75%, above the preview’s prior 6.75%–7.25% framework. This was the guidance raise the preview said investors wanted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year FY27 organic revenue guidance by 50 basis points to 7.25%-7.75%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The company framework was “organic revenue +6.75–7.25%”; the preview said the market wanted “a raise, not a reaffirm.”

surprises.description: Q1 adjusted operating margin expanded only 10 basis points to 23.7%, below the preview’s expected 40–70 basis points of year-over-year expansion. The quarter’s margin result therefore fell short of the preview’s margin bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating margin rose 10 basis points to 23.7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “~24.0–24.3%E” operating margin and said the quarter needed “+40–70bps of Y/Y expansion.”

surprises.description: Although the company raised EPS guidance, the new $5.94–$6.00 range lifts only the low end by $0.04 and leaves the high end unchanged from the preview’s $5.90–$6.00 framework. The increase was more limited than the preview’s bull case of at least $6.00–$6.05.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lifted EPS guidance to $5.94-$6.00.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The company framework was “Non-GAAP EPS $5.90–$6.00”; the bull case anticipated “FY27 EPS raised to ≥$6.00–6.05.”

surprises.description: The full-year margin outlook was trimmed: management now expects about 50 basis points of expansion rather than the prior 60 basis points, citing reinvestment. That is a setback relative to the preview’s stated FY27 margin framework, despite expected operating-profit growth of about 10%.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects “full-year operating profit to grow ~10% with ~50 basis points of margin expansion, a slight reduction from prior 60 basis point expectations due to reinvestment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s FY27 framework was “FY op. margin +60bps.”

surprises.description: The tariff burden appears much smaller than the preview’s expected $75 million Q1 hit: refunds nearly offset tariffs paid, leaving only a slight net headwind. However, management said no future refunds are included in guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tariff impacts were a slight net headwind as refunds nearly offset tariffs paid, but no future refunds are embedded in guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “~$250M tariff COGS hit, $75M of it in Q1” and flagged the tariff line as a key margin issue.

surprises.description: The reported 13.7% organic growth was boosted by an extra selling week contributing about 670 basis points, more than the preview’s expected 500–600 basis points. Excluding the week, growth was near 7%, so the underlying rate was within the preview’s clean-growth range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Organic revenue growth was 13.7%, but roughly 670 basis points (~$570 million) came from an extra selling week… implying underlying growth near 7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the extra week would add “500–600bps to Q1” and identified “~5.5–7%” as the clean growth range.

surprises.description: Cardiac Rhythm Management grew 15% globally, broadly matching the preview’s roughly 15% cardiovascular segment growth mark, but it also gained 80 basis points of share and conduction system pacing contributed more than 200 basis points to the business—specific competitive and product contributions the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cardiac Rhythm Management grew 15% globally, gaining 80 basis points of share, with conduction system pacing adding over 200 basis points to the business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s cardiovascular segment mark was “+15.2%”; it did not specify CRM share gains or conduction-system-pacing contribution.

surprises.description: Cranial and Spinal Technologies grew 13% globally, above the preview’s 10.7% implied growth mark for Neuroscience, with U.S. Core Spine up 14% and neurosurgery up 15%. Stealth AXiS pull-through was anticipated, but the reported growth was stronger than the segment mark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cranial and Spinal Technologies grew 13% globally with U.S. Core Spine up 14% and neurosurgery up 15%, boosted by the newly launched Stealth AXiS platform.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Neuroscience segment mark was “+10.7%”; it also expected acceleration from Stealth AXiS pull-through.

surprises.description: The planned MiniMed separation is expected to close before fiscal year-end, and management quantified its effects: about 50 basis points of gross-margin improvement and 100 basis points of operating-margin improvement, at a cost of only about 20 basis points of growth. The preview highlighted the separation but did not include these quantified margin benefits.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The planned MiniMed (diabetes) separation is expected to close before fiscal year-end and will lift gross margin by ~50 basis points and operating margin by ~100 basis points, while costing only ~20 basis points of growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said MiniMed was “targeted by end of CY2026” and that any “quantified accretion or firm exchange-offer date is un-modeled upside.”

surprises.description: Medtronic announced a $700 million strategic investment and distribution agreement for Cornerstone’s Sentire surgical robotics system in select non-U.S. markets, with material revenue and margin contribution expected from FY28. This was not part of the preview’s outlook or catalyst checklist.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced a $700 million strategic investment and distribution agreement for Cornerstone's Sentire surgical robotics system in select non-U.S. markets, with material revenue and margin contribution expected starting FY28.”

surprises.description: Free-cash-flow conversion improved to 70%, with management describing a path toward 80%; the preview did not discuss a cash-conversion expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow conversion improved to 70% with a path toward 80%.”

in_line: Underlying organic growth excluding the extra selling week was near 7%, at the upper end of the preview’s 5.5%–7% clean-growth range.
Cardiac Rhythm Management’s 15% global growth was broadly in line with the preview’s roughly 15.2% cardiovascular segment growth mark.

surprises.description: The preview expected gross margin around 31.5%–32.0% and modeled a decline on firearms-and-ammunition mix. Instead, gross margin rose 50 basis points to 32.5%, helped by lower freight and a one-time tariff benefit despite heavier promotions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved 50 basis points to 32.5%,” aided by “lower freight costs, and a one-time tariff benefit despite a heavier promotional cadence.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin” consensus/bar: “~31.5–32.0%”; the preview’s estimate was “31.4% (‑60bps)” and it said “mix pressure likely persists.”

surprises.description: The preview expected net debt to trend below the Q1 level of $148.4 million. Q2 net debt was $169 million—about $20.6 million above that level—even though it was down $26 million year-over-year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt was reduced by $26 million year-over-year to $169 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Look for inventory down YoY again … and net debt trending below the $148.4M Q1 level.”

surprises.description: The preview expected roughly five store closures planned for after the holiday season. Management described one closure on January 31 and only two to three additional closures in negotiation, indicating fewer closures than the preview’s approximate plan and that most additional closures were not yet settled.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management confirmed one store closure on January 31st with two to three additional closures in various stages of negotiation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~5 closures planned, post-holiday.”

surprises.description: The preview’s GAAP estimate was a loss of $0.17 per share. The reported net loss was $4.4 million, or $0.11 per share, a narrower loss than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net loss narrowed to $4.4 million (-$0.11 per share) from $7.1 million (-$0.18) a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP diluted EPS” estimate: “‑$0.17.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case assumed other categories would be roughly flat, while fishing sales declined about 2%. Management attributed the decline to western drought conditions, although sales remained nearly double-digit higher on a two-year comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fishing sales declined about 2% due to western drought conditions, though they are up nearly double digits on a two-year comp stack.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case described “everything else” beyond hunting and shooting as “roughly flat”; the preview also said positive fishing comps would help support the bull case.

in_line: Q2 net sales were $295.6 million, up 0.6%, with same-store sales essentially flat; the call explicitly said this was in line with expectations, consistent with the preview’s roughly flat sales and flat-to-+1% same-store-sales bar.
Adjusted EBITDA was $8.7 million, within the preview’s $8–9 million expectation.
The company reiterated full-year guidance, including adjusted EBITDA of $30–$36 million and capex of $20–$25 million; the preview’s base case expected the EBITDA guide to be reaffirmed.

surprises.description: Dell reported non-GAAP EPS of $7.04, far above the $4.91 consensus and even the preview’s $5.00–$5.10 buy-side working assumption. The earnings beat was substantially larger than the preview’s already-elevated expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS jumped 203% to a record $7.04.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS $4.91”; buy-side conversations were “anchored well above the tape” at “$5.00–5.10.”

surprises.description: Dell raised full-year revenue guidance to $192 billion, well above the prior $165–169 billion guide and the preview’s expectation of another raise toward roughly $170–175 billion. The size of the increase greatly exceeded the anticipated upgrade.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year revenue guidance was raised by $25 billion to $192 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The current guide was “revenue $165–169B”; the preview said consensus expected “another raise” and described a bull case of “~$175B.”

surprises.description: AI server orders reached $60.9 billion in Q2, far above the preview’s $24.4 billion prior-quarter benchmark and its bull-case threshold of orders above $25 billion. The reported order intake was more than twice that threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company booked a record $60.9 billion in AI server orders in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 AI orders of “$24.4B” and a bull-case signal of “orders >$25B.”

surprises.description: The AI backlog rose to a record $95 billion, far beyond the preview’s $51.3 billion starting point and even its bull-case threshold of more than $55 billion. Rather than merely growing or staying roughly flat, the backlog expanded dramatically.
surprises.fact_evidence: Dell exited Q2 with “a record $95 billion AI backlog.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 backlog of “$51.3B”; its bull case specified “backlog >$55B,” while its base case expected “roughly flat $50–53B.”

surprises.description: Full-year EPS guidance rose to $25.50, substantially above the prior $17.90 ± $0.25 guide and the preview’s expectation of roughly $19 or more. The EPS outlook rose much more than the preview’s anticipated profitable-growth upgrade.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The current guide was “EPS $17.90 ± $0.25”; the preview’s bull case expected “EPS $19+.”

surprises.description: ISG operating margin reached 15%, far above the preview’s expectation of about 11% and its bull-case threshold of 12% or more. The recovery from Q1’s 10.5% was much stronger than the anticipated sequential improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ISG revenue grew 89% to a record $31.8 billion with operating margin expanding 620 basis points to 15%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected ISG margin of “~11%”; its bull case specified “12%+,” after Q1’s “10.5%” and management’s commitment to sequential improvement.

surprises.description: Dell now expects AI server revenue to reach $74 billion for the full year, versus the roughly $60 billion outlook the preview identified as current. The forecast implies a materially larger AI server business than the preview’s baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI server revenue expected to triple to $74 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed current FY2027 guidance as “~$60B AI servers.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $47 billion, above the $45.1 billion consensus and also above the preview’s $46 billion-plus buy-side working assumption. The beat was meaningful, though less dramatic than the EPS and guidance surprises.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue rose 58% to a record $47 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Revenue consensus was “~$45.1B”; the preview said buy-side conversations were anchored at “revenue $46B+.”

surprises.description: ISG revenue reached $31.8 billion, above the preview’s approximately $29.8 billion estimate. The segment’s revenue outperformed expectations as well as its margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ISG revenue grew 89% to a record $31.8 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “ISG revenue | ~$29.8B.”

surprises.description: Traditional server and networking revenue surged 122% to $10.5 billion, with demand outstripping supply and Dell gaining more than 10 points of traditional server share in two quarters. The preview discussed improving supply as a possible positive signal but did not anticipate or quantify these reported sales and share gains.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Traditional server and networking revenue surged 122% to $10.5 billion, with demand outstripping supply” and Dell gained “over 10 points of traditional server share in two quarters.”

surprises.description: Dell returned a record $4.3 billion to shareholders in Q2, up from the $2.1 billion returned in Q1 cited in the preview. This was a much larger sequential acceleration than the preview could establish as its baseline, though it had identified buyback acceleration as a possible bull signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company returned an all-time record $4.3 billion to shareholders in Q2, including 9.5 million shares repurchased at an average $401, up $2.2 billion sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Dell returned “$2.1B in Q1” and listed “Buyback accelerating at current prices” as a bull-case signal.

surprises.description: Dell disclosed that full-year operating expenses are expected to be only about 8% of revenue, a 42-year low, reflecting operating leverage from modernization. The preview did not anticipate this unusually low expense ratio or identify it as an expected result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year operating expenses are guided to approximately 8% of revenue, the lowest level in the company's 42-year history, reflecting significant operating leverage from modernization.”

surprises.description: Storage revenue grew 26% to $4.9 billion, and Dell reported a sixth consecutive quarter of above-market demand for its IP products. The preview did not provide a storage outlook or flag this sustained outperformance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Storage revenue grew 26% to $4.9 billion, marking the sixth consecutive quarter of Dell IP demand growth above market.”

surprises.description: The AI factory customer count exceeded 6,500, with more than 3,300 customers added in the last three quarters. That extended the customer-base expansion beyond the preview’s cited Q1 level of more than 5,000, although the preview did not set a Q2 customer-count forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI factory customer count surpassed 6,500 with over 3,300 added in just the last three quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited an AI customer count of “>5,000” in Q1 but gave no Q2 target.

in_line: CSG revenue grew 20%, matching the preview’s expectation of approximately 20% growth.

surprises.description: MongoDB reported Q2 revenue of $772 million, above the preview’s $750 million-plus buy-side bar and well above its $734–735 million consensus estimate. The 30% growth rate was materially stronger than the preview’s 24% consensus-implied growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 total revenue reached $772 million, up 30% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “the functional bar is $750M+”; consensus revenue was “$734.4–735.1M” with “+24%” implied growth.

surprises.description: The full-year revenue outlook was raised to a range that straddles $3 billion, reaching the key threshold at its midpoint. That is a stronger raise than the preview’s roughly $2.97–3.00 billion base case, though the low end remains just below $3 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year fiscal 2027 revenue guidance was raised to $2.99–$3.03 billion (21–23% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called a raise to “≥$3.00B” the “single most important number” and described the base case as “FY27 to $2.97–3.00B.”

surprises.description: Q3 guidance points to a sharp slowdown from Q2’s growth pace: total growth is expected at 20–21% and Atlas growth at about 26%. The preview had flagged H2 consumption deceleration as a risk, but the near-term outlook makes that concern concrete even as full-year guidance rose.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance implies decelerating total growth of 20–21% and Atlas growth of ~26% as management remains prudent on consumption trends and its toughest Atlas compare.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned that “a de facto H2 caution signal” would matter and identified “macro/consumption caution” and “conservatism embedded in the second half” as bear-case tells.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS reached $1.90, beating even the preview’s $1.85-plus bull-case threshold, as well as its $1.72-plus functional bar. The preview’s listed consensus was only about $1.62.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net income rose to $163 million ($1.90 per share) from $87 million ($1.00 per share) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview set the “functional bar” at “~$1.72+” and its bull scenario at “$1.85+”; listed consensus was “$1.61–$1.62.”

surprises.description: Profitability was much stronger than the preview’s roughly 20% full-year operating-margin framing: Q2 margin reached 24%, and the company now expects about 250 basis points of full-year expansion, 100 basis points above its prior high end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 24% from 15% a year ago, with full-year operating margin expansion now guided to ~250 basis points, 100 bps above the prior high end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described FY27 non-GAAP operating margin as “~20% (high end)” and flagged “FY27 op-margin guide ≥20%” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: EA and Other accelerated sharply, with 36% growth—the segment’s strongest quarter in three years—and early demand for the newly launched Search and Vector Search products. The company also lifted its full-year EA growth outlook to about 11%, rather than the prior mid-single-digit expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EA and Other revenue grew approximately 36% year-over-year (its strongest quarter in three years), boosted by early demand for the newly launched Search and Vector Search on EA, with full-year EA guidance raised to ~11% growth from prior mid-single-digit expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q1 EA growth of “+13%” and described “EA renewals lumpy”; it did not forecast this acceleration or the full-year outlook.

surprises.description: Atlas growth held near the preview’s expected range, but its $127 million of additions exceeded the preview’s stated $117 million-plus dollar-add hurdle and set a record.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Atlas revenue grew approximately 29% year-over-year for the fifth straight quarter … adding a record $127 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “sequential net-new Atlas dollars > $117M” and identified “≥29%” growth as the thesis-intact level.

surprises.description: The company added a record 2,900 net new customers, including many AI-native companies. The preview highlighted customer additions as a metric to watch but did not anticipate this record result or the AI-native mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added a record 2,900 net new customers, bringing the total to 70,600 … with many new additions being AI-native companies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited 67,700 total customers and said to watch “$100K+ ARR customer adds and multi-product attach,” but gave no Q2 total-customer-add expectation.

surprises.description: Voyage’s customer count roughly doubled for a second consecutive quarter, and most new customers had no prior MongoDB relationship; referrals from coding agents such as Claude and Codex also point to a new route to customer acquisition that the preview had not identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Voyage customer count roughly doubled quarter-over-quarter for the second consecutive quarter, with the majority of new Voyage customers having no prior relationship to MongoDB and referrals largely coming from coding agents like Claude and Codex.”

surprises.description: Remaining performance obligations grew 91% to $1.52 billion, a strong forward-demand indicator that the preview did not discuss or set an expectation for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Remaining performance obligations grew 91% year-over-year to $1.52 billion.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow more than doubled to $138 million. The preview discussed Q1 operating cash flow and flagged an annual FCF figure, but did not state an expectation for Q2 free cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow more than doubled to $138 million from $70 million a year ago.”

in_line: Atlas revenue growth was approximately 29%, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of at least 29% and its 28–29% base-case range.
The net ARR expansion rate rose to 122%, meeting the preview’s specifically flagged 122%-plus threshold.

surprises.description: The preview expected adjusted EBITDA of roughly negative $15–19 million; FCEL reported negative $36.7 million, a substantially larger loss than the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “negative $36.7 million Adjusted EBITDA this quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “adj. EBITDA $(15)–(19)M” in the base scenario; the preview also cited Q2 adjusted EBITDA of “$(17.1)M.”

surprises.description: Revenue was expected to be about $38.8–41.3 million, with a roughly 16% year-over-year decline. Instead, revenue fell 29% to $33 million, below even the preview’s bear-case threshold of $34 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q3 fiscal 2026 revenue fell 29% year-over-year to $33 million from $46.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $38.82M (-16.3% YoY)” and “Revenue (alt.) $41.31M”; the bear case was “<$34M.”

surprises.description: The reported $3.6 billion total committed-and-awarded capacity backlog was far above the preview’s expected roughly $1.05–1.15 billion. But $2.4 billion is awarded capacity that is not guaranteed to convert to revenue; the committed portion is $1.3 billion, only modestly above the preview’s $1.3 billion bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total committed and awarded capacity backlog reached $3.6 billion,” including “$1.3 billion of committed backlog” and “a new $2.4 billion awarded capacity backlog that is not guaranteed to convert to revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “Backlog roughly flat at $1.05–1.15B”; the bull case required “Total backlog >$1.3B.”

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate the scale of the Fit Energy-related gross loss: FCEL recorded a $24.5 million gross loss, including $17 million in charges because current costs exceeded contractual pricing for Phase 0. This was a worse gross result than the prior-year quarter’s $5.1 million loss cited in the call facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “gross loss of $24.5 million (versus $5.1 million a year ago), primarily due to $17 million in charges” tied to Phase 0 of Fit Energy, “reflecting current costs exceeding contractual pricing.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the deposit-backed 30 MW Fit Energy tranche to convert into product backlog and described the remaining capacity as phased against milestones. The call clarified that only Phase 0’s 30 MW is committed; the other 350 MW is at the customer’s sole election and creates no payment obligation unless elected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “only the 30-megawatt Phase 0 is committed, with Phases 1-3 (350 MW) at the customer's sole election and carrying no payment obligation until elected.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Fit Energy 30 MW deposit-backed tranche should convert into product backlog this quarter”; the “remainder [was] phased against milestones.”

surprises.description: FCEL’s reported loss per share was worse than the preview’s consensus range, despite the year-over-year improvement in net loss. The preview had warned that share-count changes could make EPS comparisons noisy, but the reported $0.64 loss still exceeded the expected loss of roughly $0.39–$0.50 per share.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss attributable to common stockholders was $45.3 million, or $0.64 per share,” compared with $92.5 million and $3.78 per share a year ago; weighted average shares were 70.4 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS $(0.41)” with alternatives of “$(0.39) / $(0.50).”

surprises.description: After warning that the pipeline was a soft metric and looking for signed conversion evidence, the preview did not anticipate a specific 75 MW data-center capacity reservation. The agreement is a positive proof point, though definitive agreements and project timing remain pending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Subsequent to quarter end, the company closed a 75-megawatt capacity reservation agreement with a major co-location data center operator for a Texas project, with definitive agreements and timing still pending.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “signed LOIs, deposits received, contracts executed,” and listed a “named new data-center contract” as a bull-case condition.

surprises.description: The pipeline was expected to be around 4–5 GW, with about 89% data-center-weighted proposals. FCEL reported roughly 10 GW of active proposals in fiscal 2026, with approximately 97% of Q3 pipeline tied to data centers—far more pipeline growth and concentration than anticipated, though pipeline is not the same as booked business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Data center applications now account for approximately 97% of the third quarter pipeline,” which “has grown to roughly 10 gigawatts of active proposals in fiscal 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “4 GW” pipeline and expected “pipeline 4–5 GW”; it described the pipeline as “~89% data-center-weighted proposals.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the $225 million July offering to bolster liquidity and said silence on further issuance would be bullish. The reported cash balance reached $737.3 million, but the call also attributed roughly $298 million in net equity proceeds to the offering and open-market sales, indicating additional equity sales beyond the offering alone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “record $737.3 million in total cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash,” up from $440.9 million, “boosted by roughly $298 million in net equity proceeds from a July underwritten offering and open market sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “$225M upsized equity offering” and said “Silence is bullish” on further issuance; it warned that “any further equity issuance signal post the $21 July offering” mattered.

surprises.description: The preview wanted evidence that production was visibly ramping but did not anticipate a disclosed annualized rate of only 37 MW for the quarter. FCEL aims to reach 100 MW by October 2026, with the 500 MW goal still dated June 2028, leaving a substantial near-term scale-up ahead.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company operated at only a 37-megawatt annualized production rate this quarter and aims to reach 100 megawatts by October 2026,” with a goal of “500 megawatts by June 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “module production visibly ramping at Torrington” and cited the 500 MW capacity plan, but gave no quarterly production-rate estimate.

surprises.description: Management introduced a target for positive adjusted EBITDA in Q4 FY2027, a concrete profitability milestone not specified in the preview. The target is qualified by backlog conversion, delivery schedules, and cost reductions, especially notable alongside the quarter’s negative $36.7 million adjusted EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management set a new target of achieving positive Adjusted EBITDA in Q4 fiscal 2027,” contingent on “backlog conversion, customer delivery schedules, and cost reductions.”

in_line: The longer-term Torrington capacity goal and estimated investment matched the preview: 500 MW at an estimated $200–275 million of cost.

surprises.description: The preview anticipated reported EPS of $0.55–$0.65, partly from a gain on a May vessel sale, and consensus implied about $19.7 million of net income. The reported EPS was $0.46 and net income was $17.3 million, below those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income was $17.3 million” and “EPS of $0.46 for the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reported EPS could print $0.55–0.65” and “Net income | ~$19.7M implied.”

surprises.description: Revenue came in below both the $44.9 million consensus and the preview’s $43.5–$44.5 million estimate. The preview had anticipated a smaller fleet and Hormuz-related idle time, but actual revenue was still lower than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenues were $42.9 million,” driven by “fewer operational vessels and increased spot-market idle time.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026 Consensus” revenue of “$44.9M”; “Our estimate: revenue $43.5–44.5M.”

surprises.description: Liquidity rose well beyond the preview’s estimate of about $155 million by early June: it was $168.3 million at quarter-end and later exceeded $250 million after the Echo Wizard insurance proceeds were collected. The preview treated the settlement as a Q3 event to monitor, rather than anticipating that more than $77 million would already have been collected after quarter-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Liquidity grew 70% in six months from $99 million to $168.3 million by June 30, and has since climbed to over $250 million after collecting more than $77 million from the Echo Wizard insurance settlement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash was $131.2M at Q1-end and $155M by the June 5 call”; the settlement was “announced July 7, i.e. a Q3 event.”

surprises.description: Voyage expenses were materially above the preview’s roughly $5 million estimate, as higher bunker costs and Persian Gulf insurance premiums raised the bill to $7.2 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Voyage expenses rose to $7.2 million due to higher bunker costs and Persian Gulf insurance premiums.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s estimate build included “voyage expense ~$5M.”

surprises.description: Near-term 2026 charter coverage improved more than the preview’s Q1-exit figure, but the forward-year coverage did not improve and total secured revenue through 2029 was lower than the preview’s backlog figure. This left the expected defensive improvement concentrated in the remaining 2026 days rather than extending into 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “60% of remaining 2026 fleet days are secured”; “~$30 million secured for 2027 and total future secured revenues of about $90 million through 2029,” while “one-year forward coverage of 45% is below historical norms.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 exit: 55% of remaining 2026 days and 45% of forward-year days fixed, ~$100M contracted into 2029.”

surprises.description: The disruption was more severe than the preview’s cited 3% decline in global LPG exports: exports fell 8% in the first half, with sharp drops in Chinese imports and Indian demand. At the same time, rerouting increased ton-miles and drove VLGC rates to all-time highs, an offsetting rate benefit beyond the preview’s concern about idle and repositioning days.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Persian Gulf conflict and Hormuz closure cut global LPG exports 8% in H1 2026 and slashed Chinese imports 29% and Indian demand 20%, but rerouting via the Cape of Good Hope boosted ton-miles and drove VLGC rates to all-time highs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had flagged “a 3% drop in global LPG exports” and highlighted “idle/repositioning days” as a Q2 revenue and utilization item.

in_line: No Q2 share repurchases were made, consistent with the preview’s report that management had paused buybacks in Q1 because the share price had appreciated and with its base case of unchanged capital-allocation language.
Forward-year charter coverage remained at 45%, matching the preview’s Q1-exit figure rather than improving.

surprises.description: The preview treated the Eaton relationship as an early-stage narrative with no quantified contribution; on the call, ChargePoint said early-access Express Solo units had begun shipping through the collaboration. This is a modest product milestone, though no revenue or broader commercial impact was reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: Richard Wilmer noted Express Solo and its collaboration with Eaton, and said early access units began shipping.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any quantification of Eaton / Mercedes-Benz ... / PDX contribution” was listed as a catalyst; the preview also described Eaton as “early innings.”

surprises.description: The preview expected gross margin around 28.5%-29.5% in its base case and called 29% or higher a positive result. Daktronics reported 30.5%, a stronger margin outcome than that expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit margin expanded 80 basis points to 30.5%,” aided by operating leverage and favorable mix.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario gross margin was “28.5–29.5%”; the preview also said “Anything ≥29% is a clear positive.”

surprises.description: The preview did not expect a tariff refund to land in the quarter and treated a refund disclosure as only a possibility. Daktronics said about $3 million in cash-basis tariff refunds helped gross margin, though rising input costs largely offset them.
surprises.fact_evidence: “About $3 million in cash-basis tariff refunds” aided gross margin and were “largely offset by rising input costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Do not assume it lands this quarter” and “a disclosed receivable or a sizing comment on the call is a real possibility.”

surprises.description: The preview’s EPS-based calculation implied roughly $23–24 million of operating income and about a 10.0% operating margin. Daktronics reported $24.9 million of operating income, above that implied range, while remaining within its 10%-12% target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating income increased 7.2% to $24.9 million” and the company remained within its “10%-12% operating margin target range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$0.40 EPS backs into roughly $23–24M of operating income, or ~10.0% operating margin.”

surprises.description: The preview expected backlog to hold at or above $350 million, with a decline alongside weaker orders identified as a warning sign. Backlog instead entered Q2 at $311 million, and bookings and backlog both declined year over year; management attributed the movement to order timing and said substantial deals could convert in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bookings and backlog declined year-over-year, with backlog entering Q2 at $311 million,” down from $356 million entering Q1; management said several substantial deals are expected to convert to purchase orders in Q2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a backlog “holding ≥$350M” was favorable and that “a decline plus a backlog draw is the bear trigger.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a possible exit from Daktronics’ highly customized international transportation business. Management is considering an exit and has started a collective redundancy consultation affecting employees at its Ennistymon facility.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is “considering exiting its highly customized international transportation business,” with a collective redundancy consultation process affecting Ennistymon employees.

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate disclosure of SEC and NBA requests for information related to the Kawhi Leonard and Clippers investigation. Daktronics said it is cooperating, leaving an unresolved legal overhang.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cooperating with SEC and NBA requests for information regarding the investigation of Kawhi Leonard and the Clippers,” described as an unresolved legal overhang.

surprises.description: The preview gave a prior CapEx range of $14-$16 million but did not anticipate a higher investment plan. Management now plans annual CapEx of around $20 million to fund manufacturing automation.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management plans to “raise annual CapEx to around $20 million (from $14-16 million) to fund manufacturing automation.”

in_line: Net sales growth was 7.1% year over year, close to the preview’s working consensus growth estimate of 6.9%.
EPS was $0.40, matching the preview’s working consensus estimate of about $0.40.
Management reaffirmed the FY2028 targets of 7%-10% revenue CAGR, 10%-12% operating margin, and 17%-20% ROIC, as the preview’s base case expected reaffirmation rather than a change.
The preview expected Q4’s depressed free cash flow from billing and completion timing to reverse early in FY2027; the company reported $27.5 million of free cash flow in Q1.
The preview expected the buyback to continue; Daktronics repurchased $4.4 million of shares in Q1.

surprises.description: G-III guided Q3 sales to about $870 million and non-GAAP EPS to $1.34–$1.45, and said the quarter reflects the fiscal year's largest year-over-year PVH revenue reduction. The preview highlighted holiday and order-book commentary as important but did not provide a Q3 estimate, so the scale of this outlook was not quantified in advance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for net sales of about $870 million (down from $989 million) and non-GAAP EPS of $1.34-$1.45 versus $1.90 last year, reflecting the largest year-over-year PVH revenue reduction of the fiscal year.”

surprises.description: Q2 sales were $555 million, below the preview's roughly $570 million guidance and consensus and its $578 million base estimate. The reported 10% year-over-year decline was also steeper than the preview's implied 7% decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales fell 10% year-over-year to $555 million, coming in slightly below plan due to European macro softness and the winding-down of Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger licenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 guidance and consensus of “~$570M,” its base estimate of “$578M,” and an implied year-over-year decline of “−7%.”

surprises.description: Although G-III said Marc Jacobs would be slightly dilutive for the rest of FY2027 and accretive thereafter, it excluded the acquisition from current guidance and did not provide a quantified EPS dilution or a comparable FY2027 bridge. The preview's base scenario anticipated a Marc Jacobs range with the second-half drag acknowledged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Marc Jacobs acquisition is expected to be dilutive for the first 12 months (slight dilution in the remainder of fiscal 2027) and accretive thereafter, and is excluded from current guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base scenario anticipated “MJ guidance given as a range with acknowledged 2H drag”; it also called for the stub dilution and pro-forma impact to be quantified.

surprises.description: Q2 EPS of $0.26 narrowly beat the preview's $0.25 consensus and the $0.25 top of guidance, but fell short of the preview's $0.28 base estimate and its stated $0.28–$0.32 whisper range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS was $0.26, exceeding guidance of $0.15 to $0.25.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave “$0.25” consensus, a base estimate of “$0.28,” and said the whisper was “likely $0.28–0.32.”

surprises.description: G-III raised FY2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance to $2.20–$2.30 from the preview's then-current $2.15–$2.25 range, while leaving the approximately $2.71 billion sales outlook unchanged. This was a modestly stronger earnings outlook than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance to $2.20-$2.30 (from prior levels) while reiterating net sales guidance of approximately $2.71 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2027 guidance as it stands (excludes Marc Jacobs entirely): net sales ~$2.71B” and “non-GAAP EPS $2.15–2.25.”

surprises.description: Donna Karan sales grew more than 45%, above the preview's roughly 40% Q1 growth benchmark. This was stronger brand momentum than the preview's reference point.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Donna Karan sales up more than 45%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Donna Karan +~40%” as its Q1 anchor.

surprises.description: DKNY.com grew in the mid-20% range, slower than the roughly 40% growth cited in the preview for the prior quarter. Growth remained strong, but the reported pace had decelerated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “dkny.com growing in the mid-20% range year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “dkny.com +40%” as a Q1 anchor and warned that “Any deceleration in Donna Karan or a DKNY comp turning negative breaks the thesis.”

surprises.description: The company received about $134 million in tariff refunds, a sizable cash source that supported liquidity. The preview identified the remaining receivable and cash timing as an open question but did not anticipate this reported refund amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $529 million in cash and roughly $1 billion in available liquidity, aided by approximately $134 million in tariff refunds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “the remaining balance of the $140M IEEPA receivable ($102.7M recognized in Q1) and its cash timing.”

surprises.description: Inventory was down 13% year-over-year, a cleaner position than the preview's Q1 reference of an 8% decline and supportive of the preview's clean-inventory thesis into holiday.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory down 13% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q1 inventory “$417.9M (−8% Y/Y)” and said “Clean inventory into holiday supports the full-price selling narrative.”

in_line: Gross margin was 45.2%, close to the preview's approximately 45.3% expectation (about 450 basis points of expansion).
The go-forward portfolio excluding Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger grew high single digits, matching the preview's expectation that owned brands would deliver high-single-digit growth.
FY2027 net sales guidance remained approximately $2.71 billion, as in the preview.
Marc Jacobs was described as dilutive during its first year and accretive thereafter, consistent with the preview's stated expectation about the timing of its earnings impact.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $1.42 versus the preview’s $1.14 estimate, but about $0.35 per share came from one-time tariff refunds. Excluding that refund contribution, EPS was roughly $1.07—below the estimate despite the large reported beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS increased 43% to $1.42” and “roughly $0.35 of EPS came from one-time EPA/IEEPA tariff refunds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS $1.14.”

surprises.description: Net sales were $741 million, below the preview’s roughly $757 million consensus, even though sales rose year over year on new-store openings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales rose 9.1% to $741 million driven by new store openings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales $757.9M” (with another cited estimate of $756.4M).

surprises.description: Comparable sales fell 1.8%, missing the preview’s +0.3% consensus, though the decline was less severe than the preview’s roughly –1% buy-side whisper. Transactions were flat and a lower basket drove the decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable store sales declined 1.8% amid flat transactions and a lower basket.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comparable store sales: +0.3%”; the preview also cited a buy-side whisper of “~–1%.”

surprises.description: Reported gross margin reached 43.5%, far above the preview’s 40.2–40.6% estimate, but tariff refunds supplied more than the entire reported year-over-year expansion. Excluding refunds and price investment, margin was about 40.3–40.4%, only modestly above the preview’s range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 360 basis points to 43.5%, but 380bp of the benefit came from tariff refunds”; excluding refunds and price investment, gross margin “would have been ~40.3-40.4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin ~40.2–40.6% (my est.).”

surprises.description: The new full-year adjusted EPS range of $4.57–$4.65 is above the preview’s cited prior guidance of $4.45–$4.55 and above its base case of holding that range, even as the sales and comp outlook was reduced.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year adjusted EPS is now projected at “$4.57-$4.65.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance as of Q1 … adj. EPS $4.45–4.55”; the preview’s base case said “adj. EPS $4.45–4.55 held.”

surprises.description: Management put roughly $28 million of net tariff refunds into the full-year outlook, with a stated roughly 100bp gross-margin benefit partly offset by about 50bp of price investments. The preview said refunds had previously been excluded from guidance and identified their inclusion as an open question.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects roughly $28 million in net tariff refunds … for the full year, benefiting gross margin ~100bp offset by ~50bp of price investments, with margins guided to 41.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had “explicitly excluded” refunds from prior guidance; the preview asked, “Tariff refunds — in or out of guidance?”

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year buyback plan to $175 million from the preview’s approximately $125 million target, after repurchasing $137 million year to date.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased $84 million of stock in Q2 and $137 million year-to-date” and “raised its full-year buyback plan to $175 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buyback ~$125M”; the preview said an accelerated repurchase would be a possible signal to watch.

surprises.description: The call reported 50 new stores opened in Q2 versus the preview’s consensus of 15, a much faster pace than expected. The provided facts also say 42 stores opened in the first half, so the reported Q2 and first-half figures do not reconcile.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ollie's opened 50 new stores in Q2 (42 in the first half) toward a 75-store full-year target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “New stores opened: 15”; the preview also said the 75-store full-year target was reaffirmed.

surprises.description: Management quantified about $15 million of full-year price investments, including roughly $10 million in the back half, and said it was willing to spend more to protect price leadership. The preview anticipated price reinvestment in general but did not quantify this commitment or the willingness to increase it further.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans approximately $15 million in full-year price investments (~$10 million in the back half) and signaled willingness to spend more to protect its price leadership position.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management’s bias was to “widen price gaps” and reinvest margin, but gave no investment amount.

surprises.description: Weather-sensitive categories were said to have directly reduced comps by more than 100bp, with softness concentrated in the Midwest and Texas and longer drives amplifying fuel-price pressure. The preview discussed weather as a possible explanation but did not anticipate this quantified drag or these regional details.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Weather-sensitive categories like lawn/garden and room air created over 100 basis points of direct comp drag,” with softness in “the Midwest and Texas where longer drive times amplified fuel-price headwinds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged the regional split and said a repeat of weather-related weakness could mean “the weather excuse holds.”

surprises.description: Management said acquired Big Lots stores were comping better than the typical negative mid-to-high-single-digit second-year pattern, a more favorable performance signal than the preview discussed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Acquired Big Lots stores are comping better than the typical negative mid-to-high single-digit second-year pattern.”

in_line: The full-year comp outlook of flat to +0.5% was broadly consistent with the preview’s cited expectation that management could cut the guide to roughly flat; the preview’s bear scenario also placed sales at $2.92–$2.95 billion, close to the reported $2.928–$2.941 billion range.
The 75-store full-year opening target was maintained, as the preview expected.
Tariff relief affected Q2 results, consistent with the preview’s expectation that tariff relief would land during the quarter.
Management’s willingness to reinvest margin in pricing was consistent with the preview’s stated price-investment debate.

surprises.description: Petco had guided to Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $110–112 million and the preview expected no further tariff refunds. Adjusted EBITDA was $122 million including a $6.8 million net tariff refund; even excluding it, normalized EBITDA of $115 million beat the company’s outlook, though it was within the preview’s $114–116 million whisper range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $122 million (8.2% of sales), including a $6.8 million net tariff refund, while normalized adjusted EBITDA of $115 million exceeded both prior year and the company's outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA: $110–112M guide”; “The functional buy-side bar is therefore ~$114–116M”; “management explicitly said Q2 carries the anticipated tariff headwind and assumed no further refunds.”

surprises.description: The Petco Perks relaunch led to far more point redemptions than projected, creating an unexpected sales drag of mid-single-digit millions, mainly in services.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Petco Perks membership relaunch triggered point redemptions that far exceeded projections, negatively impacting Q2 sales by an estimated mid-single-digit millions, primarily in the services business.”

surprises.description: SG&A increased only $1 million despite lapping a roughly $9 million actuarial benefit, implying underlying expenses fell about $8 million. The preview highlighted whether the turnaround could deliver SG&A leverage or further cost take-out, but did not anticipate this degree of underlying expense reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A was $543 million (36.5% of sales), up only $1 million despite lapping a ~$9 million actuarial benefit, implying underlying expenses fell about $8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The distinguishing question on the call: does H2 EBITDA growth come from comp-driven SG&A leverage … or from another round of cost take-out and store closures?”

surprises.description: Petco voluntarily prepaid another $75 million of debt on September 1, bringing paydown over nine months to $170 million—more concrete and substantial deleveraging than the preview had specified as an open possibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company voluntarily prepaid an additional $75 million in debt on September 1st, bringing total pay down over the last nine months to $170 million as it targets a 2x leverage ratio.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Balance sheet — further debt paydown below $1.48B, FCF, or any refinancing/maturity commentary.”

surprises.description: The preview described a 2027 veterinary expansion decision as still ahead; management instead said new hospital openings are planned to begin in 2027, alongside double-digit growth in visits, doctor days, and vet diet sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vet business delivered double-digit growth in total pet visits, double-digit expansion in doctor days, and double-digit vet diet sales growth for both dogs and cats, with new hospital openings planned to begin in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “the 25 underutilized hospitals being optimized ahead of a 2027 expansion decision”; “any commitment to 2027 hospital expansion”

surprises.description: The total customer base returned to slight growth in Q2, an encouraging customer trend not specifically anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The total customer base inflected to slight growth in Q2.”

surprises.description: A seven-store new-format test launched in May is already showing sizable lifts in new and reactivated customers, larger baskets, improved margins, and NPS up hundreds of basis points; the preview did not flag this test or these results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A 7-store new-format market test launched in May is showing sizable lifts in new and reactivated customers, larger baskets, improved margins, and NPS up hundreds of basis points, with a broader remodel rollout targeted for 2027.”

in_line: Q2 comparable sales were positive at 0.6%, within the preview’s buy-side expectation of roughly +0.5% to +1.0%; this was also the second consecutive quarter of positive comps.
FY26 guidance was reaffirmed at flat to +1.5% net sales and $415–430 million adjusted EBITDA, as the preview expected.
Gross margin excluding the tariff refund was roughly flat year over year, broadly in line with the preview’s estimate of roughly flat gross margin.

surprises.description: REX reported diluted EPS of $1.06, far above both the preview’s $0.42 consensus and its own $0.43–$0.50 estimate. The result was more than double the preview’s modeled range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record second quarter net income of $1.06 per diluted share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS (to REX) … $0.42”; the preview’s estimate build put EPS at “~$0.43–0.50.”

surprises.description: Gross profit reached $53.3 million, well above the preview’s $22–$27 million estimate. The call also said gross profit grew about 144% year over year even excluding 45Z credits, indicating strength beyond the credits themselves.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit surged to $53.3 million from $14.3 million a year earlier,” and grew “approximately 144% year-over-year even excluding 45Z tax credits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Gross profit … ~$22–27M (14–16%).”

surprises.description: REX recognized $18.4 million of 45Z income in the quarter, substantially above the preview’s roughly $7.0–$7.3 million estimate based on a $0.10-per-gallon accrual. The preview specifically identified a higher accrual or true-up as something to watch, but the reported amount was much larger than its modeled run rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recognized approximately $18.4 million in Section 45 production tax credit income during the quarter,” flowing directly through gross profit.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “45Z credit … ~$7.0–7.3M” and said REX was “conservatively booking $0.10/gal.”

surprises.description: The EPA issued draft Class 6 injection well permits for three One Earth carbon-capture wells, a meaningful regulatory step beyond the preview’s baseline of ongoing review and a pending state application. The permits remain drafts in public comment, rather than final approvals.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On August 17, the U.S. EPA issued draft Class 6 injection well permits for three wells associated with the One Earth carbon capture project,” now in public comment.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “EPA review ongoing” and described a filing, completed technical review, or “a dated permit expectation” as the valuable disclosure to watch; its base case was “permits still pending.”

surprises.description: SG&A was $15.6 million, materially above the preview’s $9.5–$10.5 million estimate, primarily because of higher incentive compensation and restricted stock issued during the quarter. This was a meaningful cost headwind even as earnings substantially exceeded expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A expenses rose to $15.6 million from $6.2 million a year earlier,” primarily due to “higher incentive compensation and restricted stock issued during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “SG&A … ~$9.5–10.5M.”

surprises.description: Management said third-quarter results should be profitable and better than the same period last year, supported by record ethanol export demand. The preview did not identify this forward-looking earnings outlook.
