surprises.description: Management identified rising input costs—especially memory-chip pricing that shifts quarter to quarter—as a margin headwind, prompting price increases, product redesigns, and longer-term supplier contracts. The preview focused on product mix and integration risks, not this specific cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rising input costs, especially memory chips whose pricing is shifting quarter to quarter, pose a margin headwind, prompting IPS to implement price increases, redesign products for alternative memory, and secure long-term supplier contracts.”

surprises.description: The acquisition was described as giving Brady the #2 position in AIDC across an approximately $14 billion addressable market. The preview anticipated the acquisition’s roughly 70% scale relative to the existing business, but did not flag this market position or addressable-market framing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The PSS/IPS acquisition from Honeywell closed a month ago, increasing Brady's annualized top-line revenue by over 70% and giving it the #2 market position in the AIDC sector across a ~$14 billion addressable market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $1.4B Honeywell PSS acquisition … is 70% the size of the existing revenue base.”

surprises.description: Management set a target to reduce net leverage below 2x within two years while continuing dividends and buybacks. The preview flagged deleveraging as a key issue but did not provide or anticipate this specific timeline and leverage target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management targeting net leverage below 2x within two years while maintaining dividends (41st consecutive annual increase) and buybacks ($44 million authorization remaining).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Balance sheet / deleveraging path. Brady ran net cash into the deal. Q4 cash generation sets the starting point for absorbing $1.4B.”

in_line: Q4 adjusted diluted EPS was $1.48 versus the $1.47 consensus, consistent with the preview’s base-case range of $1.45–$1.49.

Europe and Australia organic growth was 2.1% in Q4, close to the preview’s expectation that the region would remain around 1–2%; full-year organic growth was 1.2%, matching the cited year-to-date weakness.

The expected IPS scale and economics were broadly affirmed: about $1.15 billion of revenue, low-double-digit segment margins, and roughly $0.80 of EPS accretion. The preview specifically asked whether the revenue and margin framing would hold.
The approximately $25 million acquisition-synergy target was consistent with the preview’s catalyst checklist, which asked whether that target would be reaffirmed.
GAAP EPS was weighed down by acquisition-related and amortization costs, as the preview had warned deal costs would push GAAP results below the guide.
FY2026 adjusted EPS of $5.29 was close to the $5.27 consensus and within the $5.20–$5.30 company guidance range.

surprises.description: The full-year adjusted EPS outlook of $1.65–$1.80 came in below the preview’s $1.90 consensus and mostly below its roughly $1.80 effective-bar estimate. Management also expects a sharp Q1 decline, with EPS turning positive only in Q4, signaling a particularly back-end-loaded recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EPS guidance was set at $1.65 to $1.80, with a sharp Q1 decline expected and EPS turning positive only by Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 adj. EPS: $1.90 | Street; TD Cowen $1.87, BofA $1.77”; the preview also says the effective bar is “closer to $1.80.”

surprises.description: The full-year organic sales outlook of approximately down 3% is weaker than the preview’s expectation of FY26 organic sales down 2% to 1% and its implied Q4 organic sales roughly flat to slightly positive. The preview had identified that expected inflection as the most checkable claim in the print.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Campbell's guided to fiscal 2026 organic net sales down approximately 3% at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY guide of −2% to −1% with management pointing to the lower end implies Q4 organic roughly flat to slightly positive”; the preview also describes the FY26 guide as “−2% to −1%.”

surprises.description: Campbell’s reduced its dividend, contrary to the preview’s base expectation that it would be held flat and its emphasis on an unambiguous affirmation. The preview identified dividend language as a central issue, but anticipated no cut signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management confirmed the dividend was reduced as a necessary decision.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dividend held flat, no cut signal”; the preview also calls for a “Dividend maintained with unambiguous language.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed price increases averaging 4%–5% across about 60% of its portfolio, with assumed elasticity of 1.5x and expected volume pressure. The preview anticipated planned pricing but described pricing as a last resort and framed the base case as “surgical,” so the breadth and expected volume trade-off are more pronounced than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company took price increases averaging 4% to 5% on about 60% of its portfolio, assuming elasticity of 1.5x, which will pressure volumes but benefit the bottom line starting in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “On the Q3 call pricing was a ‘last resort’ behind RGM and trade optimization”; the base-case commentary expected “surgical pricing.”

surprises.description: Snacks are now expected to decline high single digits in Q1, with margin recovery delayed until the second half. That is weaker near-term performance than the preview’s base case of Snacks still down about 4%–5% with margin holding around 10%–11% and its question about whether the Q4-exit margin would hold and build.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Snacks are expected to decline high single digits in Q1, hurt by lapping prior holiday shipments ahead of consumption and new trade investment, with margin recovery not occurring until the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario: “Snacks still −4/−5% but margin holds ~10–11%”; the preview asks, “Does the ~10% Q4-exit margin hold and build?”

surprises.description: Campbell’s announced a new $500 million savings program for fiscal 2027–2030, including $350 million of incremental savings, rather than merely continuing the existing program the preview expected to be reaffirmed. The incremental savings target is a favorable addition to the expected cost offsets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Campbell's announced a new $500 million cost savings program running from fiscal 2027 to 2030, including $150 million rolled over from the prior peak program and $350 million of incremental savings from headcount cuts, procurement, and supply chain optimization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base-case commentary expected “reiteration of the $375M savings program on track.”

surprises.description: Logistics inflation is expected to run around double digits before easing, an additional near-term cost pressure beyond the preview’s stated expectation of 5%–6% total inflation. The preview anticipated inflation to be front-loaded but did not flag this specific logistics magnitude.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management projects cost inflation of plus 5% to 6% throughout the year, with logistics inflation running around double digits before easing later in the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management framed 5–6% total inflation … with pressure front-loaded into 1H.”

surprises.description: Management expects full-year gross margin to decline 50–100 basis points, with a significant Q1 drop and improvement only later in the year. The preview focused on whether productivity and pricing could offset inflation and expected a credible bridge, but did not provide a specific gross-margin decline forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year gross margin is expected to be down 50 to 100 basis points, declining significantly in Q1 before improving sequentially and turning positive in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “How much is covered by productivity + the pulled-forward $100M SG&A program versus list pricing?”; the base case anticipated “inflation guide confirms 5–6% with credible offsets.”

surprises.description: Interest expense is projected to be roughly $25 million higher year over year, adding a specific financing headwind that the preview did not quantify. The preview discussed leverage and a possible hybrid instrument, but not this increase in interest expense.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Interest expense is projected to be roughly $25 million higher year-over-year, driven by the La Regina acquisition debt and refinancing of a $500 million bond maturing in March, with a hybrid issuance under consideration.”

in_line: Management’s overall cost-inflation outlook of 5%–6% was in line with the preview’s stated expectation of 5%–6% total inflation.

surprises.description: VS&Co reported adjusted EPS of $0.95, well above the preview’s $0.75–0.77 consensus range and even the preview’s $0.90+ bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS nearly tripled to $0.95 from $0.33, beating guidance of $0.65-0.75.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS ~ $0.75–0.77”; the bull case specified “$0.90+.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating income reached $124 million, beating both the preview’s roughly $100 million implied consensus and the top of company guidance by $24 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income surged 125% to $124 million, exceeding the high end of guidance ($90-100M) by $24 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating income ~$100M (implied)”; company guidance was “$90–100M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin expanded 320 basis points, exceeding the prior quarter’s 240-basis-point expansion and the preview’s bull-case threshold of 200 basis points, with most of the increase coming from stronger merchandise margin and less promotion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded 320 basis points to 38.8%, with roughly two-thirds driven by higher merchandise margin from increased regular-price selling and reduced promotions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether “the 240bp Q1 expansion repeat[s]” and described “GM +200bp+” as part of the bull case.

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year sales, adjusted operating income, and adjusted EPS ranges rather than merely maintaining or nudging up its previous guidance. The increase was real but remained below the preview’s bull-case levels of about $7.20 billion in sales and $4.75+ EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year fiscal 2026 guidance was raised to net sales of $7.10-7.18 billion … adjusted operating income of $560-590 million, and adjusted EPS of $4.45-4.70.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case said “FY nudged to high end of existing range, not raised”; it also said a raise was a catalyst and described the bull case as “~$7.20B / EPS $4.75+.”

surprises.description: VS&Co received more than $140 million in IEEPA tariff refunds, which were excluded from non-GAAP results but substantially strengthened cash and left the company with no ABL borrowings. The preview highlighted tariff exposure but did not anticipate these refunds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received IEEPA tariff refunds of over $140 million (over 95% of IEEPA tariffs paid), which were excluded from non-GAAP results, boosting the cash balance to $522 million … with no ABL borrowings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed the “tariff step-up” and tariff assumptions, but did not mention refunds.

surprises.description: Q3 guidance includes $10–20 million of operating income, meaning the company expects to be profitable in a historically loss-making quarter despite the preview’s concern that Q3 would be the first fully tariff-loaded quarter. The preview did not provide an operating-income estimate for Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for net sales of $1.57-1.60 billion (7-9% growth), with operating income of $10-20 million versus roughly break-even last year, signaling the company's return to profitability in a historically loss-making quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called Q3 “the first fully-loaded quarter” for tariffs and said its guidance was “the single highest-leverage item on the call,” but gave no Q3 operating-income forecast.

surprises.description: Sales of $1.611 billion were near the top of company guidance but came in slightly below the preview’s $1.617–1.62 billion consensus range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales increased 10% year-over-year to $1.611 billion, near the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales ~ $1.617–1.62B”; the preview noted consensus was “at or above the top of management's own guidance range.”

surprises.description: Management plans to raise marketing spend from just over 7% of sales toward the high single digits over the next couple of years, an incremental investment plan the preview did not specifically anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management plans to raise marketing spend from just over 7% of sales toward high single digits over the next couple years, funding investments like the Angels Among Us docu-series and Fashion Show.”

in_line: Sales growth of 10% and comparable-sales growth of 9% were within the preview’s expected 9–11% year-over-year sales-growth range; comps also remained well above the preview’s stated 6%-or-below concern threshold.

International growth slowed from the Q1 rate, but the preview had specifically flagged deceleration as a risk; management reported 20% growth (10% adjusted for the European digital reporting shift) and expected moderation in the back half.

surprises.description: DLTH reported adjusted EPS of $0.50 versus the preview’s $0.01 consensus, but $0.44 per share came from a $16.3 million tariff refund; excluding that contribution, EPS was about $0.06, a much narrower beat. The preview noted roughly $12 million of potential refunds and no benefit in guidance, so receiving and recognizing $16.3 million in Q2 was a larger-than-anticipated upside item.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS of $0.50, which included $16.3 million in tariff refunds contributing $0.44 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management confirmed it paid ~$12M in IEEPA tariffs and has applied for refunds with zero benefit in guidance”; “~$12M is ~9% of market cap in cash, entirely off-model. Any timing/recognition commentary is asymmetric upside.” Consensus adjusted EPS was “$0.01.”

surprises.description: DLTH raised full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance by $10 million at both ends, to $38–42 million, far beyond the preview’s expected $28–32 million hold and even above its bull-case range of $30–34 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance to $38-42 million from the prior $28-32 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the expected guide was “$28–32M” and that a hold was the base case; its bull case assumed “FY EBITDA raised to $30–34M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin expanded much more than the preview expected: roughly 59.6% excluding tariff refunds, versus a preview estimate around 57% and expected year-over-year expansion of about 200–300 basis points. The preview’s upper range for the absolute margin was 57.5%, still well below the reported level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding tariff refunds, underlying gross margin still expanded 490-520 basis points to roughly 59.6%, driven by nearly 6% higher average unit retails and direct factory sourcing savings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Gross margin ~57%” and expected YoY expansion to “roughly halve to +200–300bps”; its base case was “~57.0–57.5%.”

surprises.description: Q2 sales were modestly ahead of consensus and near the top of the preview’s guidance-implied range: $121.4 million versus $119.9 million consensus and an implied Q2 range topping out at $121.7 million. The 7.8% decline was also less severe than the preview’s 9.0% consensus decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales declined 7.8% to $121.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed consensus net sales of “$119.9M” and an implied Q2 range of “$112.4M–$121.7M,” with consensus implying “-9.0%” year over year.

surprises.description: DLTH ended the quarter with no ABL debt and generated $13 million of free cash flow, a $41 million year-over-year improvement, versus the preview’s expectation of $6 million drawn on the ABL and $6.1 million of cash. That is a stronger liquidity and debt position than the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ended the quarter with zero debt on its ABL facility (versus $32.5 million a year ago) and generated $13 million in free cash flow, a $41 million year-over-year improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Balance sheet: $6.1M cash, $6M drawn on a $100M ABL.”

surprises.description: Inventory was lower in dollars than the preview expected, but the year-over-year reduction and current-product mix were weaker than its estimates: actual inventory was down 15.5% with 85.4% current products, versus the preview’s expected 24.8% decline and 90.2% current mix. The sharp reduction in clearance inventory is a favorable counterpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total inventory fell 15.5% (down $22.9 million) to $125.2 million”; “Clearance inventory was cut 43.1% in dollars and 46.6% in units, improving the inventory mix to 85.4% current products.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Inventory -24.8% to $132.4M with 90.2% current / 9.8% clearance.”

surprises.description: The channel and customer picture was less uniformly encouraging than the preview’s expectation of positive retail comps and improving DTC: stores were flat for the first half while DTC declined 7.6%, and management said the customer base had contracted as promotions were reset. Retention and NPS improved, with NPS up 11%, providing a positive counterpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retail stores outperformed direct, delivering flat first-half sales versus a 7.6% DTC decline, though the customer base has contracted as promotions were reset even as retention and NPS (up 11%) improved.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said retail “comped +3.3%” in Q1, described DTC’s Q1 decline as “-8.7%,” and said “Any sequential improvement in DTC decline is the leading indicator for the H2 guide.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed steep declines in women’s product sales and the AKHG brand, which the preview did not quantify or flag as a segment-level risk. Management attributed them to SKU rationalization and exits from lower-margin categories, including swimwear, so the sales weakness came alongside deliberate assortment cleanup.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Women's product sales fell 15% and AKHG brand sales dropped 26% due to SKU rationalization and exiting low-margin categories like swimwear.”

in_line: Full-year net sales guidance remained $540–560 million, as the preview expected.
The second-half sales outlook remained minus 2% to plus 2%, consistent with the preview’s key expectation that the stabilization range would be reaffirmed.
Adjusted EBITDA excluding the tariff refund was $10.7 million, within the preview’s $10–11 million Q2 estimate.

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance came in well above the preview’s roughly $114M bar: the $119.5M midpoint is also above the preview’s base-case range of $112M–$116M. Management attributed the expected sequential growth to physical-AI demand from IoT.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 FY2027 revenue guidance is $115M-$124M ($119.5M midpoint), representing ~10.5% sequential growth led by physical AI demand from IoT.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bar is ~$114M”; base scenario Q3 guide midpoint “$112–116M.”

surprises.description: Ambarella raised its five-year SAM growth forecast from about 18% to about 20% annually, and said IoT will make up about 70% of the terminal-year market, primarily due to the new edge-infrastructure business. The preview did not flag this larger market outlook or mix shift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its 5-year serviceable market (SAM) forecast to grow from $8.5 billion in FY2027 to $22.9 billion in FY2032, a ~20% CAGR, up from the prior ~18% CAGR estimate”; “IoT markets now representing about 70% of the terminal year, driven primarily by the new edge infrastructure business.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed two seven-year indirect-channel partnerships, each expected to generate about $0.5B in revenue. That adds substantial prospective business not flagged in the preview, though management said meaningful revenue is still 2–3 years away.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ambarella signed two 7-year indirect channel partnerships (Capgemini and Macnica), each expected to generate approximately $0.5 billion in revenue, though meaningful revenue is 2-3 years away.”

surprises.description: Ambarella introduced a standalone AI-accelerator line and previewed the X7 SoC, an unanticipated product disclosure in the preview. The product is still in simulation, so the announcement is an early-stage opportunity rather than near-term revenue evidence.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company introduced a new standalone AI accelerator product line, previewing the X7 SoC (currently in simulation), which requires only 4MB of memory and a 4-5 watt power envelope to run large language models as an AI coprocessor.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was below the preview’s roughly 59.8% expectation, although it remained within the company’s 59.0%–60.5% guidance range. Management said it plans to pass rising supply-chain costs to customers to defend its long-term margin target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin was 59.3%, below the guidance midpoint, and management plans to pass rising supply chain costs to customers to maintain its long-term 59%-62% gross margin target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview consensus for non-GAAP gross margin was “~59.8%”; company guidance was 59.0%–60.5%.

surprises.description: Memory-cost and scarcity risks had been flagged as a potential second-half demand problem, but management reported that they had already caused a small revenue impact in Q2 and Q3 and were creating uncertainty about Q4 order volumes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rising memory prices and scarcity are creating Q4 uncertainty, as customers may reduce order volumes; management noted a small revenue impact was already seen in Q2 and Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had warned of “much higher DRAM and NAND pricing plus potential shortage in H2” and described customer demand reduction as a risk.

surprises.description: Inventory days rose from 145 to 157 rather than stabilizing or declining, moving close to the preview’s 160-day warning threshold. This occurred even though Q2 revenue was not at the low end of expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory days rose from 145 to 157 days.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said 145 days “needs to stabilize” and that days coming down or holding would support the supply-preparation explanation; it warned about 160+ days if revenue landed low.

surprises.description: The call disclosed the cancellation of an automotive-autonomy customer’s development project, an unanticipated customer/project setback. The cancellation reduced GAAP R&D expense by $9M, but management said it did not affect the non-GAAP outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A $9 million reduction in GAAP R&D expense was recognized from the cancellation of an automotive autonomy customer's development project, with no impact on non-GAAP outlook.”

surprises.description: The board authorized a new $50M share-repurchase program, which was not anticipated in the preview. No shares were repurchased during Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The board authorized a new $50 million share repurchase program valid through June 30, 2027, though no shares were repurchased during Q2.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was $0.18, one cent above the preview’s $0.17 consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS of $0.18.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Non-GAAP EPS consensus: “$0.17.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was essentially in line with expectations: $108.1M was close to the $108M guidance midpoint and within the preview’s approximately $108M–$110M consensus range.
Q2 year-over-year revenue growth of 13.2% was close to the preview’s roughly 13% expectation.

surprises.description: The preview expected Learning revenue of $99–104 million, down 10%–14%; Wiley reported $93 million, down 20%, with both Academic and Professional down 20%. Learning's adjusted EBITDA margin also fell to 15.1% from 27.4%, a sharp deterioration beyond the revenue weakness the preview highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Learning revenue fell 20% to $93 million, with both academic and professional down 20%, and segment adjusted EBITDA margin collapsed to 15.1% from 27.4% on revenue declines and mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Learning ~$99–104M (−10% to −14%) — Academic ~$54M, Professional ~$45M”; the preview also flagged another double-digit Professional decline as a bear-case concern.

surprises.description: The preview expected a roughly $25 million year-over-year revenue headwind from prior-year AI licensing projects. Management reported a $29 million headwind, $4 million greater than that estimate, though it said the comparison did not change full-year expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue faced a known $29 million headwind from AI licensing revenue that landed in the prior-year quarter, which management said does not change full-year expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~$25M unfavorable year-over-year revenue comparison in Q1 from prior-year AI licensing projects.”

surprises.description: Emerald contributed $13 million of revenue, slightly below the preview's approximately $14 million expectation for its two-month contribution. Its $5 million of adjusted EBITDA implies a margin of about 38%, essentially matching the preview's expected 37%–38% operating margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Emerald contributed $13 million of revenue and $5 million of adjusted EBITDA in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~$14M from two months of Emerald”; the preview asked whether Emerald would land at “~$14M for two months at the promised 37–38% operating margin.”

surprises.description: Wiley reported a GAAP loss of $0.23 per share, versus earnings of $0.22 a year earlier, due to restructuring and Emerald acquisition and integration costs. The preview forecast positive adjusted EPS, but did not give a GAAP EPS estimate, so the GAAP loss was not directly covered by its estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 GAAP EPS was a loss of $0.23 versus earnings of $0.22 a year ago, driven by restructuring charges and Emerald acquisition and integration costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS ~$0.46” consensus; the preview's own adjusted EPS estimate was “~$0.28–0.38.”

surprises.description: Research revenue and Publishing growth were broadly in line with the preview, but Research adjusted EBITDA grew 9% and its margin expanded 130 basis points to 29.6%. The preview did not anticipate that degree of margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Research adjusted EBITDA grew 9% with margin expanding 130 basis points to 29.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected Research revenue of “~$294–298M (+4–6%)” and Publishing organic growth, but gave no Research adjusted EBITDA or margin-growth estimate.

in_line: Wiley reaffirmed FY27 adjusted EPS guidance of $4.60–$5.05, adjusted EBITDA margin of 26.5%–27.5%, and free cash flow of $205 million, matching the preview's stated full-year guidance.
Research revenue rose 4% to $293 million and Publishing rose 12% (about 6% excluding Emerald), broadly matching the preview's Research and organic Publishing estimates.
Recurring AI revenue was $3.5 million, within the preview's expected Q1 range of $3–4 million; Wiley also remained on track for over $50 million of FY27 AI revenue, as expected.
Emerald's approximately 38% adjusted EBITDA margin, year-one EPS accretion expectation, and $30 million year-three cost-synergy target were consistent with the preview's expectations.
Net debt to EBITDA was 2.1x pro forma including Emerald synergies, matching the preview's approximately 2.1x pro forma leverage estimate.
The 33rd consecutive annual dividend increase was already flagged in the preview.

surprises.description: Matrix provided no FY2027 revenue guidance, despite the preview treating an initial guide as likely and describing $950 million–$1.0 billion as the in-line range. Management said it would wait until a permanent CFO is onboarded.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “will not provide guidance until a permanent CFO is onboarded”; A.J. Smith is serving as Interim CFO.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the release would “most likely” include the initial FY2027 revenue guide, and that “$950M–$1.0B is in line.”

surprises.description: Q4 gross margin was 8.0%, well short of the preview’s 9.5%+ watch level and below its 8.5% concern threshold. The margin did improve sharply year over year, but not to the level the preview looked for as evidence of overhead recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 gross margin was “8.0%” versus 3.8% a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch for 9.5%+ consolidated gross margin” and flagged “Below 8.5%” as putting the operating-leverage story in question.

surprises.description: Awards of $169 million and 0.7x book-to-bill fell short of the preview’s roughly $200 million base case and the approximately $220 million needed to hold backlog near $1 billion. Ending backlog was $953 million, below the preview’s roughly $981 million base-case estimate, though just above its $950 million warning level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 project awards totaled $169 million for a weak 0.7x book-to-bill,” and backlog ended at “$953 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Matrix needed “~$220M+ of awards (0.9x)” to hold backlog near $1.0 billion; its base case was “~$200M” of awards and “~$981M” exit backlog.

surprises.description: Process and Industrial Facilities remained weak rather than showing the Q4 inflection the preview was watching for: revenue was $33.6 million, down from $47.3 million a year earlier, and its margin was only 2.9%. The call facts do not establish whether the anticipated mining project started, but the segment results themselves did not show a recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: Process and Industrial Facilities revenue “dropped to $33.6 million from $47.3 million,” while its Q4 margin was “2.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the newly awarded Western US mining project “the stated inflection” and said confirmation it started on schedule was “the cleanest test” of the rebuild.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was slightly below the $247 million consensus estimate, although it remained inside the guidance-implied range and the preview’s expected $241 million–$251 million band. This was a small consensus miss, not a miss of the company’s revenue guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 revenue was “$244.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Revenue $247.0M” consensus and said a revenue print in the “$241–251M band” would meet guidance.

surprises.description: The company incurred $3.4 million of restructuring costs in Q4, an unanticipated charge that weighed on the quarter; management said future restructuring should be insignificant.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$3.4 million of restructuring costs hit Q4,” with future restructuring “expected to be insignificant.”

surprises.description: The company said it was actively evaluating a stock buyback, introducing a potential shareholder return that the preview did not identify as a possibility. It remains under evaluation, not a committed repurchase.
surprises.fact_evidence: Matrix had “$283.9 million in total liquidity” and was “actively evaluating a stock buyback.”

surprises.description: Matrix was selected for FEED work on America First Refining’s Brownsville storage tank farm, a specific project opportunity not identified in the preview. The larger award is still contingent on a final investment decision and may not enter backlog until late Q3 or early Q4 FY2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: Matrix was “selected for the FEED” on the tank farm, with a larger award “potentially converting to backlog in late Q3 or early Q4 fiscal 2027 pending FID.”

surprises.description: Year-end total liquidity was lower than the Q3 figure, despite the preview flagging roughly $20 million of expected legacy-dispute cash inflows and Q4 seasonality as reasons to check for cash generation. The call facts do not say whether the dispute proceeds arrived or explain the movement.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended the quarter with “$283.9 million in total liquidity” and “$223 million unrestricted cash,” versus Q3 total liquidity of $297.2 million in the preview.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had flagged “~$20M of cash inflow from resolving two legacy disputes” and asked investors to check Q4 cash flow because “Q4 is seasonally the cash quarter.”

in_line: Adjusted EPS of $0.16 was close to the preview’s roughly $0.17 consensus and within its stated $0.15–$0.18 range.

The return to profitability and large year-over-year earnings improvement were expected given the easy prior-year comparison; the preview explicitly cautioned that a large YoY EPS improvement was “not new information.”
The opportunity pipeline exceeded $7 billion, broadly in line with the preview’s $6.9 billion Q3 baseline.

surprises.description: Q3 net sales were $1.23 billion, above the preview’s $1.19–$1.20 billion consensus and even the $1.20–$1.22 billion buy-side range. Growth of 8.4% also exceeded the preview’s implied consensus growth of 5.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 net sales grew 8.4% to $1.23 billion (6.2% organically).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | ~$1.19–1.20B”; buy-side revenue expectations “likely sit at the high end, ~$1.20–1.22B.”

surprises.description: Toro raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance rather than merely narrowing or holding it: the midpoint rose by over $0.07 to $4.63. The preview identified a raise as needed but considered a narrow-and-hold the likeliest outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $4.60-$4.65 (midpoint $4.63) from the prior $4.50-$4.62, lifting the midpoint by over $0.07.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A narrow-and-hold at $4.50–$4.62 is the single most likely source of a negative reaction”; the base case was guidance “narrowed to ~$4.54–$4.62 (midpoint held/nudged).”

surprises.description: Full-year sales growth guidance was raised to 6.3%–6.6%, substantially above the prior 4%–6.5% range. The preview’s base case anticipated narrowing with the midpoint held or nudged, while its bull case anticipated a raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year net sales growth guidance was raised and narrowed to 6.3%-6.6% from the prior 4%-6.5% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The standing guidance was “+4.0% to +6.5%”; the base case expected it to be “narrowed to reflect year-to-date performance,” while the bull case anticipated “raising the low end of the sales range.”

surprises.description: Q3 adjusted EPS of $1.33 beat the $1.30 consensus, although it landed within the preview’s stated $1.32–$1.34 buy-side whisper range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS of $1.33.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | $1.30 (range $1.29–$1.32)”; the buy-side EPS whisper was “~$1.32–1.34.”

surprises.description: Residential sales growth of 8.6% surpassed the preview’s expected +2%–+6% range. However, its 5.9% margin remained below the preview’s high-single-digit margin expectation despite improving 400 basis points year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The residential segment grew net sales 8.6% and improved adjusted operating margin by 400 basis points year-over-year to 5.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Residential sales were estimated at “+2–6%”; the preview called for “a high-single-digit margin” and cited a “swing from 1.9% to ~8% margin.”

surprises.description: Professional sales growth of 8.8% was well above the preview’s projected 5%–6% growth. But the segment’s 20.9% margin declined 40 basis points and fell short of the preview’s 21.3% year-ago benchmark and its clean-beat threshold of 21%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The professional segment grew net sales 8.8% (6.1% organic) but adjusted operating margin declined 40 basis points to 20.9% due to product mix, higher manufacturing costs, and Tornado acquisition dilution.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Professional sales were estimated at “+5–6%”; the preview highlighted the “21.3% Q3 FY2025 comp” and said “Anything ≥21% is a clean beat.”

surprises.description: The AMP program had already reached its $125 million run-rate savings target, ahead of the preview’s expectation that it was on track to reach that target by year end. The additional comment that unrealized in-year benefits should carry into fiscal 2027 points to continued margin expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The AMP productivity program has already reached its $125 million run-rate savings target, with unrealized in-year benefits expected to carry into fiscal 2027 for continued margin expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “$95M of the $125M run-rate savings target delivered; on track to hit $125M by year end.”

surprises.description: The refund outlook was lower than the preview’s roughly $20 million full-year expectation: guidance for anticipated IEEPA refunds was reduced from $12 million to $7 million. The company also removed $5 million reclassified outside Phase 2 from Q4 residential margin, complicating the expected tariff and margin bridge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Anticipated IEEPA tariff refunds in guidance were reduced to $7 million from $12 million, with $5 million reclassified outside Phase 2 and removed from Q4 residential margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “~$20M expected refunds” and said management needed to “quantify how much of the Q3 hit was absorbed and confirm Q4 mitigation is landing.”

surprises.description: Year-to-date free-cash-flow conversion reached 128%, above the preview’s 1H rate of 124.5% and its ≥120% conversion benchmark. The company used $358 million for share repurchases, an allocation not specifically anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-to-date free cash flow reached $425 million at a 128% conversion rate, funding $358 million of share repurchases.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “1H FCF $265.5M at 124.5% conversion” and said to watch for reaffirmation of “≥120%.”

surprises.description: Inventory and working capital improved materially, driven by lower finished-goods balances. The preview discussed field inventory being below target but did not anticipate these reported company inventory and working-capital reductions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory improved $153 million year-over-year and working capital improved $217 million, driven by lower finished goods balances.”

surprises.description: The Q3 tax rate was 22.4%, above the preview’s approximately 21.7% full-year assumption, and was a larger EPS headwind than that assumption implied. The release attributed a $0.08 EPS offset to the higher tax rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 EPS benefited from $0.12 in operational performance, $0.05 from buybacks, and $0.06 from tariff refunds, partially offset by an $0.08 higher tax rate (22.4%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Standing guidance included a “tax rate ~21.7% (+300bps, ~$0.04 EPS headwind).”

surprises.description: Lululemon cut FY2026 EPS guidance to $9.48–$9.73, far below the preview’s roughly $10.94 consensus and even below the low end of its bear-case range. Revenue guidance also fell to $10.35–$10.5 billion, versus the preview’s $11.0–$11.15 billion company guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was lowered to $10.35-$10.5 billion (down 5-7%), with full-year EPS cut to $9.48-$9.73 versus $13.26 in 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 EPS” consensus “~$10.94”; the preview’s base case expected “EPS trimmed modestly to ~$10.40–10.75,” while its bear case was “~$9.50–10.00.”

surprises.description: China Mainland growth fell well short of the preview’s mid-to-high-teens expectation: revenue grew just 4% reported and declined 2% in constant currency, with comps down 8%. Management attributed the shortfall mainly to negative social-media sentiment and a weaker Tmall 618 event.
surprises.fact_evidence: “China Mainland revenue grew only 4% reported (down 2% constant currency) with comps down 8%, the primary source of the quarterly shortfall driven by negative social/media sentiment and a weaker Tmall 618 event.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed China Mainland at “mid-to-high teens” growth and described it as “the last growth engine.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $2.4 billion, below the preview’s $2.46 billion consensus, and declined 4% rather than the expected 2%–3%. Comparable sales were down 10%, contributing to the full-year guidance cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 total net revenue declined 4% (5% in constant currency) to $2.4 billion with comparable sales down 10%, driving a full-year guidance cut.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave Q2 revenue consensus of “$2.46B” and expected growth of “–3% to –2%.”

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook points to a sharp further deterioration: revenue is forecast down 10%–11%, operating margin around 6.5%, and EPS $0.93–$0.98. The preview did not provide Q3 estimates, but its base case anticipated only a modest FY EPS trim, not this degree of near-term weakness.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for revenue of $2.29-$2.32 billion (down 10-11%), operating margin of ~6.5% versus 17% a year ago, and EPS of $0.93-$0.98 versus $2.59 last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “EPS trimmed modestly to ~$10.40–10.75”; it gave no specific Q3 revenue, operating-margin, or EPS estimate.

surprises.description: Management expects North America to deteriorate from Q2’s 12% comparable-sales decline to a mid-teens decline in Q3. The preview warned that a mid-teens US decline would break the thesis, but its base case expected US comps around down 11%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North America revenue fell 8% with comparable sales down 12%, and management guides Q3 North America to worsen to a mid-teens decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “US comps ~–11%”; it said “Mid-teens = thesis break.”

surprises.description: A $134.5 million pretax IEEPA tariff refund materially lifted Q2 results, adding 560 basis points to margin and $0.86 to EPS. This was an unexpected one-off tailwind; reported operating margin was still 18.8%, below 20.7% a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 operating margin was 18.8% versus 20.7% a year ago, but included a $134.5 million pretax IEEPA tariff refund that added 560 basis points and contributed $0.86 to EPS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the FY tariff assumptions included “no recovery assumed on tariffs paid.”

surprises.description: Q3 SG&A is expected to deleverage by 800 basis points year over year, with about 450 basis points of deleverage for the full year. That is a substantial expense burden amid lower sales, even as management increases marketing and cuts discretionary costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 SG&A is expected to deleverage 800 basis points year-over-year due to lower sales, increased marketing, and expense timing, with full-year SG&A deleverage of ~450 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described 2H marketing spend as “bolder,” but did not flag this degree of SG&A deleverage.

surprises.description: Demand weakened sharply in specific product categories: leggings sales fell about 20% as guests shifted toward away-from-body silhouettes, and accessories declined 13% amid bag softness. The preview noted that recent launches had fallen short, but did not anticipate these category declines or this shift in customer preference.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Leggings sales dropped approximately 20% in Q2 as guests shift toward away-from-body silhouettes, while accessories declined 13% amid softness in bags.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had admitted recent launches “ran ‘short of expectations.’”

surprises.description: Lululemon reduced planned net new store openings to about 35, below the preview’s stated low-end plan of 40–45, and also cut pop-up stores from 65 to about 40. This indicates a deeper pullback in physical expansion than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company cut planned net new store openings to approximately 35 (from ~40), is reducing pop-up stores from 65 to ~40.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY net new stores were guided to “the low end of 40–45.”

in_line: Q2 North America comparable sales were down 12%, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of a low-double-digit decline and its base-case estimate of about down 11%.
The incoming CEO’s start next week and the deferral of strategic reassessment to her tenure were consistent with the preview’s expectation that the interim team would leave strategy for O’Neill.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was reported at $23.3 million, well above the $12–16 million Q2 guidance, because an $11.1 million tariff refund benefit was recognized. Excluding the refund, EBITDA was $12.1 million, within guidance; the refund also lifted the headline full-year outlook to $76–86 million while the underlying $65–75 million outlook stayed unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $23.3 million (10% margin), but excluding an $11.1 million tariff refund benefit, it was $12.1 million (5.2% margin), within guidance.” The full-year outlook was raised to $76–$86 million “to reflect the tariff refund,” with the underlying outlook unchanged at $65–$75 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guidance excludes Phase 1 ($9–11M) and Phase 2 ($1.5–2.5M).” The preview also described “$9–11M refund collected” as part of its bull scenario.

surprises.description: Q2 net sales of $231.7 million came in below the preview’s practical $236 million bar and just below the company’s $232 million guidance floor. That is a modest shortfall, even against the preview’s below-consensus adjusted bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales fell to $231.7 million … with comparable sales declining 6.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat $236M (guide midpoint) as the real bar.” Company Q2 guidance was “$232–240M.”

surprises.description: Comparable sales declined 6.3%, worse than the preview’s base-case expectation of a 3%–5% decline, although not as weak as its bear-case threshold. The later July improvement does not change that Q2 comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable sales declining 6.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case called for “Comps -3% to -5%”; its bear case was “Comps -7%+.”

surprises.description: Gross margin excluding the tariff refund was 33.9%, down 170 basis points year over year because of targeted promotions. That was below the preview’s roughly 35.5% base-case expectation, despite the reported gross margin rising to 38.7% with the refund benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin rose to 38.7% from 35.6%, but excluding the tariff refund, gross margin declined 170 basis points to 33.9% due to targeted promotions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “GM ~35.5%”; its bull case called for “GM ≥36%.”

surprises.description: Management said comparable sales had turned positive in July and expected comparable-sales growth in the back half, a stronger stated trend than the preview’s expectation of roughly flat back-half sales. All 11 marketing channels were improving sequentially.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable sales inflected positively in July with all 11 marketing channels improving sequentially, and management expects a return to comparable sales growth in the back half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said sales were expected to “inflect from -9% to roughly flat” in the back half, with implied H2 sales of “$458–478M (-2.8% to +1.5%).”

surprises.description: The store-optimization program was essentially complete at 177 total closures, with management expecting about $40 million of expense savings in fiscal 2026. The preview noted prior closures but did not flag completion or quantify these savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The store optimization program is essentially complete with 177 total closures … and is expected to deliver ~$40 million in expense savings in fiscal 2026.”

surprises.description: Digital monetization and app engagement were stronger than anything the preview had identified: paid revenue grew double digits on lower spend, and the app reached nearly 40% of digital revenue with roughly seven times the conversion rate of desktop/mobile web.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Paid revenue grew double digits on lower spend, now representing 12% of digital revenue (up from 9%), while the mobile app hit an all-time high of nearly 40% of digital revenue and converts at roughly 7x desktop/mobile web rates.”

in_line: The underlying full-year adjusted EBITDA outlook remained $65–75 million and net sales guidance remained $940–960 million, as in the preview’s stated guidance.
Sub-brands grew approximately 74% year-to-date and remained on track for about $110 million in 2026, or 60% growth, matching the preview’s roughly $110 million and 60% growth expectation.
Footwear remained a Q2 comparable-sales drag and management still expected it to become a sales and margin tailwind in the second half, consistent with the preview’s expected H1-to-H2 shift.
Excluding the tariff refund, Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $12.1 million was within the company’s $12–16 million guidance range.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $216.4 million, above the $214.15 million consensus and the $215 million top of guidance. That also reversed the preview’s expected growth deceleration: reported growth was 10%, versus 8.8% implied by consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY27 revenue was $216.4 million, up 10% year-over-year, accelerating from Q1 and exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus” revenue was “$214.15M”; the guide was “$213–215M” and implied “+8.8%” year-over-year.

surprises.description: AI Studio and AI teammates contributed about 25% of net new ARR, or about 22% excluding one large deal—well above the 15% full-year target and above the preview’s >20% bull-case threshold. The preview expected an AI update, but this level of contribution was stronger than its 17–19% base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI Studio and AI teammates drove approximately 25% of net new ARR (about 22% excluding one large deal), up from 17% last quarter and above the 15% full-year target set in March.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 was “17% vs. a 15% full-year target,” identified “>20%” as the bull trigger, and put the base case at “AI 17–19% of net-new ARR.”

surprises.description: The full-year revenue range’s ceiling stayed at $863.5 million, short of the preview’s hoped-for raise to at least $865 million, despite the Q2 beat. The low end did rise by $3 million, so this was not a wholly unchanged range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year FY27 revenue guidance is $858.5 million to $863.5 million (9% growth at midpoint).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 needs to move to ≥$865M to be read as a raise”; the preview also said a range “merely” reaffirmed would read as a de facto cut.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating margin reached 10%, about 110 basis points above the preview’s roughly 8.9% consensus, while EPS was $0.10 versus $0.0875 consensus. Both profitability measures outperformed expectations despite the anticipated StackAI margin drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin was 10%, expanding roughly 300 basis points year-over-year, with net income of $23.8 million or $0.10 per diluted share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 non-GAAP operating margin consensus at “~8.9%” and EPS consensus at “$0.0875”; it also expected a “~1pt operating margin drag in Q2” from StackAI.

surprises.description: Overall dollar-based NRR improved to 97%, but remained one point below the preview’s 98% in-quarter expectation. Core-customer and $100,000-plus-customer NRR both reached 98%, with the latter improving from 96%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Overall dollar-based net retention rate improved to 97% from 96%, with core customer NRR and $100,000+ customer NRR both reaching 98% (the latter up from 96%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called “in-quarter NRR 98%” the cleanest proof of improvement and said “NRR 96% / 97%” was the prior-quarter trailing/in-quarter figure.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a new second-half revenue timing headwind from consumption-based AI revenue recognition and AWM packaging, plus additional gross-margin pressure. The preview discussed PLG and StackAI pressures but did not flag these specific timing and margin effects.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The transition to consumption-based AI revenue recognition and AWM packaging creates a $1.2 million second-half revenue timing headwind, split between Q3 and Q4, plus about 150 bps of second-half gross margin pressure.”

surprises.description: Gross margin declined about 120 basis points sequentially to 87% as AI infrastructure costs rose, Stack AI was added, and the mix shifted toward AI products. The preview focused on StackAI’s operating-margin drag, not this reported gross-margin decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined about 120 basis points sequentially to 87%, driven by higher AI infrastructure costs (80 bps), the Stack AI addition (30 bps), and mix shift toward AI products.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described StackAI as carrying a “~1pt operating margin drag in Q2 and 2H.”

surprises.description: Enterprise AI adoption was evidenced by a record AI expansion agreement: a Fortune 500 media company signed a three-year multimillion-dollar deal with nearly half of contract value from AI products. More than one-quarter of customers spending over $100,000 had purchased AI Studio or an AI teammate; the preview had not specified these adoption milestones.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Over 25% of customers spending $100,000+ have now purchased AI Studio or an AI teammate,” and the company “signed its largest AI expansion deal ever,” a “3-year multimillion-dollar agreement with a Fortune 500 media company,” with AI products at “nearly half of total contract value.”

surprises.description: U.S. revenue returned to double-digit growth for the first time in more than two years. The preview did not identify this U.S. growth milestone as an expectation or a key debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. revenue grew 10% year-over-year, returning to double-digit growth for the first time in over two years.”

surprises.description: The technology vertical posted a second consecutive quarter of growth, continuing its recovery after the prior quarter’s turn positive. The preview noted the initial turn but said tech outperformance was excluded from the FY outlook, leaving continued growth as potential upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The technology vertical posted a second consecutive quarter of growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the tech vertical had “turn[ed] positive after eight quarters” in Q1, while the FY outlook “excludes tech-vertical outperformance.”

in_line: Core-customer and $100,000-plus-customer NRR both reached 98%, matching the preview’s 98% improvement benchmark for in-quarter NRR, even though overall NRR was 97%.

surprises.description: The preview did not mention an Investor Day or Analyst Day, but eGain announced that both would be held in Chicago on October 13 alongside eGain Solve. This is an unexpected event announcement, though the facts provided do not indicate its financial or operational implications.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call announced an Investor Day and Analyst Day to be held in conjunction with eGain Solve on October 13 in Chicago.

surprises.description: Revenue of $54.6 million exceeded the preview’s $53.1 million anchor and its $54.0 million alternate consensus figure. The beat was modest, and it was closer to the preview’s roughly $54 million buy-side bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 fiscal 2027 revenue grew 55% year-over-year to $54.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $53.1M (Zacks) / $54.0M (S&P agg.)”; the preview also says, “Assume the buy-side bar is $0.06 and ~$54M.”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $0.06, above the preview’s published $0.05 consensus, though it matched the preview’s higher $0.06 whisper estimate. Adjusted EBITDA of $5.5 million also topped the preview’s $5.3 million estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income more than doubled, rising 100.9% to $2.6 million ($0.06 per diluted share)”; “Adjusted EBITDA increased 68.9% to $5.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) | $0.05”; “Adj. EBITDA | ~$5.2M”; the preview also says, “the buy-side bar is $0.06.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 24.0%, just below the preview’s 24.3% estimate, and did not show the stronger recovery the preview identified as a possible validation of easing startup costs. Management instead said it shifted about $0.5 million into trade spend and spent over $1 million more on trade year over year, pressuring near-term gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved sequentially to 24.0% from 23.6% in Q1 but declined from 24.9% year-over-year”; management “intentionally shifted about $0.5 million (roughly a full point of margin) from marketing into trade spend and spent over $1 million more in trade than the prior year due to high returns.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimates: Revenue $53.5M, gross margin 24.3%”; the preview says Q2 is “the first quarter where those startup costs should begin unwinding” and describes 24.0–24.9% as “acceptable, on-track.”

surprises.description: Mama’s announced a first-ever Kroger launch for next month, an expansion the preview did not flag. The initial placement is limited to over 100 stores—about 10% of Kroger’s roughly 1,300 banner locations—with four items.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company will launch in Kroger for the first time next month, starting with over 100 stores in the Louisville division with four items … representing about 10% of Kroger's ~1,300 banner locations.”

surprises.description: Costco confirmed a second-half multi-vendor mailer across all eight regions that management forecasts will be larger than last year. The preview focused on a Costco everyday placement to watch, rather than anticipating this broader mailer.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Costco confirmed a second-half multi-vendor mailer across all eight regions forecasted to be larger than last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists “the Costco San Diego branded beef meatball everyday placement” among the items to watch.

surprises.description: Walmart distribution grew beyond the preview’s cited 2,000-plus-store footprint, reaching over 2,300 stores with nine items. This is a positive expansion beyond the distribution level the preview described, although the preview had specifically called for sell-through and repeat-rate detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Walmart distribution expanded to over 2,300 stores (up from ~2,000) with nine items.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview describes “7 Walmart chicken SKUs in 2,000+ stores” and says to watch for “actual velocity/repeat-rate commentary versus another list of door counts.”

surprises.description: The company said its larger cash balance enables larger, more transformative M&A, but the reported update remained a broad statement of capacity rather than the targets, size, or timing the preview said investors wanted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $138.6 million in cash … against only $4.8 million total debt, enabling larger and more transformative M&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said investors “need a timeline” and wanted “targets, size, timing, and whether the $94M is one deal or several.”

in_line: Management maintained its mid-to-high-20% corporate gross-margin target, consistent with the preview’s stated target.
Management reiterated confidence in double-digit revenue growth and a long-term line of sight to $1 billion in revenue, consistent with the preview’s qualitative growth anchors.

surprises.description: Oxford cut FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $1.60–$2.00 from $2.30–$2.70, a much steeper reduction than the preview’s bear case of $2.30–$2.50. The new range is also below fiscal 2025 adjusted EPS of $2.11.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Slashed full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $1.60-$2.00,” down from $2.11 in fiscal 2025.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the FY2026 adjusted EPS guide was $2.30–$2.70 and identified a trim to $2.30–$2.50 as the bear case.

surprises.description: Lilly Pulitzer weakened more than the preview’s expected sequential improvement from Q1, and management does not expect a positive trend change until spring 2027. The preview had described assortment fixes as a possible contributor to the current-year recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lilly Pulitzer's performance deteriorated more than anticipated”; entry-price dress styles fell from about 50% of the assortment in 2025 to roughly 35% in 2026, and “a positive trend change is not expected until spring 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “sequential improvement from -8.8%” and listed Lilly assortment corrections among the bridges to second-half improvement.

surprises.description: Oxford lowered FY2026 sales guidance to $1.43–$1.47 billion from $1.475–$1.505 billion. That reverses the preview’s expectation of roughly flat to slightly higher full-year sales versus FY2025.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cut full-year sales guidance to $1.43-1.47 billion,” a 3% decline to roughly flat versus $1.478 billion last year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed full-year sales guidance of $1.475–$1.505 billion versus $1.478 billion in FY2025, and said the key question was whether guidance would be reaffirmed or cut.

surprises.description: Q3 guidance points to continued sales and earnings contraction: sales of $280–$300 million are below the prior-year $307 million, and the expected adjusted loss is wider than last year’s. This conflicts with the preview’s implied second-half sales growth and adjusted-EPS improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q3 guidance calls for sales of “$280-300 million (versus $307 million last year)” and an adjusted loss per share of “$1.40 to $1.20,” wider than the $0.92 loss in Q3 2025.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview calculated implied H2 sales growth of “+1.8% to +6.2% YoY” and expected H2 adjusted EPS to improve by $0.48–$1.08 versus FY2025.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS of $1.34 was slightly above the published $1.32 consensus, but below the preview’s estimated roughly $1.40 functional buy-side bar. So the result modestly beat consensus but did not meet the higher bar the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS grew year-over-year to $1.34.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave Q2 adjusted EPS consensus of “$1.32” and estimated the functional buy-side bar at “~$1.40 adjusted EPS.”

surprises.description: Debt fell much further during Q2 than the preview’s discussion of the balance sheet and $25 million of filed tariff-refund claims earmarked for repayment would suggest. Oxford ended Q2 with $73 million of long-term debt, down from $142.7 million at Q1-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Long-term debt was cut sharply to $73 million from $143 million at the end of Q1 and $116 million at the end of fiscal 2025,” aided by $97 million of first-half operating cash flow.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted debt of “$142.7M” and said “$25M of Phase 1 tariff refund claims are filed with proceeds earmarked for debt repayment.”

surprises.description: Oxford received a larger tariff refund than the $25 million of filed claims highlighted in the preview, and substantially all of the reported $42 million arrived in cash during or shortly after Q2. The refund also reduced reported cost of goods sold, though it was excluded from adjusted results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recorded a $42 million reduction to cost of goods sold from previously paid tariff refunds (excluded from adjusted results) and received substantially all of it in cash during or shortly after Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “$25M of Phase 1 tariff refund claims” and called the timing of converting those claims into cash a live upside item.

surprises.description: Management announced an enterprise-wide operating-margin review and plans to convert select Southern Tide and Johnny Was stores to Lilly Pulitzer—specific steps not anticipated in the preview. The margin objective is constructive, but the supplied facts do not quantify the expected benefit or costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “launched an enterprise-wide review to enhance operating margins,” including “converting select Southern Tide and Johnny Was stores to Lilly Pulitzer.”

in_line: Q2 net sales of $394 million were close to the preview’s approximately $394.6 million consensus and landed near the high end of the $380–$400 million company range.
Adjusted gross margin expanded 140 basis points to 63.1%, within the preview’s expected 100–200 basis-point increase and near its approximately 63% estimate.
Tommy Bahama’s low-single-digit positive DTC comp and expectation of slightly positive full-year comps were consistent with the preview’s expectation of positive comps, slightly lower than Q1.
The plan to normalize capex to about $60 million was in line with the preview’s stated FY2026 capex expectation of approximately $60 million.

surprises.description: Q3 revenue was $116.8 million, well above the preview’s $110 million base estimate and its $114–117 million bull-case range’s lower end. That represents 13% growth, rather than the 5–7% growth expected in the base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue grew 13% year-over-year to $116.8 million,” driven primarily by large-scale data center and infrastructure projects in the U.S.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base est.: $110M (+6.1%)”; the base scenario expected “Revenue $109–111M +5–7%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $30.4 million, above the preview’s $28.5 million base estimate and its $27–29 million expected range. The result also substantially exceeded the $26.6 million EBITDA implied by the prior guidance midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 13% to $30.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base est.: $28.5M”; consensus-derived expectation was “~$27–29M,” and the guide-midpoint-implied Q3 estimate was “$26.6M.”

surprises.description: Management raised FY26 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance instead of merely narrowing the existing ranges. The new ranges’ midpoints are higher than the previous ranges’ midpoints, and the new revenue high end is above the preview’s anticipated upper-half outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 guidance: revenue to $425-$435 million (from $410-$425M), adjusted EBITDA to $103-$108 million (from $98-$105M).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the ranges “must narrow” and called narrowing to “the upper half ($418–425M / $102–105M)” the clean bull outcome.

surprises.description: FY26 free cash flow guidance increased to approximately $50 million from a floor of at least $45 million, despite the roughly $22 million equipment spend being pulled forward into 2026. The preview identified reaffirming the $45 million floor after that pre-buy as the make-or-break outcome, not raising the target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow to approximately $50 million (from at least $45M)”; the company also “pulled forward roughly $22 million of 2027 replacement CapEx into 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described FY26 FCF guidance as “≥$45M” and flagged reaffirmation of “the ≥$45M FCF floor with the $22M pre-buy fully absorbed” as the key test.

surprises.description: U.S. concrete pumping revenue grew 10%, above the preview’s 7.5% segment estimate, and adjusted EBITDA grew 18%. This was stronger than the expected deceleration from Q2, although light commercial and residential demand remained soft as anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. concrete pumping segment revenue increased 10% to $76.2 million with adjusted EBITDA up 18% to $18.4 million,” while light commercial and residential demand remained soft.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated U.S. Concrete Pumping revenue of “$74.5M” and “+7.5%,” with the segment expected to decelerate from Q2.

surprises.description: Eco-Pan revenue grew 14%, exceeding the preview’s 10.5% growth estimate, and adjusted EBITDA grew 19%. The preview expected continued growth but did not forecast this level of segment EBITDA growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Eco-Pan waste management segment revenue grew 14% to $21.9 million and adjusted EBITDA grew 19% to $8.8 million, remaining on track for a record year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Eco-Pan revenue of “$21.3M” and “+10.5%,” describing it as the “most consistent grower.”

surprises.description: U.K. revenue grew 24%, far above the preview’s 8.6% estimate, but the increase was mainly acquisition-driven. At the same time, margins remained pressured by labor inefficiency and higher fuel costs, rather than showing the recovery the preview was watching for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.K. revenue grew 24% to $18.7 million driven mainly by the Tenplait temporary power acquisition,” while underlying construction stayed soft and “margins were pressured by labor inefficiency and higher fuel costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated U.K. revenue growth of “+8.6%” with a first full quarter of the acquisition, and said to watch whether the acquisition was “accretive on day one” and whether margins showed recovery.

surprises.description: The board initiated a quarterly cash dividend of $0.13 per share, an approximately 5.6% yield at the stated stock price. The preview discussed the remaining buyback authorization and possible repurchases, but did not anticipate a new dividend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board initiated a new quarterly cash dividend of $0.13 per share ($0.52 annualized), representing a yield of approximately 5.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “$11.9M remained on the repurchase authorization” and said an aggressive repurchase could signal management’s confidence; it did not mention a dividend.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $0.09, one cent above the preview’s $0.08 base estimate, while net income attributable to common shareholders increased to $4.5 million from $3.3 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income attributable to common shareholders increased to $4.5 million ($0.09 per diluted share) from $3.3 million ($0.07).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base estimate was “$0.08” diluted EPS.

in_line: Consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin was 26%, meeting the preview’s stated threshold of at least 26%.
Light commercial and residential demand remained soft, consistent with the preview’s expectation that those markets would remain challenged.
The roughly $22 million replacement-capex pull-forward was already anticipated by the preview; the reported U.S. pumping and Eco-Pan allocations clarify its split.
Large-scale data center and infrastructure work remained the primary U.S. growth driver, consistent with the preview’s expectation that data-center projects were driving the re-acceleration.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $898 million versus the preview’s roughly $877 million consensus, and fiscal-year revenue was $3.4 billion versus about $3.33 billion expected. Both revenue figures came in around 2% above the preview’s estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue reached $898 million… exceeding the high end of guidance,” and “full-year fiscal '26 revenue of $3.4 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q4 revenue consensus of “~$877.0–877.6M” and FY26 revenue consensus of “~$3.33B.”

surprises.description: Organic net new ARR growth accelerated to 17%, above the preview’s 15% threshold for showing that the slowdown was easing. This was a clearer improvement than the expected modest recovery from Q3’s 14% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Organic net new ARR (excluding Red Canary) of $232 million accelerating to 17% growth versus 10% in the first half of fiscal '26 and 7% in fiscal '25.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said organic net new ARR “needs to hold ≥15%” and noted it “was +14% in Q3.”

surprises.description: Total ARR reached $3.8 billion, above the preview’s expected FY26 guided band of $3.740–3.749 billion. The roughly $51–60 million excess was a modest beat against the stated exit-ARR bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total ARR grew 25% to $3.8 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “ARR must land in the $3.740–3.749B guided band.”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP operating margin was 24.3%, implying operating income of about $218 million on reported revenue—above the preview’s roughly $207 million estimate. The margin also set a new record.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin hit a record 24.3% in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Non-GAAP operating income” at “~$207M.”

surprises.description: Security-for-AI bookings grew more than 50% sequentially, going beyond the preview’s expectation that AI Protect would simply grow sequentially. The 70% data-security attach rate added evidence of cross-selling, although management said the products remain early in their development.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Security for AI bookings increased more than 50% sequentially in Q4, with 70% of security-for-AI deals including a data security solution, though these products remain in early innings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s platform bar was “AI Protect growing sequentially”; it also cited AI Protect at “>$100M TTM bookings.”

surprises.description: Zero Trust Everywhere enterprises exceeded the preview’s expected range of more than 850–900, reaching more than 950 by fiscal year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Zero Trust Everywhere enterprises grew to more than 950 exiting Q4, up from over 700 in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview set a bar of “ZTE customers >850–900 (from >700).”

surprises.description: ZFlex produced more than $1.7 billion of TCV for FY26, substantially above the preview’s cited expectation of more than $1 billion in TTM TCV. Q4 TCV also surged more than 60% quarter over quarter, and Flex customers saw nearly 30% average ARR uplift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ZFlex generated over $770 million in TCV in Q4, up more than 60% quarter-over-quarter, and more than $1.7 billion for full fiscal '26, with Flex customers seeing an average ARR uplift of nearly 30%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Z-Flex >$1B TTM TCV at ~4-yr terms.”

surprises.description: Non-seat-based metered usage ARR grew more than 100% year over year, a growth rate the preview did not anticipate. The result also showed the solutions already contribute a meaningful share of new and upsell ACV.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-seat-based metered usage solutions delivered approximately 30% of new and upsell ACV with related ARR growing more than 100% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: The non-seat ACV mix was approximately 30%, below the preview’s stated bar of at least 33%. The related ARR grew rapidly, but the reported mix did not reach the preview’s target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-seat-based metered usage solutions delivered approximately 30% of new and upsell ACV.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bar was “non-seat ACV mix ≥33%.”

surprises.description: The company announced a workforce restructuring affecting about 3% of employees and expects $30–33 million of charges, neither of which was anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced a workforce restructuring affecting approximately 3% of employees with charges of $30–33 million.”

in_line: FY27 revenue and ARR guidance was broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of roughly 16–17% growth: revenue guidance is $3.908–3.938 billion and ARR guidance is $4.396–4.426 billion.
The sales-leadership transition was expected to weigh on the start of FY27; the call said two sales leaders had departed and that the transition would affect the first half, as reflected in guidance.
The FY27 free-cash-flow outlook and elevated CapEx were broadly consistent with the preview’s base case: the call cited an FCF margin of roughly 23–23.5% and CapEx remaining elevated.

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP operating margin was 31.6%, materially above the preview’s expected 29.7–30.2% range and its forecast of roughly 200 basis points of sequential compression.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP operating margin was 31.6%” and “160 basis points above the guidance midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin” consensus guide: “29.7–30.2%”; the preview also expected “~200bp sequential operating margin compression.”

surprises.description: The company raised its FY2027 ARR growth outlook to 8.5–9.0%, above the preview’s expected 8.25–8.75% range. The new top end reaches 9%, rather than merely reaffirming the prior outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its fiscal 2027 ARR growth guidance to 8.5%-9.0% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 guide: 8.25–8.75% y/y”; the preview identified whether it was “raised, reaffirmed, or narrowed to the low end” as a key catalyst.

surprises.description: IAM reached 15.1% of ARR in Q2, ahead of the preview’s roughly 14.4–14.5% glidepath. Management also put the exit-Q4 FY2027 range at 18–19%, modestly above the preview’s approximately 18% year-end expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “IAM now accounts for 15.1% of total ARR, up from 12.6% in Q1,” and is “guided to reach 18-19% of total ARR by exiting Q4 fiscal 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 needs ~14.4–14.5% to hold the glidepath”; management had “reaffirmed ~18% by fiscal year-end.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS of $1.16 exceeded both the preview’s $1.08–$1.09 consensus range and its $1.14–$1.17 base-case estimate, landing near the top of that base case.
