surprises.fact_evidence: “Total operating expenses rose 8% ($55.9 million),” with unit growth, credit card fees, and same-store employee expenses contributing; “Q2 OpEx growth [is] expected to be similar to Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operating expense growth — guided +5–7%”; “a print above 7% with wage/M&A integration commentary would offset a fuel beat.”

surprises.description: Inside same-store sales grew 3.2%, below the preview’s roughly 3.9% blended consensus. The segment results diverged: prepared food and dispensed beverage sales beat their estimate, while grocery/general merchandise fell short.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inside same-store sales grew 3.2%”; prepared food and dispensed beverage were up 4.8%, and grocery/general merchandise was up 2.7%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus sits at ~+3.9% blended.”

surprises.description: Prepared food and dispensed beverage same-store sales growth of 4.8% exceeded the preview’s 4.3% estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Prepared food and dispensed beverage same-store sales [were] up 4.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Prepared food SSS: +4.3%.”

surprises.description: Grocery and general merchandise same-store sales growth of 2.7% missed the preview’s 3.6% estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Grocery/general merchandise [same-store sales were] up 2.7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Grocery/GM SSS: +3.6%.”

surprises.description: Total gallons sold grew 2.5%, a little slower than the preview’s 2.8% consensus estimate. Same-store gallons were down 0.3%, but that remained within the preview’s FY27 guide range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “2.5% higher gallons sold”; “same-store gallons dipped 0.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total fuel gallons: 936.9M” versus “911.8M” prior year, implying about 2.8% growth.

surprises.description: Prepared food and dispensed beverage gross margin expanded 130 basis points, but management attributed the improvement mainly to lower cheese costs and a distribution-cost reclassification. The preview emphasized inside-margin performance as evidence of the mix and menu-innovation story, so the reclassification makes the reported expansion less purely operational than that framing might suggest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Prepared food and dispensed beverage gross margin expanded 130 basis points to 59.3%, driven mainly by lower cheese costs ($1.93/lb vs. $2.11) and a distribution cost reclassification.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Inside margin holding >42%” would “validate[] the mix/menu-innovation story.”

in_line: Same-store fuel gallons declined 0.3%, within the preview’s FY27 guidance range of -1% to +1%, even though it was the first negative quarter after roughly six positive quarters.
Management remained on track for the preview’s target of at least 120 stores in FY27.
The quarterly dividend remained at $0.65, as referenced in the preview.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was $0.15, well above the preview’s $0.09–$0.10 estimate—roughly 50%–67% higher than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS nearly doubled to $0.15 from $0.08” year over year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP diluted EPS: $0.09–$0.10.”

surprises.description: The company withdrew its prior $45 million full-year operating cash flow figure rather than reaffirming a path to it, replacing it with less precise “significant positive” guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: Cognyte “withdrew its prior $45 million full-year cash flow figure in favor of ‘significant positive’ guidance due to deliberate inventory investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists “operating cash flow ~$45M” as company guidance and says H2 “must generate ~$55M to hit the $45M FY target.”

surprises.description: RPO fell substantially, including short-term RPO at $313.4 million versus $363.4 million at Q1, instead of the sequential and year-over-year improvement the preview said would support the H2 ramp. Management attributed the reported decline partly to multiyear contract consumption and cancelable subscription revenue excluded from reported figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total RPO declined to $470.2 million (with $313.4 million short-term),” attributed to “$30 million of multiyear contract consumption and $42 million of cancelable subscription revenue excluded from reported figures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If short-term RPO is up sequentially and Y/Y, the H2 ramp is credible.” The preview also cited Q1 short-term RPO of $363.4 million.

surprises.description: Q2 operating cash flow was positive rather than seasonally negative as the preview expected, improving by $7.4 million from the prior-year quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Positive operating cash flow of $1.1 million in Q2 (versus negative $6.3 million a year ago).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says “Q2 is seasonally negative” and describes “Around −$5M” as in line.

surprises.description: Revenue guidance stayed at the $448 million midpoint, as expected, but the range narrowed from ±3% to ±2%, modestly reducing the stated range around the unchanged outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: Cognyte “narrowed its full-year revenue guidance to approximately $448 million (±2%), roughly 12% growth, while keeping the midpoint unchanged.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists FY27 revenue guidance of “$448M ±3%” and says to watch for a reaffirmation at $448M.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP gross margin reached 73.7%, 40 basis points above the preview’s roughly 73.3% expectation; the company also reported professional services below 8% of revenue, versus about 15% a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin expanded 154 basis points year-over-year to 73.7%, aided by the shift away from professional services, which fell to under 8% of revenue from about 15% a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Non-GAAP gross margin ~73.3%” and cited a 73.5% FY27 target.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was close to, but slightly below, the preview’s implied quarterly range, although non-GAAP operating income grew much faster than revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income grew 52.5% to $12.2 million and adjusted EBITDA rose 35.7% to $14.9 million, with profitability expanding roughly 4x faster than the 12% revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adj. EBITDA (implied) ~$15–16M” and approximately 40% year-over-year growth.

surprises.description: Software revenue grew much faster than total revenue and increased to more than 92% of sales, a sharper mix shift than the preview specifically anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total software revenue grew 20.9% to $100.8 million, now representing over 92% of total revenue versus 86% a year ago,” while total revenue grew 12%.

surprises.description: Cognyte signed more new customers in the first half than a year earlier, including a Tier 1 national security agency in a NATO member nation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cognyte signed 40 new customers in the first half versus 31 a year earlier, including a Tier 1 National Security Agency in a NATO member nation.”

surprises.description: Management said the reported growth rate understates underlying momentum: it estimated growth would be several percentage points higher if the perpetual-versus-subscription mix had remained at last year’s level.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management indicated “the accelerating shift toward subscriptions is masking underlying momentum, estimating growth would be several percentage points higher if the perpetual/subscription mix had stayed constant with last year.”

in_line: Total revenue was approximately $109 million, essentially in line with the preview’s $109.2 million consensus estimate.
The $448 million full-year revenue guidance midpoint was unchanged, as the preview expected.
Recurring revenue exceeded 50% of total revenue, reaching 51.4%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it would cross that milestone.
Management remained on track for $20 million of signed U.S. deals this year, matching the preview’s stated target.

surprises.description: Q3-to-date same-store sales are tracking above 3%, ahead of the preview’s 3.0% bogey and Evercore’s 2.5% consensus estimate. That points to a somewhat stronger near-term comp than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 currently tracking above 3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bogey: ≥3.0%”; Evercore: “Q3 +3.0% vs. cons. +2.5%.”

surprises.description: The Q2 revenue result was above the preview’s functional consensus midpoint: total revenues were $208 million versus an expected approximately $202 million. The result was still within the disclosed $189 million–$214 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenues rose 10% to $208 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ~ $202M” with a disclosed range of “$189M – $214M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was above the preview’s approximately $111 million midpoint, but the reported 7% growth understates the result excluding an advertising timing difference. The call also cited $8 million of lower costs from exiting the area director model, addressing the preview’s concern about cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 7% to $114 million”; growth “would have been 18%” absent the advertising timing difference, aided by “$8 million in lower costs from exiting the area director model.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~ $111M” with a disclosed range of “$107M – $117M”; the preview also flagged “incremental public-company G&A” as a risk to the EBITDA outlook.

surprises.description: The initial full-year guide calls for adjusted EBITDA growth of at least 20%, with management saying a G&A step-down will drive growth above its algorithm. That is more encouraging than the preview’s concern that public-company costs could pressure EBITDA, although the preview had no published EBITDA consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance calls for … adjusted EBITDA growth of at least 20% … with a step-down in G&A driving above-algorithm EBITDA growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch incremental public-company G&A and how much of it is already in the Q2 base”; the preview also warned that a clean EBITDA result could “quietly become a 2027 estimate cut.”

surprises.description: The full-year unit-growth floor is at least 8%, slightly below the preview’s approximately 8.5% reaffirmation bogey. The wording is a floor rather than a specific forecast, so the shortfall from that bogey is limited.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance calls for … net unit growth of at least 8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bogey: reaffirm ~8.5% unit growth for FY26”; “Unit growth reaffirmation at ~8.5%.”

surprises.description: Management said Q2 same-store sales growth was predominantly transaction-driven, addressing the preview’s concern that the comp might rely on price rather than traffic. That makes the reported comp composition better than the preview’s downside scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 same-store sales grew 2.3% … driven predominantly by transactions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A +2.3% comp carried by price with negative traffic is a materially worse print than the same comp on flat traffic.”

in_line: Q2 same-store sales were 2.3%, matching the preview’s pre-announced figure.
The company opened 83 stores in Q2 and 130 in the first half, with 3,378 stores and 8% net unit growth, broadly matching the preview’s unit-growth and opening expectations.
Digital channels were 43% of sales mix, in line with the preview’s stated Q2 figure.
AUVs near $1.4 million were broadly in line with the preview’s $1.376 million figure.
Management said the Cyclospora outbreak had no material impact, as the preview expected.
The domestic pipeline remained above 1,600 units, consistent with the preview’s pipeline expectation.

surprises.description: Revenue came in above the preview’s $2.97–3.00 billion total-revenue estimate: SUNB reported $3.1 billion, with rental revenue of $2.9 billion also above the preview’s roughly $2.70–2.73 billion estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 total revenue grew 11.2% to $3.1 billion” and “rental revenue grew 12.5% to $2.9 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $2.97–3.00bn”; “Rental revenue | ~$2.70–2.73bn (est.).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS substantially exceeded the preview’s $1.04–$1.08 consensus range, reaching $1.18. The preview’s bull-case EPS was $1.15.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS rose 20.4% to a first-quarter record of $1.18.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS | $1.04–1.08”; the bull scenario projected “$1.15.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA and especially its margin fell short of the preview’s expectations: EBITDA was about $1.3 billion versus an estimated $1.33–1.36 billion, and the 42.2% margin was well below the expected 44.5–45.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased 8.7% to $1.3 billion but margin declined to 42.2% from 43.2% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$1.33–1.36bn”; “Adj. EBITDA margin | ~44.5–45.5%”; the preview set a bar of “roughly −100bps YoY (≈44.8%).”

surprises.description: Rather than reaffirming FY2027 guidance unchanged as the preview expected, SUNB raised its revenue-growth ranges and EBITDA guidance above the prior ranges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised FY2027 guidance to total revenue growth of 6%-9%, rental revenue growth of 7%-10%, and adjusted EBITDA of $4.92 billion-$5.12 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Prior guidance was “+4.5% to +7.5%” total revenue growth, “+5% to +8%” rental revenue growth, and “$4.85–5.05bn” adjusted EBITDA; the preview said “the base case is a reaffirm.”

surprises.description: SUNB also raised its capital-spending ranges, indicating more investment than the preview’s already-established FY2027 capex ranges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross capital expenditure guidance was raised to $2.75 billion-$3.15 billion and net rental capex to $2.4 billion-$2.8 billion, driven by mega project, specialty and energy demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed gross rental capex of “$2.45–2.85bn” and net rental capex of “$2.05–2.45bn.”

surprises.description: Specialty rental growth was much stronger than the preview’s roughly 12% watchpoint and its 15%+ bull-case marker; specialty dollar utilization also rose more than the preview’s cited 200-basis-point prior-quarter increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North American Specialty rental revenue surged 25.3% with dollar utilization up 300 basis points to 77%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said specialty deceleration “below ~12%” would be a concern and described “specialty +15%+” in its bull scenario; it cited specialty utilization rising “200bps to 75%.”

surprises.description: General Tool growth was a clear upside to the preview’s threshold for a genuine surprise: revenue grew 7.4%, above the level the preview identified as meaningful upside for the segment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “General Tool rental revenue grew 7.4% with dollar utilization flat at 47%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “General tool above +4% would be the genuine upside surprise.”

surprises.description: The preview did not identify the FIFA World Cup as a growth driver, but management attributed a sizable portion of quarterly rental growth to it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FIFA World Cup contributed roughly 250 basis points … to rental revenue growth in the quarter.”

in_line: General Tool dollar utilization was flat at 47%, matching the preview’s expectation of flat utilization.
The company opened 13 greenfields and remained on track for roughly 55 this year, in line with the preview’s 55-greenfield expectation.
Net leverage of 1.8x remained within the preview’s cited 1–2x target range.
SUNB reaffirmed its 200-basis-point margin-improvement target, consistent with the preview’s expectation of H2-weighted margin recovery.

surprises.description: Signet’s adjusted operating income reached $107 million, well above the preview’s roughly $88 million consensus estimate, while adjusted EPS growth was 36% versus the preview’s expected 6.8%. The 140-basis-point operating-income rate expansion also contrasts with the preview’s focus on gold-cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income rose 25% to $107 million with 140 basis points of rate expansion”; “adjusted EPS growth of 36%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating income … ~$88M (implied)”; “Adj. diluted EPS … $1.72 (+6.8% YoY).”

surprises.description: Signet secured an early seven-year Bread Financial renewal with substantial benefits that the preview did not anticipate: more than $1 billion in incremental noncomp revenue and operating income over the agreement’s life, including a $200–250 million operating benefit over 36 months and about $80 million of Q3 cash.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Signed an early 7-year renewal with credit partner Bread Financial through December 2035,” expected to generate “over $1 billion in incremental noncomp revenue and operating income”; the deal is expected to provide “$200-250 million” over 36 months and “roughly $80 million in cash” in Q3.

surprises.description: Shareholder returns were set to accelerate beyond the buyback pace the preview identified as a key watch item: Signet increased its authorization by nearly $400 million, announced a $125 million ASR, and said buybacks plus dividends would return 12% of its recent market cap in the first nine months.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nearly $400 million increase to its share repurchase authorization and a $125 million ASR,” with “$575 million remaining”; combined with dividends, returns will total “12% of its recent market cap” in the first nine months.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “~$355M authorization remaining” and listed “Buyback/ASR pace” as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: The sales mix was notably uneven: comps were strong at price points above $2,000 and in timepieces, while fashion comps declined, particularly at Banter and in lower-priced metal pieces. This gives a concrete version of the preview’s concern that AUR and mix could carry results while lower-priced demand remained weak.
surprises.fact_evidence: “High single-digit comp growth occurred at price points over $2,000 and timepieces grew nearly double digits, while fashion posted a 1% comp decline driven by weakness at Banter and lower-priced metal pieces.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned of “AUR carries the comp while units go negative” and highlighted the need to watch “Bridal: units vs. AUR.”

surprises.description: Tariff refunds were quantified, but they are only a partial offset to the tariff burden: $30 million is expected this year, including $15 million in Q2, while indirect refunds are pushed to fiscal 2028. The preview anticipated that refunds could provide a near-term earnings source but had said their timing was too early to quantify.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tariff refunds of $30 million are expected this year (including $15 million in Q2), but represent less than half of the net headwind from incremental tariffs, with indirect refunds expected to benefit fiscal 2028 instead.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said refund timing was “too early to quantify” and that “Quantified refunds would be a clean, low-quality-but-real EPS source.”

surprises.description: Signet ended with cash up nearly $250 million year over year to about $525 million while inventory was down 1% despite gold-cost inflation. The preview did not flag this combination of stronger cash and lower inventory as an expected result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory ended down 1% to $2 billion despite gold cost inflation, and cash rose nearly $250 million year-over-year to about $525 million.”

in_line: Q2 same-store sales comps were up 2.2%, broadly in line with the preview’s approximately 2% consensus expectation and within the upper half of the prior guide.
A second full-year guidance increase was expected; the preview said investors were looking for a second consecutive raise.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was +$0.05 rather than the preview’s -$0.04 estimate, while adjusted EBITDA reached $7.7 million—above even the preview’s $4–6 million bull-case range. Both measures were substantially stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose to $7.7 million (6.9% of sales) from $4.7 million a year ago, while adjusted EPS improved to $0.05 from $0.01.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (adjusted) -$0.04”; the scenario analysis put “adj. EBITDA $1–3M” in the base case and “adj. EBITDA $4–6M” in the bull case.

surprises.description: Gross margin rose to 47.9%, far above the preview’s roughly 44% base-case expectation, but a one-time $4.6 million tariff refund drove the result. Excluding the refund, merchandise margin would have been about 70 basis points worse year over year, so the headline strength did not reflect stronger underlying merchandise margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A one-time $4.6 million IEPA tariff refund benefited merchandise margin and drove gross margin up 270 basis points to 47.9%, but excluding the refund merchandise margin would have been roughly 70 basis points worse than last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “GM ~44% on tariffs,” and the preview flagged “Gross margin vs. the 100bps tariff headwind.”

surprises.description: Cash and investments were $20.1 million, above the preview’s expected $13–16 million range and the $16.2 million Q1 balance. The company also reported no debt, consistent with the expectation of no revolver draw.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported a fortress balance sheet with $20.1 million of cash and investments, no debt, and $61.7 million of excess availability.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “cash ~$13–16M” and “no revolver draw”; the preview identified cash and liquidity as the key metric, starting from “$16.2M cash.”

surprises.description: Although the quarter’s -3.5% comparable-sales decline was within the preview’s expected range, monthly comps improved from -5.7% in May to -1.9% in July. That was a stronger sequential trajectory than the preview’s base case of modest improvement suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Monthly comps improved sequentially from -5.7% in May to -2.8% in June and -1.9% in July, signaling an improving sales trajectory.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case anticipated “Modest sequential improvement” and comps of “-3% to -5%”; the preview asked whether the Q1 “-3.8% comp stabilize[d] into the easier Q2 base.”

surprises.description: Management gave new detail on a multi-year store rationalization plan: about three stores are expected to close this year, with a few dozen 2027 lease renewals under review. The company expects occupancy costs and sales per square foot to improve beginning in 2027; the preview did not forecast this plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is executing a multi-year store rationalization plan closing about 3 stores this year and evaluating a few dozen lease renewals in 2027, expected to reduce occupancy costs and improve sales per square foot beginning in 2027.”

surprises.description: The preview characterized GLP-1-related sizing changes as a secular threat to DXL’s addressable market. The call confirmed that some customers are pausing purchases while losing weight, but added that a majority say they intend to return once their size stabilizes, tempering that concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GLP-1 medication adoption among a meaningful portion of customers is driving weight-loss-related purchase pauses, though a majority of these customers say they intend to return to DXL once they reach a stable size.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described GLP-1 medications as “shifting customer sizing” and called this “a secular TAM question, not a cyclical one.”

surprises.description: The call reported measurable early traction across growth initiatives that the preview did not quantify: brand awareness rose from 40% to 49% in seven months, ThermaChill demand was up 56% year to date, and FitMap had scanned more than 150,000 customers, with higher average order values and lower return rates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Early results from growth initiatives include brand awareness in the core 35-64 demographic (household income above $100,000) rising from 40% to 49% in seven months, ThermaChill private-brand demand up 56% year-to-date, and over 150,000 customers scanned via FitMap showing higher AOV and lower return rates.”

in_line: Revenue of $111.6 million was above the loose $109.3 million consensus estimate, but within the preview’s $110–113 million operational base case.
Comparable sales were down 3.5%, within the preview’s base-case range of -3% to -5%.
The board’s recommendation that stockholders vote against the Full Beauty merger was already anticipated; the preview said the board had reversed its position and now recommended voting against it.
The store/direct comp split was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation that direct would remain the healthier line: store comps were down 4.3% and direct comps were down 1.6%.
No debt and no revolver draw were consistent with the preview’s base-case expectation.

surprises.description: ODD guided Q3 revenue to decline only about 5% year over year, much better than the preview’s base-case decline of 15%–22% and its better-than-15% recovery threshold. Management said the worst of the acquisition-driven pressure is behind it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company guided Q3 net revenue to decline only ~5% year-over-year,” attributing the improvement to “the worst of the acquisition-driven pressure being behind them.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case called for “‑15% to ‑22%”; it said narrowing to “better than ‑15%” would validate recovery.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $13 million, above the preview’s $8–$10 million guidance range. The beat was sizeable relative to the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $13 million beat the $8-$10 million guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$8M–$10M” and consensus of “~$9–10M.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue reached $181 million, slightly above the preview’s $176.5–$178.2 million consensus range and at the favorable end of company guidance. The beat was modest, since the preview already expected revenue in the upper part of guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net revenue declined 25% year-over-year to $181 million, landing at the favorable end of guidance for a 25%-30% decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave consensus of “$176.5M–$178.2M” and noted that consensus sat in “the upper third of the guided range.”

surprises.description: The full-year revenue outlook implies about $656 million, above the preview’s approximate $630 million revenue anchor. That points to a better full-year revenue outcome than the preview’s illustrative estimate, even though revenue is still expected to decline year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 net revenue is expected to decline approximately 19%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a business that “should still do ~$630M of revenue this year.”

surprises.description: The full-year adjusted EBITDA outlook is now quantified at $30–$32 million rather than left at a general commitment to be positive. That gives investors a concrete target, though the preview did not provide a numerical estimate to compare against.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA [is] guided to $30-$32 million and Q3 to $18-$20 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY26 adjusted EBITDA was expected to be “positive” but “unquantified,” and called quantifying it a sign of restored confidence.

surprises.description: First-order net revenue was still down about 40% year over year. That is an improvement from Q1’s 50% decline, but it remains in the preview’s downside range rather than approaching the stronger recovery scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 first-order net revenue fell approximately 40%” year over year, driven by IL MAKIAGE.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called first orders “the forward indicator” after Q1’s “‑50%,” and its bull scenario required first orders to improve to “better than ‑25%”; its bear scenario cited “still ‑40%+.”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 68.7%, below the preview’s roughly 70% expectation for stabilization. Management attributed much of the decline to an approximately 8% AOV drop and characterized it as non-structural and recoverable, which partly softens the miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin compressed approximately 360 basis points year-over-year to 68.7%, driven largely by an ~8% AOV decline,” which management called “non-structural and recoverable.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated gross margin at “~70%” and said stabilization “at ~70%” would show remediation held.

surprises.description: Repeat-order net revenue declined about 20%, worse than the 15% decline cited for Q1. The preview had highlighted repeat orders and warned that lost first-order cohorts could weigh on future repeat activity, so the direction was a concern it had flagged, but the further deterioration was unfavorable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 ... repeat-order net revenue fell approximately 20% year-over-year,” driven by IL MAKIAGE.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q1 repeat orders at “‑15%” and warned that “Lost H1 first orders mechanically depress the 2027 repeat cohort.”

surprises.description: SpoiledChild is expected to grow at least 35% and approach $350 million of 2026 revenue, a much more specific and substantial growth outlook than the preview’s expectation that it would simply continue growing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SpoiledChild is on track to grow at least 35% and approach $350 million of net revenue in 2026,” reaching that milestone more than a year faster than IL MAKIAGE did.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said SpoiledChild “continues to grow” with “milder CPA impact,” without giving a growth rate or revenue target.

surprises.description: METHODIQ is now expected to deliver higher first-year revenue than SpoiledChild, beyond the preview’s stated expectation that it was tracking to a $25 million FY2026 target. The call did not provide a specific updated dollar target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “METHODIQ, launched less than a year ago, is expected to deliver higher first-year revenue than SpoiledChild.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said METHODIQ was “tracking to its $25M FY2026 target.”

surprises.description: The company outlined a planned move into longevity and metabolic health, including prescription injectable and peptide therapies in 2027, alongside a planned fourth brand launch. Those initiatives were not part of the preview’s diversification expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management plans to expand METHODIQ into “longevity/metabolic health including prescription injectable and peptide therapies in 2027, alongside a planned Brand 4 launch.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s diversification discussion focused on METHODIQ’s “$25M FY2026” target and SpoiledChild’s continued growth.

surprises.description: ODDITY repurchased $50 million face value of its 2030 exchangeable notes for $35 million. The preview highlighted cash and undrawn facilities but did not anticipate this discounted debt repurchase.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “repurchased $50 million face value of its 2030 exchangeable notes for $35 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Debt | $0 (plus $350M undrawn facility)” and did not mention a planned note repurchase.

in_line: The year-to-date buyback pace was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of aggressive Q2 repurchases: the preview cited $82.3 million spent in Q1 and $167.3 million remaining, while the call reported $163 million repurchased year to date and about $87 million remaining.

surprises.description: Gross margin was expected around 34.5%, with 34%+ viewed as confirmation that Q2's improvement could hold. OCC reported 37.4%, well above that level, citing manufacturing operating leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 gross profit jumped 43.9% to $9.1 million, with gross margin expanding to 37.4% from 31.7% a year earlier due to manufacturing operating leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My model (base case): revenue $24.5M, GM 34.5%”; “Sustained 34%+ on higher volume is the bull confirmation.”

surprises.description: OCC's diluted EPS of $0.21 slightly exceeded the preview's $0.20 estimate and its $0.18–0.19 model range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 net income surged to $1.9 million ($0.21 per diluted share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 FY26 est. EPS (basic/diluted): $0.20”; “EPS ~$0.18–0.19.”

surprises.description: The preview said OCC was evaluating workforce expansion and equipment additions; the call reported that it is expanding capacity and hiring across facilities, including Roanoke and Dallas. The expansion is not quantified, but it is more concrete than the preview's evaluation-stage description.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company…is expanding capacity and hiring across facilities (notably Roanoke and Dallas).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management is ‘evaluating workforce expansion and equipment additions’”; “Any capex commitment, a quantified capacity ceiling, or concrete revenue attributable to Lightera would be new information.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged a possible equity raise as a financing overhang given low cash and working-capital needs. Management instead said working capital had strengthened and that the revolver and operating cash were sufficient to fund growth, without indicating a need for an equity raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Working capital strengthened to $19.2 million from $13.9 million at fiscal year-end 2025, with management asserting the credit revolver and operating cash are sufficient to fund growth without indicating a need for an equity raise.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any equity raise into strength…is a real overhang”; the preview also noted cash of “$146K” and that growth was “working-capital hungry.”

surprises.description: OCC reported that it had begun recording initial Lightera product sales. The preview identified concrete Lightera revenue as new information, although the call did not quantify the contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has begun recording initial sales of Lightera products under its strategic collaboration.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any…concrete revenue attributable to Lightera would be new information”; “first quantified revenue contribution would be genuinely new.”

surprises.description: Sales were slightly below the $24.5 million estimate: OCC reported $24.3 million, or 22% year-over-year growth, versus the preview's implied 23% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 FY2026 net sales rose 22% year-over-year to $24.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $24.5M”; “Implied Y/Y: +23%.”

surprises.description: SG&A came in above the preview's $6.5 million model, and at 28.7% of sales it missed the preview's operating-leverage marker of below about 28%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 SG&A rose to $7 million from $5.7 million but held essentially flat at 28.7% of sales versus 28.8% a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My model (base case)…SG&A $6.5M”; “the operating leverage story requires SG&A to stay below ~28% of sales.”

in_line: Backlog and forward load reached $13.5 million, within the preview's $13–15 million base-case range, though below its bullish threshold of more than $15 million.
Revenue increased sequentially from $22.2 million to $24.3 million, meeting the preview's call for at least 8% sequential growth.
The preview expected optical-fiber shortages and longer lead times to constrain shipments; management said those remain the primary bottleneck.
Enterprise, data-center and specialty-market demand remained strong, consistent with the preview's account of OCC's growth drivers.
The preview said OCC would provide no formal guidance; no forward numerical guidance is reported in the call facts.

surprises.description: SailPoint raised its FY27 ARR target by $11 million to $1.38 billion, rather than holding the prior $1.369 billion target as the preview’s base case anticipated. The increase is positive, though it is below the preview’s bull-case threshold of $1.385 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year FY27 guidance was raised by $11 million to $1.38 billion ARR (up 23%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... FY ARR held at $1.369B”; “Bull ... FY27 ARR raised to ≥$1.385B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating margin was 20.3%, well above the preview’s 18.4% quarterly guide and its expectation of roughly 200 basis points of year-over-year compression. This was a clear reversal of the anticipated margin pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating margin was 20.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating income ... (18.4% margin)”; “Guide implies ~200bps of Y/Y compression.”

surprises.description: Total ARR reached $1.231 billion, $11 million above the guidance midpoint and above the preview’s base-case range of $1.220–$1.228 billion. It was slightly short of the preview’s bull-case threshold of $1.235 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY27 total ARR reached $1.231 billion ... exceeding the guidance midpoint by $11 million.”

surprises.description: Net new SaaS ARR was $66 million, up 34%, compared with $35 million in Q1, when reported growth was only 5%. That is a strong sequential improvement against the preview’s focus on whether SaaS additions would reaccelerate, although the call facts do not specify constant-currency growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net new SaaS ARR of $66 million (up 34%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 was $35M, +5% reported but +30%+ cc”; “The bear case is cc growth decelerating below ~25%; the bull case needs reacceleration.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $309 million, slightly below the $310.4 million consensus estimate, though still inside the $308–312 million company guide. The call attributed an approximately $5 million in-period revenue headwind to the higher SaaS mix and the timing difference between SaaS and term revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue was $309 million”; “The higher SaaS mix created an approximately $5 million revenue timing headwind.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ... $308–312M”; “Consensus ... $310.4M.”

surprises.description: SaaS accounted for 97% of net new ARR, above the 90–95% range the company had guided. The greater SaaS share supports the ARR mix, while also contributing to the reported revenue timing headwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net new SaaS ARR ... accounting for 97% of total net new ARR—above the guided 90-95% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guided 90-95% range.”

surprises.description: AI-driven ARR had already exceeded $70 million by quarter-end, putting SailPoint well ahead of pace for its $100 million fiscal year-end target. The preview discussed AI monetization as an upside lever but did not give this FY27 target or report this level of progress toward it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total AI-driven ARR already surpassed $70 million by end of Q2, putting the company well ahead of pace to hit its $100 million fiscal year-end target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$100 million fiscal year-end target.”

surprises.description: Existing customers adopting AI-driven solutions increased annual spend by more than 60%, exceeding the 25–50% uplift range discussed at Analyst Day. The reported expansion was materially above that prior benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Existing customers adopting AI-driven solutions increased their annual spend by over 60%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “25-50% uplift range discussed at Analyst Day.”

surprises.description: AI-driven solutions represented more than 30% of Q2 net new ARR, and the AI-driven pipeline had more than doubled to over $200 million since Investor Day less than three months earlier. These figures provide stronger quantified adoption and pipeline evidence than the preview had specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI-driven solutions accounted for more than 30% of net new ARR in Q2, and the AI-driven pipeline has more than doubled to over $200 million since Investor Day less than three months ago.”

surprises.description: The call reported that Entro-based POCs are shortening sales cycles to 30–45 days compared with traditional agentic suite purchases. The preview noted Entro and agentic conversion as issues to watch but did not anticipate this specific faster POC path.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Entro-based POCs are shortening sales cycles to 30-45 days versus traditional agentic suite purchases.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Organic vs. inorganic ARR” and “Agentic Fabric / non-human identity monetization” as key metrics to watch, but gave no POC-cycle expectation.

surprises.description: More than two-thirds of migrations included an AI-driven solution, and those migrations carried a 2–3x ARR uplift. The preview discussed migration pace and Modernization Flex use, but did not anticipate this degree of AI attachment or the reported uplift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Over two-thirds of migrations ... included an AI-driven solution with 2-3x ARR uplift.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “On-prem migration pace” and noted Modernization Flex was used in “~1/3 of migrations”; it did not state an expectation for AI attachment or ARR uplift.

surprises.description: RPO growth accelerated to 30% at $1.9 billion, while current RPO grew 27% to $931 million, with the call pointing to larger deal sizes. The preview did not discuss RPO or set an expectation for this forward-demand measure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “RPO accelerated to 30% growth ($1.9 billion) and current RPO grew 27% to $931 million on larger deal sizes.”

in_line: SaaS ARR growth was 36%, matching the 36% year-over-year rate reported in the preview’s Q1 baseline.
DBNRR was 113%, in line with the preview’s expectation that it would remain around 113%.

FY27 revenue guidance of approximately $1.27 billion, adjusted operating margin of about 19%, adjusted EPS of $0.32, and free cash flow of about $200 million were broadly in line with the preview’s full-year guide and consensus.

surprises.description: Korn Ferry reported $756 million of fee revenue, above the preview’s $736.8 million consensus and the $745 million high end of prior guidance; adjusted EPS of $1.43 also exceeded the $1.36 consensus. Both headline results came in stronger than the preview’s modest-growth baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY27 fee revenue grew 7% year-over-year to $756 million” and “Adjusted diluted EPS grew 9% year-over-year to $1.43.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Fee revenue | Consensus $736.8M | Company Guidance $725M – $745M” and “Diluted EPS | Consensus $1.36.”

surprises.description: The Q2 fee-revenue guide of $860–$878 million is at the upper end of, and extends above, the preview’s $845–$870 million framework for a credible guide including about two months of AMS. The two-month AMS contribution itself was expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY27 guidance calls for fee revenue of $860-$878 million (including only two months of AMS).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A credible Q2 fee revenue guide is ~$845–870M” and “Q2 guide $845–870M.”

surprises.description: Management reaffirmed the goal of lifting AMS adjusted EBITDA from $100 million to $140 million within one year, as the preview expected, but said it expects to reach the goal faster. It also said revenue synergies are the primary driver, whereas the preview did not anticipate that faster timing or specify that driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management targets $40 million of incremental run-rate EBITDA from AMS (raising it from $100 million to $140 million) within one year of closing, and expects to achieve it faster, driven primarily by revenue synergies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has targeted ~$140M EBITDA within one year post-close.”

surprises.description: Estimated remaining fees grew 14% year over year, ahead of the preview’s expected 10% growth, and the combined backlog was $3.5 billion, modestly above the preview’s approximately $3.4 billion estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Estimated remaining fees under existing contracts grew 14% year-over-year to $1.92 billion, with the combined backlog reaching $3.5 billion including AMS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$1.9B at Q4 FY26, +10% YoY” and “Bull requires… combined remaining fees (~$3.4B).”

surprises.description: New-business activity showed strength across the company: consolidated new business grew 12%, new wins included about $160 million of RPO with half from new logos, and internal referrals rose about 300 basis points. The preview had highlighted decelerating new business and Middle East-related demand risk, though the reported 12% figure is consolidated rather than the ex-RPO measure it wanted to assess.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated new business grew 12% year-over-year with growth across all regions and industries, while internal referral rate rose ~300 basis points to 29.4% of fee revenue”; “RPO new wins reached approximately $160 million in the quarter, with 50% coming from new logos.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Decelerated in Q4 FY26, which management attributed to Middle East geopolitical disruption dampening activity” and “New business ex-RPO growth rate — did the Middle East drag persist through the July quarter, or was it a one-quarter air pocket?”

surprises.description: APAC grew only 1% amid China weakness, a regional headwind the preview did not flag. The picture was mixed rather than uniformly weak: the Americas grew 9% and EMEA grew 4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Regional performance was uneven: Americas grew 9% to $442 million, EMEA grew 4% to $228 million, and APAC inflected to just 1% growth at $87 million amid China weakness.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA margin was 17%, in line with the preview’s expectation of an approximately flat 17% margin.
The preview expected the quarter to contain no AMS revenue because the acquisition closed after quarter-end; the reported Q1 results were standalone, and Q2 guidance included only two months of AMS.
Prioritizing debt paydown over buybacks was consistent with the preview’s expectation that buybacks could pause to deleverage after the acquisition.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.47, well above the preview’s $0.37 consensus and its $0.34–$0.35 estimate. This was a substantial upside surprise even though revenue fell short of consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EPS came in at $0.47” and beat the company’s own expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus” EPS was “$0.37”; the preview’s estimate was “$0.34–$0.35.”

surprises.description: The company raised the low end of full-year adjusted EPS guidance by $0.10 to $1.50 while keeping the $1.65 high end, rather than narrowing guidance toward the low end or cutting it as the preview warned was possible.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Caleres raised the low end of full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $1.50-$1.65 while maintaining the high end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called out a possible “narrow-to-low-end or an outright cut” and said narrowing toward “~$1.45–$1.60” was a base case.

surprises.description: Full-year GAAP EPS guidance of $2.80–$2.95 is far above the prior $1.44–$1.69 GAAP range cited in the preview. The preview expected the tariff refund to be excluded from guidance, while the call reported a large refund and much higher GAAP guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP EPS [is] guided to $2.80-$2.95”; the company also received “$57.4 million in IEPA tariff refunds,” excluded from adjusted results.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company guidance of “$1.44–$1.69 GAAP” and said the “IEEPA tariff refund” was “excluded from guidance.”

surprises.description: Caleres received $57.4 million in tariff refunds, turning the preview’s uncertain potential cash or receivable event into a reported receipt. The amount was close to the preview’s estimate, but the receipt itself was not assured there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $57.4 million in IEPA tariff refunds ($55.6 million reduced cost of sales, $1.8 million interest income), excluded from adjusted results.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “any receivable booked, cash received, or inclusion in guidance” and described management as having withheld it amid uncertainty.

surprises.description: Sales of $695 million were below the preview’s $702.5 million consensus and $706 million estimate. The reported 5.6% increase also depended on Stuart Weitzman: excluding its sales, total sales declined 0.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total sales rose 5.6% to $695 million, though excluding Stuart Weitzman sales declined 0.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview put consensus sales at “$702.5M” and its estimate at “$706M.”

surprises.description: Consolidated gross-margin expansion was just short of the company’s guided range and the preview’s estimate: it rose 340 basis points to 46.8%, versus guidance for 345–375 basis points of expansion and an estimated margin around 47.0%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated gross margin (excluding the tariff refund) expanded 340 basis points to 46.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited company guidance of “+345–375 bps” and estimated gross margin at “~47.0%.”

surprises.description: Famous Footwear comps fell 5.9%, worse than the preview’s roughly 4.5% estimate, although still within the company’s expected mid-single-digit decline. The decline was attributed to later back-to-school timing and a shift away from lifestyle athletic products.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Famous Footwear was the key weak spot with sales down 6.3% and comparable sales down 5.9%, pressured by a later back-to-school season and a shift away from lifestyle athletic products.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Famous Footwear comps at “−4.5%” and cited company guidance for comps “down MSD.”

surprises.description: After the weak quarter-to-date Famous comps, comps turned flat through Labor Day, with fashion comps positive and more than 10 points ahead of athletic. That is a better late-season trend than the quarter’s results suggested and led management to invest more in fashion inventory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Quarter-to-date through Labor Day, Famous Footwear comps turned flat, with fashion comps positive and outperforming athletic by over 10 points, prompting increased fashion inventory investment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the “last five weeks” and August-to-date data were key, and noted management expected “stronger Famous performance during peak periods like back-to-school and holiday.”

surprises.description: Brand Portfolio organic sales grew 8.2%, below the preview’s expectation that organic growth would be in the low double digits. This suggests the reported portfolio growth was less robust on an organic basis than the preview hoped.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Brand portfolio organic sales grew 8.2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether organic growth excluding Stuart Weitzman was “still tracking low-DD” and described low-double-digit organic growth as the expected rate.

surprises.description: Brand Portfolio gross margin jumped 880 basis points to 49.1%, a particularly strong segment result not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of consolidated margin pressure and markdown risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: The portfolio “gross margin jumped 880 basis points to 49.1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the consolidated gross-margin target a “heroic ask” amid promotional pressure and highlighted Famous Footwear markdowns; it gave no expectation for this magnitude of Brand Portfolio margin expansion.

surprises.description: International sales rose more than 50%, with high-teens organic growth, and management called international the company’s greatest growth vector despite it representing less than 10% of total sales. The preview focused on overall Brand Portfolio growth and did not flag this as a major growth engine.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International sales rose over 50% (up high teens organically), positioning international—currently under 10% of total—as the company’s greatest growth vector.”

surprises.description: Sam Edelman delivered mid-teens sales growth and reached the #9 position in dollar-volume women’s fashion footwear, with leading positions in flats, pumps, and loafers—brand-specific momentum the preview did not discuss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sam Edelman posted mid-teens sales growth and is now the #9 dollar-volume brand in women’s fashion footwear, holding the #1 flat, #1 pump, and #1 loafer positions through spring.”

in_line: Q3 tariff assumptions were broadly as anticipated: management said new tariffs will largely replace prior IEPA tariffs, while the preview said the planned tariff reinstatement had been expected.

Famous Footwear’s gross-margin pressure and promotional activity were consistent with the preview’s warnings about markdowns and the segment’s recent margin weakness, although management’s expectation that similar pressure will persist through the back half confirms the risk.

surprises.description: Academy reported gross margin of 40.4%, far above the preview’s estimated 35.0%-35.5%. The gap was largely driven by tariff refunds, which management said added 510 basis points, so the unusually high margin was not presented as recurring.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded roughly 440 basis points to 40.4%,” driven by “510 basis points of tariff refunds”; management flagged the benefit as “non-recurring.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~35.0–35.5% (est.)”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $2.31, above the preview’s $2.12 consensus estimate, a beat of about 9%. Tariff refunds net of reinvestments contributed only about six cents, so the EPS result exceeded expectations by more than that temporary benefit alone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS grew 19.1% to $2.31,” while tariff refunds net of strategic reinvestments “added only about six cents to EPS in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS | $2.12”

surprises.description: Management raised full-year gross margin guidance to 35.5%-36.0% from 34.5%-35.0%, rather than leaving the prior range intact as the preview’s base case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management raised gross margin guidance to “35.5%-36.0%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed standing guidance of “GM 34.5–35.0%” and said the base case was to “reaffirm sales/EPS.”

surprises.description: Academy raised adjusted full-year EPS guidance to $6.50-$6.90 from $6.40-$6.80, instead of reaffirming the prior range as expected in the preview’s base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management lifted adjusted EPS guidance to “$6.50-$6.90.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed standing adjusted EPS guidance of “$6.40–6.80” and described the base case as “reaffirm sales/EPS.”

surprises.description: The comp outlook was firmer in the commentary than the preview’s base case: management kept the full-year 0%-2% range rather than narrowing it to 0%-1%, indicated roughly 1% comps for the back half, and reported low-single-digit positive Q3 comps through Labor Day.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management reaffirmed “flat-to-plus-2% comps,” guided to “roughly 1% back-half comps,” and said Q3 was running “low single-digit positive comps through Labor Day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called narrowing to “0–1%” the base case and said “a quantified positive QTD comp is the single most bullish thing management can say.”

surprises.description: The call described a pronounced split in customer traffic: visits from households earning under $50,000 fell high single digits, worse than their low-single-digit decline in Q1, while traffic from households earning over $100,000 rose high single digits. The preview flagged lower-income consumers as a risk, but did not anticipate this degree of divergence.
surprises.fact_evidence: Traffic from households earning “under $50K fell high single digits (worse than Q1's low single-digit decline),” while traffic from households “above $100K rose high single digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bear scenario cited “low-income consumer + gas prices.”

surprises.description: Basket results showed that higher ticket did not translate into more shopping activity: ticket rose 4.5%, but units per transaction fell and total transactions were down about 2%. The preview expected roughly flat comps but did not specify this transaction-and-ticket mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ticket up 4.5% (driven by higher AUR) offset by units per transaction down and total transactions down about 2%,” with shopping described as “episodic, event-driven.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the Q2 comp was expected to be “roughly flat”; it did not give an expectation for transactions or ticket.

surprises.description: The relaunched MyAcademy Rewards card showed strong reported engagement, with applications up 15%, approval rates up over 900 basis points, and card spend up roughly 20%. The preview did not identify this program or provide an expectation for its performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: The program drove “credit card applications up 15%, approval rates up over 900 basis points, and card spend up roughly 20%”; membership was “over 15 million” and on track for 16 million by year end.

surprises.description: Management signaled a reduced buyback pace in the second half, despite having repurchased about $181 million in the first half and retaining $256 million of authorization. The preview highlighted buyback pace as important but did not forecast a second-half slowdown.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company repurchased “approximately $181 million of stock” in the first half, had “$256 million remaining on authorization,” and “signaled reduced buyback pace in the back half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “buyback pace” and “buyback dollars in the quarter vs. Q1's $99.3M.”

surprises.description: Net sales of about $1.6 billion came in slightly below the preview’s $1.62-$1.66 billion goalpost range, although they were close to its lower end and sales grew 3% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net sales rose 3% to $1.6 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “$1.62–1.66B” as the “real goalposts.”

in_line: Q2 comparable sales declined 0.4%, broadly consistent with the preview’s roughly flat expectation and its implied range of about -1% to +0.5%.
Full-year sales guidance was reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s base case of reaffirmed sales guidance.
New stores remained a growth engine, consistent with the preview’s expectation that new stores were carrying much of the growth and its focus on new-store productivity.

surprises.description: Full-year operating income guidance was $540–550 million, far above the preview’s expected $390–410 million range. The company also said American Eagle’s outlook had softened, but the reported full-year range was still substantially higher than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year operating income is guided to $540 million to $550 million on mid-single-digit comp growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 operating income guidance of $390–410M”; the base case expected “FY $390–410M reiterated.”

surprises.description: Reported Q2 operating income, EPS, and gross margin were dramatically above the preview’s expectations, but tariff refunds drove the gap: operating income included about $161 million of benefit, leaving underlying operating profit near the expected level. Gross margin was 48.7% rather than the preview’s estimated 37.0–37.4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 operating income was $211 million versus $103 million last year, but included a net tariff refund benefit of approximately $161 million, meaning underlying operating profit was roughly $50 million”; “Gross margin expanded 980 basis points to 48.7%, but tariff refunds contributed 1,300 basis points”; “Q2 EPS was $0.79.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operating income: ~$48–50M”; “Diluted EPS: $0.21”; “Gross margin: ~37.0–37.4% (est.)”; the preview said the anticipated “~$140M net cash benefit” from tariff refunds was “excluded from guidance.”

surprises.description: American Eagle’s full-year outlook was weaker than its previously expected low-single-digit-positive comps: the company now expects the brand to be flat, citing it as the main reason for trimming prior expectations. The preview had already flagged American Eagle as a key debate, but expected roughly flat Q2 comps rather than this full-year outlook change.
surprises.fact_evidence: The full-year outlook was “a slight trim to prior expectations driven mainly by American Eagle's flat versus previously expected low-single-digit-positive outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Previously expected low-single-digit-positive outlook.”

surprises.description: Underlying merchandise margins were weaker than the preview’s margin-offset debate allowed for: merchandise margin deleveraged 330 basis points because of American Eagle markdowns, and seasonal and fashion-product markdown pressure is expected to continue into Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Merchandise margin actually deleveraged 330 basis points due to markdowns at American Eagle”; “ongoing markdown pressure from seasonal and fashion product at American Eagle is expected to persist into Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch whether merchandise margin (AUR, markdown rate) offsets” tariff costs, and described the bull case as involving “lower markdowns.”

surprises.description: Revenue modestly exceeded the $1.37 billion consensus estimate, reaching $1.4 billion, although comparable sales were about in line with expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue was $1.4 billion, up 8% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue: $1.37B”; comparable sales were expected at “~+6% (implied).”

in_line: Comparable sales grew 6%, at the high end of guidance and roughly in line with the preview’s ~6% expectation.
Aerie/OFFLINE comps grew 19%, within the preview’s implied ~18–20% range.
American Eagle comps declined 1%, roughly in line with the preview’s ~flat expectation.
Underlying operating profit was roughly $50 million, in line with the preview’s $48–50 million expectation.

surprises.description: AeroVironment’s Q1 adjusted EPS was $0.59, well above the preview’s consensus range of $0.20–$0.32 and its roughly $0.20 guidance-phasing estimate. The preview expected flat to down year-over-year EPS, but EPS instead rose 84%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS jumped 84% year-over-year to $0.59 from $0.32, driven by product gross margin improving to 40% from 36%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Published consensus sits above [guidance-implied phasing]”; sources listed Q1 adjusted EPS of “$0.25” and “$0.32,” while “Company phasing math” implied “~$0.20.”

surprises.description: Q1 revenue of $480 million exceeded the preview’s $456.1 million cited Street consensus and even the high end of its displayed vendor range, $474.6 million. It also came in above the roughly $440 million implied by company phasing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AeroVironment reported Q1 FY2027 revenue of $480 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed revenue estimates of “$456.1M,” “$459M,” and “$474.6M,” and calculated “Company phasing math” of “~$440M.”

surprises.description: Bookings and backlog were stronger than the preview’s concern about a potentially soft in-quarter bookings optic. Q1 bookings were $683 million at 1.4x book-to-bill, while funded backlog reached $1.5 billion, up from the $1.2 billion entering the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 bookings totaled $683 million for a 1.4x book-to-bill ratio”; “record funded backlog of $1.5 billion (up 37% year-over-year).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management might use E-HEL and the counter-UAS budget “to offset a soft in-quarter bookings optic,” and cited entering funded backlog of “$1.2B” and Q4 bookings of “$572M (0.9x book-to-bill).”

surprises.description: Management put forward a much larger prospective LOCUST opportunity than anything quantified in the preview: it expects the business to exceed $500 million annually within roughly a year and potentially outgrow the loitering munitions business within five years. The preview discussed LOCUST only as part of the known E-HEL award and did not present this growth outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects LOCUST to become a franchise exceeding $500 million per year within roughly a year and potentially larger than the loitering munitions business within five years, operating at under $10 per shot.”

surprises.description: Space, Cyber and Directed Energy posted negative $9 million adjusted EBITDA, a deeper loss than the preview’s base-case expectation of a still-negative but “modestly” negative result and worse than the segment’s FY26 negative $3 million. The preview had identified the segment’s progress toward profitability as a key debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Space, Cyber and Directed Energy segment posted negative $9 million adjusted EBITDA and 21% revenue decline year-over-year due to the SCAR contract termination … and discontinued government programs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “SCDE still modestly negative” and cited FY26 SCDE adjusted EBITDA of “-$3M.”

surprises.description: Q1 SG&A was elevated at 18% of revenue and included a $4.2 million bad-debt reserve, an expense the preview did not flag. Management said the full-year ratio should be 14–16%, making the near-term cost pressure partly offset by its projected normalization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted SG&A rose to $85 million (18% of revenue) from $65 million (14%), including a nonrecurring $4.2 million bad debt reserve, though full-year SG&A is projected at 14-16% of revenue.”

surprises.description: AeroVironment also reported its first international LOCUST direct commercial sale, a discrete commercial win not anticipated in the preview. The call facts provide no contract value, so its scale cannot be compared with an expected number.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Plus a first international LOCUST direct commercial sale.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed FY2027 revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and non-GAAP EPS guidance unchanged, as the preview’s central expectation explicitly called for a guidance reaffirmation.
The company guided to negative FY2027 free cash flow with CapEx at 12–14% of revenue, matching the preview’s expectation of negative FCF and that CapEx range.
Revenue weighting of 45% to the first half and 55% to the second half, and adjusted EBITDA weighting of roughly one-third/two-thirds, matched the preview’s stated phasing assumptions.

The E-HEL production award was already described in the preview as announced after quarter-end and expected to be a Q2, rather than Q1, booking; its mention on the call was not a new Q1 bookings surprise.

surprises.description: LAKE reported diluted EPS of -$0.50 versus the preview’s -$0.05 consensus estimate. The $3.2 million non-cash goodwill impairment tied to LHD Germany was an unanticipated contributor to the loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recorded a net loss of $4.9 million ($0.50 per share) versus net income of $0.8 million a year ago, including a non-cash $3.2 million goodwill impairment tied to LHD Germany.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) … −$0.05.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached 37.7%, well above the preview’s modeled 34–35% range and its 35% level that would validate the recovery thesis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanding 410 basis points sequentially to 37.7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. gross margin … model ~34–35%”; “35%+ validates it.”

surprises.description: Revenue was below the $51.48 million consensus, and growth excluding the divested product lines was only 2.8%, far short of the preview’s anticipated high-single- to low-double-digit organic growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net sales were $50.1 million”; sales were “up 2.8% when excluding $3.7 million of prior-year revenue from divested product lines.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue … $51.48M”; “Organic, ex-divestiture growth could be high-single to low-double digits.”

surprises.description: Fire revenue grew just 2% year over year, below the preview’s expectation that the fire business would accelerate beyond Q1’s 11% growth; some fire orders also shifted into Q4. Separately, fire services revenue surged 78%, with the ISP business contributing $3.5 million, substantially above the preview’s 10–15% base-case growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fire revenue grew 2% year-over-year”; “Fire services revenue grew 78% year-over-year, with the independent service provider (ISP) business contributing $3.5 million”; management flagged “some fire orders shifting into Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If Fire Services doesn't accelerate above +11%, the backlog claim looks like it converted into throughput constraints rather than revenue”; base case: “Fire Services +10–15%.”

surprises.description: Foreign exchange was a much larger earnings headwind than the preview highlighted: management cited a $1.3 million impact and said it was exploring hedging strategies, especially for Argentina and Europe.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Foreign exchange was a significant $1.3 million headwind versus just $43,000 a year ago, prompting management to explore hedging strategies, particularly for Argentina and European exposures.”

surprises.description: First-half operating cash flow was $5.4 million, a $15.1 million year-over-year improvement, providing stronger interim progress toward the preview’s full-year positive-cash-flow target than the preview quantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow was $5.4 million in the first half of fiscal 2027, a $15.1 million year-over-year improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management targets … positive operating cash flow for FY27.”

surprises.description: Management gave a concrete OpEx objective of lowering the expense ratio from about 32% of sales toward the mid-to-high 20s, a quantified efficiency goal not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cited “a goal to reduce OpEx from ~32% of sales toward the mid-to-high 20s.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had “explicitly declined to quantify margin targets.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA excluding FX was $2.7 million, within the preview’s modeled $2–4 million range, and the preview expected a sharp year-over-year decline from the $5.1 million comparison.
Management’s sequential revenue and margin growth outlook for Q3 and Q4 was consistent with the preview’s expectation that margin gains would be more visible in H2.

The UK firefighter PPE framework was already flagged in the preview; the call described the award and future contract opportunity but did not provide a specific LAKE contract value or first-order sizing.

surprises.description: Q3 revenue was $43.8 million, below the preview’s roughly $47 million estimate and the approximately $50 million consensus, despite the preview treating revenue as a low-signal metric. The reported total was also down from $47.8 million a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 FY2026 total net revenue declined to $43.8 million from $47.8 million a year earlier,” driven by “lighter-than-expected lemon sales volume and the transition of citrus brokerage operations to Sunkist.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total net revenue … ~$47M” in the preview’s estimate build; consensus revenue was “~$50M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was positive, as management had promised, but at $3.9 million it fell below the preview’s $5.5–$7.5 million base range and the $5 million level the preview said would validate the Sunkist savings thesis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose to $3.9 million in Q3 FY2026 versus $3.0 million in the prior-year quarter, despite results coming in below management's expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adjusted EBITDA … ~$6.5M” and said “Anything ≥$5M validates the Sunkist thesis”; it also noted management committed to “positive adjusted EBITDA in both Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was only $0.02, well below the preview’s approximately $0.08 operating estimate; the quarter also showed a $0.17-per-share GAAP loss rather than the positive $0.18–$0.19 consensus estimate cited in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported a Q3 net loss of $3 million ($0.17 per diluted share), widening from a $1 million loss ($0.06 per share) a year earlier, though adjusted diluted EPS turned positive at $0.02.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s estimate build put “Adjusted EPS” at “~$0.08”; its consensus table listed “EPS (GAAP/adj.)” at “$0.18–$0.19.”

surprises.description: Fresh lemon volume guidance was moved to the low end of the prior range rather than simply being reiterated, reflecting higher Argentine imports and oversupply in the U.S. market.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fresh lemon volume guidance was cut to the low end at 4.0 million to 4.25 million cartons for FY2026 due to higher lemon imports from Argentina oversupplying the U.S. market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY2026 lemon guidance was “4.0–4.5M cartons” and listed “FY26 lemon (4.0–4.5M cartons) … guidance reiterated” as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: FY2026 avocado volume guidance was raised substantially above the range the preview expected to be reiterated, although the lower realized price makes the volume upgrade less favorable than the headline alone suggests.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Avocado volume guidance was raised to 7.0-7.25 million pounds for FY2026, well above the prior 5.5-6.5 million pound range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the FY2026 guide as “5.5–6.5M lbs” and expected it to be “reiterated.”

surprises.description: Avocado pricing was weaker than the preview’s expected range: the reported average was $1.15 per pound, versus the preview’s roughly $1.35 estimate and cited $1.30–$1.40 spot pricing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average avocado pricing fell to $1.15 per pound from $1.50 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q3 avocados at “~5.0M lbs @ ~$1.35” and cited “Spot cited at $1.30–1.40/lb for peak sizes.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a much larger future avocado crop than the preview had discussed: FY2027 production is expected to exceed 10 million pounds, with further acreage coming into production over the following years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects FY2027 avocado production to exceed 10 million pounds, an approximately 30% increase over FY2026,” driven by planted acreage and “400 additional non-bearing acres coming online in 2-4 years.”

surprises.description: The company laid out a broader quantified monetization pipeline and FY2027 operating-improvement target: it identified more than $200 million of assets for monetization and cited about $180 million of real estate proceeds over seven fiscal years plus $4 million of operating improvements in FY2027. The preview discussed asset sales and Harvest at Limoneira, but not this broader quantified plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company identified over $200 million in real estate, non-strategic land and water rights for monetization” and “anticipates ~$180 million in real estate proceeds over seven fiscal years plus $4 million in operating improvements in FY2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed “the ~$5M FY26 distribution” and “the $155M/5-year proceeds framing” for Harvest at Limoneira.

surprises.description: Debt was higher at quarter-end than the April 30 balance cited in the preview, while cash remained very limited. That leaves the balance sheet under pressure ahead of the covenant measurement, even though cash was slightly above the preview’s April figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Long-term debt rose to $100.7 million as of July 31, 2026, up from $72.5 million at the end of FY2025, while cash stood at just $2.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “At 4/30/26: cash $0.9M, long-term debt $94.1M” and said to watch “pro-forma leverage against the Oct 31 covenant test.”

surprises.description: The Windfall sale was expected, but the company also said it would retain the 2026 crop economics and receive a $200,000 annual farming fee, adding ongoing economics beyond the sale proceeds.
surprises.fact_evidence: The “$15 million all-cash sale of Windfall Farms” is expected to close September 14, with “retained 2026 crop economics and a $200,000/year farming fee.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Windfall Farms $15M all-cash closes September 14, 2026” and described proceeds as intended for deleveraging.

in_line: Fresh lemon shipments were 1.373 million cartons, within the preview’s estimated 1.3–1.5 million range and above its 1.3 million minimum; the $19.88 net price per carton was within the expected $19–$21 range.
Adjusted EBITDA turned positive, consistent with management’s stated commitment to positive adjusted EBITDA in Q3, although the result was below the preview’s modeled range.
The Windfall Farms sale remained a $15 million all-cash transaction expected to close September 14, 2026, as the preview anticipated.
The preview expected a Colorado River water-rights monetization event in Q4 FY2026; management’s stated Q4 timing was consistent with that expectation.

surprises.description: Investors were watching for a CooperSurgical sale or a clear step forward in the process; instead, the Board concluded its review and chose to retain the business. The stated reason was that offers did not reflect intrinsic value.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Board “unanimously concluded its strategic review and decided to retain CooperSurgical,” citing offers that failed to reflect intrinsic value.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the sale “a binary strategic catalyst” and said a definitive update could land before the call; it also described retaining CSI as a bear-case outcome.

surprises.description: Q4 guidance was materially below the preview’s implied Q4 earnings level: EPS of $1.05–$1.09 versus roughly $1.19 implied by the prior FY26 guide.
