The revenue range of $1.057–$1.080 billion also falls below the roughly $1.13 billion Q4 implied by the prior annual revenue midpoint after the reported Q3 segment results.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 guidance calls for revenue of “$1.057-$1.080 billion” and non-GAAP EPS of “$1.05-$1.09,” with margins pressured by increased CooperVision commercial investments, FX headwinds, and lower tariff refunds.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the FY26 EPS midpoint implied Q4 EPS of “~$1.19” and the FY26 revenue midpoint implied H2 revenue of “~$2.194B.”

surprises.description: CooperVision revenue was well below the preview’s estimate, at $717 million and essentially flat year over year versus an expected $735–740 million and 4–5% growth. Management attributed the weaker reported result to U.S. channel destocking and said a similar inventory reduction should continue in Q4, while underlying U.S. consumption remained in the mid-single digits.
surprises.fact_evidence: CooperVision revenue was “essentially flat year-over-year at $717 million”; the Americas would have grown about 5% absent “proactive U.S. channel inventory reductions,” and a similar reduction is expected in Q4.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated CooperVision revenue at “~$735–740M” and described expected growth of “+4–5%”; it also said the whisper for organic growth was “~4–4.5%.”

surprises.description: CooperSurgical revenue also came in below the preview’s estimate, at $349 million versus $355–360 million expected. Its 3% organic growth was within the preview’s expected range, so the surprise is the lower reported revenue rather than the organic growth rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: CooperSurgical revenue was “$349 million,” with organic growth of 3%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated CooperSurgical revenue at “~$355–360M” and expected “+2–3%” growth.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS of $1.15 exceeded the preview’s $1.11–$1.12 consensus range. The preview noted Cooper’s history of repeated EPS beats, so the result was better than the estimate but not an entirely unexpected pattern.
surprises.fact_evidence: Non-GAAP EPS grew 4% to “$1.15,” marking the 11th consecutive quarter of beating consensus earnings expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed non-GAAP diluted EPS consensus at “$1.11–$1.12.”

surprises.description: The Board approved a much larger capital-return commitment than the preview could quantify: a $1 billion increase in repurchase authorization, alongside $339 million of Q3 repurchases. This adds a concrete, substantial buyback signal to the previously stated aggressive posture.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Board approved a “$1 billion increase to share repurchase authorization,” bringing capacity to about $1.5 billion; Cooper repurchased $339 million in Q3 and $445 million year to date.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged the “size of buyback executed in Q3 and any new authorization” as a key watch item and noted only $13 million had been repurchased in Q2.

surprises.description: A favorable HMRC examination resolution produced a large discrete tax benefit and extended non-GAAP tax benefits for at least another decade, an unanticipated positive development.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company recognized a discrete tax benefit of “~$307 million” following favorable resolution of an HMRC examination, providing non-GAAP tax benefits for “at least 10 additional years.”

surprises.description: A scheduled GILTI increase is expected to raise the non-GAAP effective tax rate by about two percentage points in FY27, an adverse future tax headwind not flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The scheduled GILTI increase is expected to move the non-GAAP effective tax rate from roughly 15.5% this year to roughly 17.5% in fiscal 2027.

surprises.description: Tariff refunds contributed about $0.03 to Q3 non-GAAP EPS. The preview highlighted uncertainty over whether tariff refunds would materialize, so their actual contribution was a modest positive.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q3 non-GAAP EPS included “~$0.03 from tariff refunds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said whether the excluded “~$15M in refunds materializes” mattered.

in_line: CooperSurgical organic growth was 3%, within the preview’s expected 2–3% range.

surprises.description: Skillsoft cut FY2027 revenue guidance to $380–390 million from $388–406 million, below the preview’s expected reaffirmation. Management attributed the reduction to accelerating weakness and AI disruption in its coding-focused consumer business, a specific risk the preview had not identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $380-390 million from the prior $388-406 million range, driven by accelerating weakness and AI disruption in its coding-focused consumer business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 guide reaffirmed at $388–406M” was the base case; the preview also called guidance action “the binary.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $33.4 million, well above the preview’s $26–28 million estimate, and the margin reached 34% versus an expected 27–28%. The preview anticipated cost discipline holding margins around 28%; the reported 12% reduction in selling and marketing expenses helped produce a much stronger result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations rose 7% to $33.4 million, with margin expanding to 34% from 31% a year earlier, aided by a 12% cut in selling and marketing expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$26–28M”; “Adj. EBITDA margin ~27–28%.” The base case described “cost discipline” holding “the ~28% margin.”

surprises.description: The reported quarterly dollar retention rate was 95%, below the preview’s 100% threshold for confirming the prior-quarter improvement. It was better than the preview’s downside case of a relapse into the low 90s, but it did not sustain the Q1 rate of 105%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Dollar retention rate improved to 95% from 94% year-over-year, though the LTM DRR slipped to 98% from 99%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A second consecutive quarter ≥100% validates the go-to-market redesign; a relapse into the low 90s guts the H2 ramp story.”

surprises.description: The Global Knowledge disposal is expected to consume about $15 million of FY2027 cash, plus roughly $4 million of Q3 advisory costs. That is above the preview’s cited $8–10 million of guided separation costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Global Knowledge disposal is estimated to consume about $15 million of fiscal 2027 cash ($12 million already incurred through July 31), plus ~$4 million of Q3 advisory costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bear scenario cited “GK separation costs run above the $8–10M guided.”

surprises.description: The preview identified refinancing progress on the 2028 term loan as a key debate and said silence or a repeat of general priority language would be negative. The call facts report no concrete refinancing step, only that addressing upcoming maturities remains management’s top financial priority.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Addressing upcoming debt maturities [was] identified as management's top financial priority following the Global Knowledge divestiture.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything concrete — advisors engaged, lender conversations, a term sheet, an amend-and-extend — is a bigger stock event”; “Silence or a repeat of ‘we're evaluating all alternatives with discipline and urgency’ is a negative.”

surprises.description: The call provided specific early AI-product adoption indicators that the preview had not flagged: Casey conversation-simulator learners and using organizations grew year over year, and AI Coach was being piloted by seven organizations. These are positive early signs, though the facts do not quantify bookings from that adoption.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Casey conversation-simulator learners [were] up 23% year-over-year and using organizations up 9%, plus AI Coach now piloted by seven organizations out of 30-plus early-access customers.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of $98.2 million was close to the $99.0 million consensus and within the preview’s $98–100 million base-case range; the core enterprise business was roughly flat as the preview’s base case expected.
Q2 consolidated free cash flow of negative $20.5 million was within the preview’s estimated negative $15–25 million range, and the preview expected seasonal cash consumption.

The company maintained FY2027 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $108–116 million and free cash flow guidance of $14–22 million, consistent with the preview’s focus on whether the cash-flow guide would survive.
LTM dollar retention was 98%, matching the preview’s cited 98% level.

surprises.description: The preview expected Q3 adjusted EBITDA to reach roughly breakeven, but Gloo guided to a $3.5 million loss. Management now targets adjusted EBITDA profitability in Q4 2026, one quarter later than the preview’s key expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for revenue of $55 million and adjusted EBITDA of -$3.5 million”; management committed to “reaching adjusted EBITDA profitability in Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the implied Q3/Q4 revenue was “roughly Q3 ~$52M and Q4 ~$57M,” and called “Q3 breakeven” the “make-or-break item”; it also said that if Q3 breakeven were “pushed to Q4,” the profitability narrative would break.

surprises.description: Gloo raised its FY2026 revenue guidance to $200 million, rather than merely reaffirming the preview’s expected $195 million. The increase is inclusive of Cedarstone, though the call did not provide a clean organic-growth figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance by $5 million to $200 million, inclusive of the Cedarstone acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 revenue guidance of “$195.0M” and said the base case was that FY guidance would be “reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue exceeded the $44 million guide and consensus by $2.6 million, a roughly 6% beat. The preview had cautioned that anything below a 3–5% beat could signal decelerating momentum.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 fiscal 2026 revenue grew 188% year-over-year to $46.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 revenue guidance and consensus at “$44.0M” and said “Anything less than a ~3–5% beat reads as decelerating momentum.”

surprises.description: Quarter-end cash was below the preview’s estimated range and below its $40 million risk threshold. The July offering brought in more net proceeds than the preview’s rough estimate, but did not prevent the ending cash balance from coming in lower than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: Gloo “raised $23.7 million net in a follow-on offering” and “ended the quarter with $39.3 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “~$42–46M” cash at July 31 and said “Below ~$40M” would reopen dilution risk; it estimated “~$21M net” from the July offering.

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of $55 million is above the preview’s approximate $52 million expectation, suggesting a stronger near-term revenue run rate than the preview’s H2 build implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for revenue of $55 million,” driven by peak advertising and fundraising season for Masterworks and Westfall Gold.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s H2 math implied “roughly Q3 ~$52M.”

surprises.description: The call did not provide the clean organic-growth disclosure the preview identified as the highest-value disclosure; instead, it said platform growth was driven substantially by acquisitions. That leaves the preview’s concern about how much growth is acquired unresolved.
surprises.fact_evidence: Platform solutions revenue rose 209% and platform revenue rose 170%, “both driven substantially by acquisitions like Masterworks, Westfall Gold, and EMD”; the call facts provide no organic-growth percentage.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called a “clean organic figure” the “single highest-value disclosure” and said “Silence on it is a negative.”

surprises.description: Cost of revenue improved substantially year over year, an unexpectedly favorable margin development given the preview’s concern that a greater services mix could weigh on revenue quality.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cost of revenue improved 10.8 percentage points to 64.0% of total revenue from 74.8% a year earlier,” aided by scale and favorable acquisition mix.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned that Cedarstone’s outsourced accounting and fractional CFO work was “services, not software,” and that a mix “drifting toward solutions justifies a lower multiple.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was slightly better than expected, at a loss of $8.3 million versus the preview’s $8.5 million loss estimate. The improvement is small compared with the more consequential shortfall against the preview’s Q3 breakeven expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA improved $3.2 million sequentially to -$8.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 adjusted EBITDA guidance and consensus at “–$8.5M.”

surprises.description: Gloo reported a first customer above $10 million in annual contract value and more than 30 customers above $1 million, providing a customer-scale milestone the preview did not forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company now has more than 30 customers with over $1 million in annual contract value and reached its first customer exceeding $10 million in annual contract value.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a $4.4 million restructuring charge tied mainly to severance, which the preview did not flag. Management also said it plans to invest in additional salespeople, so integration-related cuts are not the only operating-cost move.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company took a $4.4 million restructuring charge in Q2, primarily for severance related to integrating business lines, while planning to invest in additional salespeople.”

surprises.description: Gloo said its $13.2 million senior secured loan was extended to April 2028, a financing-term update not anticipated in the preview and potentially easing near-term refinancing pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “extended its $13.2 million senior secured loan to April 2028.”

surprises.description: Management said future acquisitions are targeted to use a 20–25% cash structure, an unanticipated detail that could limit cash use in future deals. The call also quantified Cedarstone’s customer contribution at more than 250 new mid-market customers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Cedarstone acquisition added over 250 new mid-market customers with strong Masterworks cross-selling potential,” and management targeted a “20-25% cash structure for future deals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Cedarstone as an acquisition of outsourced accounting and fractional CFO services and raised concern about “Cedarstone cash consideration still to come,” but did not specify its customer contribution or a target cash structure for future deals.

surprises.description: The cash management fee rate was 55 bps, below the preview’s expected 56–57 bps range and at the preview’s stated bear-case threshold. That puts more pressure on the cash revenue model than the base case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The annualized cash management fee rate fell 6 basis points year-over-year to 55 basis points,” driven by the APY-to-APR conversion at lower Fed funds rates and higher client incentive costs.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected a “fee rate 0.56–0.57%”; it said a rate “below ~0.55%” would be a bear-case trigger.

surprises.description: Cash management revenue was $61.8 million, below the preview’s estimated $62–64 million. This was a modest shortfall even though total revenue landed near the preview’s overall estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash management revenue declined 10% to $61.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated cash revenue at “~$62–64M.”

surprises.description: Cash management assets fell 4% year-over-year, a steeper decline than the roughly 2% decline the preview cited. Quarter-end cash assets were still around the preview’s expected $44–45 billion range, but the year-over-year contraction was worse.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash management assets fell 4% year-over-year to $44.9 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said cash management assets were “down ~2% YoY” and projected “cash assets flat ~$44–45B.”

surprises.description: Management attributed cash outflows in part to the 2023 and 2024 client cohorts lagging in investment adoption after joining during peak rates. The preview raised the possibility of rate-cycle effects or competitor-driven share loss, but did not anticipate this cohort-specific explanation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2023 and 2024 client cohorts, which joined during peak rates, have lagged in investment adoption and driven cash outflows.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether cash attrition was “a rate-cycle artifact or genuine share loss to higher-yielding competitors,” without identifying these cohorts as a driver.

surprises.description: Management said targeted incentives improved cash net deposits in July and August to their best level since March. The preview was looking for cash deposits to turn positive or at least for the June outflow to shrink, so this is encouraging progress, though the call facts do not say whether deposits actually turned positive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Targeted incentives improved July and August cash net deposits to the best level since March.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said cash net deposits needed “to turn positive, or at least shrink the outflow from -$235M.”

surprises.description: The call reported 1.1 million funded clients, far below the preview’s last disclosed figure of 1.49 million for June, even as the call described funded clients as up 14% year-over-year. The provided materials do not reconcile the difference, so the implication for client growth is unclear.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Funded clients rose 14% year-over-year to 1.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s metrics table listed “Jun 30 … Funded clients 1.49M.”

surprises.description: GAAP diluted EPS was $0.10, slightly above the preview’s bottom-up expectation of roughly $0.06–$0.09 for GAAP EPS. It was still below the preview’s $0.13–$0.14 public estimates, which the preview warned could reflect adjusted rather than GAAP conventions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP diluted EPS was $0.10.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “GAAP EPS lands ~$0.06–$0.09” if SBC stayed near $17 million per quarter.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a one-time $3–$3.5 million employer tax expense next quarter tied to former employee option exercises, an unexpected near-term expense and margin headwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management flagged a one-time employer tax expense of $3 million to $3.5 million next quarter tied to former employee option exercises.”

surprises.description: Investment advisory revenue reached $28.8 million, modestly above the preview’s estimate of about $28 million. The advisory business therefore performed a little better than the preview’s build implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Investment advisory revenue grew 31% to $28.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated advisory revenue at “≈ $28M.”

in_line: Total revenue of $91.9 million was essentially in line with the preview’s roughly $92 million estimate and its $91–93 million bottom-up range.

Quarter-end platform assets of $99 billion were within the preview’s $99–101 billion base-case range; the subsequent August level of $100.9 billion was also consistent with the anticipated record-asset headline.
Adjusted EBITDA margin was 41%, matching the preview’s expected 40–41% range, and the company remained above the 40% rule-of-40 threshold the preview highlighted.

Advisory assets of $54.1 billion were close to the preview’s roughly $54 billion estimate; asset-weighted cross-product adoption just under 64% was consistent with the preview’s expectation of adoption above 63%.
The $30 million quarterly repurchase was broadly similar to the prior quarter’s roughly $27 million repurchase; the facts do not report an expanded authorization.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was ZAR 6.51 for FY26, above the preview’s guidance-based expected range of ZAR 5.50–6.00; Q4 EPS of ZAR 2.40 was also well above the preview’s implied high end of about ZAR 1.76.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS grew 210% to ZAR 6.51”; “Q4 adjusted EPS rose from ZAR 0.90 to ZAR 2.40.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EPS | ZAR 5.50–6.00”; the preview’s implied Q4 adj. EPS range was “1.26” to “1.76.”

surprises.description: Merchant revenue did not turn to positive growth in Q4: it fell 10%, while the preview expected a return to positive growth. The decline came despite higher transaction volumes, as take rates fell, and Merchant adjusted EBITDA also dropped sharply.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 net revenue declining 10% to ZAR 729 million as take rates fell (ADP take rate down 25%) despite acquiring TPV growing 27% and ADP TPV growing 31%”; “Merchant segment adjusted EBITDA declined 33% to ZAR 122 million in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Merchant revenue growth turns positive” and described the base case as “Merchant flat.”

surprises.description: The FY27 EBITDA guide includes Bank Zero, contrary to the preview’s base-case expectation of an ex-Bank Zero guide. Its ZAR 1.45 billion low end is also below the preview’s expected ex-deal range of ZAR 1.5–1.6 billion, although the guide reaches ZAR 1.6 billion at the top end.
surprises.fact_evidence: FY27 guidance is “group adjusted EBITDA of ZAR 1.45–1.6 billion,” “inclusive of Bank Zero.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the base case as “FY27 guided ex-Bank Zero at ZAR 1.5–1.6bn EBITDA” and said a clean ex-Bank Zero guide was most likely.

surprises.description: Management now expects Bank Zero to close before year-end, earlier than the preview’s framing of a deal still awaiting regulatory approval with a long-stop date of 31 January 2027. The call also outlined a deposit-funded migration of lending books that could sharply reduce debt and leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: Bank Zero “is expected to close before year-end”; the acquisition is expected to cut leverage “to below 1x by June 2027” and could bring gross debt “near-zero” by June 2028 through migration of lending books to customer-deposit funding.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the deal “has not closed,” that regulatory sign-off was outstanding, and that the long-stop date had been extended to “31 Jan 2027”; it also flagged how the deal would be funded as an open question.

surprises.description: Year-end leverage came in better than the preview’s already-improved Q3 level and the company’s target: net debt to adjusted EBITDA was 1.9x rather than about 2.1x, and below the 2.0x target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt to group adjusted EBITDA fell to 1.9x, below its 2x target and down from 2.9x a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported leverage at “2.1x at Q3 vs a 2.0x target.”

surprises.description: Enterprise delivered strong growth and management identified it as the fastest-growing segment for FY27, a development the preview did not flag among its expected segment outcomes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enterprise net revenue grew 34% to ZAR 255 million in Q4 with core net revenue up 45% for the year, and segment adjusted EBITDA rose 155% to ZAR 54 million”; management expects it to be “the fastest-growing segment in FY27.”

surprises.description: Management warned that one-off and restructuring costs in Merchant will pressure Q1 FY27 results, an additional near-term headwind not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “flagged one-off and restructuring costs that will pressure Q1 FY27 results.”

surprises.description: Management set specific FY29 ambitions—including ZAR 11 billion in net revenue, an EBITDA margin above 25%, and adjusted EPS above ZAR 18—that were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management set FY29 ambitions of “net revenue of circa ZAR 11 billion (over 20% CAGR), EBITDA margin above 25%, and adjusted EPS exceeding ZAR 18,” alongside targets for consumers, merchants, and Enterprise TPV.

in_line: FY26 net revenue of ZAR 6.33 billion was within the preview’s company-guidance range of ZAR 6.2–6.5 billion.
FY26 adjusted EBITDA of ZAR 1.27 billion was within the ZAR 1.25–1.35 billion guidance range and consistent with the preview’s expectation that it would be near the bottom end.
FY26 GAAP net income was positive, as the preview expected, which had identified positive full-year net income as the company’s stated guidance.
Q4 group adjusted EBITDA of ZAR 367 million was within the preview’s implied Q4 range of ZAR 338–438 million and its base-case range of ZAR 350–390 million.
Consumer growth was strong but broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation that Consumer momentum would carry the quarter.

surprises.description: Navan reported Q2 revenue of $233 million, about 6% above the $220.5 million consensus and above even the preview’s $230–235 million bull-case range only at its lower end. The headline beat was stronger than the preview’s base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue rose 35% year-over-year to $233 million, both exceeding expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Sell-side consensus sits at $220.5M”; the preview’s bull case forecast revenue of “$230–235M.”

surprises.description: GBV exceeded $3 billion, versus preview consensus of $2.86 billion, and grew 45% rather than the expected 37%. Bookings therefore came in materially above the already strong growth anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total GBV grew 45% year-over-year to more than $3 billion in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross Booking Volume … Consensus $2.86B (+37%).”

surprises.description: Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow reached $28 million, well above the preview’s expected $2 million and a sharp improvement from the prior-year burn. The cash and short-term investment balance also came in above the preview’s $681 million figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow turned positive at $28 million on a trailing basis versus a $33 million burn a year ago, with $820 million in cash and short-term investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “TTM FCF +$2M (vs. −$52.4M prior year)” and “$681M cash and short-term investments.”

surprises.description: Navan raised FY27 non-GAAP operating income guidance to $82–86 million from $76–80 million. That is a larger profit outlook than the preview’s existing guide, and it accompanies the revenue raise rather than leaving the upside entirely to spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its full-year FY27 … non-GAAP operating income guidance to $82-86 million (9% margin), marking the second raise this year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 non-GAAP op income $76–80M (~9% margin)” and “Watch whether op income is raised alongside revenue.”

surprises.description: Navan disclosed a Q3 operating-income outlook of $35.5–36.5 million, or a 14% margin. That is a pronounced step-up from Q2’s 7% reported margin and above the 9% full-year margin outlook, though the preview did not provide a specific Q3 margin estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for … non-GAAP operating income of $35.5-36.5 million (14% margin).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Q2 margin guide implies a ~460bp sequential non-GAAP operating margin compression” and “H2 must carry $38–42M: either margins step up hard or the op-income guide gets raised too.”

surprises.description: Sales-led enterprise demand had a strong quantified indicator not called out in the preview: new signed GBV reached $4 billion over the trailing 12 months, up 60%. The preview noted rising RFP activity, but this signed-bookings figure adds a stronger leading indicator of future revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New signed GBV for the sales-led growth (SLG) enterprise business reached $4 billion over the trailing 12 months, up 60% versus Q2 last year, serving as a leading indicator of future revenue.”

surprises.description: Navan said it now serves 50 S&P 500 companies, up from 45 last quarter, exceeding the preview’s cited count of 45. The preview had highlighted enterprise-logo growth, so the additional five companies were a favorable update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company now serves 50 companies in the S&P 500, up from 45 last quarter, with rising win rates and ASPs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “45 at Q1, up from 28 a year prior.”

surprises.description: Product-led growth revenue more than doubled year over year, a strong result for a business line the preview did not quantify or identify as a specific Q2 expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Product-led growth revenue more than doubled year-over-year.”

surprises.description: Subscription revenue grew 39% to $21 million, another strong revenue stream update that the preview had not specifically anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Subscription revenue was $21 million (up 39%).”

surprises.description: Navan reported that its AI agent resolved about 60% of customer interactions and that its own models accounted for half of usage, up from 30% in Q1. This puts specific operating results behind the preview’s discussion of possible AI-driven support savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI agent Ava resolved approximately 60% of customer interactions in Q2, driving structural gross margin gains, with Navan-owned AI models rising to 50% of usage from 30% in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s commentary tells included “AI-driven support cost savings.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP gross margin topped 75% for the first time, up 200 basis points year over year. The preview focused on operating-margin pressure and take rate, but did not anticipate this gross-margin milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin exceeded 75% for the first time in company history (up 200 bps year-over-year).”

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP operating margin was 7%, versus the preview’s roughly 6.4% margin implied by the company’s guide, so it beat that guide. However, it fell short of the preview’s 8% catalyst threshold and its higher-margin bull-case scenarios.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin improved to 7% from 5% a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income … ~$14M” on consensus revenue, or “~6.4% margin”; the preview also flagged “Non-GAAP operating margin ≥8%” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: Payment volume grew 34%, just below the preview’s 35%+ marker for a genuine positive surprise. It was nevertheless above the preview’s concern about another sub-30% quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Payment volumes reached $1.3 billion (up 34%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “+35%+ is a genuine positive surprise; another sub-30% quarter says Navan is a travel company with a card attached.”

surprises.description: The BoomPop acquisition adds a newly disclosed FY27 cost: very low-single-digit revenue impact and a mid-single-digit operating-income drag, with accretion not expected until FY28. Its meetings-and-events opportunity and savings potential provide the longer-term upside, but the near-term drag was not in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The BoomPop acquisition targets the meetings and events category (roughly 30% of business travel TAM) with ~30% savings rates, but will have only very low-single-digit revenue impact and mid-single-digit operating income drag in FY27 before becoming accretive in FY28.”

in_line: FY27 revenue guidance was raised to $927–933 million, with a midpoint of $930 million, in line with the preview’s $925–935 million bogey.
First-half RFP volume tripled year over year, matching the preview’s cited roughly 200% increase in RFP activity.
Payment growth at 34% was close to the preview’s 35%+ positive-surprise marker and clearly above its sub-30% concern.

surprises.description: The preview said the market expected roughly flat FY2027 revenue and framed a decline as a bear trigger. Management instead guided to a mid-single-digit revenue decline, a meaningful step below that expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company guided fiscal 2027 revenue to decline in the mid-single-digit range.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street sits at ~$1.52B (roughly flat).” A guide to “another year of decline” was identified as “the bear trigger.”

surprises.description: The FY2027 adjusted EBITDA guide was only $10–$15 million, below the preview’s $25 million-plus bull-case floor. The guide also absorbs roughly $12 million of additional variable compensation expense, while the preview’s base case anticipated no hard EBITDA number.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company guided fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA of $10 to $15 million, which “absorbs roughly $12 million of additional variable compensation expense.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “flat-to-up revenue with a $25M+ EBITDA floor” as the bull trigger, while its base scenario expected FY2027 guidance to be framed qualitatively, “no hard EBITDA number.”

surprises.description: The company moved beyond the preview’s warning to watch for covenant language: it amended its credit agreement for covenant relief and retained an adviser to evaluate raising capital, including equity and asset divestitures. Those financing and divestiture options point to greater pressure than the preview’s monitoring language alone suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “amended its credit agreement to extend covenant relief and retain a portion of asset-sale proceeds,” and retained Guggenheim Securities to evaluate capital-raising options including debt, equity, and divestitures of non-strategic assets.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch FY26 FCF, revolver capacity, and any covenant language” and listed “first mention of covenant headroom or refinancing” as a bear signal.

surprises.description: Gross margin contracted rather than providing the expansion the preview wanted as proof that cost savings were working: full-year adjusted gross margin fell, and Q4 margin was below the prior-year quarter even with a tariff-refund benefit. The roughly $7 million refund is not expected to recur in FY2027, making the reported Q4 margin a favorable one-off rather than a durable improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year adjusted gross margin fell to 38% from 39.1%; Q4 margin was 34.7% and included an approximately $7 million tariff refund benefit that is not expected to recur in fiscal 2027.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “Expanding GM on falling revenue is the proof point that cost-out is real; contraction says they're buying volume with promotion,” and cited Q4 FY2025 gross margin of 35.5%.

surprises.description: Gourmet Foods and Gift Baskets revenue fell 15.4%, far weaker than the preview’s expectation that the segment would hold roughly flat. Easter timing partly explains the Q4 decline, but the reported segment contraction was still substantial.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 Gourmet Foods and Gift Baskets revenue declined 15.4%. The Easter timing shift reduced that segment’s revenue by roughly 2.5 to 3.5 percentage points and overall Q4 revenue by about 1.5%, with no full-year impact.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s secondary watch list described “Gourmet Foods holding flat (Q3 $106.9M, ~flat).”

surprises.description: BloomNet returned to growth, contrary to the preview’s concern that the historically stable segment was now declining. Its Q4 increase also reversed the decline reported for Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: BloomNet revenue increased 1.9% in Q4.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “BloomNet trend (Q3 −5.9% — the historically stable, high-margin franchise segment is now declining).”

surprises.description: Net debt rose well above the preview’s Q3 estimate, and the company ended the year with only $11 million of cash. The preview anticipated a cash-consumptive quarter, but the reported net debt was roughly $34–$37 million above its cited Q3 level.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net debt rose to $128 million from $114 million a year earlier, with cash of $11 million, $139 million in term debt, and no revolver borrowings.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q3 exit net debt of “~$91M (management cited $94.3M)” and said, “Q4 is a cash-consumptive quarter.”

surprises.description: FY2026 adjusted EBITDA came in slightly above the top of the breakeven ±$2 million guide, and the Q4 loss was smaller than the preview’s derived estimate. This was a modest positive versus the guide, rather than the serious guide miss the preview warned about.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year adjusted EBITDA was $2.9 million; Q4 adjusted EBITDA loss was $31 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited FY2026 guidance of “breakeven ±$2M” and derived Q4 adjusted EBITDA of approximately “−$32M to −$34M.”

in_line: Q4 revenue of $293.1 million was slightly below the preview’s derived $295–$300 million range, but within its base-case range of $288–$300 million; full-year revenue of approximately $1.5 billion was close to the preview’s ~$1.51 billion estimate.

Consumer Floral and Gift revenue declined 13.4%: weaker than the preview’s threshold for a genuine positive surprise (better than roughly −12%), but consistent with its base-case expectation of a mid-teens decline and an improvement from Q3’s −18.7%.
The company achieved the previewed $50 million cost-savings target and identified the expected additional $15–$20 million of savings for FY2027.

surprises.description: Designer Brands raised FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $0.47–$0.52 from $0.28–$0.38, a much larger increase than the preview’s base case of reaffirming the range with high-end language.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year adjusted diluted EPS guidance to $0.47-$0.52,” from prior guidance of “$0.28-$0.38.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “FY guide reaffirmed with ‘high end’ language intact”; UBS was also described as expecting a reaffirmation.

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached 47.9%, far above the preview’s 44.8% estimate. The gain was partly boosted by a tariff refund claim—280 basis points of the 430-basis-point expansion—while underlying improvement was 150 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded 430 basis points to 47.9%,” including “280 basis points” from a “$20.2 million tariff refund claim,” with “150 basis points of underlying improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated gross margin of “44.8%,” or “+110 bps,” and said tariff impacts and refund claims were expected to be largely offset by new tariffs.

surprises.description: Q2 sales were below the preview’s $742 million base-case estimate, with sales down about 1% rather than up 0.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales fell approximately 1% year-over-year to $730.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bottom-up estimate was “$742M (+0.3% Y/Y),” with an implied range of “$735–750M.”

surprises.description: Retail comps were weaker than the preview’s expectation that retail would be flat to slightly up: comparable sales fell 2.4%, and retail segment sales declined 2%. Sandals explained roughly 200 basis points of the retail decline, leaving sales approximately flat excluding sandals.
surprises.fact_evidence: Comparable store sales were “down 2.4%,” retail segment sales “declined 2%,” and seasonal sandals accounted for “roughly 200 basis points” of the retail decline; excluding sandals, retail sales were “approximately flat.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had guided Q2 retail to “flat to slightly up” and identified the retail comp as the key inflection test.

surprises.description: The company also raised its sales outlook, narrowing the downside and moving the range’s low end to flat growth. This was a smaller improvement than the EPS guidance increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year sales guidance was lifted “to flat-to-up 1% from prior negative 1% to positive 1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed the existing FY2026 net sales guide as “−1% to +1%” and expected a reaffirmation in its base case.

surprises.description: Brand Portfolio sales grew 18%, above the preview’s 12–15% Q2 build, despite being slightly below the prior quarter’s 19.4% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Brand Portfolio sales grew 18%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 build assumed “Brand Portfolio +12–15%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS of $0.34 edged above the preview’s $0.32 bottom-up estimate, though it was nearly flat with the prior-year $0.33 and the tariff benefits were offset by higher taxes and interest expense.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 adjusted net income was “$19.2 million ($0.34 per diluted share), only modestly above last year's $16.4 million ($0.33), as tariff benefits were offset by higher taxes and interest expense.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bottom-up Q2 estimate was “$0.32” adjusted EPS.

surprises.description: Debt fell further than the preview’s balance-sheet snapshot implied: it was $423.1 million, below the preview’s cited $475.3 million level, and liquidity was somewhat higher than the cited $189 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: Total debt was reduced “to $423.1 million from $516.3 million a year ago,” and the company ended the quarter with “roughly $198 million in total liquidity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited debt of “$475.3M” and liquidity of “$189M.”

in_line: The Q3 incentive-compensation comparison remained a profitability headwind, consistent with the preview’s warning about a roughly $10 million Q3 incentive-compensation headwind.
Brand Portfolio growth remained strong, consistent with the preview’s expectation of sustained growth after Q1’s 19.4% increase, although the reported 18% was modestly above the preview’s Q2 build.

surprises.description: Q4 diluted EPS was $0.02, half the preview’s current $0.04 estimate. The preview cautioned that its published full-year EPS figure was unreliable, so the more current quarterly estimate is the relevant comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 net income fell to $666,000 ($0.02) from $2.4 million ($0.09)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “TipRanks' next-quarter estimate of $0.04 (range $0.03–$0.04) is the more current mark and is what I use.”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA was $5.8 million, below the preview’s expected $6.0–$6.2 million. The preview also set a $1.6 million Q4 floor, but the provided call facts do not state Q4 adjusted EBITDA, so that quarterly comparison cannot be confirmed here.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EBITDA increased to $5.8 million from $5.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 adjusted EBITDA should land ~$6.0–6.2M vs. $5.3M in FY2025 (+13–17%).”

surprises.description: Gross margin improved more than the preview anticipated: fiscal 2026 reached 51.9%, up 260 basis points, and Q4 reached a record 53%, versus an expected roughly 100-basis-point full-year improvement and about 52% for Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2026 gross margin improved 260 basis points to 51.9%, with Q4 hitting a record 53%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The story this table tells: ... gross margin +450bp in FY25, another ~100bp in FY26”; Q4 gross margin estimate: “~52%.”

surprises.description: Transaction revenue showed better stabilization than the preview’s roughly 8% Q4 decline estimate: its year-over-year decline narrowed to 6.7% from 11% in Q3. Management also expects only a low-single-digit decline in FY2027, rather than the further steep decline the preview warned could make revenue negative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Transaction revenue's year-over-year decline improved to 6.7% in Q4 from 11% in Q3, and management expects only a low-single-digit decline in fiscal 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q4 transaction revenue estimate was “~$6.7M” versus “$7.3M” a year earlier; the preview said “another double-digit decline means FY2027 revenue goes negative outright.”

surprises.description: AI/MCP sales showed commercial traction beyond the preview’s pipeline question: Q4 AI-related bookings were about $800,000, MCP deals were almost entirely upsells, and adding MCP/agentic AI access roughly doubled contract value on average. The preview had asked for closed AI business rather than another pipeline figure but gave no booking target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI-related bookings reached about $800,000 in Q4, representing 125% sequential growth”; “Adding MCP/agentic AI access roughly doubled contract value on average, MCP deals were almost entirely upsells to existing customers, and about three-quarters of MCP usage now comes from paid plans.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 is the first full quarter — look for closed ARR, not pipeline. Repeating the pipeline number without conversion is a tell”; the Q3 pipeline was “exceeding $1 million in opportunities.”

surprises.description: B2C ARR declined by about $380,000 over the year to roughly $6.3 million, rather than remaining flat around $6.4 million as the preview described it in the recent quarters. The hoped-for B2C stabilization or sequential turn was not evident in the reported full-year figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “About $6.3 million in B2C ARR, which declined by roughly $380,000 for the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “B2C ARR has been flat at $6.4M for two quarters after declines — first sequential increase would confirm the turn.”

surprises.description: Platform deployment additions rebounded to 29 in Q4, compared with 15 in Q3, and average sales price rose 4.7%. That was better than the recent collapse in deployment additions that the preview had highlighted, though it had not set a Q4 deployment estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added 105 net new platform deployments during the year (29 in Q4) to reach 1,276 total, while average sales price increased 4.7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said net new deployments “collapsed from 47 in Q2 to 15 in Q3” and noted that Q4 was “the first quarter those fixes could show up.”

surprises.description: Management gave a positive FY2027 profitability and cash-flow outlook, saying both should grow, although it offered no top-line guidance. The directional commitment was more than the preview’s base case of silence, but it was not a numeric target or full growth algorithm.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided to further EBITDA and cash flow growth in fiscal 2027 despite offering no top-line guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Silence is the base case; anything concrete is a genuine catalyst either way”; the preview looked for “even a directional ‘return to double-digit ARR growth’ or an EBITDA target.”

surprises.description: Fiscal 2026 revenue of $48.3 million was slightly above the preview’s $48.17 million full-year estimate, though the difference was very small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total fiscal 2026 revenue declined slightly to $48.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The only published full-year figure is FY2026 revenue $48.17M / EPS $0.13.”

surprises.description: Cash ended the year at nearly $13 million, above the preview’s $12.1 million figure, and management said it was evaluating buybacks and other capital options. However, it did not announce a buyback authorization, so the concrete action flagged as a potential catalyst was not delivered.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company holds nearly $13 million in cash with no debt after funding four quarters of Scite earn-out payments”; management said the stock was trading “far below fair value” and it was “evaluating buybacks and other capital options.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called a “buyback authorization” the “highest-ROI capital allocation available” and listed it as a catalyst; it also cited cash of “$12.1M, no debt.”

in_line: Total ARR was $22.5 million, up 7.8% year over year, in line with the preview’s roughly $22.4 million exit ARR estimate and expected 7–8% growth.
B2B ARR was about $16.2 million, up 14.1% year over year, matching the preview’s threshold of at least $16.2 million and expectation that B2B growth would hold around 14%.
No overall FY2027 top-line guidance was provided, consistent with the preview’s base case of no guidance.

surprises.description: Lovesac recognized about $20 million of tariff refunds through cost of merchandise sold, far more than the roughly $3.4 million already received and embedded in the preview’s gross-margin guide. That lifted reported gross margin to 68.4% and contributed $0.86 per share to EPS of $0.51, versus the preview’s expected EPS loss of roughly $0.36–$0.39.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company received approximately $21 million in IEPA tariff refunds, with $20 million recognized through cost of merchandise sold, contributing an $0.86 per diluted share benefit to reported Q2 EPS of $0.51. Gross margin rose to 68.4%, while gross margin excluding the refunds was approximately 56%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “~$3.4–3.6M of IEEPA refunds are embedded in the guide” and cited expected Q2 EPS of “$(0.36) to $(0.39).”

surprises.description: Lovesac cut its FY27 outlook rather than reiterating the prior $700–740 million sales and $35–46 million Adjusted EBITDA ranges. The new sales range is $690–710 million and Adjusted EBITDA is $31.5–35.5 million, with net income now guided to $0.5–18.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company cut its full-year outlook to net sales of $690–710 million, net income of $0.5–18.5 million, and Adjusted EBITDA of $31.5–35.5 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called reiteration of “$700–740M / $35–46M EBITDA” the base case and warned that “any Q2 wobble compresses an already back-loaded year.”

surprises.description: Omnichannel comparable sales fell 1.9%, a weaker result than the preview’s roughly flat whisper and worse than the prior quarter’s 1.0% decline. Headline revenue was near consensus, but comps showed weaker underlying demand than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: Omnichannel comparable sales declined 1.9%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the “whisper is roughly flat” for omnichannel comparable sales and noted Q1 FY27 comps of “−1.0%.”

surprises.description: Major product launches are now expected to contribute meaningfully in Q4 rather than Q3, and Q3 is guided to a $9–12 million net loss. That pushes more of the planned second-half recovery into the final quarter than the preview’s late-summer launch timing suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q3 guidance calls for net sales of $140–150 million and a net loss of $9–12 million, reflecting product launches shifted toward Q4; four major launches are planned for the second half, with meaningful revenue impact concentrated in Q4.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said domestic Sactionals manufacturing was “Guided to start ‘late summer’ — inside this quarter” and described product and marketing efforts as starting to culminate toward year-end. It also said a quantified Q3 range would be constructive.

surprises.description: The under-$6,000 Sactionals segment remained pressured and had not returned to growth despite promotional and pricing changes. The preview specifically looked for opening-price campaigns to stabilize the low end, so that improvement did not materialize.
surprises.fact_evidence: Sactionals configurations over $6,000 grew double digits, while the under-$6,000 segment remained pressured and had not yet returned to growth despite promotional and pricing adjustments.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case required opening-price campaigns to “stabilize the low end” and flagged whether high-end transaction strength would broaden.

surprises.description: Lovesac repurchased more stock in Q2 than the preview’s concern about a passive quarter implied: first-half repurchases reached $7.2 million, up from the $2.4 million deployed in Q1 alone. The remaining authorization fell to $46.9 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company repurchased approximately $7.2 million of stock in the first half, with $46.9 million remaining under authorization.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “only $2.4M deployed in Q1” and said a passive quarter could read as a lack of conviction; it cited $51.7 million remaining after Q1.

in_line: Net sales of $161.2 million were close to the preview’s $161.55 million consensus and within the company’s $157–166 million Q2 guidance range.

Gross margin excluding the tariff refunds was about 56%, down 40 basis points year over year, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of underlying margin around 55.3–56.3% and flat to slightly down versus the prior year.
Sactionals configurations over $6,000 grew double digits, consistent with the preview’s expectation that strength in higher-priced configurations would continue.

surprises.description: Comparable sales rose 2.7% (2.8% on a go-forward basis), above the preview’s implied +1.5% to +2% range. The preview’s bull case began at +2.5%, so the result was stronger than the central expectation and reached the bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 comparable sales growth of 2.7% (2.8% on a go-forward basis).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comparable sales (O+L+M): ~+1.5% to +2% implied by revenue consensus”; bull case: “+2.5% to +3.5%.”

surprises.description: Net sales of $4.9 billion topped the preview’s $4.77–$4.82 billion consensus range and even exceeded its base-case range. This was a modest but clear upside to the expected sales result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net sales up 1.1% to $4.9 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $4.82B” from Zacks and “$4.77–4.78B” from LSEG/Investing.com; base case “$4.80–4.85B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.63, well above the preview’s $0.35–$0.37 consensus, but the reported result included a roughly $0.23 tariff-refund benefit. Excluding that benefit, EPS was about $0.40, still above the company’s guidance high end and up 14% year over year, but within the preview’s $0.39–$0.43 buy-side bogey.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $0.63 versus $0.35 a year ago, but included a roughly $0.23 net tariff refund benefit; excluding this, adjusted EPS rose 14% year-over-year and beat the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street $0.35–$0.37 EPS”; the buy-side bogey was “~$0.39–$0.43.”

surprises.description: Reported gross margin reached 41.5%, well above the preview’s roughly 39.6%–39.7% bogey. But the underlying expansion was only about 10 basis points, so the large headline margin beat did not represent a similarly large improvement in underlying margin quality.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin reached 41.5% of net sales versus 39.7% last year, but underlying gross margin (excluding tariff and fuel impacts) expanded only about 10 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bogey is ~39.6–39.7%”; the preview also said to “strip [a tariff-refund] benefit out before crediting the beat” and highlighted “GM ≥39.6%, ex-tariff-refund.”

surprises.description: Macy’s raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $2.15–$2.35 and comparable-sales guidance to +1.0% to +1.5%. The EPS range’s high end was above the preview’s expected $2.15–$2.30 area, but second-half sales assumptions were unchanged, falling short of the preview’s call for an explicit second-half improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was raised to adjusted diluted EPS of $2.15 to $2.35 and comparable sales of up 1.0% to 1.5%, with second-half sales assumptions unchanged from prior outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected FY EPS of “$2.15–$2.30” in its base case and said “anything that doesn’t also raise 2H will read as a downgrade of the back half.”

surprises.description: The Q3 comp outlook of down 0.5% to up 0.5% was weaker than the preview’s warning threshold: it said a guide below roughly +1% would signal caution. The stated 3.2% prior-year comp makes the comparison tougher, but the guidance still landed below the preview’s expected level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance implies a comp sales range of down 0.5% to up 0.5% … against a tougher prior-year comp of 3.2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has guided conservatively and beaten for five straight quarters, so a Q3 comp guide below ~+1% signals real caution.”

surprises.description: The Macy’s nameplate grew comps only 1.1%, below the preview’s aspiration for the nameplate to turn “solidly positive” and well below the companywide comp result. Reimagined stores still outperformed the nameplate at 1.9%, but that spread did not widen from the Q1 spread implied by the preview’s figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Macy’s nameplate grew comps 1.1%, with reimagined stores outperforming at 1.9%; these ~200 reimagined locations now represent nearly 60% of go-forward stores and 75% of go-forward store sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “Macy’s nameplate comp turning solidly positive” and asked whether the Reimagine-200 spread was “widening.” Its Q1 figures were Macy’s +1.6% and Reimagine 200 +2.4%.

surprises.description: Bloomingdale’s reached its highest second-quarter sales volume in its 154-year history, a milestone the preview did not anticipate. Its 11.3% comp growth itself was consistent with the preview’s expectation that the business would remain double-digit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bloomingdale’s posted 11.3% comparable sales growth … achieving the highest second-quarter sales volume in its 154-year history.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Bloomingdale’s was “going for an eighth straight positive quarter” and expected it to “stay[] double-digit.”

surprises.description: The company received the full $116 million in tariff refunds, including $18 million after quarter-end, whereas the preview framed refunds as a possible one-time item and otherwise cited tariff and fuel costs as a drag. Macy’s said it would put most of the refund back into the business rather than send it to the bottom line.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received all $116 million of expected tariff refunds ($98 million in Q2 plus $18 million after quarter-end) and is flowing only ~$20 million (~$0.05 EPS) to the bottom line while reinvesting the rest.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Tariff + fuel drag: $0.10–$0.20 FY, $0.03–$0.04 in Q2” and listed “IEEPA tariff refunds” among the one-timers to watch.

surprises.description: First-half free cash flow was a $262 million inflow, and shareholder returns included $100 million of buybacks in the quarter—twice the $50 million buyback amount cited for Q1. This was stronger cash generation and a faster buyback pace than the preview’s stated Q1 baseline, although the preview had flagged capital returns as an item to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was an inflow of $262 million in the first half versus an outflow of $88 million last year, and the company returned $201 million to shareholders (dividends plus $100 million buybacks) with ~$1 billion remaining on its buyback authorization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “buyback pace” and cited “$50M in Q1, $1.07B remaining.”

in_line: Bloomingdale’s 11.3% comparable-sales growth was in line with the preview’s expectation that it would remain double-digit.

surprises.description: Vince reported adjusted EBITDA of $18 million, far above the preview’s roughly $7 million guidance-implied figure, and adjusted diluted EPS of $1.02 versus the preview’s $0.11–$0.27 consensus range. A $10.4 million tariff refund was included in the results, while the preview said any quantified refund would be upside not in the estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $18 million” and adjusted diluted EPS was “$1.02,” including “a $10.4 million tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave guidance-implied adjusted EBITDA of “~$7.0M” and said, “A quantified refund would be pure upside not in any model”; adjusted EPS consensus was “$0.11 to $0.27.”

surprises.description: Even with reported gross margin at 60.9%, the margin excluding the tariff refund fell 290 basis points, a much weaker underlying result than the preview’s expected tariff-related pressure suggested. The preview identified gross margin as a key debate and described roughly 50 basis points of adjusted operating-margin compression as expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin rose to 60.9% from 50.4%, but excluding the tariff refund benefit, gross margin actually declined 290 basis points due to higher product and freight input costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said guidance implied “~50 bps of adjusted margin compression, driven by tariffs,” and described that as “expected, not a miss.”

surprises.description: Vince raised FY2026 guidance to 8%–10% net sales growth and a 9%–9.5% adjusted EBITDA margin, above the preview’s stale pre-raise guide of 7%–8% sales growth and 5.5%–6.0% adjusted EBITDA margin. The preview treated the forward guide as the main catalyst and its base case contemplated a reiterated guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year fiscal 2026 Vince guidance to net sales growth of 8% to 10%, with adjusted EBITDA margin of approximately 9% to 9.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 guidance of “+7–8%” sales growth and “5.5–6.0%” adjusted EBITDA margin, and said its base case was “FY guide reiterated ex-OVO.”

surprises.description: The OVO operating business came with a disclosed scale and growth target that the preview said had not yet been quantified: nearly $50 million of calendar 2025 net sales and a target of more than $100 million by FY2030, with low double-digit adjusted EBITDA margins. This provides concrete economics where the preview had only noted that the run-rate was undisclosed.
surprises.fact_evidence: OVO was “generating nearly $50 million in calendar 2025 net sales” and has a target of “$100 million-plus revenue by fiscal 2030 with low double-digit adjusted EBITDA margins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called OVO deal economics “still undisclosed,” said its revenue and EBITDA run-rate were unknown, and noted that “any hard number here” would provide new information.

surprises.description: Wholesale sales grew 10.4% year over year, accelerating from the 5.9% growth cited for Q1 in the preview, rather than merely relying on continued DTC strength. That is evidence of the wholesale reacceleration the preview identified as an important condition for the bullish case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wholesale [was] up 10.4% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case needed “wholesale reacceleration” and identified fall/holiday wholesale order-book commentary as a leading indicator; it cited Q1 wholesale growth of “+5.9%.”

surprises.description: The balance sheet improved despite the preview’s concern that Vince would need to fund OVO and holiday inventory from a thin cash position: long-term debt was reduced to $12.3 million, and inventory was below its year-ago level. The preview had highlighted borrowings of $29.1 million and warned about funding strain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Long-term debt [was] reduced to $12.3 million and net inventory [was] down to $73.4 million from $76.7 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 borrowings of “$29.1M” and warned Vince had to fund OVO and holiday inventory “off a thin cash position.”

in_line: Q2 sales were close to the pre-announced high-end expectation: $81.8 million and 11.7% growth versus the preview’s roughly $82 million high-end estimate and 12% growth.
OVO being neutral to earnings in FY2026 and accretive in FY2027 matched the timing already described in the preview.

surprises.description: CULP reported $54 million of sales, above the preview’s $53.2 million consensus and $52.8 million base estimate. That is a modest beat, especially given the quarter had one fewer selling week than the year-ago quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net sales rose to $54 million from $50.7 million year-over-year despite one fewer selling week.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed revenue consensus of “$53.20M” and a base estimate of “$52.8M.”

surprises.description: Bedding sales reached $31.8 million, above the preview’s $30.8 million estimate. More notably, bedding gross margin rose to 13.6%, above the preview’s expectation that it would recover toward low double digits; management said the margin gain did not include allocated tariff recoveries.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bedding segment sales grew 13.2% to $31.8 million with gross margin expanding to 13.6% from 10.5%, a gain management said was not aided by any allocated tariff recoveries.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated bedding sales of “$30.8M” and said bedding margin needed to “move toward low double digits.”

surprises.description: Gross profit excluding tariff recoveries was $8.4 million, or 15.6% of sales, versus the preview’s estimate of $7.4 million and 14.0%. The underlying margin and profit were therefore stronger than expected even without counting the one-time recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding tariff recoveries, gross profit was $8.4 million (15.6% of sales), up roughly 17% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated gross profit of “$7.4M (14.0%).”

surprises.description: Net debt was $3.1 million, below the preview’s roughly $5 million estimate, and management said it is targeting net cash by fiscal year-end. The company also used the full tariff recovery to pay off all higher-rate U.S. debt, a stronger balance-sheet outcome than the preview’s estimate implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reduced net debt approximately 70% to $3.1 million” and “used the full tariff recovery to pay off all higher-rate U.S. debt”; management is “targeting a net cash position by fiscal year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Net debt @ 8/2/26 ~$5M (from $10.8M).”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a CFO transition not flagged in the preview: Ken Bolling will retire effective September 14, with COO Mary Beth Hunsberger succeeding him and Bolling consulting through December. The disclosure is new, but the provided facts do not establish whether the change is good or bad for shareholders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CFO Ken Bolling will retire and be succeeded by COO Mary Beth Hunsberger effective September 14, 2026, with Bolling staying on in a consulting capacity through December.”

surprises.description: Management also highlighted substantial assets not discussed in the preview: approximately $95 million of U.S. federal NOL carryforwards associated with about $20 million of future tax benefits, and a Stokesdale hub estimated to be worth $40 million versus a $12 million book value. These are potentially valuable resources, though no monetization plan was reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company holds approximately $95 million in U.S. federal net operating loss carryforwards (~$20 million in future tax benefits) and owns its Stokesdale, NC hub with an estimated $40 million market value versus $12 million book value.”

in_line: The approximately $7 million tariff recovery came through in the quarter, as the preview expected; the reported $0.47 EPS was close to the preview’s $0.44 estimate and was understood to be largely refund-driven.
Adjusted EBITDA excluding tariff recoveries was positive $566,000, broadly in line with the preview’s estimate of about $0.4 million and its expectation of break-even to positive adjusted EBITDA.
Upholstery sales were essentially flat at $22.2 million, close to the preview’s $22.0 million estimate and its expectation of modest or flat performance.
The Q2 outlook called for sequential sales consistency and modest year-over-year growth, consistent with the preview’s expectation of constructive Q2 language and modest improvement.

surprises.description: The preview called the first combined-company FY27 guide the decisive event and cited $604.6 million of revenue consensus. Instead, the reported guidance is for the six-month July–December transition period; the supplied call facts give no FY27 revenue or earnings guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is transitioning to a December fiscal year-end and guided the 6-month transition period (July-December 2026) to net sales of $287-291 million, adjusted EBITDA of $29-32 million, and adjusted EPS of $0.66-0.76.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “First guide for the combined company. FY27 guidance, not the Q4 print, is the real event”; FY27 revenue consensus was “$604.60M.”

surprises.description: Legacy Q4 sales were above the preview’s guidance-implied standalone estimate: $96.6 million versus about $93 million. The reported 21.5% growth also exceeded the preview’s implied 17.0% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 legacy net sales grew 21.5% to $96.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Revenue | Q4 standalone (guidance-implied) | $93.0M (+17.0% YoY).”

surprises.description: Legacy Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin substantially exceeded the preview’s guidance-implied 15.9%: the reported margin was 19.3%, a 3.4 percentage-point gap.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin expanding 730 basis points to 19.3%, driven by premium X-Series mix and lower discounts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated a “15.9% margin” for Q4 standalone.

surprises.description: Full-year company sales beat the published consensus estimate, reaching $348.9 million against $338.25 million. The preview cautioned that reported results would include the acquisition and would not be comparable to standalone guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total company fiscal 2026 net sales reached $348.9 million (up 22.8% YoY).”

surprises.description: Legacy full-year adjusted EBITDA exceeded the preview’s cited $40 million standalone FY26 guidance, reaching $43.8 million. Legacy sales also finished slightly above the cited $312 million sales guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Legacy fiscal 2026 net sales were $315.6 million … and legacy adjusted EBITDA rose 79.6% to $43.8 million, exceeding prior increased guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the May 7 standalone FY26 guide was “$312M sales / $40M adj. EBITDA.”

surprises.description: The acquired segment brought in more six-week revenue than the preview’s roughly $31 million stub estimate, but its $1.8 million of adjusted EBITDA was below the preview’s estimated $3–5 million contribution. Management cautioned that the short period does not show the segment’s true earnings power.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The newly acquired Recreation and Sport Fishing segment added $33.3 million in revenue but only $1.8 million of adjusted EBITDA during its 6-week window, which management said does not reflect its true earnings power.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “+ MPX stub (47 days)” of “~$31M” revenue and “~$3–5M” adjusted EBITDA.

surprises.description: Both businesses’ dealer inventories were down substantially rather than showing a channel refill: legacy inventory fell about 30%, and Chaparral/Robalo inventory fell about 20%. Legacy turns were also better than pre-pandemic levels, easing the inventory and margin concern flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Legacy field inventory ended the year down approximately 30% YoY with turns better than pre-pandemic levels, while Chaparral and Robalo inventory was down about 20%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Dealer inventory and retail registrations” as a key metric, asked whether there would be “any shift toward channel refill,” and identified an “inventory step-up hit to gross margin” as a bear risk.

surprises.description: Retail results were better than the weak industry and recent unit-volume backdrop implied: MasterCraft retail rose low-single digits and Robalo grew high-single digits while the broader powerboat industry declined mid- to high-single digits.
surprises.fact_evidence: “MasterCraft retail rose low-single digits and Robalo grew high-single digits, both outperforming a broader powerboat industry that declined mid- to high-single digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “MCFT's own unit volumes are falling” and described the marine retail market as a risk to the outlook.

surprises.description: The post-acquisition balance sheet was stronger than the preview’s downside scenario allowed for: the company ended the year with cash, no debt, and full revolver availability, while also generating $22.3 million of free cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the year with $43.9 million in cash, no debt, full availability on its $75 million revolver, and generated $22.3 million in free cash flow after $8.1 million capex.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the post-deal net cash/debt position a key disclosure and included “modest net debt” in its bear case; it also said the combined company’s cash generation profile was “unproven.”

surprises.description: Management put a concrete decline on near-term demand and responded by pausing Chaparral Surf Series production and moderating Chaparral/Robalo volumes. The preview warned of weak marine demand, but did not specify a 5%–10% decline or these production actions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects retail demand to decline approximately 5% to 10% over the next six months and has paused Chaparral Surf Series production while moderating Chaparral/Robalo volumes to align with retail.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “MCFT's own unit volumes are falling” and identified a challenged marine retail environment as a risk, but gave no quantified next-six-month decline or production pause.

surprises.description: The reported $10.1 million non-cash Crest brand impairment was a specific additional charge not identified in the preview’s discussion of purchase accounting. It contributed to the Q4 GAAP loss, alongside acquisition-related purchase accounting and transaction costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 GAAP net loss of $7.0 million (-$0.35 per share) versus $5.5 million income ($0.33) a year prior, driven by a $10.1 million non-cash Crest brand impairment plus acquisition-related purchase accounting and transaction costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview anticipated poor GAAP results from purchase accounting, but discussed inventory step-up, amortization of acquired intangibles, and goodwill—not a Crest brand impairment.

surprises.description: The preview expected a first quantified synergy target and timeline, but the supplied call facts report no quantified target or timeline. That leaves the deal’s synergy opportunity unquantified in the reported information.
surprises.fact_evidence: The supplied call facts contain no quantified synergy target or timeline.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “First hard number lands here” and that “continued qualitative language is a disappointment.”

in_line: The preview expected a six-week acquisition contribution in Q4; the reported acquired-business contribution covered six weeks.
The preview warned that GAAP results could look poor because of purchase accounting. The reported Q4 GAAP loss, in contrast to adjusted operating results, was consistent with that warning.

surprises.description: SHOE reported Q2 net sales of $284.3 million, about 5% below the $299.19 million consensus in the preview and below the company’s own expectations. This was a materially weaker sales result than the preview’s roughly $298–300 million base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 fiscal 2026 net sales declined 7.2% to $284.3 million”; sales “falling short of the company's own expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Q2 FY26 Consensus | $299.19M”; base scenario “~$298–300M.”

surprises.description: Comparable sales fell 7.1%, far worse than the preview’s estimated decline of 2% to 3%. The comp result missed even the preview’s bear-case estimate of roughly down 6%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable store sales down 7.1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comparable sales | ~−2% to −3% (my est.)”; bear scenario: “Comp ~−6%.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin contracted 690 basis points, worse than the preview’s already cautious expectation of a decline exceeding 500 basis points and worse than its bear-case estimate of about 650 basis points. Management attributed part of the merchandise-margin decline to the expired prior-year pricing benefit and the rest to promotions and inventory liquidation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit margin fell 690 basis points to 31.9%”; roughly 390 basis points of the merchandise-margin decline came from “lapping a temporary prior-year pre-tariff pricing benefit” and about 240 basis points from “promotions and inventory liquidation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 compression was forecast as “potentially exceeding 500 basis points”; bear scenario: “~32.3% (−650 bps).”

surprises.description: The company cut full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $0.75–$0.90 instead of reaffirming the prior $1.40–$1.60 range. The new range is roughly 40%–53% below the midpoint of the old range, a much steeper reset than the preview’s bear-case cut to about $1.10–$1.30.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lowered full-year fiscal 2026 guidance to … adjusted EPS of $0.75-0.90.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year FY2026 guidance (reaffirmed at Q1…) … Adjusted EPS $1.40–$1.60”; bear scenario anticipated a cut “to ~$1.10–$1.30.”

surprises.description: Full-year net sales guidance was also reduced to $1.1–$1.111 billion, below the prior $1.125–$1.147 billion range. The preview’s central expectation was that the existing full-year guidance would be reaffirmed, not cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lowered full-year fiscal 2026 guidance to net sales of $1.1-1.111 billion (down 2-3%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Prior guidance: “Net sales $1.125–$1.147B (−1% to +1%)”; the preview described reaffirmation of the FY26 guide as the central case.

surprises.description: The new full-year gross-margin outlook of 32.5%–32.7% is well below the preview’s approximately 34% expectation. The company now expects 390–410 basis points of compression rather than the previously guided 260 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year guidance includes “gross margin of 32.5-32.7% (390-410 bps of compression).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Prior guidance: “Gross margin ~34% (−260 bps vs. FY25).”
