surprises.description: The preview looked for the back-to-school reset to create a stronger second-half recovery, with its base case repeating management’s “down first half, up second half” framing. Instead, management expects roughly flat Q3 comps, says growth is deferred to Q4, and guides second-half comps to only down 1% to up 1% while assuming no improvement in promotions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects roughly flat comps in Q3 with growth deferred to Q4”; it “does not assume any improvement in the promotional environment for the second half” and guides second-half comps to “down 1% to up 1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said BTS and fall were “the primary earnings opportunity”; its base case expected management to repeat “down first half, up second half.”

surprises.description: Within the weak quarter, online comparable sales rose 18.8% while comparable store sales fell 9.5%. The preview did not anticipate this sharp divergence between the e-commerce and store channels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable online sales up 18.8% in Q2, even as comparable store sales fell 9.5%.”

surprises.description: Management identified store traffic—not conversion—as the main problem: conversion had reached multi-year highs, and the response was to intensify advertising rather than rely on deeper discounting. That differs from the preview’s emphasis on promotional liquidation as a key part of the quarter’s margin and inventory story.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Store traffic was identified as the core problem while conversion improved to multi-year highs in both banners, prompting a shift toward intensified advertising rather than deeper discounting.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “first-half promotional liquidation runs to hit the inventory target” and highlighted promotional intensity as a key driver to watch.

surprises.description: The inventory-reduction objective was narrowed to the low end of the preview’s $50–$65 million year-end target, with management citing weaker sales. The quarter-end inventory itself was down year over year, but the intended reduction is now less ambitious than the top of the prior range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory ended down 5.0% to $426.6 million,” with a target of “approximately $50 million reduction by year-end” and the company “now aiming for the low end of that range due to weaker sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Inventory down $50–65M by year-end.”

in_line: The company remained debt-free, consistent with the preview’s description of a zero-debt balance sheet; cash and marketable securities were $131.6 million versus the preview’s $129.3 million reference point.
The stated expectation that margin could recover toward roughly 35% in fiscal 2027 was consistent with the preview’s reference to a 2027 rebound “back into the 30 fives.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was about $671,000, well above the preview’s roughly $300,000 base-case model, even as the company expanded its commercial organization. This was a substantially stronger quarter than the modeled baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA surged to approximately $671,000” and marked “the fifth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled Adj. EBITDA at “~$0.3M” in the base case.

surprises.description: Oncology services margin reached 51%, above the preview’s approximately 48% model and its 48% threshold for confirming the in-housing benefit. Gross margin also expanded to 50%, while oncology revenue costs fell despite higher revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Oncology services margin improving to 51% from 43%”; gross margin “expanded to 50% from 43%.” Cost of oncology revenue “fell roughly $500,000 to $7.5 million despite higher revenue,” primarily from bringing radiolabeling in-house.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the oncology services margin model was “~48%” and that “holding ≥48% would confirm the in-housing benefit is structural rather than a Q4 one-off.”

surprises.description: Data licensing brought in $893,000—more than the entire prior fiscal year’s licensing revenue—an unexpectedly strong contribution for the quarter, though management cautioned that it will remain lumpy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Data licensing revenue reached $893,000 in the quarter—more than all of fiscal 2026 combined,” but management cautioned “it will remain lumpy.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY26 had shifted to “smaller licensing agreements” and described licensing as “violently lumpy”; it noted that any large one-time deal could inflate revenue.

surprises.description: Revenue of $15.2 million narrowly exceeded the $15.05 million consensus estimate. The beat was small, though revenue also rose about 10% sequentially from Q4, slightly more than the preview’s stated 9% sequential ask.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q1 revenue was “$15.2 million,” up from $14 million a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed consensus revenue of “$15.05M” and said consensus asked for “+9% sequential.”

surprises.description: Sales and marketing expense was $3 million, modestly above the preview’s $2.8 million Q4-run-rate assumption. Management attributed the increase to a deliberate expansion of the commercial organization, indicating somewhat higher spending than that model implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sales and marketing expense rose to $3 million from $1.8 million a year earlier due to a deliberate expansion of the commercial organization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said its estimates were “built off reported FY26 quarterly actuals and Q4 opex run-rate,” including “$2.8M S&M,” and described FY27 priorities as including “financial discipline” and “selective investment.”

in_line: The fifth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA matched the preview’s expectation that the streak would continue.

Cash ended at approximately $4.4 million, within the preview’s $4.0–$4.5 million base-case range. The preview also expected continued Corellia funding efforts; the call described pursuit of outside funding or a licensing partnership, without reporting a completed deal.

The reported GAAP net loss, which included a large noncash expense, is broadly consistent with the preview’s base-case EPS estimate of approximately $(0.03); the preview had cautioned that the consensus EPS basis was ambiguous.

surprises.description: Revenue of $87.1 million exceeded the preview’s $80 million base estimate, although it also came in well above the stale $62.6 million consensus cited there. The result was stronger than the preview’s already-strong quarter forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached an all-time high of $87.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Q2 2026 base est.” revenue: “$80M”; consensus revenue: “$62.6M.”

surprises.description: Net income and EPS fell short of the preview’s own base estimates, despite beating the cited consensus EPS. Net income was $34.8 million and EPS $0.75 versus the preview’s estimates of about $43.5 million and $0.95.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income was $34.8 million (EPS $0.75).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base estimate was “Net income … ~$43.5M” and “EPS (basic) … ~$0.95”; it also cited consensus EPS of “$0.58.”

surprises.description: Tanker revenue realization was stronger than the preview’s rate assumptions: tanker TCE was near $71,500 per day, above the preview’s peer benchmarks around $51,900–$53,000 and its $45,000/day marker for strong MR realization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 daily fleet revenue exceeded $50,000” and “tanker TCE near $71,500/day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited MR peer spot rates of “$51,900/day” and “$53,000/day,” and said “If MR spot prints above ~$45,000/day, IMPP captured the market.”

surprises.description: Operational utilization was far below the preview’s watch threshold: it came in at 73.5%, versus the preview’s concern about utilization slipping below roughly 85%. Six drydockings caused off-hire, with seven more scheduled by year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operational utilization fell to 73.5% due to 6 drydockings,” with “7 more drydockings scheduled by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch for utilization slipping below ~85%” and its bull case assumed “utilization >90%.”

surprises.description: Drydocking costs were substantially above the preview’s estimate, reaching $7.5 million versus its $1.5 million forecast. This was a much larger cost drag than the model allowed for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Drydocking costs hit $7.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Drydocking … $1.5M.”

surprises.description: Voyage costs rose much more than the preview’s model allowed for: the preview budgeted $15 million of voyage expenses, while the call reported a $14.4 million increase, attributed to more spot days and higher Brent prices.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Voyage costs rose $14.4 million (58% more spot days plus Brent averaging $97 vs $67).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Voyage expenses … $15.0M” and identified voyage-expense inflation as a possible bear-case factor.

surprises.description: Suezmax market rates ended Q2 well above the preview’s cited peer benchmark, exceeding $145,000 per day versus the preview’s $121,800/day Teekay reference, and at times surpassed $200,000 per day.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Suezmax daily rates surged to over $145,000 by end of Q2 2026” and “at times exceeded $200,000/day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$121,800/day (Teekay, 60% of days through mid-May)” as the Q2 Suezmax benchmark.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a profitable August sale of the Suez Enchanted that the preview had not anticipated. The sale generated a profit exceeding $32 million, though it occurred after Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company sold the 2007-built tanker Suez Enchanted in August for a profit exceeding $32 million.”

surprises.description: Cash and time deposits were higher than the preview’s cited liquidity level, rising to $245.2 million at quarter-end and roughly $260 million afterward, while the company remained debt-free.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and time deposits rose to $245.2 million as of June 30 and have since increased to roughly $260 million,” with the company “fully debt-free.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$212.6M liquidity and zero debt” and said “Fully self-funded is the base case.”

surprises.description: Some of the company’s dry bulk vessels remained stranded in the Strait of Hormuz since late May, a company-specific disruption not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of the dry bulk fleet.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Some dry bulk vessels remain stranded in the Strait of Hormuz since late May.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the dry bulk market as “~flat” and said IMPP’s “drybulk half … was flat.”

in_line: The company remained debt-free, consistent with the preview’s zero-debt and self-funded-capex base case.
The stated target of a 25-vessel fleet was consistent with the preview’s reference to a 25-ship target.

surprises.description: FEIM reported $23.5 million of Q1 revenue, far above the preview’s $17.85 million consensus and above the preview’s $19.5–21.0 million bull-case range. The preview said record quarters were expected in later quarters, making an all-time record in Q1 an additional upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue hit an all-time record of $23.5 million, up 70% year-over-year and 52% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $17.85M”; “The record-revenue language is a fiscal-year statement, not a Q1 commitment”; bull scenario: “Revenue $19.5–21.0M.”

surprises.description: Reported gross margin reached 45.8%, exceeding the preview’s 40% recovery benchmark and its 42% bull-case threshold. That is a stronger recovery than the preview’s base case of 37–41%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved 9 percentage points to 45.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for ≥40% reported”; base scenario: “reported GM 37–41%”; bull scenario: “reported GM ≥42%.”

surprises.description: Quarterly EPS was $0.41 versus the preview’s $0.15 consensus, a substantial beat even though the preview cautioned that EPS was a less reliable measure than revenue, margin, and backlog. Operating income and margin also showed strong profitability, rather than an earnings result dependent only on a possible tax benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income surged to approximately $4.2 million ($0.41 per share)”; “operating margin reached 22% (operating income of $5.2 million versus $364,000 a year ago).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) | $0.15”; the preview said to “Anchor on revenue, gross margin, and backlog instead” because EPS could include part of the anticipated tax benefit.

surprises.description: Management reaffirmed the FY2029 targets as expected, but went further by suggesting the $150 million revenue goal could be reached sooner and be substantially larger. That upside ambition was not part of the preview’s stated expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reaffirmed its fiscal 2029 targets of $150 million+ in annual revenue, 50% minimum gross margin, and 30% minimum operating margin, while suggesting the revenue target could be reached sooner and be substantially larger.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY29 targets ($150M / 50% GM / 30% OM) — reaffirmed, refined, or quietly softened.”

surprises.description: Management described unusually strong near-term conversion visibility: about 65% of funded backlog is expected to become revenue within 12 months, with unfunded backlog visibility multiple times the funded amount. The preview focused on whether awards would convert and warned about timing slippage, but did not anticipate this degree of stated conversion visibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately 65% of the $129 million funded backlog is expected to convert to revenue within the next 12 months, with additional unfunded backlog visibility described as multiple times the funded portion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case required awards to have “entered production, not just booking,” while the bear case could involve “slower” backlog conversion and programs spanning “one to three years.”

surprises.description: For a secured communications production contract already involving more than 1,000 systems, customers are asking for monthly production to rise by over 50% and have promised follow-on orders. This is an additional demand and production-acceleration signal beyond the preview’s general concern about getting new programs into production.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A secured communications production contract for over 1,000 systems is seeing customer requests to increase monthly production by more than 50% alongside promised follow-on orders.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case required a “high-rate production” transition to show up in units shipped; it did not mention these production increase requests or follow-on orders.

in_line: Funded backlog was $129 million, within the preview’s $120–130 million watch range; the preview also identified $120 million as a key catalyst level.
Management reaffirmed the FY2029 targets of at least $150 million revenue, 50% gross margin, and 30% operating margin, as the preview expected.
The preview expected operating leverage as revenue grew; SG&A was 18% of revenue versus 26% a year earlier, although absolute spending increased by $0.5 million.

surprises.description: TEN reported Q2 EPS of $4.40, far above the $2.48 consensus and also above the preview’s $3.60 base case. The result was close to the preview’s $4.50 bull case, but substantially stronger than the central expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net income jumped to $139.3 million from $26.8 million (EPS of $4.40 vs $0.67).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) $2.48”; the scenario analysis gave “Base ... EPS ~$3.60” and “Bull ... EPS ~ $4.50.”

surprises.description: Profit-sharing contributed $30.5 million in Q2 and $71 million in H1, and management expects a significant further increase in H2. The preview highlighted profit-sharing as a potential earnings driver and sought a Q2 figure, but gave no expectation for this level or for a further H2 increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Profit-sharing arrangements contributed $71 million in H1 2026 versus $10 million a year earlier ... with Q2 alone contributing $30.5 million, and management expects a significant further increase in the second half.”

surprises.description: Management signaled that a dividend increase would be announced after the November strategy meeting, contrary to the preview’s expectation of no change to the capital-return cadence. The $1.60 paid in calendar 2026 also exceeded the preview’s stated $1.50 aggregate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company paid dividends totaling $1.60 per share in calendar 2026 ($0.60 plus $1.00) ... with management signaling a dividend increase to be announced after the November strategy meeting.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “2026 aggregate is $1.50”; “expect no new declaration” and “no change to capital return cadence.”

surprises.description: Management is considering redeeming the $120 million Series E preferred shares, which could add $0.30–$0.40 per share to the bottom line. The preview did not flag this potential earnings benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is considering redeeming the $120 million Series E perpetual preferred at a 9.25% coupon, which could add $0.30-$0.40 per share to the bottom line.”

surprises.description: TEN’s 26-vessel newbuilding program was reported to have appreciated at least 30%, to an estimated $3.8–$3.9 billion value versus roughly $3.1 billion in cost. The preview discussed the program mainly as a funding and capex concern, without anticipating this reported increase in its value.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 26-vessel, roughly $3.1 billion newbuilding program has already appreciated at least 30% (estimated ~$3.8-3.9 billion in value).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch capex schedule vs. cash generation — this is the bear's argument for why free cash doesn't reach shareholders.”

surprises.description: The reported TCE rate of $43,503 per day was below the preview’s $46,000–$52,000 watch range and its $47,500 base-case estimate, though it was above the roughly $39,700 consensus-implied figure. That makes the rate result weaker than the preview’s central operating assumptions but better than the implied consensus bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The fleet's time charter equivalent rate rose 41% to $43,503 per day from $30,754.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to look for “$46,000–$52,000” and modeled a base case of “TCE/day ~$47,500”; it also cited “implied ~$39,700.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $170.4 million, below the preview’s $192 million base case, although above its $168 million bear case. This was a weaker operating-profit result than the preview’s central scenario despite the much higher reported EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased ... 81% to $170.4 million in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 scenario table estimated “Base ... Adj. EBITDA ~$192M” and “Bear ... Adj. EBITDA ~$168M.”

surprises.description: TEN reported net debt to capitalization of about 44.5% and cash of $466 million, ahead of the preview’s monitored 48.4% leverage threshold and its cited Q1 cash balance of $321.4 million. The balance sheet was therefore stronger than the preview’s stated hurdle and starting-point figures suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pro forma 81-vessel fleet has a fair market value of approximately $4.9 billion against $2 billion of debt, with net debt to capitalization around 44.5% and cash of $466 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to look for “Net debt/cap below 48.4%” and cited Q1 “cash $321.4M.”

in_line: Forward committed earnings of approximately $3.5 billion matched the preview’s reference to backlog of more than $3.5 billion.

The sale of two older Suezmaxes for more than $100 million in proceeds, with the gain to be recorded later, matched the preview’s note that the two vessels had been sold for more than $100 million and that the sale was a Q3/Q4 event.

surprises.description: The preview expected Copart to give a non-answer about its reported CCC bid, but the call announced an agreed acquisition of ACV Auctions instead. Copart said the all-cash tender offer would be funded from cash on hand, with no financing conditions, and is expected to close by year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: Copart announced that it had agreed to acquire ACV Auctions. The transaction is an all-cash tender offer funded from cash on hand with no financing conditions, and the company expects to close by the end of the calendar year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Expect the question; expect a non-answer” on CCC Intelligent Solutions; a premium CCC deal “likely runs $5–6B+, exceeding the $4.2B cash pile and putting debt on a historically debt-free company.”

surprises.description: The preview framed M&A discipline as a key issue, with the bull case expecting Adair to be walk-away-ready on CCC. Instead, Adair said the ACV deal does not preclude future acquisitions, signaling continued openness to further deals.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adair stated that the ACV deal does not preclude future acquisitions.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the call would test “how Adair frames M&A discipline” and described the bull case as CCC being “framed as disciplined/walk-away-ready.”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $21.2 million, about 3% above the preview’s $20.6 million estimate; full-year revenue of $71.7 million also slightly exceeded the $71.16 million estimate. The beat was modest, though, rather than the $22 million-plus revenue bull-case outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue set a company record at $21.2 million”; full-year fiscal 2026 revenue was “$71.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 Consensus” revenue: “~$20.6M”; full-year revenue consensus: “$71.16M.”

surprises.description: Q4 gross margin reached 39.4%, above the preview’s roughly 37% expectation and even the 38% bull-case threshold. Management attributed the improvement to higher-margin mix and resolved yield and throughput problems, rather than price increases or one-time items.
surprises.fact_evidence: Gross margin “reached 39.4% in Q4,” driven by “higher-margin product mix and resolved yield/throughput problems rather than price increases or one-time items.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q4 gross margin at “~37%,” said “Anything ≥37% validates the ramp,” and set “GM ≥38%” in its bull case.

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EBITDA was $2.1 million, above the preview’s $1.4–$1.8 million estimate, and its 10% revenue margin reached the top of the preview’s bull-case range. This marked a fourth consecutive profitable quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 adjusted EBITDA was “$2.1 million (10% of revenue),” the “fourth straight profitable quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q4 adjusted EBITDA at “~$1.4–1.8M” and described expansion “toward 8–10%” as the proof point.

surprises.description: LightPath disclosed that it had already raised $50 million in a June primary offering, leaving it with $93.2 million in cash and effectively no debt. The preview flagged the possibility of another raise, but did not anticipate that a substantial offering had already occurred; it strengthens funding capacity while also representing equity issuance.
surprises.fact_evidence: LightPath ended fiscal 2026 with “$93.2 million in cash and effectively no debt after a June primary offering raised $50 million,” to fund capacity expansion, working capital, and potential acquisitions.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$55.2M cash at March 31” and said to watch for “any language pointing toward another raise.”

surprises.description: Management said the Army delayed the NGSRI interceptor program by a few months. The preview emphasized the need for confirmation that the Lockheed Martin work was on schedule, so the delay is a negative development, although management characterized it as low-risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The NGSRI interceptor program was delayed a few months by the Army but management views it as low-risk.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said investors wanted “confirmation the LM seeker-head work is funded and on schedule.”

surprises.description: Management reported that camera systems are designed into or being evaluated on seven missile/seeker platforms, including three with Lockheed Martin. The preview sought reassurance on the Lockheed Martin opportunity but did not anticipate this broader platform count.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its camera systems are now designed into or evaluated on seven missile/seeker platforms (three with Lockheed Martin).”

surprises.description: Detector lead times have lengthened from six months to more than ten, prompting LightPath to build inventory ahead of demand. This creates a supply and working-capital burden that the preview did not specifically flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Detector lead times have stretched from six to over ten months, prompting inventory buildup ahead of demand.”

in_line: June 30 backlog was $110.9 million, within the preview’s expected $105–112 million range; the two July orders totaling $24 million were also anticipated, and the reported amount is consistent with the preview’s expectation that current backlog would be north of $125 million.

Assemblies, modules, and cameras remained a large and growing part of the business: 43% of Q4 revenue and 44% of full-year revenue, consistent with the preview’s focus on sustained systems-mix growth.
The China operation’s $4.5 million sale, payable over five years, and the removal of roughly $4.5 million of annual revenue were anticipated in the preview.

The $15.6 million non-cash earn-out remeasurement charge and its effect on GAAP results were broadly consistent with the preview’s warning to expect a sizable mark; the preview also highlighted the possibility that the June 30 mark would produce a charge.
Higher fiscal 2027 CapEx and glass-capacity pressure were consistent with the preview’s warning that demand exceeded available capacity and that investors should watch for a CapEx step-up.

surprises.description: Net new ARR fell about 36–37% year over year. The preview expected the freemium strategy and deferred Creative Cloud pricing actions to weigh on individual-subscriber ARR, but did not indicate a decline of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net new ARR declined approximately 36-37% year-over-year,” attributed to “the intentional freemium funnel strategy prioritizing user acquisition over near-term monetization and deferred Creative Cloud pricing actions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had chosen to “accelerate freemium MAU growth and defer previously planned Creative Cloud ‘line optimizations’”; the strategy “lowers our second-half ARR growth expectations from individual subscribers.”

surprises.description: RPO growth slowed to 8%, its first single-digit growth since early fiscal 2023, with cRPO growth at 9%. The preview highlighted RPO and cRPO as the key forward-demand read, but did not set a specific Q3 growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “RPO growth decelerated to 8% (its first single-digit growth since early fiscal 2023) and cRPO grew 9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called RPO/cRPO “the cleanest forward-demand read for the enterprise” and “the hardest number to dress up,” without specifying a Q3 growth bar.

surprises.description: Q3 revenue and non-GAAP EPS both beat the preview’s consensus and Adobe’s guidance: revenue was $6.76 billion versus consensus of $6.69–$6.70 billion and guidance topping out at $6.72 billion; non-GAAP EPS was $6.13 versus consensus of $6.08–$6.09 and guidance topping out at $6.10.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 FY2026 revenue of $6.76 billion” and “non-GAAP EPS of $6.13.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed consensus revenue of “$6.69–6.70B” and non-GAAP EPS of “$6.08–6.09,” with Q3 guidance of “$6.67B – $6.72B” revenue and “$6.05 – $6.10” non-GAAP EPS.

surprises.description: Both subscription segments came in just above the top of their previewed ranges: BP&C revenue was $1.91 billion versus a $1.89 billion high end, and C&MP was $4.65 billion versus a $4.64 billion high end. Their reported growth rates were otherwise close to the preview’s expected growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: BP&C subscription revenue was “$1.91 billion (up 15% CC)” and C&MP subscription revenue was “$4.65 billion (up 12% CC).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave BP&C subscription revenue guidance of “$1.87B – $1.89B” and C&MP of “$4.61B – $4.64B,” with growth expectations of approximately 15% and 12%, respectively.

surprises.description: Adobe raised its full-year revenue and non-GAAP EPS guidance, with the revenue midpoint rising by about $50 million and the EPS range moving up from $24.35–$24.45 to $24.45–$24.50. The increase was modest and did not reach the preview’s bull-case thresholds.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adobe raised FY2026 revenue guidance to “$26.576-$26.626 billion” and non-GAAP EPS to “$24.45-$24.50,” a “roughly $50 million midpoint raise.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited the existing FY26 guide as “$26.5–2.6B” revenue and “$24.35–24.45” non-GAAP EPS; its bull case called for revenue raised to “≥$26.7B and EPS ≥$24.60.”

in_line: Adobe reiterated its FY26 ending ARR growth objective of 10.2%, as the preview’s base case expected.
AI-first ARR exceeded the preview’s $650 million watch level, and Firefly ARR growth of 40% quarter over quarter was above the preview’s roughly 30% sequential-growth threshold.
Q4 revenue guidance of $6.8–$6.85 billion was broadly within the preview’s implied $6.79–$6.89 billion range; the preview had characterized that as requiring only modest sequential growth.
BP&C and C&MP subscription revenue growth of 15% and 12% CC, respectively, matched the preview’s approximate growth expectations despite coming slightly above the dollar ranges.
The CEO transition timing and roles matched what the preview already reported: Anil Chakravarthy becomes President and CEO on December 1, with Shantanu Narayen moving to Executive Chair.

surprises.description: Oracle reported non-GAAP EPS of $1.92, well above the preview consensus of $1.74. The roughly 10% beat was substantially larger than the preview’s expectation of a modest, largely de-risked quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS rose 30% to $1.92.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS | Consensus | $1.74”; the preview also said “the quarter itself is largely de-risked.”

surprises.description: Oracle delivered 850 megawatts of AI capacity and more than 300,000 GPUs since Q4 end—nearly three times the entire Q4 delivery—while utilization remained near 98%. The preview framed OCI as a capacity-delivery risk, but this scale of delivery showed capacity coming online rapidly without utilization falling.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Oracle delivered 850 megawatts of AI capacity with over 300,000 GPUs since Q4 end—nearly 3x the entire Q4 delivery and 73% of all capacity delivered last fiscal year—while GPU utilization remained at 97.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “This is a capacity-delivery question, not a demand question”; the preview said a shortfall would mean “data centers landed late” and cited Q4 GPU utilization of 97.5%.

surprises.description: Oracle’s operating cash flow and free cash flow were better than the preview’s expected Q1 cash burn: free cash flow was negative $5 billion rather than the forecast negative $8–12 billion, despite $28 billion of CapEx. The record $23 billion of operating cash flow helped narrow the shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 CapEx was $28 billion, producing negative free cash flow of $5 billion, though cash flow from operations hit a record $23 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Expect Q1 FCF around negative $8–12B.”

surprises.description: Oracle raised its full-year EPS outlook to $8.10 from the previously reaffirmed $8.05. The revenue target remained around $90 billion, so the change was a modest upward revision rather than a broad reset of the annual plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year fiscal 2027 guidance to at least $90 billion in total revenue (up 34%) and $8.10 in non-GAAP EPS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year FY27 … $90B revenue (+34%) and $8.05 non-GAAP EPS … both reaffirmed in June.”

surprises.description: Oracle said it closed more than $30 billion in additional AI contracts without requiring additional capital from the company. That was favorable against the preview’s focus on who would fund the backlog and its concern about financing and capital needs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company closed more than $30 billion in additional AI contracts in Q1 without requiring additional capital from Oracle, using financing models like prepayments and bring-your-own-hardware arrangements.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The stock is not trading on the P&L. It is trading on RPO direction, capex, and who is funding the backlog”; the preview also identified new financing as a bear trigger.

surprises.description: Revenue was slightly above consensus, with 30% year-over-year growth versus the preview’s implied 28%. The beat was positive but relatively small compared with the EPS beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 total revenue reached a record $19.3 billion, up 30% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Consensus | $19.13B”; the preview gave implied growth of “+28%.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating margin was 42%, below the preview’s 43–44% consensus estimate, although it held roughly flat despite gross-margin pressure from the data-center ramp. This missed the stated margin estimate but was more resilient than a step-down would imply.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income [was] up 31% to $8.2 billion and operating margin holding roughly flat at 42% despite declining gross margins from data center ramp-up.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP op. margin | ~43–44% | guided to ‘step down’ on DC ramp.”

surprises.description: Q1 revenue grew sequentially for the first time in a Q1, breaking Oracle’s historical pattern of a lighter quarter after a record Q4. The preview did not quantify a sequential-growth expectation, but this result ran counter to the seasonal pattern described on the call.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[Revenue] grew sequentially for the first time in a Q1, breaking the historical pattern of a lighter Q1 following a record Q4.”

surprises.description: GPUs reaching renewal in Q1, most of them at least four years old, were renewed or resold at a 20% premium to prior contracts. The preview did not anticipate evidence that older hardware could retain or increase its contract value.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GPUs that came up for renewal in Q1, the majority being 4 years or older, were renewed or resold at a 20% premium to prior contracts.”

in_line: OCI revenue was $7.4 billion, up 121% year over year, within the preview’s implied $7.2–7.6 billion range and 110–125% growth range.
Cloud Apps grew 10%, matching the preview’s roughly 10% expectation for SaaS growth.

RPO increased sequentially to roughly $664 billion, within the preview’s $620–670 billion base range and $630–680 billion buy-side anchor. The roughly half of RPO expected to convert over 36 months was also close to the preview’s 12% within 12 months plus 34% in months 13–36.
Full-year CapEx guidance of $90–95 billion gross and net cash CapEx of no more than $70 billion was consistent with the preview’s expected $90–95 billion gross and roughly $70 billion net outlay.
The decline in gross margins from the data-center ramp was consistent with the preview’s warning that gross margins would step down because of ramp timing.

surprises.description: IBEX’s FY2027 revenue guide of $700–715 million came in above the preview’s modeled base range of $680–695 million, and its $90–94 million adjusted EBITDA guide was slightly above the modeled $88–92 million range. The guidance still implies slower revenue growth than FY2026, but it was stronger than the preview’s central expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY2027 guidance projects revenue of $700-715 million (9-11% growth) and adjusted EBITDA of $90-94 million (9-14% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... FY27 guided $680–695M / $88–92M”; the preview also modeled an initial guide of “$680–700M” revenue and “$88–93M” adj. EBITDA.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue of $164.3 million exceeded the preview’s $158–160 million consensus range and even the $162.2 million high end of the guide-implied range. Its 12% growth also topped the preview’s expected Q4 growth of roughly 8–10%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue grew 12% to a record $164.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$158–160M”; guidance implied “Q4 revenue $158.2–162.2M (+7.6% to +10.3%).”

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EBITDA was slightly below the preview’s ~$20.8 million estimate, and the 12.3% margin was below its roughly 13.0% expectation. The reported pressures were new-client training, nearshore-to-offshore transfers, and higher fuel prices; the preview had specifically sought an explanation other than AI-related pricing concessions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 adjusted EBITDA slipped to $20.2 million (12.3% margin) from $20.5 million (13.9%) a year earlier, pressured by new client training costs, nearshore-to-offshore work transfers, and higher fuel prices.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$20.8M”; “Adj. EBITDA margin | ~13.0%”; the preview said management needed to attribute any shortfall to “investment ... rather than price.”

surprises.description: The Sierra partnership update went beyond general enthusiasm, providing deployment activity across five verticals and quantified proof-of-concept resolution rates and CSAT scores, including a named BJ’s Wholesale example. However, the update did not provide the revenue or pipeline figures the preview wanted to establish monetization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Sierra AI partnership drove double-digit client AI agent deployments across five verticals, with proof-of-concept resolution rates of 20%+ (Philippine Airlines) to 40%+ (BJ's Wholesale) and CSAT scores above 4.7 out of 5.0.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management needed “named logos beyond Philippine Airlines, AI/digital revenue disclosure, or a quantified pipeline,” and warned that “Qualitative enthusiasm ... will be read as an absence of evidence.”

surprises.description: Customer expansion showed additional strength: IBEX added nine trophy logos in Q4, while revenue from its top 10 clients grew 22%, above the 19% top-10 growth noted in the preview for Q3. The preview had flagged client retention and large-client expansion as important measures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added nine new trophy logos in Q4 (17 for the full year), with revenue from its top five, top 10, and top 25 clients growing 24%, 22%, and 15% respectively.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “top-10 concentration 54% with largest client at only 9%” and said the top-10 cohort had grown “+19% in Q3.”

surprises.description: Net cash rose to $30.9 million, well above the approximately $14 million the preview cited, with record full-year free cash flow of $31.2 million. FY2026 capex of $27.8 million, by contrast, was within the preview’s expected $25–30 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year free cash flow reached a record $31.2 million and net cash improved to $30.9 million (from $13.7 million a year earlier), while capex rose to $27.8 million (4.3% of revenue) from $18.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “net cash ~$14.0M” and said FY2026 capex “was raised to $25–30M.”

surprises.description: Q4’s 10% tax rate reflected discrete benefits, while management indicated a normalized 20–22% rate going forward. The lower rate benefited the reported quarter, but the normalization implies a future tax headwind that the preview had not flagged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4's tax rate fell to 10% from 19% due to discrete benefits, but management guided to a normalized 20-22% tax rate going forward, implying a future earnings headwind.”

surprises.description: FY2026 revenue finished modestly above the preview’s approximately $640 million guide-midpoint expectation and above the company’s $638–642 million guidance range. The gap was small compared with the larger Q4 beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year FY2026 revenue rose 15.4% to $644.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “FY2026 full year (implied at guide midpoint): revenue ~$640M (+14.6%)” and cited company guidance of “$638–642M.”

in_line: Adjusted EPS was $0.85, matching the preview’s $0.85 consensus estimate.
FY2026 capex of $27.8 million fell within the preview’s expected $25–30 million range.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $155.2 million, slightly above the top of the $154.0–$155.0 million pre-announced range and above the $154.43 million consensus. The beat was narrow, but it exceeded the range investors had been told to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net revenue grew 24.1% year-over-year to $155.2 million” and came in “above the high end of IPO estimates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 revenue” was pre-announced at “$154.0M – $155.0M”; consensus was “$154.43M.”

surprises.description: Profitability also came in above the pre-announced upper bounds: adjusted EBITDA was $25.4 million versus a $25.30 million high end, and net income was $12.4 million versus a $12.00 million high end. Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 16.4%, modestly above the preview’s roughly 16.2% calculation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 54% to $25.4 million with margin expanding to 16.4%,” while “net income nearly doubled to $12.4 million from $6.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave adjusted EBITDA of “$24.92M – $25.30M,” net income of “$11.73M – $12.00M,” and calculated adjusted EBITDA margin of “~16.2%.”

surprises.description: The FY2026 revenue guide is a little above consensus: even its $602 million low end exceeds the $601.33 million estimate. The range implies H2 revenue modestly above the preview’s $334.5 million estimate, though it still points to a sharp slowdown from H1 growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year 2026 guidance calls for “net revenue of $602-606 million (18.6%-19.5% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY2026 revenue consensus was “$601.33M”; the preview calculated implied H2 revenue of “$334.5M” and H2 growth of “+13.0%.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a meaningful decline in DTC revenue per customer despite growing its active-customer base. Newly acquired customers were lower-spending, which diluted DTC net revenue per customer by 1.4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LTM active customers grew ~23% to 1.2 million, but DTC net revenue per customer declined 1.4% to $417 due to the dilutive mix of lower-spending newly acquired customers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified Active Customer adds as an open KPI and listed “strong Active Customer adds” as a bullish signal; it did not flag falling revenue per customer.

surprises.description: International growth was notably strong, including rapid customer growth in France, a market the preview had identified as an area where the company might disclose more but did not forecast. International revenue reached about one-fifth of the total.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International revenue grew 36.8% to $31.2 million (about 20% of total),” and new customer growth in France accelerated to “over 180% year-over-year in the first half of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “international contribution” among the metrics that were open for disclosure, without giving an expectation for its growth.

surprises.description: Wholesale revenue grew far faster than total revenue, driven by existing partners’ higher order volumes. That adds a channel-mix shift not quantified in the preview and partly offset the quarter’s gross-margin expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wholesale and other net revenue jumped 48.7% to $19.9 million,” driven mainly by “higher order volumes from existing partners”; faster wholesale growth partially offset gross-margin expansion.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed channel mix as an open KPI, but gave no wholesale growth expectation.

surprises.description: Reformation laid out a rapid store-expansion plan: from 70 stores at quarter-end, it expects to reach 79–80 by year-end and aims to double the fleet over five years. The preview flagged store cadence as an open question but had no specific expansion target.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company had “70 stores at quarter-end (17 opened over the prior 12 months)” and plans to reach “79-80 stores by year-end,” targeting “a doubling of the fleet over the next five years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “store-opening cadence and new-store productivity” as open questions, without a store-count target.

surprises.description: Management provided concrete evidence that store openings can lift local demand, citing a sharp acceleration in Chicago customer growth and faster DTC revenue growth after openings. The preview had identified new-store productivity as unknown but did not anticipate this quantified market-halo example.
surprises.fact_evidence: In Chicago, new-customer growth accelerated “from 28% to 50% year-over-year” and DTC revenue growth rose “nearly 1.5x after openings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “new-store productivity” as an open question and noted that the company might disclose it, but gave no expected halo effect.

surprises.description: The company disclosed that it borrowed ahead of its IPO to fund a large dividend, then used most of the IPO proceeds to repay debt. The dividend represents a shareholder cash distribution, while the repayment reduced leverage, making the newly disclosed financing history a mixed development.
surprises.fact_evidence: Ahead of the IPO, Reformation raised “$92 million in term loans to fund ~$90 million ($1.63/share) in dividends,” then used “~$110 million of $132.2 million net IPO proceeds to repay debt,” cutting net leverage to “~0.9x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the IPO proceeds split was unconfirmed and noted Q1 cash of about $41.2 million, but did not describe the dividend-funded borrowing or subsequent debt repayment.

in_line: Gross margin was 66.7%, at the top of the preview’s expected 66.6%–66.7% range. The call attributed expansion primarily to lower blended tariff rates and higher AUR, partly offset by faster wholesale growth.

The full-year guide still implies a marked H2 growth deceleration from H1, broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of roughly 13% H2 growth; management also said Q3 growth should exceed Q4 because of tougher holiday and tariff-normalization comparisons.

surprises.description: Identical sales excluding fuel grew only 0.2%, well below the preview’s +1.0%–1.3% expectation, and Kroger cut its full-year range to +0.2%–0.8%. The preview expected a narrower +1.0%–1.5% range, so both the quarter and the revised outlook were weaker than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Identical sales without fuel grew just 0.2%”; Kroger “lowered its full-year identical sales without fuel guidance to 0.2%-0.8%, down sharply from its initial 1%-2% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ID sales ex-fuel | ~+1.0–1.3% (buy-side)”; the preview also said the sell-side expected management to “narrow[] FY26 ID sales to +1.0–1.5%.”

surprises.description: Despite the sales shortfall, Kroger held its full-year adjusted FIFO operating-profit and adjusted EPS ranges unchanged. That contrasts with the preview’s expectation of an EPS trim to $5.00–$5.20.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company maintained full-year guidance for adjusted FIFO operating profit of $5.0-$5.2 billion and adjusted EPS of $5.10-$5.30 despite the lower sales outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The sell-side consensus expectation is that management narrows FY26 ID sales to +1.0–1.5% and trims adjusted EPS to $5.00–$5.20.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $1.09 exceeded the preview’s $1.05–$1.06 consensus range, a roughly 3%–4% beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $1.09, representing 5% growth versus last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS | $1.05–$1.06.”

surprises.description: FIFO gross margin excluding fuel rose 13 basis points, better than the preview’s flat-to-down-20-basis-point expectation. The preview identified this as the most important metric and said flat-to-positive would be the best outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FIFO gross margin rate excluding fuel rose 13 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FIFO gross margin rate | Flat to –20 bps”; the preview called “Flat-to-positive” the “single best bull outcome.”

surprises.description: OG&A rate rose 33 basis points, worse than the preview’s expected 10–20-basis-point increase. Wage investments and healthcare costs added pressure, with sales deleverage also contributing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OG&A rate increased 33 basis points due to wage investments, higher healthcare costs and sales deleverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “OG&A +10–20 bps”; the preview flagged further OG&A deleverage as a key risk.

surprises.description: The Cyclospora outbreak hit late in the quarter and is expected to keep weighing on Q3 sales. The preview discussed sales and pharmacy pressures but did not anticipate this specific outbreak or its carryover into the next quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Cyclospora outbreak hit late in the quarter after most competitors had closed their quarters, and lingering impacts are expected to weigh on Q3 sales.”

surprises.description: Adjusted e-commerce sales grew 20%, above the preview’s expected 17%–19%, and Kroger reported a second consecutive quarter of profitable e-commerce growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted e-commerce sales grew 20%” and delivered “a second consecutive quarter of profitable e-commerce growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted eCommerce growth | ~+17–19%.”

surprises.description: Retail media grew 24%, its best growth since 2021. The preview highlighted digital economics as a key profit offset but gave no current-quarter retail-media growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retail media grew 24% (best since 2021).”

surprises.description: Kroger said the Inflation Reduction Act pharmacy headwind is projected to rise to approximately 150 basis points in Q4 as new high-cost drugs, including GLP-1s, enter the formulary in January, while stating there is no profit impact. The preview mentioned pharmacy reimbursement headwinds generally but did not flag this specific timing or scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Inflation Reduction Act pharmacy headwind is projected to accelerate to approximately 150 basis points in Q4 as new high-cost drugs including GLP-1s enter the formulary in January, with no profit impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “pharmacy reimbursement headwinds” as a secondary issue to watch.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $15.8M, down 13% year over year, rather than the preview’s $20.9M base estimate or $21.53M consensus, both of which implied growth. Cash rewards rose 77% and were deducted from revenue, while Q2 total transaction value was flat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue fell 13% year-over-year to $15.8 million”; “Cash rewards…rose 77% year-over-year to $5.1 million…masking underlying growth as total transaction value held flat at $20.9 million.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA remained loss-making at $1.6M, versus the preview’s expectation of a $0.9M profit. Even on a constant-FX basis, the company reported a $0.9M EBITDA loss, not a positive quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed…to $1.6 million in Q2”; “constant-FX EBITDA loss narrowed 64% to $0.9 million in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base…Adj. EBITDA +$0.9M”; the preview said a positive quarter “should” print and described a second positive quarter as the expectation.

surprises.description: Hong Kong revenue was flat at $7.8M rather than the preview’s $10.0M estimate and expected 28% growth. That falls well short of the preview’s view of Hong Kong as the growth engine.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hong Kong revenue held flat at $7.8 million” in Q2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Hong Kong…Q2'26E $10.0M…YoY +28%”; “Deceleration below ~+20% kills the base case.”

surprises.description: Singapore revenue fell 20% to $6.2M instead of reaching the preview’s $8.7M estimate and 12% growth forecast. The preview also identified a possible reacceleration as a bull-case driver, but the quarter instead declined.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Singapore revenue fell 20% to $6.2 million on cash-reward deployment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Singapore…Q2'26E $8.7M…YoY +12%”; bull case: “SG re-accelerates toward Q4'25's +56%.”

surprises.description: Despite flat Hong Kong revenue, its segment profit rose to $0.5M from $0.1M a year earlier, an improvement not forecast in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hong Kong…segment profit rising to $0.5 million from $0.1 million a year earlier.”

surprises.description: Singapore delivered a first-half segment profit of $0.2M, turning around from a $0.5M loss a year earlier. The preview focused on Singapore revenue growth and possible reacceleration, not a first-half segment-profit turnaround.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Singapore…delivered a first-half segment profit of $0.2 million, a turnaround from a $0.5 million loss a year earlier.”

in_line: Cash ended at $28.2M and was stable versus March, broadly matching the preview’s $27–28M estimate and its flat-to-up cash marker.
Wealth and insurance reached 30% of revenue, in line with the preview’s 30%+ bull marker for the mix.
Approval rates reached 48%, consistent with the preview’s cited improvement to 48% and its expectation that better approvals would help offset funnel declines.

surprises.description: Rent the Runway reported Q2 revenue of $97.7 million, above both the preview’s $91–95 million guidance range and its $94.5 million estimate. The beat was larger than the preview’s base case and even exceeded its $96–98 million bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record Q2 revenue of $97.7 million… exceeding the guidance range communicated in June.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 guidance: $91–95M”; “My estimate: $94.5M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 12.9%, far above the preview’s expected 5–8% guidance range and 6.5% estimate. The result substantially outperformed expectations for a modest improvement over last year’s 4.4% margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $12.6 million (12.9% of revenue) in Q2, a sharp improvement from $3.6 million (4.4%) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA: 5–8% of revenue”; “My estimate: $6.1M (6.5%).”

surprises.description: Gross margin rose to 36.1%, sharply reversing the margin pressure the preview expected. The preview modeled 27.5% and warned that revenue-share costs could keep margins near 27% or below.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit margin expanded roughly 609 basis points to 36.1%, driven by lower fulfillment costs (down 370 bps) and reduced rental product depreciation and revenue share costs (down 240 bps).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin… My estimate: 27.5%”; “Watch whether the mix effect is stabilizing (27%+) or still deteriorating (sub-26%).”

surprises.description: Ending active subscribers fell to 140,826, down 3.8% year over year, rather than reaching the preview’s 158,000 estimate or even its roughly 152,000 bear-case threshold. The decline was attributed to higher pauses and less promotional acquisition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ending active subscribers fell 3.8% year-over-year to 140,826, hurt by higher pause activity and reduced promotional acquisition compared to 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Ending active subscribers… My estimate: 158,000 (+7.9%).”; “Anything below ~152K ending actives (+4% YoY) confirms the bear case.”

surprises.description: The company guided to a negative Q3 adjusted EBITDA margin of 3% to 6%, a sharp reversal from Q2’s 12.9% margin and weaker than the preview’s expected positive 4–7% FY2026 margin range. Management cited seasonal pauses and higher revenue-share inventory costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 adjusted EBITDA is guided to negative 3% to negative 6% of revenue due to seasonal pause activity and higher revenue-share inventory costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance… adjusted EBITDA margin 4–7%.”

surprises.description: Rent the Runway raised its FY2026 rental product investment guidance to $53–55 million, above the preview’s expected $45–50 million. The higher planned spend contrasts with the preview’s expectation that investment would remain reduced amid cash-flow concerns.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its full-year rental product investment guidance to $53–55 million (up from $45–50 million) to ensure fuller stocking for second-half events and launches, though still below fiscal 2025’s $75 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Rental product acquired $45–50M (vs. $74.9M in FY2025).”; “rental product acquired is guided down ~$25M YoY.”

surprises.description: The company announced a $15 million backstopped rights offering and a new $10 million term loan. The preview discussed financing as a possible risk if cash burn continued, but did not anticipate this specific capital raise; it adds liquidity while bringing additional financing and potential dilution considerations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management announced a $15 million backstopped rights offering plus a new $10 million term loan from the same investor group that led the 2025 refinancing to bolster liquidity.”

surprises.description: Paige Thomas was named permanent CEO effective September 14, resolving the leadership uncertainty highlighted in the preview. The preview identified a permanent appointment as a live catalyst but had no disclosed search timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company appointed Paige Thomas, formerly Chief Commercial Officer and ex-CEO of Saks OFF 5TH, as permanent CEO effective September 14, with interim CEO Teri Bariquit becoming Nonexecutive Chair.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Permanent CEO search / strategic direction”; “No search timeline has been disclosed.”

surprises.description: Rent the Runway paused Marketplace, on-site advertising and monetization, and new B2B dry-cleaning partnerships, rather than advancing the diversification initiatives the preview highlighted as areas to watch. Management is instead concentrating resources on core rental and resale execution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rent the Runway paused several initiatives including Marketplace, on-site advertising/monetization, and new B2B dry cleaning partnerships to refocus resources on core rental and resale execution.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Also watch… the new diversification lines (RTR Marketplace, B2B dry-cleaning pilot, advertising).”

in_line: The preview warned that second-half growth would step down sharply as the company lapped 2025 price increases and faced tougher comparisons. Q3 revenue guidance of $87–90 million, implying only flat to 3% year-over-year growth, is consistent with that anticipated slowdown.

surprises.description: Q1 revenue was $31 million, above the preview’s $30.3 million bogey as well as the $29.6 million consensus estimate. The beat was positive but not as large as the preview’s $31.5 million bull case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 revenue grew 60% year-over-year to $31 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue vs. $29.6M … My bogey: $30.3M”; the bull case listed “$31.5M.”

surprises.description: Kestra raised its long-term gross-margin target from 70% to the mid-70% range, with 70% now expected for FY2029. The preview discussed the 70% margin bridge but did not anticipate a higher target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its long-term gross margin target to the mid-70% range within the next 2-3 years, up from the prior 70% goal, expecting to deliver 70% for full-year fiscal 2029.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to “the 70%-GM long-term bridge” and cited the prior “~700bps of gross margin expansion” guidance.

surprises.description: A significant national payer expanded coverage to non-ischemic patients on guideline-directed medical therapy, a newly reported access development not anticipated in the preview. The preview noted that this group represents over 60% of the typical WCD population.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A significant national payer expanded coverage to non-ischemic patients on guideline-directed medical therapy for the first time,” and “over 60% of the typical WCD population is non-ischemic.”

surprises.description: Kestra estimated its WCD market share at about 15%, above the preview’s estimate of about 12%. That suggests a larger share position than the preview assumed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Kestra estimates about 15% U.S. market share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described KMTS as “at ~12% share.”

surprises.description: Reported total liquidity was roughly $320 million, below the preview’s estimate of about $357 million. The call cited $245 million in cash and investments and the $200 million term loan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company holds $245 million in cash and investments as of July 31 and roughly $320 million in total liquidity, bolstered by a new $200 million nondilutive term loan announced in July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY26 closed with “$262.2M cash & investments plus a newly-secured $200M term loan (~$357M total liquidity).”

in_line: FY2027 revenue guidance was raised to $141 million, within the preview’s anticipated $139–141 million range; the preview also explicitly expected the second half to be weighted toward growth as new representatives ramp.

Gross margin was 56.5%, matching the preview’s 56–57% modeled range and its 56.5% bogey; the 11th consecutive quarter of sequential expansion matched the preview’s expectation of an 11-quarter streak.
In-network fittings reached the low-80% range, consistent with the preview’s expectation of low-to-mid-80s mix and its threshold of at least 80%.

surprises.description: The preview expected no announced refinancing solution as the base case and identified a Personal Care sale as the likely asset-sale upside. Hain instead agreed to sell its international business for $323 million cash, with $305–310 million of net proceeds expected to reduce debt; however, closing depends on obtaining a maturity-extending credit amendment within 30 days, so the financing condition is not yet secured.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hain agreed to sell its international business to private equity firm Aurelius for $323 million in cash, with net proceeds expected between $305 million and $310 million”; the sale is “contingent on securing a credit agreement amendment to extend maturity,” and lenders can terminate if the amendment is not obtained within 30 days. After the transaction, debt would be approximately $250 million, down about 55%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No refinancing announcement has been made since the May 11 Q3 report”; the base case was “no resolution” on the December maturity. “Personal Care is held for sale and still unsold. Any proceeds go straight to the maturity problem. A signed Personal Care deal is the most likely positive surprise after a refi itself.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q4 organic sales would decline 4%–6%. Hain reported a smaller 2% decline, a better result than that expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Overall Q4 organic net sales declined 2% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic net sales: ~−4% to −6% (est.)”; the base scenario also assumed “organic ≈ −5%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was expected to be about $20–24 million, but Hain reported $19 million. That was slightly below the low end of the preview’s estimated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of $19 million (7.1% margin) down slightly from $20 million a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$20–24M (est.)”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was expected to be a loss of $0.03 per share, while Hain reported a loss of $0.05, a deeper loss than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An adjusted net loss of $0.05 per diluted share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS: −$0.03.”

surprises.description: The international segment’s sales decline improved, but its profitability weakened sharply: adjusted gross margin fell 555 basis points and adjusted EBITDA dropped 41% amid cost inflation. The preview highlighted international sales trends but did not anticipate this margin and EBITDA deterioration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International segment organic net sales declined 4% year-over-year (improving from an 8% decline in Q3), but adjusted gross margin fell 555 basis points to 16.6% and adjusted EBITDA dropped 41% due to cost inflation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q3 International organic sales as “−8%” and said management expected Q4 organic trends to improve; it gave no expectation for International segment margin or EBITDA.

surprises.description: A zero-based budgeting review identified more than $16 million in annual run-rate savings, an unpreviewed cost-reduction opportunity. Realizing it is also expected to cost roughly $20 million, mostly in fiscal 2027, which tempers the savings benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A zero-based budgeting review identified more than $16 million of annual run-rate cost savings, expected to cost roughly $20 million to implement (70% in fiscal 2027).”

surprises.description: Hain said it would increase marketing investment by about 100 basis points of net sales to support three brands. The preview did not flag this planned spending increase, which may support the brands but adds expense.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to increase marketing investment by approximately 100 basis points of net sales to support Celestial Seasonings, Greek Gods, and Earth's Best.”

surprises.description: Hain reduced net debt by $151 million during fiscal 2026, ending at $500 million. The preview emphasized the maturity and liquidity risk but did not anticipate this amount of in-year debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reduced net debt by $151 million (about 25%) during fiscal 2026 to $500 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on the “$549.8M of debt maturing December 22, 2026” and flagged positive full-year free cash flow as a commitment, but did not state an expectation for the amount of net debt reduction.

in_line: Full-year free cash flow was positive, as the preview said management had repeatedly committed to positive FY26 free cash flow: Hain reported $58 million versus a $3 million outflow the prior year.

North America’s nearly 1,200-basis-point gross-margin expansion to 31.1% and 14.4% adjusted EBITDA margin were consistent with the preview’s post-Snacks framing of gross margin above 30% and low-double-digit EBITDA margin.
International organic sales improved to a 4% decline from an 8% decline in Q3, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Q4 organic trends would improve.
No traditional guidance was provided, consistent with the preview’s expectation that FY27 guidance would not be provided before the strategic review.

surprises.description: Instead of the preview’s base-case gross margin of 27–29% and concern that new tariffs could pressure margins, Hooker reported 31.8%, up 690 basis points. The call said results benefited significantly from tariff recoveries after the Supreme Court invalidated IEPA tariffs, an outcome the preview did not expect to be reflected in results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved 690 basis points to 31.8% and gross profit rose $2.9 million, driven largely by tariff recoveries.” Results “benefited significantly from tariff recoveries” following the decision invalidating IEPA tariffs.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “GM 27–29% (some HB give-back).” The preview also said Q1 had “no receivable booked” for tariff claims and expected “certain tariffs to be levied on our imported goods later this fiscal year.”

surprises.description: Hooker earned $1.7 million rather than the small loss implied by the $(0.02) EPS consensus, and reported its third consecutive profitable quarter rather than the preview’s anticipated second consecutive one. This was a clear step beyond the expected turnaround print.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated net income of $1.7 million in Q2 FY2027,” marking “its third consecutive profitable quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus EPS was “$(0.02).” The preview described the expected outcome as a “second consecutive quarter of positive operating income.”

surprises.description: Domestic Upholstery moved from a $689,000 operating loss in Q1 to $833,000 of operating income, exceeding the preview’s breakeven bull-case threshold. Its gross margin also expanded 450 basis points to 23%.
surprises.fact_evidence: Domestic Upholstery gross margin “improved 450 basis points to 23%,” and the segment swung to “$833,000 operating income from a $408,000 loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called Domestic Upholstery “the one segment that hasn’t turned” and said “Breakeven here is worth roughly $0.05/quarter”; its bull scenario anticipated “DU at/near breakeven.”

surprises.description: Hooker Branded held and slightly exceeded the preview’s margin threshold: its gross margin was nearly 40%, versus 39.4% in Q1 and the preview’s 36% hold threshold. The preview’s base case allowed for some margin give-back.
surprises.fact_evidence: Hooker Branded sales fell 4.5%, but “gross margin expanded 1,000 basis points to nearly 40%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “If Q2 HB margin holds ≥36%, the re-rate case is intact” and its base scenario assumed “some HB give-back.”

surprises.description: Hooker Branded backlog grew nearly 35% year over year, improving on the 30% year-over-year growth reported in Q1 and surpassing the preview’s concern that the prior build could flatten. The call facts do not give a sequential backlog figure, so the preview’s sequential test cannot be confirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Hooker Branded backlog “surged nearly 35% versus the prior year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 HB backlog growth of “+30%” and warned that “a backlog that flattens or declines sequentially would signal the +30% HB build was a one-time load-in.”

surprises.description: Margaritaville shipments had begun in Q2, earlier than the preview’s expectation that shipments would start in H2. The preview’s expected commitments of roughly 100 galleries and 10 freestanding stores were confirmed, and no revenue sizing was provided.
surprises.fact_evidence: The rollout had commitments for “approximately 100 in-store galleries and 10 freestanding retail stores,” with “shipments beginning in Q2” and expected to build through the second half of FY2027 and into FY2028.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Margaritaville ships in H2” and cited commitments for “100 in-store galleries + 10 freestanding stores.”

surprises.description: The ‘all other’ segment suffered a steep Q2 sales drop and an operating loss because hospitality shipments were heavily concentrated in Q1. The preview did not flag this project-timing pattern as a specific risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: ‘All other’ sales “plunge[d] about 66% ($2.8 million) due to hospitality project timing,” with “roughly 80% of first-half shipments occurring in Q1,” resulting in a Q2 operating loss.

surprises.description: Cash generation and the cash balance exceeded the preview’s already-positive expectation: cash was $18.7 million at quarter-end and about $21 million by the day before the call, alongside $24 million of first-half operating cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: Cash and equivalents rose to “$18.7 million at quarter end” and were “roughly $21 million” the day before the call; the company generated “$24 million” from operations in the first six months.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s secondary checklist cited cash as expected to be “over $15M” by the June call.

in_line: Consolidated net sales fell about 9%, consistent with the preview’s base-case expectation of a mid-to-high-single-digit decline on continuing operations and its $63–67 million base revenue range; sales pressure across segments was also anticipated. Hooker Branded sales were down 4.5%, close to the Q1 decline of 4.8%.
The company maintained zero outstanding credit-facility borrowings and continued reducing inventory, consistent with the preview’s debt-free balance-sheet and inventory-discipline expectations.

surprises.description: The preview put Q3 sales consensus at $23.28 million and its base case at $22.5–23.2 million; RF Industries reported a record $24 million, modestly above both.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record quarterly revenue of $24 million in Q3 FY2026,” up 21% year-over-year and 16% sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Q3 FY26 Consensus | $23.28M”; the base scenario projected “Revenue | $22.5–23.2M.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated non-GAAP EPS of $0.20, while RF Industries reported $0.19 per diluted share—a slight shortfall despite near-doubling year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net income nearly doubled to $2.2 million ($0.19 per diluted share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (non-GAAP) | Q3 FY26 Consensus | $0.20.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 35.6%, above the preview’s roughly 35% estimate and its 35% watch threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit margin expanded 160 basis points to 35.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin (my est.): ~35%”; the watch table said “≥35%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA came in modestly above the preview’s $2.6 million estimate, at $2.7 million, and reached 11.1% of sales—above the company’s long-term 10% goal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose approximately 71% to $2.7 million, reaching 11.1% of sales and surpassing the company’s long-term 10% goal.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA (my est.): ~$2.6M.”

surprises.description: Bookings of $22.5 million were within the preview’s base-case range, but the 0.94x book-to-bill missed its stated >1.0x signal, and backlog at $19.8 million remained just below the preview’s >$20 million benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 bookings were $22.5 million for a book-to-bill ratio of about 0.94x, with backlog rising to $19.8 million as of the call from $18.6 million at July 31.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called “Book-to-bill >1.0x” the line and said “Backlog … >$20M”; its base case expected “Bookings / Backlog | $20–23M / $20–21M.”

surprises.description: DAC moved from qualitative potential to a quantified growth business: management now expects more than $10 million in annual sales and sees it expanding beyond traditional telecom, more concrete than the preview’s hoped-for dollar figure or named customer.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The DAC business, previously immaterial, is now expected to exceed $10 million in annual sales and is viewed as a key growth engine expanding beyond traditional telecom.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said DAC was “Qualitative only” and that “A dollar figure or named customer” would be good to see.

surprises.description: Management said Q4 sales should be roughly the same as or above Q3’s $24 million, giving a directional next-quarter outlook beyond the preview’s focus on Q3 sequential growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q4 FY2026 sales to be roughly the same or above the Q3 level of $24 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had guided Q3 sales to “increase sequentially over Q2” and identified formal guidance as a potential catalyst, but gave no Q4 sales outlook.

surprises.description: A single wireless carrier accounted for about 17% of Q3 sales, adding a notable customer-concentration exposure; the preview had flagged concentration risk but cited a largest A&D customer at about 14% and called for growth with diversification.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A single wireless carrier represented about 17% of Q3 sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Largest A&D customer ~14% of revenue” and listed “Growth w/ diversification” as the watch item.

surprises.description: NEMA 4 and edge-data-center opportunities are expected to become material mainly in fiscal 2027 rather than this year, tempering the near-term contribution from the data-center opportunity set.
surprises.fact_evidence: “NEMA 4/edge data center opportunities are expected to become material contributors mainly in fiscal 2027 rather than this year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the “AI/edge-datacenter adjacency” as carrying the multiple and highlighted DAC as a key catalyst, without specifying that material contributions would be delayed until FY2027.

in_line: Small cell/integrated systems began accelerating in Q3, consistent with the preview’s expectation of visible acceleration, although management said the business remained below year-start expectations in dollars.
Cash rose and revolver borrowings declined, matching the preview’s stated preference for revolver paydown.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $261.4 million, about 13% above the preview’s roughly $231 million estimate. Adjusted gross profit also grew 10.6%, clearing the preview’s stated $60 million bull-signal threshold implied by the $60.4 million year-ago figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue rose 18.5% to $261.4 million while adjusted gross profit grew 10.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: ~$231M”; “AGP above ~$60M with EBITDA leverage on top is the clean bull signal.”

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EBITDA reached $10.4 million, above the preview’s derived $8.5–9.5 million range and its roughly $9 million base case. The 240-basis-point margin expansion was at the top of the preview’s expected 150–240-basis-point range, rather than an additional surprise.
